questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes presents for review. He currently takes metformin 2 g/day and gliclazide 160 mg/day. and a recent HbA1c was 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%). His complaint is of weight loss, burning proximal muscle pain and weakness. On examination there is left-sided quadriceps wasting. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for his diabetes and associated complications?
questions.explanation: The aetiology of diabetic amyotrophy, the diagnosis here, is unknown. It affects the lumbar sacral plexus lower motor neurones. Transition to insulin therapy is recommended because it is likely to improve his glucose control, and may impact progression of neuropathy. Recovery of diabetic amyotrophy happens over 3-4 months, but only 50% achieve complete recovery. Trials of immunomodulatory agents in managing the condition have been disappointing. A: Increased metformin dose. There is little evidence that increasing metformin dose above 2 g/day has any additional impact on glycaemic control. B: Increased gliclazide dose. Like metformin, the dose response curve for gliclazide is relatively flat at high doses. The increment in glucose control between 160 and 320 mg/day is therefore small. D: Amitriptyline. Amitriptyline, although effective in treating neuropathic pain, won't impact on progression of neuropathy. E: Tramadol. Opiate-based analgesics aren't recommended for the treatment of diabetic neuropathy because they are less effective than agents such as tricyclic anti-depressants, and are addictive.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man with mild learning disability is referred to the Emergency Department for review. He has recently moved into sheltered accommodation in the area and is noted by staff to have made multiple complaints about muscular weakness and pins and needles affecting both hands. He has been noted by the GP to have hypocalcaemia and a raised level of parathyroid hormone. On examination, there is obvious subcutaneous calcification and he has a short fifth metacarpal on each hand. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this patient?
options: C. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation
questions.explanation: This individual has pseudohypoparathyroidism. It is associated with short stature, short metacarpals, subcutaneous calcification and variable intellectual impairment. The G-protein-coupled receptor for parathyroid hormone (PTH) becomes unresponsive to the hormone, hence patients become hypocalcaemic in the face of normal or elevated PTH levels. Variable degrees of resistance involving other G-protein-mediated receptors, such as those linked to thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) activity, may also be seen. Calcium and vitamin D is the intervention of choice. Calcium levels should be monitored frequently during treatment as rapid rises may occur. A: Parathyroidectomy. The hypocalcaemia seen here is consistent with parathyroid resistance rather than functional parathyroid excess; hence parathyroidectomy is not appropriate. B: Calcium supplementation. Calcium supplementation alone is inadequate to restore normal calcium levels. D: Parathyroid hormone administration. Given this is a syndrome of parathyroid hormone resistance, supplementation of PTH will not restore normal calcium metabolism. E: Calcitonin administration. Calcitonin is used IV as a treatment for acute hypercalcaemia.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman with limited exposure to medical services presents to the Endocrinology Clinic. She has never had a period and previously felt this was due to having a short height, but she has recently decided to seek advice. On examination, she is significantly shorter than would be expected, given her parental height; her nipples are widely spaced and there is a suspicion of a high-arched palate. There appears to be a failure of secondary sexual characteristics. Her blood pressure is elevated at 149/90 mmHg. Investigations reveal a follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level of >40 IU/L on at least two occasions. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely complication in this patient?
questions.explanation: There is a strong suspicion that this patient has Turner syndrome and that access to health services has been patchy. Features include short stature, webbing of the neck, micrognathia, low-set ears, a high-arched palate, widely spaced nipples and cubitus valgus, some of which are clearly present here. Turner syndrome occurs due to the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, and diagnosis is by lymphocyte karyotyping. Turner syndrome is associated with a number of other associated abnormalities, including aortic coarctation and other left-sided congenital heart defects, osteoporosis, hypothyroidism, lymphoedema, skeletal abnormalities and congenital malformations of the renal tract. Due to the genetic defect in Turner syndrome, cortical bone is thin, putting patients at greater risk of osteoporosis. Furthermore, in this patient who has been diagnosed with Turner syndrome later in life and who has not received any treatment with oestrogen, her risk of reduced bone density and osteoporosis is higher. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scanning should be completed for this patient. C: Graves' disease. Autoimmune thyroid disease is found in up to half of patients with Turner syndrome and therefore, thyroid function should be measured. However, this is more commonly Hashimoto's thyroiditis, rather than Graves' disease. A: Aortic dissection. Patients with Turner syndrome are at risk of aortic dissection, although the mechanism for this is poorly understood, and not necessarily related to the recognised risk of hypertension and cardiac abnormalities in patients with Turner syndrome. Cardiovascular screening is given high priority in affected patients. However, the risk of aortic dissection is lower than that of osteoporosis. B: Gonadoblastoma. Some patients with Turner syndrome may have a fragmented Y chromosome-specific sequence identified on karyotyping and this puts them at risk of gonadoblastoma, which is a benign tumour. The risk of this is lower than osteoporosis. D: Hepatitis. Thirty to 40% of patients with Turner syndrome have elevated transaminases, and treatment with oestrogen may decrease liver enzymes. However, the risk of hepatitis is lower than that of osteoporosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with hypertension that is refractory to multiple antihypertensive medications. He has no other past medical history of note. His regular medications include amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide. He reports a family history of early-onset hypertension and ischaemic stroke. His temperature is 36.7°C, his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular and his BP is 165/95 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 98% on air. Investigations show Sodium 145 mmol/L, Potassium 2.8 mmol/L, Urea 5.0 mmol/L, Creatinine 70 µmol/L, Aldosterone 50 pmol/L, Renin 0.2 pmol/mL/hour. A venous blood gas shows pH 7.59, Bicarbonate 38 mmol/L, Glucose 5.5 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: Liddle syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by a genetic defect in the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) found in the renal collecting tubules that results in increased Na+ reabsorption. The syndrome presents with a biochemical picture of hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Patients will also have low renin and aldosterone activity in a physiological effort to reduce BP. A: Bartter syndrome. Bartter syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle. This causes loss of Na+, K+ and chloride in the urine. Fluid loss associated with Na+ excretion leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that promotes potassium and H+ exchange for Na+ and bicarbonate reabsorption in the distal tubules, hence causing metabolic alkalosis and worsening hypokalaemia. Bartter syndrome is not in keeping with this patient's presentation. B: Cushing syndrome. Excess levels of serum cortisol cause Cushing syndrome. It is characterised by central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump and abdominal striae. Patients can also present with hypertension. Biochemically, there is hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Since cortisol has some mineralocorticoid activity, Na retention and K+ excretion can also be present. The lack of physical characteristics makes Cushing syndrome unlikely. C: Gitelman syndrome. Gitelman syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that belongs to the family of salt-losing tubulopathies. It is caused by a mutation in the SLC12A3 gene encoding the thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride transporter, and its presentation mimics thiazide diuretic use, with hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia being additional features. The condition typically presents in adulthood, and other symptoms and signs include abdominal pain and nocturia, as well as other features including excessive thirst, tetany and chondrocalcinosis. This patient's clinical presentation is not in keeping with Gitelman syndrome. E: Primary hyperaldosteronism. Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn syndrome, is characterised by excessive production of aldosterone, leading to hypertension, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and low plasma renin activity. It is a very important differential diagnosis to consider for this patient. However, the blood results demonstrate low aldosterone and renin levels, making primary hyperaldosteronism unlikely.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman is admitted via the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of weakness, nausea, and malaise. Unfortunately, she has not brought all of her regular medications with her. She tells you that she is a tablet-controlled diabetic, with high blood pressure (BP) and kidney problems. She has with her a packet of lisinopril which she takes at 10 mg/day In addition, she has a packet of gliclazide which she takes at 80 mg/day. She takes several other tablets, which she left on the sideboard at home when the ambulance collected her. She attended an outpatient appointment two weeks ago when she was prescribed a new medication. She does not know the name of this medication and does not have it with her; she was told that it was a medication also used to treat people with liver problems and had been taking one tablet a day. On examination, she is overweight and appears unwell. She has evidence of mild biventricular cardiac insufficiency, with elevated jugular venous pressure and pitting oedema of her ankles. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Urgent biochemical analysis reveals Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 7.1 mmol/L, Urea 11.0 mmol/L, Creatinine 146 µmol/L. Appropriate treatment is instigated. What is the most likely cause for this patient's presentation on this occasion?
options: A. A recent 2-day course of ibuprofen 400 mg three x daily (tid)/as required (prn) for backache
B. Recent commencement of spironolactone 50 mg
C. Recent commencement of digoxin 62.5 µg once daily (od)
D. Recent commencement of bisoprolol fumarate 2.5 mg od
E. Recent commencement of amiloride hydrochloride 5 mg twice daily (bd)
questions.explanation: This woman has life-threatening hyperkalaemia, with evidence of cardiotoxicity on ECG (tall tented T waves), requiring urgent intervention to prevent potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias. All of the drugs listed can be associated with hyperkalaemia. However, we know that this lady has renal disease. In addition, we know that she is already taking an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Following the Randomised Aldactone Evaluation Study (RALES) clinical trial, when it was shown that aldosterone antagonists can reduce mortality in severe chronic congestive cardiac failure when given in conjunction with an ACE inhibitor, the prescription rates of spironolactone increased, along with hospital admission rates and deaths from hyperkalaemia. Although this medication can be given safely with ACE inhibitors, and indeed be beneficial, there is a risk of causing life-threatening hyperkalaemia, particularly in those with renal impairment. The combination of ACE inhibitor therapy with spironolactone therefore needs to be carefully considered and monitored to avoid significant side-effects. The standard dose used for heart failure is at a lower level than that seen here (around 25-50 mg daily). A: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents can be associated with hyperkalaemia in the context of renal impairment, although we might expect this with a longer duration of use if this were the cause in this case. C: Digoxin toxicity can be increased by hypokalaemia, although it is hyperkalaemia which is seen here. D: Non-selective b blockade can lead to hyperkalaemia by decreasing the uptake of potassium from extracellular into intracellular spaces. This would not be expected with the highly selective b1 blocker bisoprolol. E: Amiloride can cause hyperkalaemia in similar situations; however, it is not so commonly used in current practice.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with palpitations. Approximately 3 weeks ago she had suffered with flu and since then she has been getting occasional palpitations, anxiety attacks and loose bowel motions. Her weight has remained stable and she has previously been fit and well. Examination reveals a tender thyroid, but no enlargement or focal masses. Her pulse rate is 110/min and regular. Thyroid function tests show TSH 0.3 mu/L, T4 190 nmol/L, T3 3.21 nmol/L, ESR 45 mm/h. What is the next most appropriate management step?
questions.explanation: Subacute thyroiditis is transient inflammation of the thyroid, which typically occurs in females in the fourth and fifth decade. Patients can have a preceding viral infection followed by mild symptoms of hyperthyroidism. The thyroid gland is usually tender by this time. If bloods are taken early, the patient can display a low thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and raised thyroxine (T4)/tri-iodothyronine (T3). The mainstay of treatment is management of pain over the thyroid with NSAIDs. Prednisolone can be used if NSAIDS are ineffective. The symptoms should resolve but can take weeks to a few months to do so, and the patient's thyroid status should be monitored. Some patients are left hypothyroid after the inflammation has settled. Propranolol may be considered if palpitations or anxiety are particularly severe. A: Carbimazole is used for Graves' thyrotoxicosis. It is a pro-drug which, after absorption, is converted to the active form, methimazole. Methimazole prevents thyroid peroxidase enzyme (TPO) from coupling and iodinating the tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, hence reducing the production of the thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). In De Quervain's thyroiditis, the transient rise of T3 and T4 is self-limiting and doesn't require anti-thyroid medication. B: This is used in Graves' thyrotoxicosis. It shares the same mechanism of action as carbimazole, but moreover inhibits the enzyme 5'-deiodinase which converts T4 to the more active form T3. D: This is used in Graves' thyrotoxicosis when not complicated by thyroid eye disease, as there is a chance that it may aggravate its course. E: This is considered in the case of a toxic adenoma or when the cytology results following fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of a nodule raise the suspicion of malignancy.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman is discovered at home by her family, demonstrating confusion and poor responsiveness. She is brought into the hospital and assessed in the Emergency Department. Her family cannot recall her past medical history, but they think that she may have asthma and depression. When they last saw her, 3 days ago, she had a productive cough. On examination, the junior doctor thinks her face appears puffy, and they find a small scar in the middle of her neck. She is hypothermic, has a heart rate of 45 beats per minute (bpm), and a blood pressure of 92/65 mmHg. Her Glasgow coma score (GCS) is 9/15 An arterial blood gas confirms type Il respiratory failure. Investigations revealed Hb 112 g/L, WCC 8.2 x 10^9/L, PLT 165 x 10^9/L, Na+ 131 mmol/L, K+ 4.3 mmol/L, Urea 6.5 mmol/L, Cr 114 µmol/L, Blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L, TSH 25.2 µu/ml, T3 2.6 pmol/L, T4 3.6 pmol/L. What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myxoedema coma may develop following a long history of undiagnosed hypothyroidism or may occur in a patient with known hypothyroidism with an additional decompensating event such as infection or surgery. The clues in this scenario that point to this diagnosis are the scar on her neck which could be a thyroidectomy scar (which would mean the patient is likely to have hypothyroidism) and the report of a productive cough 3 days before the admission. The other clinical signs are consistent with myxoedema coma, including type Il respiratory failure, hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, tissue oedema and reduced Glasgow Coma Score (GCS). In severe hypothyroidism, it is common to find hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. B: Serotonin syndrome ought to be considered as the patient has a history of depression, and therefore, it is possible that she takes a medication that raises the level of serotonin. While serotonin syndrome can cause impaired consciousness, the other clinical findings are not consistent with this diagnosis, as you would also expect hyperthermia, hypertension and tachycardia. A: The past medical history of asthma, for which it is possible that the patient takes a long-term steroid inhaler, coupled with the presentations of hypotension and hypoglycaemia are consistent with an adrenal crisis. However, this diagnosis does not explain the impaired level of consciousness or the facial oedema. It is possible to have adrenal insufficiency in addition to myxoedema coma, but the primary diagnosis is myxoedema coma. C: Subclinical hypothyroidism tends to be asymptomatic; this would, therefore, not explain these clinical findings. In subclinical hypothyroidism, the thyroid-stimulating hormone level is elevated, but the thyroxine level is in the normal range. E: In a thyroid storm, patients experience reduced consciousness but will also have hyperthermia, tachycardia, diarrhoea and jaundice. These signs do not typically occur in myxoedema coma.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with tiredness, weight loss, and diarrhoea. She has also been suffering from heavy periods over the past few months. On examination, she looks tanned, but is very thin and emaciated. Her blood pressure (BP) is 115/80 mmHg. Her pulse is 84 beats per minute (bpm) and regular and she has a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Investigations reveal Hb 91 g/l (normocytic), WCC 6.1 x 10^9/L, PLT 195 x 10^9/L, Na+ 132 mmol/L, K+ 5.8 mmol/L, Ferritin 25 µg/L, Folate 4.0 µg/l, Corrected Ca2+ 2.35 mmol/L, Albumin 28 g/L, ALT 42 U/L, TSH 8.3 µU/L, fasting Glucose 8.5 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Type 2 polyglandular syndrome is characterised by adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes; hypogonadism, coeliac disease and myasthenia gravis may also be seen. The hyponatraemia, elevated fasting glucose and elevated TSH all support this as the diagnosis. B: This is characterised by mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. A: This may explain the diarrhoea, but it would not explain the hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia seen here, nor the postural drop in blood pressure. D: Type 3 polyglandular syndrome is characterised by autoimmune thyroiditis, but the other associated autoimmune diseases don't fit with a diagnosis of either type 1 or type 2 disease. E: Although HIV infection may present with significant weight loss and diarrhoea, the abnormalities seen on blood testing are much more consistent with autoimmune polyglandular syndrome.

questions.question: A 37-year-old man with a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He takes a basal bolus insulin regime of 22 units of long-acting insulin (Insulotard®) per day and 6 units of short-acting insulin (Actrapid®) with each meal. His main problem is unpredictable hypoglycaemic episodes, which occur during the day, normally a few hours after each meal. He has peripheral neuropathy affecting the soles of both feet, but is otherwise well. Examination reveals a BP of 105/80 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. His BMI is 21. Investigations show Hb 132 g/l, WCC 7.1 x 10^9/L, PLT 199 x 10^9/L, Na+ 137 mmol/L, K+ 4.4 mmol/L, Cr 102 µmol/l, Glucose 6.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 53 mmol/mol (7.0%). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Arrange a 72 continuous glucose monitor recording
B. Change the Insulotard® to insulin glargine
C. Reduce the dose of the Actrapid®
D. Reduce the dose of Insulotard®
E. Refer for Dose Adjustment for Normal Eating (DAFNE) education.
questions.explanation: In this situation it is possible that the patient has never been educated about matching short-acting insulin to the carbohydrates consumed with the meal. In the first instance he is likely to benefit from DAFNE education, teaching him to take appropriate short-acting insulin for the meal he has eaten. Reducing the dose of his insulin is likely to lead to deterioration in his glycaemic control. D: Reduce the dose of Insulotard®. This would have most impact on nocturnal rather than daytime hypoglycaemia. A: Arrange a 72 continuous glucose monitor recording. Although continuous glucose monitoring may elucidate the daytime hypoglycaemia episodes, it won't initiate the change in behaviour which is driven by DAFNE education. B: Change the Insulotard® to insulin glargine. This is more likely to impact on fasting hypoglycaemia during the overnight period, rather than daytime hypo episodes. C: Reduce the dose of the Actrapid®. A blanket reduction in the dose of Actrapid® is likely to drive hyperglycaemia; as such, it should be avoided here if possible.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) where she asks for her cholesterol to be measured. She has a past history of polycystic ovary disease (PCOD) and diet-controlled diabetes mellitus. She drinks a glass of wine each night and swims most days. She is currently on the oral contraceptive pill. Investigations reveal LDL cholesterol 5.5 mmol/L, Triglycerides 2.5 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 0.8 mmol/L. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the low HDL cholesterol levels?
questions.explanation: Low levels of HDL are associated with an increased risk of ischaemic heart disease. Diabetes causes low HDL and raised triglycerides. HMG CoA reductase inhibitors are used in primary and secondary prevention of coronary events. Statins are particularly considered for patients with diabetes mellitus and are recommended now for all diabetics above 40 years of age in the JBS2 guidelines. They are also used in other patients with high calculated cardiovascular risk. A: Mild to moderate alcohol consumption is associated with an increase in HDL. B: Exercise is an effective way of increasing HDL cholesterol levels. C: Increased oestrogen levels, as caused by the contraceptive pill, lead to higher HDL levels. E: Women have naturally higher HDL levels compared to men, due to higher oestrogen levels.

questions.question: A 54-year-old taxi driver presents to the Diabetes Clinic for review. He is finding it increasingly difficult to work because of increased drowsiness and episodes of sweating and nausea. He reports having to take sugary snacks to work with him to help him focus. His current medications for type II diabetes are metformin 1 g twice daily (bd) and gliclazide 80 mg bd. He has symptoms of erectile dysfunction, for which he takes sildenafil, and numbness in both feet. He is otherwise well and works five days a week as a bus driver. His BP is 135/82 mmHg, and his BMI is 35 kg/m2 Investigations show Hb 132 g/l, WCC 7.1 x 10^9/L, PLT 181 x 10^9/L, Na+ 137 mmol/l, K+ 4.3 mmol/l, Creatinine 113 µmol/L, HbA1c 54 mmol/mol (7.1%), Urine microalbuminuria stix: Positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Change the Gliclazide for Sitagliptin
B. Change the Gliclazide for Liraglutide
C. Reduce the dose of Metformin
questions.explanation: This patient has symptoms of hypoglycaemia, characterised by drowsiness, sweating and nausea, combined with the need for sugary snacks. In this situation, it is the sulfonylurea (SU) that is driving hunger and episodes of hypoglycaemia and potentially contributing to weight gain. Over time, this will drive an increase in insulin requirements and lead to a deterioration in glycaemic control. As such, the best option is to change the SU for a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitor, given HbA1c control is relatively good. An alternative to sitagliptin would be a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor, which now has associated class benefits in heart failure and renal impairment. He should, of course, also be encouraged to lose weight. B: Although liraglutide will improve glycaemic control, it is injectable and would at least initially lead to significant gastrointestinal upset. In this patient, therefore, it would usually be considered as another option after the second oral failure. Furthermore, the addition of a GLP-1 mimetic, such as liraglutide, should not be considered until failure of diabetic control with triple therapy (eg metformin, sulfonylurea, SGLT-2 inhibitor). C: Metformin per se does not lead to hypoglycaemia and has a positive impact on diabetes outcomes. As such, it is gliclazide that should be substituted, rather than reducing the dose of, or stopping, metformin. D: Reducing to one medication only may drive a significant deterioration in glycaemic control. For this reason, substitution of gliclazide, rather than stopping it, is the most appropriate next step. E: It would be inappropriate to commence this patient on an insulin regimen at this stage. He is describing symptoms of hypoglycaemia and is working as a courier. Insulin may further exacerbate his symptoms of hypoglycaemia and affect his ability to work (patients must stop driving group 2 vehicles until the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency has made a formal decision). Alternative methods, such as adjusting his oral hypoglycaemic regimen, should be considered initially.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is admitted to Intensive Care following surgery for peritonitis after a ruptured appendix. After 7 days, his blood tests return the following: Hb 112 g/l, WCC 8.2 x 10^9/l, PLT 165 x 10^9/L, Na+ 131 mmol/L, K+ 4.3 mmol/L, Urea 6.5 mmol/L, Cr 85 µmol/L, TSH 3 µu/ml, T3 2.8 pmol/L, T4 10 pmol/L. What is the most likely explanation for the blood test results?
questions.explanation: Sick euthyroid syndrome may occur in any severe illness, organic or psychiatric. It develops due to a disruption of the deiodinases that are usually involved in synthesising T4 and T3. As a result, T4 and T3 levels fall, but the TSH level remains within the normal range. So far, no evidence has been found of any benefit in treating this condition, and it resolves upon resolution of the underlying condition. A: Hyperthyroidism would present with a suppressed TSH level, and raised T3 or T4 level, or both. Instead, we see a normal TSH level coupled with reduced T3 and T4. B: Hypothyroidism would present with an elevated TSH level, and reduced T3 or T4 level, or both. In contrast, we see a normal TSH level coupled with reduced T3 and T4. C: In subclinical hyperthyroidism, the TSH level will be suppressed, but the thyroid hormones remain within the normal range. In contrast, here we see a normal TSH level but suppressed levels of the thyroid hormones. E: In subclinical hypothyroidism, the TSH level will be elevated, but the thyroid hormones remain within the normal range. Instead, this patient presents with a normal TSH level and suppressed levels of thyroid hormones.

questions.question: A 36-year-old female who is 36-weeks pregnant attends hospital in labour. She has a tense, woody abdomen and the cardiotocograph (CTG) confirms fetal distress. She is found to have a placental abruption and has an emergency C-section. The major haemorrhage protocol is activated due to heavy blood loss in excess of 3 litres. After being discharged from the hospital, she visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining that she is unable to produce any milk. She has also been feeling fatigued. Her GP suspects that she may have Sheehan syndrome. Which anatomical structure has infarcted, resulting in this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Sheehan syndrome results from profound postpartum blood loss which causes an infarction of the pituitary gland. Most commonly, this disrupts the production of growth hormone and prolactin, which results in agalactorrhea. However, production of the other anterior pituitary hormones may also be disrupted (gonadotropins, adrenocorticotropic hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)). C: Hypothalamic dysfunction can disrupt the release of hormones that act on the pituitary gland and result in the release of anterior pituitary gland hormones. However, in Sheehan syndrome, it is the pituitary gland itself that infarcts and not the hypothalamus. A: The pituitary gland infarcts in Sheehan syndrome, which can result in hypopituitarism. This can result in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency, which causes secondary adrenal insufficiency; the adrenal gland itself, however, does not infarct. B: Breast lactocytes are the normal site of milk production. The insult in Sheehan syndrome is not to the lactocytes themselves but rather to the pituitary gland which secretes prolactin, which stimulates the lactocytes to produce milk. E: Sheehan syndrome is due to infarction of the pituitary gland. This can cause hypopituitarism (including TSH deficiency), which will give rise to the symptoms of hypothyroidism. The thyroid gland itself is unaffected

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents to clinic and complains of tiredness, weakness and loss of body hair. He has recently split up with his partner and he cites loss of sexual function as one reason for this occurring. There is no past medical history of note apart from mild essential hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine. On examination, pulse is 90 beats per minute (bpm) and blood pressure (BP) 100/50 mmHg. He is of normal appearance and has normal secondary sexual characteristics, although his body hair is fine and sparse. He also has bitemporal hemianopia. Routine bloods reveal mildly elevated potassium of 5.5 mmol/L. TSH is in the normal range. What test would be most useful from those listed?
questions.explanation: This clinical history is highly suggestive of a pituitary macroadenoma. As the patient is of normal appearance, the differential diagnosis is that of prolactinoma or a non-functioning pituitary adenoma. Therefore, serum prolactin is therefore of great importance. A Synacthen™™ test is an adequate measure of cortisol reserve and would be the next most important test. MRI pituitary is important to document the size and invasion of the pituitary tumour, but would be done after a Synacthen™™ test and serum prolactin to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the most appropriate surgical approach. A: A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in the diagnostic workup for Cushing syndrome, which is effectively ruled out here by the normal appearance and normal blood pressure. B: Insulin tolerance testing is used in the work-up for growth hormone deficiency, which at this stage isn't appropriate until an MRI has taken place and other pituitary hormones have been profiled. D: Cortisol is subject to pulsatile release, and therefore random measurement is not useful in the work-up for possible pituitary tumour. E: Both hypo- and hyperglycaemia may be associated with pituitary disease, although a random glucose is unlikely to be helpful here.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by the Emergency Department. She has had three episodes of collapse over the past five months. There is also a history of increased hunger, which has been accompanied by gradual weight gain. On further questioning, family history reveals no useful information. You elect to admit her for a period of fasting. The morning after admission, some 16 hours without food, she complains of feeling faint. Investigations reveal Glucose 2.1 mmol/L, Insulin 7 mU/L with increased proportion of pro-insulin, C-peptide Elevated, Cortisol 550 nmol/L. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: After a 15 h fast, the cut-off normal limits for glucose are 2.5 mmol/L and 5 mU/l for insulin. As such, this patient has an inappropriately low glucose and raised insulin level. By 24 h, fasting leads to a detection rate of 78% for insulinoma. If the fast is extended to 72 h, this detection rate increases to 98%. Insulinomas have an incidence of 1-2/million/year, are commoner in women and may be associated with the MEN-1 syndrome in around 10%; 90% of them are less than 2 cm in size. More of the insulin released by an insulinoma remains as pro-insulin, so that pro-insulin levels are often raised as a proportion of total insulin levels. D: A glucagonoma would lead to hyperglycaemia, rather than hypoglycaemia. A: As she is in hospital, abuse of insulin secretagogues is unlikely. B: Abuse of insulin would lead to raised insulin levels without a corresponding rise in c-peptide. E: The cortisol levels in this patient are appropriately towards the upper end of the normal range, making Addison's disease very unlikely.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the Hypertension Clinic with difficult-to-control blood pressure. He is now taking ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg, but his blood pressure is still 153/88 mmHg. Investigations show Sodium 145 mmol/L, Potassium 3.0 mmol/L, Urea 5.2 mmol/L, Creatinine 85 µmol/L. Renal ultrasound scan shows Kidneys normal size. Which of the following represents the best investigation for this patient?
options: A. Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol level
B. Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol levels after washout of antihypertensives
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors may increase plasma renin activity, and calcium antagonists may reduce aldosterone. Hence, renin, aldosterone and cortisol should be measured after a 2-week washout period to confirm primary hyperaldosteronism, the most likely diagnosis here. Resection of adenoma leads to resolution of hypertension in around 70% of patients where a discrete adenoma has been identified. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia may be managed with spironolactone for many years; dexamethasone is the treatment of choice for those with glucocorticoid-suppressible hyperaldosteronism. A: These investigations are in the context of suspected secondary hypertension (young patient requiring three antihypertensive agents). These need to be performed after washout of his medication, since ACE inhibitors may increase plasma renin activity and calcium antagonists may reduce aldosterone. C: It may reveal end organ damage (left ventricular hypertrophy) but it will not clarify the cause of the hypertension. D: In young patients with hypertension that is difficult to control, renal artery stenosis is one of the differential diagnoses. In this scenario though, normal-sized kidneys preclude this diagnosis. E: This is one of the tests used to detect autonomous aldosterone secretion. Patients should increase their sodium intake to more than 6 g/day for 3 days with diet and sodium chloride tabs. Potassium supplementation and daily potassium measurements are required for patients with hypokalaemia. Patients perform 24 h urine collection starting on day 3 for sodium and aldosterone. A 24 h urinary aldosterone excretion of more than 12 mcg is consistent with primary aldosteronism, whereas 24 h urinary sodium of 200 mEq indicates adequate intake. This test should not be performed in patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure or arrhythmias.

questions.question: A 51-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of hot flushes and night sweats for the past few weeks. In addition, she states that she has not been able to concentrate and that her sleep is disturbed at night. She is accompanied by her husband who states that she has been having mood swings of late. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg and her heart rate is 78 bpm. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2 Abdominal examination is normal. She is started on hormone replacement therapy. However, she wants to know more regarding the benefits of hormone replacement therapy. Which of the following is associated with hormone replacement therapy?
options: A. Decreases the risk of colorectal cancer
B. Decreases the risk of dementia in older women
C. Increases the occurrence of osteoporosis
D. Decreases the risk of gall bladder disease
E. Increases the risk of diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: The incidence of colorectal cancer is decreased in women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT), making this the most likely answer. Long term follow up of patients taking HRT demonstrated that when colorectal tumours do occur, however, they are found at a more advanced stage. This indicates that the underlying pathophysiology of colorectal cancer may be altered by HRT, although the mechanism remains unknown. C: The risk of fracture and occurrence of osteoporosis is decreased (33% decreased risk for hip fracture) by hormone replacement therapy. B: Consistent, statistically significant changes to the risk of dementia have not been demonstrated in patients taking hormone replacement therapy. D: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) causes a definite increase in the risk of cholecystitis (57% increased risk). For every 185 patients treated with HRT, it is estimated one extra patient will require a cholecystectomy. E: There is a decreased risk of type II diabetes mellitus (up to 19%) in individuals taking hormone replacement therapy. A reduction in insulin resistance has been proposed as an underlying mechanism.

questions.question: You are called to interpret the results of a synacthen test on the Oncology Ward. The patient is a 60-year-old woman who is in hospital for chemotherapy for breast cancer. She has tolerated her therapy poorly and is currently suffering from multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, pulse 120/min regular, BP 90/60 mmHg. Her JVP is not seen, her heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. There is evidence of a right mastectomy. Abdominal and neurological examination is normal. Short synacthen test: Time 0 min - cortisol 90 nmol/l, Time 30 min - cortisol 130 nmol/l, Time 60 min - cortisol 145 nmol/l. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most important component of your immediate management?
options: B. 1 litre IV normal saline over 12
D. Hydrocortisone oral 20 mg AM, 10 mg PM
questions.explanation: This patient's rise in cortisol demonstrates an inadequate response to synacthen. The 30 min value should rise above 550 nmol/l. Therefore, this lady has acute adrenal insufficiency. The treatment for this is intravenous saline - at least 6-hourly initially, as her blood pressure is on the low side. Hydrocortisone should be given at a dose of 50 mg IV QDS. Lower doses will not be sufficient. Fludrocortisone should be started but is not necessary for emergency treatment. The aetiology of the adrenal insufficiency should be elucidated, but in this lady is likely to be due to metastatic spread, most commonly from a breast or lung primary. A: IV dextrose may further exacerbate any underlying hyponatraemia, and is unlikely to represent adequate fluid replacement for this patient. B: Although normal saline will contribute to total body sodium, this represents an inadequate fluid replacement regimen and won't correct underlying hypoadrenalism. D: This is an adequate maintenance regimen for hypoadrenalism, although it is inappropriate here due to vomiting, and because of likely greater corticosteroid requirements due to her intercurrent illness. E: This patient is acutely unwell with a very poor cortisol response to synacthen, and thus higher doses of corticosteroids will almost certainly be required.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man is admitted with confusion. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is on home nebulisers and oxygen. His relatives have noticed increased breathlessness and vomiting, which has meant he has been unable to keep down his rescue course of prednisolone. General examination reveals skin bruises and dry mucous membranes. Other past history of note includes treated hypothyroidism. On chest auscultation, there are bibasal inspiratory crepitations with prolonged expiratory wheeze. His pulse is 78/min, blood pressure 85/54 mmHg, temperature 37.5°C. Chest radiography shows chronic obstructive airways changes and an electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm. Investigations show Hb 132 g/l, WCC 14 x 10^9/L, PLT 470 x 10^9/L, Na+ 125 mmol/L, K+ 5.3 mmol/L, Urea 17.2 mmol/L, Cr 130 µmol/L, Glucose 2.8 mmol/L. You give him a bolus of IV glucose and start IV fluid replacement with normal saline. Which of the following is the next best immediate management step?
questions.explanation: Acute adrenal insufficiency in this patient is most likely due to a chest infection and prior suppression of the adrenocortical axis by exogenous steroids. Patients present with hypotension and confusion. Examination may reveal evidence of prior treatment with steroids. Biochemistry shows hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and an increased urea. Treatment includes correction of hypoglycaemia, administration of glucocorticoids and adequate hydration. B: Whilst these may be appropriate, antibiotics should follow corticosteroids in this case in terms of urgency given the significant electrolyte disturbance and hypotension. C: Potassium is towards the upper end of the normal range and is likely to fall rapidly as a result of rehydration and initiation of corticosteroid therapy. D: Calcium resonium is unpleasant to take and is not required here, because potassium will almost certainly fall once fluid replacement and steroid therapy is initiated. Its main use is in the management of hyperkalaemia occurring as a result of acute on chronic kidney disease. E: IV aminophylline use is not encouraged in acute exacerbations of COPD because of the high risk of atrial arrhythmias; it may be used in cases where other options have been exhausted.

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of excess facial hair and acne. On examination, her BMI is elevated at 29 kg/m2. Her BP is raised at 155/92 mmHg and her pulse is 80/min and regular. You notice excess hair around her beard line, upper chest and lower abdomen. There are no purple striae on abdominal examination. The examination of external genitalia is normal. On further questioning, she tells you that her periods are irregular, only occurring every 3 months, and they are heavy when they do occur. Which one of the following would be an appropriate initial investigation?
questions.explanation: The suspected diagnosis here is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). According to the Rotterdam Consensus, two of the following three criteria are required for the diagnosis of the PCOS: oligo-/anovulation hyperandrogenism clinical (hirsutism or less commonly male pattern alopecia) or biochemical (raised free androgen index or free testosterone) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. D: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test. This is used when Cushing syndrome is clinically suspected and the overnight dexamethasone suppression test results are equivocal. A: Plasma ACTH. There is no clear clinical evidence of cortisol excess in this scenario. Even if Cushing syndrome was suspected, an overnight dexamethasone suppression test or high-dose dexamethasone suppression test would be the initial investigation in order to establish the presence of hypercortisolism. If hypercortisolim was confirmed, a suppressed ACTH would point towards an adrenal cause whereas raised ACTH would indicate a pituitary cause. B: MRI pituitary. This would be useful only if Cushing syndrome was confirmed via overnight dexamethasone or high-dose dexamethasone suppression test and a central cause for hypercortisolism was suspected. E: 17-hydroxyprogesterone. This is usually raised (>1000 ng/dl) in cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Females with severe CAH due to deficiencies of 21-hydroxylase, 11-beta-hydroxylase or 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase have ambiguous genitalia at birth (classic virilising adrenal hyperplasia). Females with mild 21-hydroxylase deficiency are identified later in childhood because of precocious pubic hair, clitoromegaly or both, often accompanied by accelerated growth and skeletal maturation (simple virilising adrenal hyperplasia). Females with still milder deficiencies of 21-hydroxylase or 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity may present in adolescence or adulthood with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism and/or infertility (non-classic adrenal hyperplasia).

questions.question: A 64-year-old type II diabetic presents to her General Practitioner (GP) for review. She has poor blood glucose control and is taking maximal doses of metformin and gliclazide. You elect to substitute insulin glargine for her gliclazide. Which of the following options best describes the amino acid modifications seen in glargine insulin?
options: A. Glycine is at position A21, two arginines are added to the B chain
B. Aspartic acid is at position B28
C. Glycine is at position B28
D. Aspartic acid is at position A21
E. Proline is at position A21
questions.explanation: The clue is in the name - 'glargine' is an amalgam of glycine and arginine. Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin analogue. It has recently been joined by another insulin analogue, insulin detemir.. The main use for insulin analogues is in improving glycaemic control in type 1 diabetes. Some patients may be limited in haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) reductions due to post-meal hypoglycaemia or nocturnal hypoglycaemia, and the use of short- and/or long-acting insulin analogues may improve glycaemic control with reduced incidence of hypoglycaemia compared to conventional insulins. Additional studies of glargine insulin in type 2 diabetes have demonstrated a reduction in nocturnal hypoglycaemia. D: Aspartic acid is at position A21. Insulin aspart is a short-acting insulin analogue which has an aspartic acid residue at position B28. It is a manufactured form of human insulin. It was created through recombinant DNA technology so that the amino acid, B28, which is normally proline, is substituted with an aspartic acid residue. This analogue has increased charge repulsion, which prevents the formation of hexamers, to create a faster-acting insulin. B: Aspartic acid is at position B28. Insulin aspart is a short-acting insulin analogue which has an aspartic acid residue at position B28. It is used as prandial insulin. In our scenario, since the patient was on maximum doses of gliclazide and metformin, the next step would be to add in basal insulin such as glargine. If this doesn't work, there is the option to advance to a basal bolus regimen where basal insulin is administered once daily, and a type of fast-acting insulin as aspart is used to cover post-prandial hyperglycaemia. C: Glycine is at position B28. Insulin aspart is a short-acting insulin analogue which has an aspartic acid residue at position B28. E: Proline is at position A21. Insulin lispro was the first insulin analogue to enter the market. Engineered through recombinant DNA technology, the penultimate lysine and proline residues on the C-terminal end of the B-chain are reversed. This modification does not alter receptor binding, but blocks the formation of insulin dimers and hexamers. This allows larger amounts of active monomeric insulin to become immediately available for postprandial injections.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with the ulcer below on her foot. Her posterior tibial pulses are easily felt, but her dorsalis pedis pulses are not palpable. Pinprick and vibration perception are absent from the knee down. Which of the following represents the likely aetiology of this ulcer?
options: C. Combined neuropathy and arterial insufficiency
questions.explanation: This is a typical neuropathic ulcer, with callus forming the edge and a clean base. These are commonly found on the pressure points of the feet and are painless. Ten per cent of people have absent dorsalis pedis pulses; therefore, their absence does not indicate ischaemia. Off-loading is the key intervention with respect to driving successful ulcer healing, although many patients find this difficult to achieve. C: Combined neuropathy and arterial insufficiency. There are no features such as pallor, cold extremities and trophic changes including loss of hair and nail dystrophy to suggest arterial insufficiency. A: Primary infection. Around 50% of diabetic foot ulcers may become infected, although primary infection is not the usual cause of plantar lesions like this. D: Venous insufficiency. Venous insufficiency results in ulceration with slough and debris formation, primarily over the medial malleolus. E: Arterial insufficiency. Arterial insufficiency results in loss of temperature in the feet, pallor and trophic changes including loss of hair and nail dystrophy. These changes are not seen here.

questions.question: An 18-year-old hirsute woman, who is obese, is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with a prolactin of 850 mU/L (normal range: 90-520 mU/l) and no menses for the past three months. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 125/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 70 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m2. What is the most important next step?
options: D. Serum FSH and LH levels
questions.explanation: The first test to do when seeing anyone with hyperprolactinaemia is to exclude pregnancy, as it is the most common cause. Obesity and hirsutism are common and may not indicate any underlying pathology. Prolactin is normally <450 mU/l, but can rise tenfold in pregnancy. A serum prolactin of >3000 mU/l is suggestive of a tumour. However, treatment with dopamine antagonists can give a prolactin of 900-3600 mU/L. C: Serum testosterone levels. Given that this patients symptoms of amenorrhoea are recent, pregnancy is more likely than an alternative diagnosis such as polycystic ovarian syndrome. A: Serum 17-hydroxy-progesterone levels. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is associated with hirsutism, although given that the patient has had a normal menstrual cycle until 3 months earlier, pregnancy is the more likely cause of her presentation here. B: Pituitary MRI. The prolactin level seen here is not particularly elevated, making a tumour less likely as the cause of her symptoms. Large pituitary tumours can compress or interrupt the pituitary stalk, leading to prolactin in the range of 900-6000 mU/L. However, macroprolactinomas are generally defined as a prolactin of >6000 mU/L. First-line therapy for prolactinoma is with dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline. D: Serum FSH and LH levels. Calculation of the LH:FSH ratio is most useful in the evaluation of possible polycystic ovarian syndrome, which is unlikely here given the recent onset of amenorrhoea.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman is referred by her General Practitioner to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of excessive hairiness. She is particularly concerned as this affects her face and the upper part of her chest. Her periods have been irregular ever since they began at the age of 12. On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m2 Her testosterone level is measured at 3.2 nmol/L (normal range: 0.5-3.0 nmol/l) and there is a raised luteinising hormone/follicle-stimulating hormone (LH/FSH) ratio. What is the best long-term management for this lady?
questions.explanation: This woman has evidence of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) as evidenced by her clinical presentation, moderately raised testosterone level and reversal of the LH/FSH ratio. Given that her elevated BMI is approaching the obese range, the best management is loss of weight. Loss of weight leads to decreased insulin resistance, increases in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and reduction in levels of free androgens. A 5% weight loss is said to result in a 40% improvement in hirsuitism. It will also significantly reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes over the longer term. D: Metformin. Like pioglitazone, metformin reduces insulin resistance and has a modest effect on weight reduction in women with PCOS. B: Pioglitazone. The insulin sensitiser pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity and restores ovulatory function in a significant number of patients with PCOS. It is, however, usually avoided over the long term because of adverse effects including weight gain, fluid retention and decreased bone mineral density. C: Combined oral contraceptive pill. Although the pill will regularise the menstrual cycle and improve hirsutism, over the longer term weight loss is more beneficial with respect to the patient's health. E: Cyproterone acetate and ethinyloestradiol. Cyproterone acetate and ethinyloestradiol do reduce hirsuitism, although where patients can manage to lose weight this is the preferred intervention, accompanied by electrolysis.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with type II diabetes mellitus is seen in the Diabetic Clinic for follow-up. He has been diabetic for nearly 10 years now, diet controlled for four years and since that time on gliclazide and metformin. Unfortunately, he has missed many of his follow-up appointments. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 124/74 mmHg. He has no evidence of peripheral neuropathy. Investigations from the previous appointment revealed the following: Haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) 45.36 mmol/mol (6.3%), Protein Negative, Glucose Negative, Leucocytes Negative, Nitrites Negative, Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/L, Urea 6.8 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 98 µmol/L. A 24 hour urine collection was carried out which demonstrated 180 mg of albumin in the sample. Which management step is most likely to improve his overall prognosis with respect to renal and other complications?
options: A. Commencing an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor in the first instance
C. Optimising blood pressure control with other agents besides ACE inhibitors in the first instance
E. Commencing angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) in the first instance
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors have been shown to improve outcome in microalbuminuria in diabetic kidney disease and reduce progression to frank proteinuria and kidney disease. Additionally, they show cardiovascular (CV) outcome benefits in large randomised controlled trials (RCTs). Their use in this context has therefore become widespread. D: Commencing betablockade. There is no evidence that beta blockade will improve renal prognosis aside from blood pressure control. B: Optimising glycaemic control. Optimising glycaemic control is likely to reduce microvascular complications as evidenced by the UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS). In this case however, there is little further optimisation which could be made based on the HbA1c result given, and further attempts to improve the situation might well lead to unacceptable side-effects such as hypoglycaemia. C: Optimising blood pressure control with other agents besides ACE inhibitors in the first instance. Although blood pressure control is important in delaying renal progression, ACE inhibition, in particular, has been proven to improve outcome in microalbuminuria in diabetic kidney disease and reduce progression to frank proteinuria and kidney disease. Therefore, ACE inhibition should be used in the first instance. E: Commencing angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) in the first instance. There is growing evidence that ARBs have similar benefits to ACE inhibitors in heart failure and other indications, and they may have a lower incidence of side-effects. Whilst evidence of renoprotection from clinical trials is strong however, evidence of ischaemic CV outcome benefit is less clear. Just taking valsartan as one example: whilst a reduction in hospitalisations was seen in the main heart failure study, there was no reduction in mortality seen. For this reason, at the present time ACE inhibitors remain first-line in most cases.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus treated with metformin is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) in a semi-comatose state. She is also taking ramipril, bendroflumethiazide and digoxin for atrial fibrillation (AF). You understand she also takes sleeping pills and codeine-based pain relief for arthritis and has recently split from her husband.  Investigations reveal the following: Bicarbonate (HCO32-): 19 mmol/L (Normal: 24-30 mmol/l) Glucose: 57 mmol/L (Normal: 3.5-5.5 mmol/L) Sodium (Na+): 149 mmol/L (Normal: 135-145 mmol/l) Potassium (K+): 4.7 mmol/L (Normal: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L) Creatinine (Cr): 134 µmol/L (Normal: 50-120 µmol/L)  Blood gases reveal the following: pH: 7.41 (Normal: 7.35-7.45) pCO2: 3.2 kPa (Normal: 4.6-6.0 kPa) pO2: 8.8 kPa (Normal: 10.5-13.5 kPa)  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This woman has markedly high blood glucose yet the pH is within the normal range, with bicarbonate of 19 mmol/l. It is likely that she is suffering from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, which is characterised by profound hyperglycaemia and diuresis. Non-compliance with diet and medication may have precipitated her presentation. Treatment centres on aggressive fluid replacement with normal saline, and treatment of hyperglycaemia using a fixed-rate IV insulin regimen. She may well be converted back to oral therapy once the acute metabolic disturbance is corrected.  A: Acute kidney disease. The lack of significant acidosis and only mildly elevated creatinine count against acute kidney disease as the reason for her presentation here. B: Diabetic ketoacidosis. Diabetic ketoacidosis is seen in patients with type II diabetes but is seen very late in the disease when patients have significant insulinopaenia, and is associated with metabolic acidosis not seen here. D: Codeine overdose. Codeine overdose is associated with respiratory acidosis, not seen on the laboratory values here. E: Lactic acidosis. Although lactic acidosis is associated with metformin use, the bicarbonate of 19 effectively rules that out here.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with a previous psychiatric history presents to the Emergency Department for review with severe left loin pain. Medication of note includes paroxetine, which was started some 6 months earlier by her GP. On examination, her BP is elevated at 155/80 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular and she is in pain. Examination of the abdomen reveals severe left loin pain.  Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb): 132 g/L White cell count (WCC): 9.9 x 10^9/L Platelets (PLT): 188 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 137 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.2 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr): 124 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+): 3.2 mmol/L Phosphate (PO43-): 0.7 mmol/L KUB: Evidence of left renal stones  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: In this case, there is confirmed nephrolithiasis and a history of previous psychiatric disorder. In the presence of hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, this is highly suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. The condition occurs most frequently in postmenopausal women, and the prevalence in this group may be as high as 3%. The differential here is between parathyroid hyperplasia and a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Technetium (99mTc) sestamibi scanning has a high specificity and sensitivity for parathyroid adenoma. This patient already has symptoms of primary hyperparathyroidism, so that surgery is the definitive management. A sestamibi scan is most likely to inform on the location of any adenoma prior to a surgical approach.  A: Hypoparathyroidism. This is associated with low levels of calcium and elevated phosphate because of PTH deficiency. C: Secondary hyperparathyroidism. Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs as a result of chronic renal impairment, and creatinine here is relatively normal at 124. D: Multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is not associated with renal stone disease, and is rarely associated with significant hypercalcaemia. E: Paget's disease. Paget's disease is associated with normal calcium. Mild elevation in calcium may be seen in patients with Paget's who have prolonged bed rest.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the clinic with increasing anxiety, palpitations and heat intolerance. He has lost 3 kg in weight over the past month. He is taking long-term maintenance amiodarone therapy at a dose of 200 mg daily, along with warfarin because of a low ejection fraction due to previous myocardial infarction, and two previous episodes of paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia. He has refused an ICD in the past. On examination his BP is 123/82 mmHg, with pulse 95/min. His BMI is 21. There are bilateral crackles at both lung bases consistent with mild cardiac failure.  Investigations: Haemoglobin: 124 g/l White cell count (WCC): 6.1 x 10^9/L Platelets: 199 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 139 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.5 mmol/L Creatinine: 132 µmol/l Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH): <0.05 µU/L Thyroid uptake scan: normal Thyroid autoantibodies: +ve  Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: The normal thyroid uptake scan and presence of thyroid autoantibodies drives us towards a likely diagnosis of type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT). AIT type 1 affects patients with latent thyroid disorders, presentation being driven by the high levels of iodine contained in amiodarone. Optimal management of AIT type 1 involves the use of high-dose thionamides and discontinuation of the amiodarone if possible. Given that this man is taking amiodarone for VT, the possibility of an ICD should be re-discussed. Without discontinuation of amiodarone, persistently high levels of iodine reduce the effectiveness of therapy.  B: Subtotal thyroidectomy. Any thyroid surgery is likely to carry significant risks in this patient because of poor cardiac function, and should therefore be avoided. C: Lugol's iodine. Lugol's iodine is a short-term measure designed to treat hyperthyroidism, allowing for a window of intervention for surgery. D: Radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine is usually ineffective in managing AIT type 1 due to the excess iodine afforded by long-term amiodarone treatment. E: Propranolol. This would impact on symptoms but may exacerbate cardiac failure. It wouldn't treat the underlying thyrotoxicosis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman with Graves' disease attends clinic for follow-up of her thyroid status. She is currently taking propranolol and carbimazole. In the clinic she complains of sore eyes and double vision, particularly at extremes of gaze. Examination reveals marked proptosis. Her blood pressure is normal at 122/82, pulse is 60 and regular. She has tried artificial tears and eye patches with no relief. Which of the following would be the initial treatment of choice to improve the ophthalmopathy?
questions.explanation: Graves' disease causes ophthalmopathy with signs of lid lag, lid retraction (related to thyrotoxicosis), proptosis and diplopia (related to Graves' itself). There are usually two phases: an initial inflammatory phase followed by a fibrotic stage. If the symptoms are mild, patients can be managed with lubricants, eye patches and smoking cessation. This lady has active disease (pain, eyelid redness and swelling), which is sight-threatening (exophthalmos, diplopia and loss of colour vision). For sight-threatening dysthyroid optic neuropathy, the initial treatment option is IV glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 500 mg once weekly and subsequently tapering down).  D: Surgical decompression. This may be done to decompress the orbit, improve proptosis and address strabismus, but is performed 1-2 weeks after IV glucocorticoids if the response is poor. A: Radioiodine. Radioiodine is a definitive treatment option for relapsed Graves' thyrotoxicosis. There is concern that radioiodine could exacerbate Graves' ophthalmopathy. Patients with active Graves' ophthalmopathy receiving radioiodine treatment should be offered steroid cover. Radioiodine treatment can safely be given to patients with inactive Graves' ophthalmopathy provided hypothyroidism is avoided. B: Ibuprofen. This is used as first-line treatment for symptom control in cases of subacute thyroiditis. E: Orbital radiotherapy. This is an alternative option to reduce acute orbital inflammation, but it is not recommended for dysthyroid optic neuropathy.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man who is a known alcohol abuser is under investigation for hyponatraemia. He drinks several lagers daily, he is otherwise well and not on any medication. He smokes 15 cigarettes/day. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, chest and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal: Chest X-ray: Normal, Computed tomography (CT) of the head: Normal, Thyroid function: Normal, Sodium (Na+): 115 mmol/L, Potassium (K+): 4.5 mmol/l, Urea: 3.5 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr): 110 µmol/l, Glucose: 4.5 mmol/L, Plasma osmolality: 255 mosmol/kg, Calculated osmolality: 243 mosmol/kg. What is the cause of the hyponatraemia?
options: E. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
questions.explanation: Beer potomania is a recognised cause of hyponatraemia in alcohol misusers. The electrolyte imbalance normally corrects itself with cessation of alcohol. The osmolar gap is due to the presence of osmotically active ethanol in the blood.  A: Addison's disease. Addison's disease is due to deficiency in corticosteroids. Therefore, we would expect a high potassium and a postural drop in blood pressure or low blood pressure. C: Hypothyroidism. The osmolar gap would be normal. There may be associated symptoms such as weight gain, low mood, reduced appetite and intolerance to the cold. D: Salt-losing nephropathy. There may be variety of causes of salt-losing nephropathy including urea-induced osmotic diuresis, glomerulotubular imbalance and impaired tubular salt resorption. The osmolar gap would be normal. E: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion. It is defined by hyponatraemia and hypo-osmolality resulting from inappropriate and continued secretion of ADH. Patients would be euvolaemic and the osmolar gap would be normal.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman, who has a 10-month-old baby, presents with neck and throat pain over the area of her thyroid. She tells you that she had a flu-like illness a week or so before the pain began. Her partner, who also attends the appointment, tells you she has been nervous and agitated over the past week. On examination, there is a mild diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland and it is tender to palpation. Her BP is 141/82 mmHg, and her pulse is 85/min and regular at rest. She has a slight tremor.  Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin (Hb): 121 g/L White cell count (WCC): 6.1 x 10^9/L Platelets (PLT): 170 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 139 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.6 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr): 100 µmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): <0.05 U/L Anti-TPO: Negative Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 62 mm/hour fT4: 24.3 pmol/l Radioiodine uptake on the isotope scan is decreased.  Which of the following forms of thyroiditis is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: De Quervain's thyroiditis, also known as subacute thyroiditis, is characterised by acute onset of thyroid tenderness after a short viral illness, with raised ESR but negative anti-thyroid antibodies. It is thought to be linked to a response to viral infection, although a range of different viruses such as influenza and Coxsackie B have been implemented in its development. The early stages are characterised by a period of thyrotoxicosis, and radioisotope scanning reveals decreased thyroid uptake. As the disease progresses, there are phases of euthyroidism and hypothyroidism, followed by a period of recovery to a euthyroid state once again. Management centres on controlling pain, with either non-steroidals or corticosteroids, and managing the symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, normally with beta blockade.  A: Hashimoto's. Hashimoto's thyroiditis, also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, is an autoimmune disease in which the thyroid gland is gradually destroyed. Early on there may be no symptoms. Over time the thyroid may enlarge, forming a painless goitre. Some people eventually develop hypothyroidism with its accompanying weight gain, feeling tired, constipation, depression and general pains. The thyroid function tests in this scenario are in keeping with thyrotoxicosis. It is very unusual for Hashimoto's thyroiditis to present with negative anti-TPO antibodies. Neither is pain in the neck a feature of the disease. C: Riedel's. Riedel's thyroiditis, also known as chronic sclerosing thyroiditis, is a rare, chronic inflammatory disease of the thyroid gland characterised by a dense fibrosis that replaces normal thyroid parenchyma. The fibrotic process invades adjacent structures of the neck and extends beyond the thyroid capsule. This feature differentiates it from other inflammatory or fibrotic disorders of the thyroid. Extension beyond the thyroid also differentiates this from the fibrosing variant of Hashimoto thyroiditis. This intense fibrosis leads to a 'hard' feel of the gland. D: Graves'. Graves' disease, also known as toxic diffuse goitre, is an autoimmune disease characterised by hyperthyroidism due to circulating autoantibodies. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to and activate thyrotropin receptors, causing the thyroid gland to grow and the thyroid follicles to increase synthesis of thyroid hormone. Graves' disease, along with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, is classified as an autoimmune thyroid disorder. In some patients, Graves' disease represents part of more extensive autoimmune processes leading to dysfunction of multiple organs (e.g. polyglandular autoimmune syndromes). Graves' disease is associated with pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, diabetes mellitus type 1, autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, systemic sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Painful goitre or neck pain with flu-like symptoms is not a characteristic of this condition. E: Postpartum. The peak incidence for postpartum thyroiditis is at month 6 post-delivery. There is an initial period of thyrotoxicosis, followed by hypothyroidism, then recovery, although a significant percentage - perhaps as high as 40% - eventually become permanently hypothyroid. Flu-like symptoms are not a feature.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with complaints of numbness, tingling and burning sensation in both feet for the past six months. These have worsened over the past two months and are interfering with his sleep. Past medical history is significant for type II diabetes mellitus (past 20 years), for which he is on metformin, glimepiride and injected human insulin. In addition, the patient says that he had two visits to the Emergency Department in the past year for urinary retention. On examination, his blood pressure is 136/86 mmHg and his heart rate is 76 bpm. Sensory examination reveals impaired pressure perception on 10-g monofilament testing.  Investigations: Urea: 3.6 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr): 84 µmol/L Sodium (Na+): 142 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.2 mmol/L HbA1c: 74 mmol/L  Which of the following medications should be used for the treatment of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, in a patient presenting with diabetic neuropathy, management includes choosing from any one of the first-line drugs, which are: amitriptyline, gabapentin, duloxetine and pregabalin. Amitriptyline cannot be used in this patient, which therefore makes pregabalin the drug of choice to treat this patient.  A: Amitriptyline. This patient is presenting with a long duration of diabetes mellitus that is poorly controlled likely has diabetic neuropathy, based on his symptoms and sensory examination. Although amitriptyline is recommended as a first-line agent in the management of diabetic neuropathy, as per NICE guidelines, in elderly patients with a history of urinary retention, amitriptyline may precipitate another episode of acute urinary retention and hence is best avoided in this patient. B: Carbamazepine. Carbamazepine is used in the management of trigeminal neuralgia, rather than of diabetic neuropathy. D: Tramadol. Tramadol should be considered only in patients requiring acute rescue therapy. E: Venlafaxine. Venlafaxine should not be used in non-specialist settings, according to NICE guidelines.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner (GP) with flu-like symptoms, neck tenderness and swelling, sweating, palpitations and anxiety. She has lost 4 kg in weight over the past two weeks and feels that she is unable to sleep because of 'nerves'. She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. Examination reveals a fine tremor at rest; her blood pressure is 125/85 mmHg, and her pulse is 95 bpm and regular. She has a smooth, tender, mildly enlarged thyroid. Her body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m2.  Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb): 131 g/l White cell count (WCC): 6.1 x 10^9/l Platelets (PLT): 203 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 137 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.5 mmol/L Creatinine: 100 µmol/L Glucose: 4.1 mmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH): <0.05 u/L Thyroid autoantibodies: Negative  Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is subacute thyroiditis where the underlying problem is not over-production of thyroid hormone, but increased release. As such, the period of thyrotoxicosis lasting up to six weeks is followed by a short euthyroid phase, a period of hypothyroidism and then recovery. Propranolol can be used to treat her symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, whereas non-steroidals are the intervention of choice for thyroid tenderness.  C: Prophylthiouracil. Like carbimazole, propylthiouracil has no role in the treatment of subacute thyroiditis, because the disease is caused by increased thyroid hormone release, not over-production. A: Carbimazole. Anti-thyroid drugs are of no value in the treatment of subacute thyroiditis, because the disease is caused by acute inflammation of the gland which drives increased release of thyroid hormone, rather than increased production. For this reason, thionamides are not of value as a treatment. B: Perchlorate. Perchlorate blocks thyroid uptake of iodine. It is of value in acute control of thyrotoxicosis. It is used for the treatment of thyrotoxicosis in patients who need urgent control of their symptoms, for instance when they have evidence of cardiac decompensation. E: Radioiodine. Radioiodine is used in the treatment of Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma. It has no role in the treatment of subacute thyroiditis.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is referred with difficult-to-treat hypertension. She is currently taking ramipril 10 mg daily and bendrofluazide 2.5 mg daily, yet recent blood pressure was 165/90 mmHg. Past medical history in the family of subarachnoid haemorrhage was noted. She is currently being treated with amitriptyline for depression. Circulating calcitonin levels are elevated. Examination in the clinic reveals a patient of normal body habitus, with a blood pressure of 170/90 mmHg. Abdominal ultrasound is suspicious of a left adrenal mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her blood pressure prior to surgery?
questions.explanation: This patient has difficult hypertension, a left adrenal mass and raised calcitonin levels. The suspicion is that she has MEN-2a. Given the adrenal mass and hypertension, 24 h urinary catecholamines should be assessed to rule out phaeochromocytoma. Amitriptyline can interfere with catecholamine measurements and should be discontinued for 4 days prior to the measurements. Phenoxybenzamine is the most potent available alpha blocker, is non-selective and irreversible, and it is therefore the treatment of choice for phaeochromocytoma. Starting dose is 10 mg bd, which should be increased up to a maximum of 20 mg qds. Intravenous phenoxybenzamine is commonly used for the 3 days prior to surgery to ensure complete alpha blockade.  A: Amlodipine. Calcium channel blockers are not effective in controlling blood pressure pre-operatively in phaeochromocytoma when used as monotherapy. They may be used as an adjunct to beta blockade. B: Valsartan. Dual blockade of the RAS system with ACE inhibitors and ARBs isn't recommended because of the risk of hyperkalaemia, and it is ineffective in controlling blood pressure in phaeochromocytoma because increased angiotensin II isn't the primary problem. C: Atenolol. When beta blockers are used in the absence of complete alpha blockade, a paradoxical rise in blood pressure can be seen in phaeochromocytoma; as such, they are only used once phenoxybenzamine therapy is established. E: Propranolol. Non-selective beta blockers can be used to control tachycardia post-complete alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man with a 40-year history of type I diabetes now managed with a basal bolus insulin regime comes to the clinic for review. He has relatively good control with a HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol (7.5%) but has not managed his diabetes appropriately in previous years. He suffers from microalbuminuria, CKD3 renal impairment, lack of sensation in the soles of his feet and, on this occasion, he has mentioned problems with maintaining the quality of his erections. On examination his blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg; pulse is 75 bpm and regular, he has a postural drop of 15 mmHg diastolic on standing. There is diminished fine touch and proprioception affecting both feet. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: The patient's long history of type I diabetes, postural drop of 15mmHg diastolic on standing and his erectile dysfunction would be indicative of an autonomic neuropathy. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors are first-line treatment for his erectile dysfunction, although it is often required at high doses in patients with diabetes.
