Prostaglandin E1 either by intraurethral pessary or intra-cavernous injection is second-line treatment. Other options such as vacuum pump devices, penile prothesis and apomorphine can be considered.  D: Sensory neuropathy. Although there is evidence of proprioceptive sensory neuropathy in the clinical stem, it is not likely to be the cause of the erectile dysfunction. The postural hypotension is a strong suggestion of autonomic dysfunction. B: Motor neuropathy. There is nothing in the clinical history to indicate a motor neuropathy. The postural hypotension is a pointer towards the cause being an autonomic neuropathy. C: Psychological dysfunction. Although psychological dysfunction is a factor in all causes of erectile dysfunction, the clinical scenario indicates autonomic neuropathy as the cause here. Psychological therapies could be used in conjunction, but not as a first-line treatment. E: Vascular disease. Although patients with diabetes will have concurrent vascular disease and poor blood supply, it is more likely given the autonomic symptoms that this is the cause of the patient's erectile dysfunction.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man who suffers from epilepsy presents to his general practitioner (GP) for review. His medication has recently been changed after an increase in his fit frequency, and he is now taking carbamazepine. In the past week, he has complained of increasing headaches, tiredness and lethargy. In addition, his wife reports that he appears intermittently confused at x. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: We are told that this patient has recently commenced carbamazepine therapy, and we are also aware that he is complaining of symptoms that may suggest hyponatraemia. Syndrome of Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion (SIADH), is a recognised side effect of carbamazepine therapy. Other drugs that may result in SIADH include vincristine, vinblastine, cyclophosphamide, chlorpropamide, clofibrate, phenothiazines and monamine oxidase uptake inhibitors. Criteria for diagnosis include normal renal, adrenal and thyroid function, with hyponatraemia and hypotonic plasma (<270 mosmol/kg). In addition, urine osmolality should be inappropriately high and there should be excessive renal sodium loss of at least 20 mmol/L In this case the best treatment option would be to consider switching to another suitable anti-epileptic agent.  A: Complex partial seizures. A complex partial seizure, now known as a focal impaired awareness seizure according to the updated classification system from the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), starts focally within the brain and causes impairment of consciousness. In most patients, focal impaired awareness seizures represent underlying temporal lobe epilepsy. Focal impaired awareness seizures typically last 30-120 s. Longer seizures may occur when these become generalised with full-body convulsions or transform to a state of partial status epilepticus. They are characterized by aura, automatisms and impaired consciousness. B: Temporal lobe epilepsy. Temporal lobe seizures often begin with a motionless stare followed by oral or manual automatisms, symptoms and signs which are not present in this scenario. C: Drug-related hypernatraemia. This is strictly defined as a hyperosmolar condition caused by a decrease in total body water relative to electrolyte content. Hypernatremia is a 'water problem', not a problem of sodium homeostasis. Patients developing hypernatremia outside of the hospital are generally elderly people who are mentally and physically impaired, often with an acute infection. E: Intra-cranial tumour. Manifestations of intra-cranial tumours nay be non-specific and include headache (new onset or different in nature), altered mental status, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, limb weakness, gait disturbance, focal seizures, fixed visual changes, speech deficits and focal sensory abnormalities.

questions.question: A male and female couple visit their General Practitioner (GP). They both have dwarfism, which is due to achondroplasia, and they would like a referral to a specialist Obstetric Clinic as they have become pregnant for the first time. What mode of inheritance best describes that seen in achondroplasia?
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is caused by a mutation on the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene which causes individuals to have short arms and legs, with a torso of normal length. Since both patients have achondroplasia, there is a 75% chance that their child will have it too.  D: X-linked dominant. An example of a condition that is inherited in an X-linked dominant way is Fragile X syndrome. B: Autosomal recessive. Conditions that are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion include cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease. C: Mitochondrial. In mitochondrial inheritance, the condition is passed from the mother to the offspring. An example of such a condition is maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD). E: X-linked recessive. An example of a condition that is inherited in an X-linked recessive way is haemophilia.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic with recurrent palpitations. She continues to hold down her job as a nurse on the Cardiology Ward of the local hospital but feels increasingly tired. There is no past medical history of note and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, her BP is 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. Her BMI is 25. Her TSH is 0.15 mU/L (0.4-5), free T4 is 20.0 pmol/l (10-22) and free T3 is 9.3 pmol/l (5-10). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The TSH is below the lower limit of normal, and the T3 and T4 are at the upper limit of the normal range. This picture fits best with a diagnosis of subclinical thyrotoxicosis. Patients with subclinical thyrotoxicosis are at increased risk of incident atrial fibrillation and coronary heart disease (although ischaemic events are very unlikely in a patient of this age). At this stage no treatment is indicated, although thyroid function tests should be repeated in another 2-3 months.  C: Sick euthyroid syndrome. Sick euthyroid syndrome is associated with a significant non-thyroidal illness, where T3 and T4 are reduced; recovery is spontaneous and no intervention is required. B: Pituitary failure. Pituitary failure would be associated with a low TSH, and T3 and T4 below the lower limit of normal. Other features such as postural hypotension would also be expected. D: Addison's disease. Addison's is usually associated with a hypothyroid picture on blood testing. E: Thyrotoxicosis factitia. Although this patient having taken a small dose of thyroid hormone can't be excluded, abuse of thyroid hormone is more likely to lead to T4 outside the upper limit of the normal range.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man has been seen in the clinic for recurrent oral candida infections over the past year. He was previously fit and well. HIV antibody and polymerase chain reaction tests are negative. In terms of his biochemical profile, the patient has a normal oral glucose tolerance test, normal urea and electrolytes and normal TSH. His bone profile results: Corrected Calcium (Ca2+): 2.01 mmol/L (2.2-2.7 mmol/l) Phosphate (PO43-): 1.65 mmol/L (1.1-1.45 mmol/l) Parathyroid hormone (PTH): 1.0 pmol/L (1.5-7.6 pmol/L) Vitamin D: 23 nmol/L (<25 nmol/L)  Which of the following is the most likely pathology?
questions.explanation: Type 1 polyglandular autoimmune syndrome comprises mucocutaneous candidiasis, chronic hypoparathyroidism and autoimmune hypoadrenalism. The three major components tend to present in the chronological order of candidiasis, followed by hypoparathyroidism, followed by adrenal insufficiency. Hypoparathyroidism chronologically follows the mucocutaneous candidiasis and presents with hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and low parathyroid hormone. Other autoimmune pathologies associated with the condition include type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, hypothyroidism and vitiligo. Treatment includes antifungals, vitamin D, calcium and glucocorticoid replacement.  A: Type 2 polyglandular syndrome. Type 2 polyglandular syndrome comprises autoimmune hypoadrenalism, in combination with thyroid autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease) and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus. Primary hypogonadism, myasthenia gravis and coeliac disease are also commonly seen in this syndrome. B: Secondary hyperparathyroidism. The biochemical profile would have been different in this condition, with a low Vitamin D, hypocalcaemia and a high PTH. C: Primary hyperparathyroidism. This is not part of the polygandular autoimmune syndromes and manifests with hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia and normal/high parathyroid hormone levels. E: Hyperthyroidism. The patient has a normal TSH. Moreover, hyperthyroidism can be accompanied by mild hypercalcaemia.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman is attending clinic for follow-up. She has a history of multiple previous fractures and precocious puberty. On examination, she has café-au-lait skin pigmentation. Her pulse rate is 100 beats/min and regular and she has sweaty palms. Her thyroid function tests showed a raised fT4 at 23.4 pmol/L and a low TSH at 0.09 mIU/L. Her bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH and Vitamin D) is normal. Which of the following is the most likely pathology?
questions.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome is due to a mutation in a G-protein. This results in variable clinical presentations: • Precocious puberty (typically gonadotropin-independent). This includes breast development, genital maturation (with or without pubic hair growth), increased height velocity and macroorchidism in males. • Café-au-lait pigmentation. This consists of spots ranging from light brown to dark brown in colour. These often display a segmental distribution and frequently are predominant on one side of the body without crossing the midline; these spots must be differentiated from those characteristic of neurofibromatosis. • Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Multiple pathological fractures may be prominent early in the history; in many cases, bony involvement is found to predominate clinically on one side; clinical manifestations include gait anomalies, visible bony deformities (including abnormal bone growths of the skull), bone pain and joint stiffness with pain. • Hyperthyroidism, which in infants can result in failure to thrive. There is an increased risk of osteosarcoma and other connective tissue tumours, especially if the patient has had multiple radiographs of affected areas. In relation to precocious puberty, the patient is at increased risk of developing breast carcinoma. The increased risk of osteosarcoma is in the setting of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, although it still has an overall incidence of only around 1%.  A: Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is one of the most common chromosomal abnormalities and it is caused by the absence of one set of genes from the short arm of one X chromosome. Typical characteristics of this condition include short stature (heights below the 50th percentile), absent breast development and ovarian failure with primary or secondary amenorrhea. Other features include high arched palate, sometimes with dental crowding or malocclusion, hypoplastic nails, webbed neck, short fourth and fifth metacarpals and metatarsals, shield chest and lymphoedema. B: Neurofibromatosis type 1. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a multi-system genetic disorder whose main components are: Cutaneous findings, most notably café-au-lait spots and axillary freckling; Skeletal dysplasias such as pseudarthrosis; Benign and malignant nervous system tumors, most notably benign neurofibromas. C: Paget's disease. It is a disorder of bone remodelling with increased osteoclastic activity and bone resorption followed by compensatory osteoblastic activity. The structure of the newly formed bone is disorganized, resulting in weakness and fracture susceptibility. It is more prevalent above the age of 65, and markedly raised ALP is typical with normal calcium and phosphate levels. E: Osteitis fibrosa cystica. This is a skeletal disorder resulting in loss of bone mass, which is replaced with fibrous tissue (peri-trabecular fibrosis) and the formation of cyst-like brown tumours in and around the bone. Osteitis fibrosis cystica is caused by hyperparathyroidism, which stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption. Clinical presentation is one of hyperparathyroidism with the addition of bone fractures. PTH and serum calcium will also be elevated.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman with type I diabetes who has recently broken up with her boyfriend is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by the emergency services. Her parents say that she has become increasingly drowsy over the past 12 hours. She is usually managed with a basal bolus insulin regime but examination of the hospital records reveals two previous admissions with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), and her most recent HbA1c was 80.33 mmol/mol (9.5%). On examination, she is drowsy. Her blood pressure (BP) is 95/65 mmHg. Her pulse is 105 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She is apyrexial. Her respiratory rate is 31 breaths per minute. There is vague abdominal pain on examination of the abdomen.  Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin (Hb): 121 g/L White cell count (WCC): 6.7 x 10^9/L Platelets (PLT): 201 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 143 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 5.9 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr): 180 µmol/L Glucose: 34.1 mmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO32-): 13.0 mmol/L pH: 7.2 Urine (catheter): Ketones +++, blood +, protein -  You begin an insulin infusion and appropriate IV fluid replacement. Which other therapy would you also instigate?
questions.explanation: Patients with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) are at increased risk of venous thromboembolism because of volume depletion, hyperglycaemia and their decreased conscious level. As such, standard prophylaxis against deep vein thrombosis is an important component of management.  B: IV phosphate. Although extracellular phosphate may be depleted once insulin therapy is instigated, phosphate replacement isn't considered a routine component of the management of DKA. A: IV sodium bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate is also not used routinely and is only recommended in severe acidosis or circulatory collapse as an adjunct to insulin and fluid resuscitation. D: IV antibiotics. The normal white count isn't consistent with signs of acute infection. E: IV mannitol. IV mannitol has a role to play in the management of acute cerebral oedema, but in this case is only likely to exacerbate volume depletion.

questions.question: A 51-year-old obese woman with type II diabetes presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. She has completed a period of diet and exercise since her diagnosis three months ago, and she currently takes metformin 1 g twice a day. There is also a history of hypertension and dyslipidaemia, which are managed with ramipril and atorvastatin. On examination, her body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg. Her home blood glucose monitoring is reviewed and found to have average fasting sugar levels of around 8.8 mmol/L with postprandial excursions of up to 15.5 mmol/L  Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb): 141 g/l White cell count (WCC): 4.5 x 10^9/L Platelets (PLT): 142 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 141 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.8 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr): 130 µmol/L Haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c): 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%)  Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step for this patient?
questions.explanation: Dapagliflozin is a sodium/glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, which promotes the loss of glucose and sodium in the urine. As such, it has potential advantages for glucose, weight and blood pressure control. It also has favourable effects on chronic kidney disease and therefore should be preferentially used when there are concomitant diabetes and chronic kidney disease, as in this case.  C: Liraglutide. Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist and has favourable effects on chronic kidney disease resulting from diabetes. It may be considered as a treatment only after at least two other treatments have been tried first. B: Gliclazide. Although gliclazide is effective in controlling blood glucose in the short term, over the longer term, it promotes weight gain. It may also cause significant hypoglycaemia. D: Pioglitazone. In an obese woman, the use of pioglitazone risks driving further weight gain and, over the longer term, can result in fluid retention and loss of bone mineral density. Therefore, it should be avoided in this patient. E: Sitagliptin. Sitagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase IV inhibitor, which is weight-neutral, although not associated with positive cardiovascular outcomes. As such, it is considered a potential alternative to metformin in patients who cannot tolerate metformin.

questions.question: A 50-year-old type II diabetic man presents to the Diabetic Clinic as a new patient referred from his General Practitioner (GP). He has a past history of hypertension, heart failure and hypothyroidism. On examination, his body mass index (BMI) is 36 kg/m2 He is currently on metformin 500 mg twice a day and has excellent compliance. He was previously on gliclazide in addition to metformin, but this was stopped when he was admitted to hospital following a collapse. His HbA1c is 85.79 mmol/mol (10%). Which one of the following treatments would be the most suitable?
options: D. Add in nocturnal isophane insulin
questions.explanation: Despite excellent compliance with treatment, this patient's HbA1c remains well above the target range at 85.79 mmol/mol (10%). As treatment intensification with a sulphonylurea or pioglitazone is contraindicated in this case, and the patient's BMI is greater than 35, NICE advocates the use of a GLP-1 agonist such as liraglutide. Liraglutide binds to and activates the GLP-1 receptor to increase insulin secretion, suppress glucagon secretion and slow gastric emptying. This should only be continued if a patient has a reduction in HbA1c of at least 11 mmol/mol and a weight loss of at least 3% of initial body weight in 6 months.  A: Add in Pioglitazone. Pioglitazone is contraindicated in this patient due to the history of heart failure. B: Add in glimepiride. Sulphonylureas would usually be used as a second-line treatment in addition to metformin. However, the patient has already previously been on a sulphonylurea which was stopped due to an episode of collapse. It is therefore unlikely that a sulphonylurea would be trialled again due to the risk of hypoglycaemia. D: Add in nocturnal isophane insulin. The addition of insulin to the patient's current dose of metformin may be the best way to improve his HbA1c. The most common way to do this is to introduce a once-daily, bedtime injection of long-acting insulin to be given in addition to the patient's current oral hypoglycaemic agents (for example, Humulin I). However, the implication in this question is that the patient has previously had a problem with hypoglycaemia. Insulin should therefore be avoided unless absolutely necessary. E: Increase metformin to 1g bd. It is very unlikely that the patient will reach the target HbA1c of 7.5% or lower through monotherapy, and increasing the dose of metformin further is more likely to result in GI side effects.

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with palpitations, anxiety, and heat intolerance. On examination, she has a small, smooth goitre on palpation of her neck. Her blood pressure (BP) is 122/72 mmHg, while her pulse is 88 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is a fine tremor at rest and she has sweaty palms. Urea and electrolytes are unremarkable. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is < 0.01, and both her T4 and T3 are elevated. Thyroid scanning reveals a uniformly increased uptake of technetium. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis has a female:male ratio of 10:1 in the UK and affects 2% of the female population. Graves' disease is the commonest cause of thyrotoxicosis. It is associated with uniformly increased uptake on thyroid scanning. Treatment involves a period of block-replace therapy with carbimazole and thyroxine; this is followed in some patients by remission. In others the condition recurs and radioiodine therapy is the treatment of choice.  E: Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is associated with hypothyroidism and decreased uptake on the technetium scan, rather than thyrotoxicosis. B: Subacute thyroiditis. Subacute thyroiditis is associated with symptoms of hyperthyroidism, although other symptoms include a tender goitre and a short, flu-like illness, neither of which are reported here. Anti-thyroid drugs are not used in therapy; non-steroidals or a short course of prednisolone may be required. C: Toxic adenoma. The fact that there is a small, smooth goitre and uniform technetium uptake rules out a toxic adenoma. D: Toxic multi-nodular goitre. Toxic multinodular goitre is associated with a non-smooth goitre, thyrotoxicosis and patchy increased uptake on the technetium scan.

questions.question: A 23-year-old final year medical student presents to the student health service complaining of increased hairiness and trouble with acne. Her periods are erratic and she is an intermittent user of the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, her body mass index is 31 and her blood pressure is mildly elevated at 145/89 mmHg. She has slight thinning of the hair on the front of her head, increased hair around her moustache and beard line, and hair around her nipples and lower abdomen.  Investigations: LH/FSH ratio: Increased Testosterone level: 5 nmol/l (Normal: 1-2.5 nmol/L)  Which of the following is the investigation most likely to confirm the diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: This patient's clinical picture is suggestive of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), and transvaginal ultrasound is said to have 91% diagnostic sensitivity for the condition in experienced hands. As per Rotterdam criteria, the presence of 12 or more follicular cysts in both ovaries measuring 2 to 9 mm and increased ovarian stroma is sufficient to make the diagnosis. Cyproterone acetate is useful for suppression of ovarian androgens, and electrolysis is useful for reducing hirsutism. Metformin increases insulin sensitivity, and therefore has positive effects on associated metabolic features and helps restore ovulatory function. Weight loss is, however, the gold-standard treatment for PCOS and improves ovulation, androgen levels, hirsutism and metabolic features associated with insulin resistance. A loss in weight of only 5% reduces hirsutism by up to 40%.  C: 17-OH progesterone levels. This test is used as screening for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Females with severe CAH due to deficiencies of 21-hydroxylase, 11-beta-hydroxylase or 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase have ambiguous genitalia at birth. Females with mild 21-hydroxylase deficiency are identified later in childhood because of precocious pubic hair, clitoromegaly or both. Females with still milder deficiencies may present in adolescence or adulthood with oligomenorrhea, hirsutism and/or infertility. Our case could phenotypically resemble non-classic adrenal hyperplasia, although the biochemical profile and the excess weight point towards PCOS. B: Pituitary MRI. This would be the investigation of choice if a pituitary adenoma was suspected as a cause of amenorrhea. In that case, however, FSH and LH would be suppressed. D: Adrenal ultrasound scan. Adrenocortical carcinomas are uncommon malignancies. Physical examination findings in patients with hormonally active adrenal carcinomas include Virilisation, Cushing syndrome, Feminization. The imaging of choice is dedicated MRI of the adrenal glands. E: Karyotyping. Karyotyping is performed when a genetic cause for primary ovarian insufficiency is suspected, such as fragile X mutation.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to the clinic for review. She has problems with hirsutism, acne affecting her face and upper chest and irregular periods. She feels that she went through puberty earlier than her peers at the age of 10.5 years old. There is no medication history of note and no other past medical history. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 122/72 mmHg and a pulse of 72 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 25 kg/m2 There is hairiness affecting the moustache and beard lines, hair affecting the upper chest and a number of boils and pustules consistent with acne.  Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb): 131 g/l White cell count (WCC): 8.9 x 10^9/L Platelets (PLT): 188 x 10^9/l Sodium (Na+): 137 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.3 mmol/l Creatinine: 90 µmol/L Glucose: 4.8 mmol/L Testosterone: 7 nmol/l 17 OH-progesterone: 20 nmol/L (elevated)  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Unlike classical CAH, which is associated with salt wasting, non-classical CAH is associated with virilisation without salt wasting. The most common form is 21-hydroxylase deficiency which leads to raised levels of testosterone and 17 OH-progesterone. If fertility is desired, then ovulation induction is the treatment of choice. If an improvement in symptoms of hirsutism is needed, then anti-androgens are the treatment of choice.  C: Polycystic ovarian syndrome. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is diagnosed if patients have irregular periods, high levels of testosterone and hirsutism. All of those are present in this case. However, the elevated levels of progesterone in this case make the diagnosis unlikely. A: Adrenal tumour. Adrenal tumours are usually associated with other features of hyperadrenalism such as hypertension, hyperglycaemia and weight gain. Isolated hirsutism is rare in patients with an adrenal tumour. D: Testicular feminisation. Testicular feminisation is not associated with hirsutism. Patients are genetically male but have female sexual characteristics. Patients will have undescended testes which can be found on ultrasound or can cause hernias when patients reach puberty. Diagnosis in confirmed through genetic screening. E: Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is not associated with hirsutism. It is a genetic condition where women are completely or partly missing an X chromosome. They are often of short stature, with a webbed neck and low-set ears.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for an annual review. She has a background of polycystic kidney disease and chronic kidney disease (CKD) and is on the waiting list for a kidney transplant. She reports having intermittent abdominal pain and generalised aches over the past two weeks and feels thirsty. Her routine bloods reveal the following:  Investigation | 6 months previously | Results now Haemoglobin (Hb) | 95 g/l | 92 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.2x10^9/L | 8.7x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 254x10^9/L | 231x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139 mmol/L | 137 mmol/L Potassium (K) | 5.7 mmol/L | 5.6 mmol/L Urea | 9.2 mmol/L | 9.4 mmol/L Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 9.4 pmol/L | 9.9 pmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 334 µmol/L | 365 µmol/L Calcium (Ca2+) | 2.4 mmol/L | 3.1 mmol/L  What condition has this patient developed, which would explain the calcium level now?
questions.explanation: Persistent secondary hyperparathyroidism, where there is a raised parathyroid hormone (PTH) level, leading to hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands, is likely here. A persistently raised phosphate level, which occurs in chronic kidney disease (CKD), resets the calcium sensitivity of the parathyroid gland; therefore, even after the calcium level has normalised, there is continued secretion of PTH, which causes hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia causes symptoms of increased thirst, abdominal pain and generalised aches and pains, which are seen in this patient's presentation.  B: Primary hyperparathyroidism. Primary hyperparathyroidism is typically caused by a parathyroid adenoma which produces PTH, leading to hypercalcaemia. In the context of CKD and a persistently raised PTH level, it is more likely that this patient has tertiary hyperparathyroidism, where a persistently raised PTH level has led to hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands. A: Hypoparathyroidism. In hypoparathyroidism, there is an inadequate amount of PTH released in the blood and this causes hypocalcaemia. By contrast, this patient demonstrates elevated levels of PTH. One cause of this is damage to the parathyroid glands during neck surgery, such as during thyroidectomy. C: Pseudohypoparathyroidism. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is a rare condition where there is resistance to PTH. The PTH level will be raised, and the patient will have hypocalcaemia. D: Secondary hyperparathyroidism. This patient had secondary hyperparathyroidism six months previously. This occurs when persistently low calcium levels cause a persistently high PTH level and is typically associated with CKD.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman presents to the clinic with polyuria, polydipsia and lethargy. She had undergone a total thyroidectomy some 2 years previously. On examination her BP is 148/89 mmHg, her pulse 80/min and regular. She has a neck scar consistent with thyroidectomy.  Investigations: Haemoglobin: 121 g/l White cell count (WCC): 7.3 x 10^9/L Platelets: 201 x 10^9/L Sodium (Na+): 139 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 4.3 mmol/l Creatinine: 155 µmol/L Corrected Ca2+: 2.9 mmol/l PTH: 10.1 pmol/l Glucose: 8.1 mmol/l  Which of the following is the most likely overarching diagnosis in this patient?
options: A. Thyroid carcinoma with new recurrence
questions.explanation: MEN-2 is associated with the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma, hyperparathyroidism and phaeochromocytoma. It is likely that the previous thyroidectomy was due to medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Given that medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN-2a tends to be less aggressive than in 2b, the presence of hypercalcaemia and the fact that the PTH is inappropriately elevated, the most likely diagnosis is one of hyperparathyroidism. The raised blood pressure and evidence of glucose intolerance also raises the possibility of co-existent phaeochromocytoma. Prior to any surgical intervention for hyperparathyroidism it is crucial to rule out phaeochromocytoma as a co-existent diagnosis.  C: MEN-1. MEN-1 is associated with parathyroid adenomas, pituitary adenomas and pancreatic endocrine tumours, but not with phaeochromocytoma. It is not associated with medullary thyroid cancer. A: Thyroid carcinoma with new recurrence. This would not account for the elevated serum calcium seen here. B: Secondary hyperparathyroidism. This is essentially ruled out by the patient's renal function, which is only mildly abnormal, probably as a result of dehydration. D: MEN-2b. MEN-2b is associated with a marfanoid habitus, not reported here as part of the scenario.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) for a 10 week early pregnancy check. She complains of mild lethargy and he checks some thyroid function tests. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is 0.3 mU/L (normal range: 0.4-5 mU/l) and free thyroxine (T4) is 27 pmol/L (normal range: 10-22 pmol/l). He diagnoses thyrotoxicosis and refers her to you for an opinion. What is the best next management step for this patient?
options: E. Refer for thyroid uptake scan
questions.explanation: This patient has no symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, with a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level just below the normal range and a thyroxine (T4) just above the normal range. It is a feature of normal pregnancy that triiodothyronine (T3) and T4 levels show a slight increase in the first trimester due to human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG) stimulation. TSH may be mildly suppressed in up to 13.5% of pregnancies during the first trimester, and this is considered a normal variant. Thyroid-binding globulin has a twofold increase in concentration during pregnancy as a result of reduced hepatic clearance and increased synthesis under oestrogen stimulus. The rise plateaus out at week 20 and then begins to fall in the postpartum period. When there are TSH receptor antibodies present at high concentration they may cross the placenta.  D: Refer for radioiodine. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because of the risk of causing hypothyroidism in the unborn child. B: Start carbimazole therapy. Carbimazole is used for treating bona fide thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy, and is used late in pregnancy because of potential risks of propylthiouracil and maternal hepatotoxicity. C: Start propylthiouracil therapy. Propylthiouracil is used for treating thyrotoxicosis in early pregnancy, but in this case the abnormal TFTs are likely to be related to normal physiology. E: Refer for thyroid uptake scan. This won't inform management in this case, and isotope scanning is avoided if possible in pregnancy.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-month history of headache and visual disturbance. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a pituitary adenoma. Baseline pituitary function tests were normal, except serum prolactin level of 15 000 mu/l (<450 mu/l) Unfortunately, her symptoms failed to respond to both bromocriptine and cabergoline. Therefore, trans-sphenoidal surgery (TSS) was organised and undertaken successfully. However, in the first 6 hours post-surgery, her urine output was 2.5 litres. Otherwise, she was well, with no particular symptoms or complications. Urgent biochemical tests were performed.  Results are shown below: Plasma osmolality: 295 mOsmol/kg Urine osmolality: 300 mosmol/kg Sodium (Na+): 147 mmol/L Potassium (K+): 5.0 mmol/L Urea: 7.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr): 105 µmol/L Glucose: 5.8 mmol/l 0900 h cortisol: 400 nmol/L  What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
options: A. Encourage the patient to drink as much as they want
B. Fluid restriction of up to 1000 ml per day
E. IV desmopressin whilst matching fluid output with appropriate replacement
questions.explanation: DI post-pituitary surgery is very common. All patients should be monitored for signs of DI, such as urine output of >800 ml/h over four consecutive hours. The symptom of thirst is unusual. Urgent paired osmolality and electrolytes should be requested if there is any suspicion of DI. Plasma osmolality of > 285 mOsmol/kg, with paired urine osmolality of <500 mosmol/kg, suggests DI. This may settle a few days after surgery though, so in the initial period, ensuring adequate fluid replacement is reasonable, but many patients may also need short-term use of desmopressin. Initially, this should IV as nasal absorption can be variable immediately post trans-sphenoidal surgery. Only some patients will require long-term DDAVP replacement.  C: Intravenous (IV) hydrocortisone 200 mg. Hydrocortisone is not the treatment of diabetes insipidus (DI). She does not have Addison's disease because there would be hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypercalcaemia. Symptoms of Addison's disease would include hypotension, syncope, severe vomiting and diarrhoea, resulting in dehydration. A: Encourage the patient to drink as much as they want. To ensure adequate fluid replacement is important initially; encouraging the patient to drink as much as they want is not necessarily keeping a close monitor of urine output as patients may not drink enough. B: Fluid restriction of up to 1000 ml per day. Fluid restriction would not be appropriate; dehydration may ensue. D: Immediate intranasal desmpressin (DDAVP). Only some patients will require long-term DDAVP replacement for DI post-pituitary surgery. Use of DDAVP in the short term may be of value if the patient is unable to keep up with losses, although this should be reassessed.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman presents to the First Seizure Clinic. She is accompanied by her community psychiatric nurse. The nurse provides a witness account of the attacks. Each episode has occurred in the community day hospital. The patient would fall to the floor screaming. She would then thrash around both her arms followed by her legs. During the episodes, she is unresponsive, holding her eyes tightly shut. Afterwards, she is able to converse with staff in the centre. She has never injured herself, but often complains of headache post-event. The patient claims to have no memory of events. Systems enquiry reveals no other symptoms. Past medical history includes schizophrenia, well controlled on depot chlorpromazine. She is a lifetime smoker with mild airways disease. Physical examination reveals tar staining of fingers only. Investigations: Toxicology screen Negative; Interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) Formal report: 'Minor slowing of alpha waves, with increased voltage theta activity and diffuse fast activity'; Serum prolactin 900 u/ml (Normal 59-619 u/ml). You reassure her that the seizures are unlikely to cause significant harm. What other step would you advise?
questions.explanation: The differentiation of true seizures from psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (NES) is challenging. It is usually detailed history from the patient and a witness, rather than laboratory testing, that will give the diagnosis. However, the gold standard investigation to confirm diagnosis is video-EEG recording of habitual events. In this scenario the story is highly suggestive of NES. Pointers to a 'non-organic' aetiology include rapid post-ictal recovery, bizarre limb movements and eye clenching, attacks in public places and lack of injury. Candidates should not be distracted by the interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) and prolactin results. The use of interictal EEG, especially in late-onset epilepsy, is limited by poor sensitivity and, to some degree, specificity. In this case the abnormalities detected would be in keeping with typical anti-psychotic use. In this case other causes of raised prolactin which may influence the choice of anti-psychotic medication, namely pregnancy, should be excluded. D: Lumbar puncture. There are no indications of an infective or inflammatory cause for these episodes, meaning that lumbar puncture is not of value here. B: MRI pituitary fossa. The elevation in prolactin seen here is very modest, and MRI of the pituitary risks diagnostic confusion because of identification of an abnormality which may have nothing to do with the current presentation. C: Dynamic pituitary function testing. Given the very modest increase in prolactin and absence of symptoms of pituitary dysfunction, dynamic pituitary function testing isn't indicated. E: Commence sodium valproate. Given that these are most likely non-epileptic seizures, there is no value in using sodium valproate in this patient. It may actually lead to adverse effects on her behaviour in the context of previous psychiatric illness.

questions.question: A 45-year-old teacher presents with a tingling sensation in the fingers of both hands, especially the thumb and index fingers, which is worse at night and disturbs his sleep. He also describes aching pain in his forearms, exacerbated by carrying heavy objects. He describes polydipsia and generalised aches and pains, and his wife has commented that he must have put on weight as his wedding ring no longer fits. Clinical examination confirms reproducible sensory loss to pinprick in both hands, particularly over the thumb, index and middle fingers, but is otherwise unremarkable. His blood pressure is 150/96 mmHg. His general practitioner has recently performed a fasting glucose which was 8.4 mmol/l. You suspect he has carpal tunnel syndrome and arrange nerve conduction studies. He has abnormal facial features, including macroglossia and prognathism. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step in his management?
options: C. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa
questions.explanation: This man has presented with bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome which, in association with macroglossia, prognathism, frontal bossing, enlarged hands, arthralgia, diabetes and hypertension (although a one-off measurement), strongly suggests a diagnosis of acromegaly. This is a rare disease, usually presenting at 30-50 years, and is due to hypersecretion of GH from a pituitary tumour. Random GH measurement may show increased secretion, but levels vary diurnally and are therefore not diagnostic. IGF-1 in contrast has a long half life and is directly correlated to growth hormone levels. It can therefore be used as an initial screen and followed later with an OGTT. The OGTT is definitive, with samples collected for glucose and GH at intervals of 30 minutes (0-150 minutes). Normally, GH is suppressed, but not in acromegaly (levels may rise). A: Random growth hormone (GH) level. GH levels display diurnal variation, and therefore a random level may be falsely normal or low. C: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa. The first step in the management is to confirm the GH excess via OGTT. Subsequently, MRI/computed tomography (CT) of the pituitary is used to visualise the tumour and trans-sphenoidal surgery is usually the treatment of choice. Irradiation is used in older patients or following failed surgery. If the OGTT confirms the diagnosis, then MRI/CT plus surgery and investigation/management of other complications (visual fields, pituitary function, echocardiogram, etc.) is indicated. D: Pituitary function tests. Pituitary function tests are indicated once the diagnosis of acromegaly is confirmed. A full pituitary profile would include testing the thyroid, gonadal and adrenal axis (thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine (fT4), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinising hormone (LH), testosterone, cortisol). E: Visual field testing. Formal visual field assessment is indicated once the presence of an adenoma is confirmed on MRI pituitary.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man with a history of hypothyroidism managed with thyroxine replacement comes to the clinic for review. He has increasing tiredness. Other symptoms of note include depression and one episode of renal colic. Investigations: TSH 2.1 mu/L (0.17-3.2), Haemoglobin 113 g/l (135-175), WCC 4.2 x 10^9/L (4-11), Na+ 139 mmol/L (135-145), K+ 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Creatinine 237 µmol/L (50-120), Corrected Ca2+ 2.10 mmol/L (2.20-2.60), 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol 10 ng/L (20-50), PTH 13 pmol/L (1-6). Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?
questions.explanation: This man has a PTH just above twice the normal level and chronic kidney disease. Management of his secondary hyperparathyroidism involves appropriate vitamin D replacement, normally given twice per week. Surgery may be considered if parathyroidism does not respond to medical management. B: Ergocalciferol. This is less effective in managing hyperparathyroidism, because of defective hydroxylation of vitamin D in the kidney. C: Cinacalcet. Cinacalcet is only used for managing symptomatic hyperparathyroidism in patients with chronic kidney disease on renal replacement therapy or in those who are unable to undergo surgery. D: Sevelamer. Sevelamer is a phosphate binder used for managing hyperphosphataemia in patients with chronic renal impairment. E: Parathyroidectomy. Parathyroidectomy is the next step in patients who fail to respond to medical intervention for hyperparathyroidism.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with an ulcer over the left medial malleolus on her left leg. She has a history of obesity and hypertension, and has been recently diagnosed with type II diabetes. On examination, she has obvious bilateral varicose veins; there is no evidence of diabetic neuropathy. Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin 140 g/l, WCC 6.1 x 10^9/L, Platelets 310 x 10^9/L, Na+ 140 mmol/L, K+ 5.0 mmol/L, Creatinine 140 µmol/L, Glucose 8.1 mmol/L, ABPI 0.9. Which of the following options offers the best chance for complete healing of the ulcer?
questions.explanation: The shallow pre tibial lesion with exudate is consistent with venous ulceration. Multi-layer bandaging is most useful in reducing lower limb oedema and improving the chances of healing of venous ulcers. It is also crucial for patients to rest and keep the leg up where possible. An ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) measurement is essential before beginning bandaging, as if there is significant arterial insufficiency, blood supply to the lower limb may be threatened. An ABPI of 0.8 has become a pivotal figure in the management of leg ulceration, defining the cut-off point for high-compression bandaging, and is frequently taken as indicating the presence of a so-called 'mixed ulcer'. A: Lower limb angioplasty. Lower limb angioplasty will improve arterial supply and has no significant impact on venous insufficiency. C: Maggot therapy. Although maggot therapy may be useful for debridement, it isn't the primary driver for healing of venous ulcers. D: Surgical debridement. Surgical debridement is only useful where there is significant necrotic tissue that risks extensive soft tissue infection. E: Fucidin ointment. Antibiotic ointment has not been shown to drive faster healing of venous ulcers.

questions.question: You review a 28-year-old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis in the thyroid clinic. She has been stable on 100 µg of thyroxine for the past few years and recent TSH was measured at 2.9 mU/l some 6 months ago (normal range 0.4-5). The reason for this appointment is that she is 12 weeks pregnant. How would you manage her thyroxine therapy during this pregnancy?
options: A. Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 100 mcg
B. Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 25-50 mcg
C. Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 25 mcg
D. Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 50 mcg
E. Keep her thyroxine dose unchanged
questions.explanation: In patients already on thyroxine when they become pregnant, thyroid function tests should be assessed at 6-8 weeks' gestation and then at 16-20 and 28-32 weeks. Average increase in thyroxine requirements is 25-50 µg, and the increased need for thyroxine ceases immediately after delivery. In patients with positive thyroid autoantibodies there is a twofold increased risk of spontaneous abortion. In patients who are suboptimally treated for hypothyroidism there is a 21% risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension. Maternal hypothyroidism is also associated with increased risk of pregnancy-induced anaemia and postpartum haemorrhage; for these reasons it is crucial that patients with hypothyroidism are followed up appropriately during pregnancy. TSH should be monitored, and guidelines suggest aiming to keep TSH below 3.0. D: Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 50 mcg. Even if this patient wasn't pregnant, halving her thyroxine dose risks symptomatic hypothyroidism. A: Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 100 mcg. This runs the risk of symptomatic hyperthyroidism in pregnancy, increasing the risk of spontaneous abortion. C: Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 25 mcg. Thyroid hormone requirements increase by an average of 30% in pregnancy; as such, this is not the appropriate course of action. E: Keep her thyroxine dose unchanged. The 30% increase in thyroid hormone requirements in pregnancy will mean this patient slips into hypothyroidism as her pregnancy progresses.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with a history of type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease and depression is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion which his partner has noticed over the past two to three weeks. Medications include metformin, sitagliptin, bendroflumethiazide, lisinopril and fluoxetine. On examination, his blood pressure is 138/72 mmHg and pulse is 70 bpm and regular. He appears to be euvolaemic. He is mildly confused when you review him. Investigations: Hb 119 g/l, WCC 5.6 x 10^9/L, PLT 281 x 10^9/L, CRP 12 mg/l, Na+ 128 mmol/L, K+ 4.3 mmol/l, Creatinine 100 μmol/l, Glucose 6.7 mmol/l. His chest X-ray is normal. Which of the following is the best way to manage this patient's hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation: This patient has hyponatraemia, which is commonly seen in conjunction with long-term use of thiazide diuretics. Since his blood pressure is relatively well controlled, and there is no sign of fluid overload on the chest x-ray, there are therefore likely to be no adverse consequences of discontinuing treatment with bendroflumethiazide. Taking this step will improve the chances of fluid restriction correcting his serum sodium levels over subsequent days. A: 3% saline infusion. 3% saline is reserved for the treatment of life-threatening hyponatraemia. In this situation, fluid replacement must happen in a high dependency setting, so that it can be tightly controlled, with regular monitoring of serum sodium levels. B: Demeclocycline. Demeclocycline, which induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, is the most appropriate option in the event that the patient fails to respond to fluid restriction alone with respect to his serum sodium level. C: Intravenous furosemide. The chest x-ray is normal. Furosemide is usually only considered appropriate for treatment of hyponatraemia where there is salt and water overload, eg in cardiac failure. D: Sodium chloride (NaCl) tablets. Salt tablets are unpleasant to take and may negatively impact on this patient's blood pressure. They are therefore not an appropriate option here.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with central chest pain suspicious of angina. She has a history of resistant hypertension, currently managed by her GP with Ramipril, amlodipine and indapamide. She tells you that her mother suffered from Conn syndrome and she is concerned she may have the same problem. Her BP is 155/95 pulse is 84 and regular. Her BMI is 22. What abnormality would you expect to find in the patient's workup if she was suffering from Conn syndrome?
questions.explanation: Conn syndrome, a cause of secondary hypertension, is usually due to an aldosterone-secreting adenoma which leads to hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism. The rule of thumb is that in patients prescribed an ACE inhibitor, hypokalaemia is highly suggestive of the condition. It was previously thought that adrenal adenomas were responsible for the majority of cases of hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism, but it's now realised that the split is much more 50:50. Aldosterone has an action on the distal tubule of the kidney to increase sodium resorption and enhance potassium and hydrogen ion loss. Renin levels are suppressed and do not rise with an upright posture. Medical treatment includes a low-sodium diet with an aldosterone receptor antagonist (spironolactone). Surgical therapy is usually indicated after localisation of adenoma. C: Metabolic acidosis. Mineralocorticoid excess leads to presentation with elevated bicarbonate and a metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis. A: Hyponatraemia. Hyponatraemia is associated with adrenal insufficiency, not with hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism. B: Elevated serum creatinine. This patient may yet develop intrinsic renal damage as a result of chronic hypertension, and thus creatinine values may well be normal. E: Hypernatraemia. Although serum sodium may well be at the upper end of the normal range, frank hypernatraemia is often not seen in patients with Conn syndrome.

questions.question: An 18-year-old girl with a history of anorexia presents to her General Practitioner with nausea and abdominal pain. Investigations: Urea 20 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/L, Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 3.64 mmol/L, Plasma parathyroid hormone (PTH) 9.8 pmol/l (Normal 0.9-5.4). Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride is started. Following fluid resuscitation, what would be the next step in management?
options: D. Referral for admission to inpatient Psychiatry Unit
questions.explanation: The initial diagnosis here is hypercalcaemia, which can cause a severe gastrointestinal disturbance. Serum levels of > 3.5 mmol/l are associated with cardiac arrhythmias, coma and pancreatitis, and urgent treatment is required. The raised PTH level suggests that the elevated Ca2+ level is secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism, and in a young woman, the most likely cause would be parathyroid adenoma. Hypercalcaemia is often associated with severe dehydration which increases the risk of renal damage. Following aggressive rehydration to prevent renal tubular damage, the bisphosphonate pamidronate is the treatment of choice to reduce osteoclastic activity, and hence bone resorption of Ca2+. A: Emergency surgery. Emergency surgery is only required in cases of resistant hypercalcaemia not responding to intravenous fluids and pamidronate. Indications for elective parathyroid surgery include the following: serum Ca2+ level > 0.25 mmol/l above the upper limit of normal, marked hypercalciuria (> 400 mg/day) or renal stones, creatinine clearance <30% of normal, marked bone density reduction with a T-score < 2.5 at any site, age < 50 years (if the problem is left untreated, many of these younger patients eventually develop complications of primary hyperparathyroidism), a patient for whom surveillance and follow-up are difficult or impossible. B: Oral prednisolone. This can be used in the management of hypercalcaemia due to sarcoid or lymphomas. In this case, the cause of hypercalcaemia is most likely primary hyperparathyroidism due to an adenoma or gland hyperplasia. D: Referral for admission to inpatient Psychiatry Unit. Although this patient has a history of anorexia, which can present with electrolyte abnormalities, this patient only presents with isolated hypercalcaemia. As this patient also has a raised PTH level, this is unlikely to be due to anorexia, and therefore, inpatient Psychiatry Unit admission is not an appropriate course of action. E: Subcutaneous calcitonin. Calcitonin reduces Ca2+ levels via inhibition of osteoclastic activity in bone and inhibition of renal tubular cell reabsorption of Ca2+ and phosphate, allowing these to be excreted in the urine. It can be used as first-line, along with fluids and bisphosphonates, in cases of hypercalcaemia due to multiple myeloma or cancer.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with frequent headaches, excessive sweating, reduction in peripheral vision, deepening of her voice and amenorrhoea. She has also noticed a prominence of her lower jaw. On examination, there is mild hirsutism. Visual tests show bitemporal hemianopia. Investigations reveal a fasting blood glucose of 7.8 mmol/L and a 2 hour post-prandial value of 12.5 mmol/l. Prolactin is elevated at 1000. Her blood pressure (BP) is elevated at 165/99 mmHg. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows a 20 mm pituitary adenoma. What would be the most appropriate first line management in this case?
options: A. Cabergoline followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery
C. External radiotherapy followed by octreotide
D. Somatostatin analogue followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery
E. Pegvisomant in combination with a somatostatin analogue
questions.explanation: Tumor resection via transsphenoidal surgery is the optimal primary treatment in most patients. Data supporting use of endoscopic over microscopic approaches remain incomplete and further comparative outcome studies are needed before one approach can be recommended over the other. Currently, the choice of technique depends on neurosurgeon expertise and preference. Craniotomy is very rarely indicated in patients with acromegaly. Intraoperative MRI and other techniques to aid in intraoperative visualization of tumor remnants remain investigational. C: External radiotherapy followed by octreotide. Radiotherapy is not the first-line treatment of choice in patients with a pituitary adenoma and has been shown to reduce prolactin levels in only approximately 25% of patients. There is also the risk of hypopituitarism as well as localised neurological damage. Radiotherapy can be considered further down the line if the patient is hypersecretory and if the tumour is not fully resected. Octreotide can be used to treat patients with acromegaly, but again this option would not be the first-line treatment. A: Cabergoline followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery. Cabergoline is a very effective treatment for prolactinoma. This patient has a raised prolactin level, but this is likely to be due to pressure effect rather than as a result of a primary prolactinoma. Regardless, carbegoline is likely to be given in isolation rather than with trans-sphenoidal surgery. D: Somatostatin analogue followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery. Medical therapy is recommended for patients who do not achieve biochemical control after surgery. Primary medical therapy is reserved for those with contraindication to or who refuse surgery, and may be considered in select patients considered at poor risk for good outcomes and surgical success. Randomized studies suggest improvement in postoperative remission after pretreatment with SRL for 3-6 months. However, data are conflicting and, in many instances, results were not sustained during long-term follow-up. E: Pegvisomant in combination with a somatostatin analogue. Pegvisomant and somatostatins are commonly used individually in clinical practice, but are only licensed for use in combination in patients where there is an effective response with somatostatin analogues alone.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 2-week history of lower leg pain, particularly his left leg. His legs feel heavy when he walks, and his left ankle is more swollen than usual. Despite taking shorter walks, the pain has persisted and is only relieved on elevation. His past medical history includes hypertension, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. The ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is 0.9. His lower limbs are examined and there is a noticeable lesion on his left lower leg. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient has evidence of venous insufficiency, given the increased pigment deposition around the lower leg and foot, with venous eczema. There is a moderately-sized venous ulcer with less well-defined margins on the lower aspect of the leg. Usually, the medial malleolus is most commonly affected. A history of aching lower legs that feel heavy and swollen with the improvement of symptoms is also suggestive of chronic venous insufficiency and venous ulcer development. Provided the ABPI is 0.8 or above, compression bandaging can be safely applied to the affected limb(s). This is one of the most effective ways of treating venous ulceration. C: Topical corticosteroids. Topical corticosteroids are used in the management of some cases of dermatitis and pyoderma gangrenosum. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare skin disorder characterised by a painful nodule that rapidly progresses to a large, ulcerative lesion. It is associated with autoimmune conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. A classical presentation is a lesion with purple-coloured outer edges. This is not seen here, making pyoderma gangrenosum a less likely diagnosis. B: Oral flucloxacillin. Oral flucloxacillin is used in the first-line treatment of cellulitis. Evidence of cellulitis includes lower limb erythema, swelling, pain and fever. The mild redness that can be seen surrounding this patient's ulcer most likely represents inflammation and venous eczema rather than an infective process. D: Topical fusidic acid. Topical fusidic acid is used in the treatment of infective lesions. However, the lack of cellulitic changes and signs of chronic venous insufficiency make venous ulceration the more likely diagnosis. E: Urgent angioplasty. Urgent angioplasty is the treatment of choice for critical limb ischaemia, which is characterised by a cold, pale, pulseless, painful limb with paraesthesia and paralysis. Arterial ulceration usually appears more defined, with punched-out edges. Although this patient has a history of smoking, which increases the likelihood for peripheral vascular disease, the appearance of the ulcer, combined with the presentation, makes arterial disease less likely. Pain relieved on elevation is more typical of venous insufficiency than arterial.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with a history of 'funny turns' over the last two years. She complains of intermittent episodes of feeling sweaty and faint and having double vision. She tells you that she often feels better after a strong cup of tea with three sugars. She has no medical history of note and is taking no tablets. Her mother had diabetes mellitus and her father had epilepsy. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol occasionally. Her examination is completely normal. Investigations reveal the following: Urea 6.8 mmol/l, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.93 mmol/l, Phosphate (PO43-) 0.84 mmol/l, Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l, Creatinine (Cr) 84µmol/l, Glucose 5.3 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An insulinoma should be suspected in this patient, given her 2-year history of 'funny turns' and the fact that she feels better after a strong cup of tea. Furthermore the blood tests reveal an elevated calcium, raising the suspicion of associated hyperparathyroidism. Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN)-1 should be suspected here, which may be a combination of a pituitary tumour (often a macroadenoma), hyperparathyroidism and a pancreatic islet tumour. Of course all these conditions may not necessarily occur at the same point in time. The MEN 1 gene has an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance. Any individual with a relative with MEN 1 should be screened. Mutational analysis of the coding region has a sensitivity of about 95% in MEN 1 patients. Relatives without the mutation can be reassured and do not require regular screening. Screening includes serum calcium and prolactin in all patients; 90% of MEN 1 patients present with hypercalcaemia. A: Petit mal epilepsy. This is a common type of epilepsy syndrome presenting in children in the first decade. A seizure is characterised by a brief staring episode with behavioural arrest. A 3 Hz spike-and-slow-wave discharge on electroencephalogram (EEG) is generally associated with this seizure. B: Recurrent TIAs. Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord or retinal ischaemia, without acute infarction. The duration of symptom/sign is <24 h and resolution is not related to consumption of any food/beverage. D: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Paroxysmal AF (PAF) is defined as an episode of AF that reverts to sinus rhythm spontaneously or with intervention within seven days. Symptoms can be irregular palpitations, shortness of breath, dyspnoea on exertion, a sensation of light-headedness or less commonly fatigue, weakness or generalised malaise. In acute presentations, heart rate is controlled by a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. If spontaneous reversion doesn't occur and there is haemodynamic compromise, electrical cardioversion is considered or, alternatively, pharmacological conversion with flecainide or amiodarone. E: Phaeochromocytoma. Phaechromocytoma are rare catecholamine-secreting tumours occurring in <0.2% of patients with hypertension. Most (about 70%) are sporadic. Classical symptoms are headaches, sweating and tachycardia. Other symptoms include palpitations, tremor, pallor, dyspnoea, generalised weakness, and panic attack-type symptoms. Most common sign is sustained or paroxysmal hypertension. Symptoms usually resolve spontaneously without intervention.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman who has a history of hypertension is operated on by Neurosurgeons for an intracranial haemorrhage. Over the next few days her serum sodium level progressively declines and by the third day has fallen to 118 mmol/l despite fluid restriction to 1 litre per day. Her blood pressure (BP) has maintained steady at 145/85 mmHg. Her chest X-ray is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Urine osmolarity 700 mOsmol/l (Normal 50-1200 mOsmol/l), Urine Sodium (Na+) 80 mmol/L (Normal < 20 mmo/l), Serum Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l (Normal 3.5-5.0 mmol/L). Which of the following fits best with the diagnosis in this patient?
options: B. Secretion of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
questions.explanation: The chest x-ray here is normal, with no signs of fluid overload or tumour. SIADH is well known to occur after head injury, central nervous system (CNS) infection or intracranial haemorrhage. It is associated with hyponatraemia and hypotonic plasma, raised urine osmolality and excessive urinary sodium excretion (often >50 mmol/l). SIADH is often a transient phenomenon and resolves after a few days; in patients who fail to respond to fluid restriction, demeclocycline, which induces partial diabetes insipidus, may be a treatment option. D: Hypovolaemia. The steady maintenance of blood pressure above 140 mmHg systolic effectively rules out significant hypovolaemia. A: Addisonian crisis. Addisonian crisis is associated with significant salt wasting and consequent hypotension, not present here, making Addison's less likely as the underlying cause of her hyponatraemia. C: Cranial diabetes insipidus. Cranial diabetes insipidus is associated with hypernatraemia and hypotension, rather than the picture seen here. E: Fluid overload. Fluid overload is both associated with hyponatraemia and signs of heart failure or peripheral oedema, neither of which is seen in the scenario here.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a three month history of diarrhoea. On examination, he is found to have blood pressure (BP) of 180/100 mmHg. A firm, enlarged thyroid is also noted. On taking his history, the patient mentions that his father had an operation to remove a gland and had a scar on his neck. His uncle also had the same gland removed due to cancer and has also had kidney failure. Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin 110 g/l, WCC 4.0 x 10^9/l, Platelet 450 x 10^9/L, Sodium 135 mmol/L, Potassium 3.5 mmol/L, Creatinine 80 µmol/l, Urea 5.5 mmol/L, Corrected calcium 2.72 mmol/L. What is a possible unifying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: It is important to note that this patient has a thyroid mass, hypertension and hypercalcaemia. MEN 2A is defined by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which causes diarrhoea; pheochromocytoma, which causes hypertension; and hyperparathyroidism caused by parathyroid gland hyperplasia, which causes hypercalcaemia. MEN 2A is a unifying diagnosis for this patient. A: Carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid tumours arise from the enterochromaffin cells in the intestine and the main bronchi and do not usually manifest as thyroid masses. These tumours secrete peptides such as 5-hydroxytryptophan. Carcinoid syndrome is a manifestation of advanced disease and is characterised by facial flushing, diarrhoea and wheezing. B: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 1. MEN 1 affects the parathyroid glands, the pancreatic islets and the anterior pituitary. Associated tumours include lipomas, angiofibromas or those located in the adrenal gland cortex. This patient has a distinct thyroid mass which is not in keeping with MEN 1. D: Phaeochromocytoma. Phaeochromocytoma is an adrenal tumour known to secrete large amounts of catecholamines. It is associated with a variety of symptoms including headache, palpitations, sweating and anxiety. Hypertension, which may be sustained or paroxysmal, is believed to be the most consistent clinical sign. E: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)oma. VIPomas in adults are neuroendocrine islet cell tumours of the pancreas that produce high amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Other secreted hormones may include secreted gastrin and pancreatic polypeptide. Episodic diarrhoea is often the presenting symptom. These presenting symptoms do not fit with this patient's symptoms, making it an unlikely diagnosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with a 2-month history of decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. He has no known past medical history of note and does not take any regular medication. On examination, his vital signs are within normal limits. He is noticeably tall, with pronounced gynaecomastia and sparse body hair. Investigations: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) 45 mlU/mL (2-20 mIU/ml), Luteinising hormone (LH) 130 mlU/ml (1.1-110 mlU/ml), Testosterone 3 nmol/l (10-30 nmol/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is characterised by an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). The condition is associated with primary testicular failure and hypogonadism. Patients with Klinefelter syndrome typically present with small testes, gynaecomastia and sparse body hair. They may also be tall, with weaker muscles, and some patients may have learning disability or behavioural disturbances, particularly in childhood. Laboratory tests show low testosterone levels and elevated LH and FSH levels due to primary testicular failure. A: Androgen insensitivity syndrome. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is a condition characterised by resistance to the action of androgens, resulting in incomplete masculinisation of the external genitalia in individuals with a 46,XY karyotype. AIS typically presents with female external genitalia or ambiguous genitalia in phenotypic females. The presence of gynaecomastia and sparse body hair in this patient is inconsistent with AIS. B: Kallmann syndrome. Kallmann syndrome is a type of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. The condition is characterised by inadequate production of testosterone secondary to hypothalamic dysfunction and failure to produce gonadotrophin-releasing hormone. It is typically associated with low serum testosterone levels and low or normal LH and FSH levels. The presence of elevated LH and FSH levels in this patient makes hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism less likely. D: Leydig cell tumour. Leydig cell tumours are rare and typically present with signs of androgen excess rather than with hypogonadism. Signs and symptoms of Leydig cell tumours include virilisation and precocious puberty. Additionally, Leydig cell tumours usually result in elevated testosterone levels rather than in low levels, as seen in this patient. E: Prader-Willi syndrome. Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disorder with multiple clinical features, including short stature, global developmental delay and hypogonadism. Patients may experience incomplete sexual development, including genital hypoplasia. However, this patient's presentation is not in keeping with Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic. She has had type I diabetes for eight years, and until recently it has been well controlled; however, recently, she has been having numerous hypoglycaemic attacks. These 'hypos' can be at any time of the day and follow no pattern. Her periods are regular. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg with a postural drop of 10 mmHg. She is on a basal-bolus regime, taking insulin eight units three x per day and glargine insulin 15 units at night. Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin 100 g/l, WCC 6.3 x 10^9/L, Platelets 193 x 10^9/L, Sodium 130 mmol/L, Potassium 4.4 mmol/L, Creatinine 100 µmol/L, MCV 93 fl, Urea 8.0 mmol/L. Which of the following is most likely to determine the underlying diagnosis?
options: B. Paired serum and urine osmolality
questions.explanation: Type I diabetes is associated with many autoimmune diseases, including Addison's (primary autoimmune adrenal failure). It commonly presents with weight loss and malaise. In patients with diabetes, it presents more commonly as hypoglycaemia. Hyponatraemia is present in 90% and hyperkalaemia in 65%. A normocytic normochromic anaemia is often present, sometimes with an associated eosinophilia. B: Paired serum and urine osmolality. The presence of unexplained hypoglycaemia in the presence of a low serum sodium steers us more towards adrenal insufficiency, which must be excluded before a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) can be considered. A: Serum ferritin. This patient has normocytic anaemia, which is much more likely to be related to adrenal failure rather than to low iron stores. C: Continuous glucose monitoring. CGM will confirm a diagnosis of unpredictable hypoglycaemia, although won't contribute to elucidating the cause. E: Transferrin saturation. However, haemochromatosis does present with diabetes mellitus and can be associated with adrenal failure, due to the effect of the menstrual cycle it presents in older women, usually post-menopause.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease as a result of long-standing reflux nephropathy goes to her GP complaining of tiredness. She currently takes ramipril and indapamide for hypertension. On examination, her BP is 142/88 mmHg and she looks pale and washed-out. Her pulse is 72 bpm and regular. Investigations: Hb 104 g/L, WCC 5.6 x 10^9/L, PLT 198 x 10^9/L, Na+ 139 mmol/L, K+ 5.2 mmol/L, Creatinine 232 µmol/L, TSH 1.5 U/l (<0.5-4.5), Total T4 45 nmol/l (58-161), Free T4 24 pmol/l (9-27), Total T3 0.8 nmol/L (0.9-2.8). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) deficiency is a non-harmful condition that is either acquired or inherited. The thyroid hormones - thyroxine (T4) and 3,5,3'-triiodothyronine (T3) - circulate in the blood by reversibly binding to carrier proteins. Although only 0.3% or less of T3 and T4 circulates unbound, it is this free hormone fraction that is metabolically active at the tissue and cellular level. The three main proteins that carry the majority (>95%) of thyroid hormones are TBG), transthyretin (TTR, or prealbumin) and albumin. Thyroid hormone binding to TBG is characterised by low capacity but high avidity. Inherited or acquired variations in the concentration and/or affinity of these proteins may produce substantial changes in serum total thyroid hormone levels as measured by commercially available assays. Notably, these changes do not result in illness (i.e. hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism), because the concentration of free thyroid hormones does not change. A deficiency in thyroid hormone-binding proteins is suspected when abnormally low serum total thyroid hormone concentrations are encountered in clinically euthyroid subjects in the presence of normal serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). More specifically, low TBG is suggested because this protein carries the majority of the serum thyroid hormones. Thyroid function tests (TFTs) in patients with TBG deficiency show normal TSH and free T4, but low total T4 and, occasionally, low total T3 serum concentrations. The most important clinical aspect of TBG deficiency states is recognition of these disorders and avoidance of unnecessary and potentially harmful thyroid hormone replacement therapy. D: lodine deficiency. lodine deficiency results in a goitre. In terms of thyroid function tests, it is characterised by low fT4 and raised TSH. sometimes fT3 can be normal/raised because of the increased fT3 to fT4 conversion as a compensatory mechanism. A: Hashimotos's thyroiditis. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition causing hypothyroidism with low fT3 and fT4 and raised TSH. The anti-TPO antibodies are also raised. In this scenario, the thyroid function tests are not in keeping with Hashimoto's. B: Pituitary failure. In cases of pituitary failure resulting in secondary hypothyroidism, the TSH is below the lowest limit of normal, with low fT3 and fT4. Pituitary disorders usually affect first the gonadal axis, then the adrenal axis and lastly the thyroid axis; therefore secondary hypothyroidism would also be associated with symptoms of gonadal and adrenal failure (amenorrhea, hyperpigmentation, nausea and vomiting). C: Sick euthyroid syndrome. Sick euthyroid syndrome is particularly common in patients with chronic kidney disease, and is characterised by small reductions in both free T3 and free T4 and normal or suppressed TSH. It is also seen in the context of severe illness in patients admitted to the ITU, severe sepsis, cardiac and liver failure, end-stage malignancy and starvation. Whether thyroid replacement is of any value in this situation is a subject of continued debate. What persuades us against sick euthyroid syndrome here is the normal free T4 against a background of reduced total T3 and T4, and the lack of a precipitant acute illness.

questions.question: A 21-year-old student with type 1 diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department by her flat-mates. She has been suffering from a cold for a few days. On examination, her GCS is 12, and she has a respiratory rate of 40/min. Finger-prick blood glucose in the department is measured at 38.1 mmol/l and this is confirmed on venous sampling. Arterial blood gases reveal a pH of 7.05 and serum bicarbonate of 12 mmol/l. Electrolytes are abnormal, with potassium of 5.9 mmol/l, urea of 15.5 mmol/L and creatinine of 193 mmol/L. She is 63kg in weight. Which of the following options would represent the most appropriate initial treatment for her?
options: A. 1 litre of normal saline over 8 h
B. 1 litre of normal saline stat
C. 1 litre of Hartmann's over 4 h
D. 1 mmol of sodium bicarbonate/kg IV over 30 min
questions.explanation: This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis, the likely precipitant of which has been her recent respiratory infection. Initial investigations of choice for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include blood for urea, electrolytes and glucose, full blood count, arterial blood gases, blood and urine cultures, chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG). Initial management involves 2 of 1 M saline administered over 2 h unless the patient has cardiovascular or fluid management issues. Potassium administration is set according to serum potassium (intravenous (IV) insulin may result in rapid potassium reduction); the recommended dosage ranges from 40 mmol/L K+ added per litre bag of 1 M/saline if serum potassium is <3 mmol/l, to no potassium added if serum potassium is 6.0 mmol/l or above. Where potassium is <3, management on the ITU where central venous access delivery of potassium can be carried out, is preferred. An IV fixed-rate insulin infusion is also started to combat hyperglycaemia. E: Intubation and ventilation. This patient's GCS is 12, so although she is confused, her conscious level can be monitored for deterioration at this stage. There may be rapid improvement in response to fluid resuscitation and insulin. A: 1 litre of normal saline over 8 h. Patients presenting with DKA may be fluid depleted by up to 5 l. As such, delivering 1 l over 8 h is far too slow an infusion rate. C: 1 litre of Hartmann's over 4 h.
