It's argued that Hartmann's shouldn't be used as initial fluid replacement because it delivers a lactate load, and patients already have a high lactate/pyruvate ratio in DKA. D: 1 mmol of sodium bicarbonate/kg IV over 30 min. At this stage the initial response to aggressive fluid resuscitation and insulin delivered IV should be assessed before commencing sodium bicarbonate. In practice for DKA, sodium bicarbonate is only really considered in the peri-arrest situation.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with thirst, polyuria, and constipation. Her family also feel that she has been depressed over the last few weeks, which is unusual for her. Examination is unremarkable apart from generalised abdominal tenderness and a scar noted on the left breast from a previous lumpectomy for breast carcinoma. Investigations reveal the following: Urea 10.0 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/L, Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 3.84 mmol/L, Plasma parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels 0.8 pmol/L. Which single initial management choice would be most appropriate from the list below?
questions.explanation: The initial diagnosis here is hypercalcaemia, which can cause severe gastrointestinal disturbance. Serum levels >3.5 mmol/l are associated with cardiac arrhythmias, coma and pancreatitis and urgent treatment is required. The low parathyroid hormone precludes parathyroid disease as a cause, and in this age group (particularly with a previous malignancy) metastatic bone disease would be high on a list of differential diagnoses. Hypercalcaemia is often associated with severe dehydration that increases the risk of renal damage. The bisphosphonate pamidronate is the treatment of choice to reduce osteoclast activity and hence bone resorption of calcium, but should always be preceded by aggressive rehydration to prevent renal tubular damage. In the case described here, these would therefore be used as a next step following IV fluids. B: Oral furosemide. In cases of hypercalcaemia, furosemide is not routinely recommended in the Society for Endocrinology Guidelines, and it should only be given with fluid resuscitation if there is evidence of ventricular strain and pulmonary oedema. C: IV steroids. Prednisolone is used to treat hypercalcaemia associated with sarcoid. D: IV pamidronate. Pamindronate is a bisphosphonate used in the acute management of hypercalcaemia after the initial phase of fluid resuscitation; therefore, it would be a good second-line treatment option. E: Denosumab. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It is a RANKL inhibitor and works by inhibiting the osteoclastic activity in bone, thereby preserving the bone mass.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic. He presents with short stature (less than the lower 3rd centile) with his weight being between the 10th and 15th centiles. On examination, he has no pubic hair and pre-pubertal testes. There is no family history and he is currently well apart from a six month history of headaches. Appropriate investigations and imaging studies are arranged for the patient, and the result of the computed tomography (CT) scan of the head shows the presence of a suprasellar calcified cyst with the cyst content having the same density as the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Craniopharyngioma is a slow-growing, calcified cystic tumour arising from the remnants of the craniopharyngeal duct. It compromises 4.2% of all childhood tumours and is slightly more common in males than females. The symptoms develop very slowly and usually manifest once the tumour has attained a diameter of 3 cm. The commonest presentation in young patients is growth failure and delayed puberty. The radiological hallmark of a craniopharyngioma is the presence of a suprasellar calcified cyst, with calcification being more common in children than in adults. Using imaging studies, CT is most useful in demonstrating the calcifications whereas MRI is essential for defining the local anatomy prior to surgical intervention. Surgery is the management of choice and may attempt to resect the tumour in total, or to reduce the size followed by postoperative radiotherapy treatment. C: Low-grade astrocytoma. Astrocytomas commonly present with headaches and seizures, or with other symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. A: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The most common symptom of idiopathic intracranial hypertension is headache, but it should not cause developmental delay. CT of the head may show ventricles that are slightly reduced in size. D: Neurosarcoidosis. Neurosarcoidosis presents with a cranial neuropathy in 60-70%, usually involving the 7th cranial nerve. Aseptic meningitis occurs in around 20%. E: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is also known as superior orbital fissure syndrome. It describes a rare, granulomatous inflammatory process adjacent to the cavernous sinus or within the superior orbital fissure and/or orbital apex. The syndrome manifests as hemicranial or periorbital pain, ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman on long-term therapy for depression has been referred by the Psychiatric Services. She presented acutely via the community psychiatric nurse with increasing drowsiness and confusion. According to her carer, she had complained of increasing thirst and going to the bathroom over the past few days, and appeared to have been drinking more fluids over the past few weeks. Investigations: Sodium (Na+) 156 mmol/l, Urea 20 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 205 µmol/L, Chloride (Cl-) 112 mmol/L, Glucose 6.1 mmol/l, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.6 mmol/L. Which of the following medications is likely to be responsible for this lady's presentation?
questions.explanation: This lady's long history of depression is likely to be related to bipolar disorder, which has resulted in a long-term script for lithium and her presentation with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI), as shown by her hypernatraemia and picture of dehydration on blood testing. Causes of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus include an X-linked inherited disorder, an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, lithium, demeclocycline, chronic renal disease, post-obstructive uropathy, hypercalcaemia and hyperglycaemia. Therapy should only be stopped with the advice of her psychiatrist, although her symptoms are highly unlikely to improve unless the lithium therapy is ceased. Bendroflumethiazide and indomethacin may be useful in nephrogenic DI due to their local action on the kidney in cases that fail to respond to cessation of lithium: because both increase lithium levels they can't be given at the same time. Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a treatment for cranial diabetes insipidus and so is of little value here. B: Fluoxetine. Like paroxetine, fluoxetine is an SSRI and is not associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. A: Paroxetine. Paroxetine is a selective serotonin uptake inhibitor (SSRI), which is rarely associated with the serotonin syndrome but is not associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. D: Amitriptyline. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant which may be associated with syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) rather than diabetes insipidus. E: Chlorpromazine. The main concern with chlorpromazine, a dopamine antagonist, is the development of tardive dyskinesia.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of an eight month history of constant sweating and occasionally being feverish. She found her recent summer holiday to Turkey unbearable and had to return to the UK early. She has also noticed that she has lost weight over the last year, though her appetite remains fine. On examination, she is afebrile but tachycardic. Her palms are sweaty. No goitre is palpable. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E) and liver function tests (LFT) are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Episodic bouts of sweating may be due to hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma or carcinoid. However, a patient reporting night sweats suggests a diagnosis of Hodgkin's disease or tuberculosis. Hodgkin's disease tends to feature localised lymphadenopathy, weight loss, pruritus and fever. Patients with thyrotoxicosis report constant sweating and heat intolerance. There may be no evidence of enlargement of the thyroid gland. Taking her age and sex into account, thyrotoxicosis is the most likely diagnosis. D: Infection undefined organism. Apart from the weight loss and the sweats, there are no other symptoms which would point towards an infection. Moreover, the FBC is normal (no neutrophilia, or lymphocytosis in the case of viral infections). Also, liver function tests are normal, which precludes hepatitis or Epstein-Barr. The natural history of the disease is also too long (8 months). A: Hodgkin's lymphoma. Hodgkin's disease tends to feature localised lymphadenopathy, weight loss, pruritus and fever, splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly. In our case, the physical examination is not in keeping with Hodgkin's lymphoma. B: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Signs and symptoms of low-grade non-Hodgkin's lymphomas are: peripheral adenopathy: painless and slowly progressive; can spontaneously regress; primary extra-nodal involvement and B symptoms: uncommon at presentation; however, common with advanced, malignant transformation or end-stage disease; bone marrow: frequent involvement; may be associated with cytopenias(s); fatigue/weakness more common in advanced-stage disease. In our case, FBC is normal and there is no evidence of lymphadenopathy. E: Phaeochromocytoma. Classically, pheochromocytoma manifests as spells with the following four characteristics: headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, severe hypertension. In our scenario, apart from weight loss and sweating, which are non-specific, there is nothing else pointing towards a diagnosis of phaechromocytoma.

questions.question: You are asked to check the blood results on a 32-year-old man who was admitted earlier in the day on the medical take. He is very overweight and has been admitted with an infective exacerbation of asthma. He is being treated with oral prednisolone 60 mg once a day, four hourly 5 mg salbutamol nebulisers with amoxicillin 500 mgs twice a day and erythromycin 250 mg twice a day. Besides his normal inhalers, he does not take any regular medications. He is a smoker. The team commented that it was very difficult to gain venous access. Investigations reveal the following: Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 6.9 mmol/L, Urea 4.0 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 82 µmol/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 139 mg/L, Glucose 5.8 mmol/l. You visit him on the ward. He is having a nebuliser and reading the newspaper. What is the best course of action?
options: A. Urgent calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% intravenous (iv) followed by insulin/dextrose infusion
B. Urgent electrocardiogram (ECG), followed by calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% iv followed by insulin/dextrose infusion
C. Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample, and hold off further treatment until this result is returned
D. Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available
E. Urgent ECG. Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available in the meantime
questions.explanation: This young man has no recognised reasons for hyperkalaemia. He is not on any medications which would predispose him to high potassium; indeed, his regular salbutamol treatment is likely to give him low serum potassium by driving potassium into the cells. His urea and electrolytes are otherwise normal. His glucose is normal. The most likely cause of the high potassium in this case is either mild haemolysis not picked up in the laboratory, or the long use of a tourniquet during blood taking, leading to relative tissue acidosis when the sample was taken and therefore a high potassium. It is likely to be artefactual. However, it would be prudent to check for evidence of cardiac toxicity which is easy to do with an ECG. It would also be worth rechecking the potassium, and if a blood gas machine is available it may be worth rechecking the potassium locally pending the formal laboratory result. C: Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample, and hold off further treatment until this result is returned. If hyperkalaemia is true, then cardiac toxicity could be fatal; therefore although a repeat sample is need, an urgent ECG should be performed. A: Urgent calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% intravenous (iv) followed by insulin/dextrose infusion. As explained above, it is important to determine whether there is any cardiac toxicity and also to confirm hyperkalaemia. B: Urgent electrocardiogram (ECG), followed by calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% iv followed by insulin/dextrose infusion. Calcium gluconate is given if there are any cardiac electrical changes. The high potassium may be an artefact therefore it is important to check validity. D: Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available. As above, urgent ECG is needed to check for any cardiac toxicity.

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy attends the clinic. He is worried as he has failed to enter puberty. He would like to form relationships with women but at the current time this is impossible. On examination he is 6ft 2 inches in height and has absent secondary sexual hair, a small penis and testes. On further questioning he admits to not having any sense of smell to speak of. Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L, White cell count (WCC) 6.2 x 10^9/L, Platelets 231 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l, Creatinine 100 µmol/L, Testosterone Very low, Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) Low, Luteinizing hormone (LH) Low. Given the likely diagnosis, what appearance would you expect to see on cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)?
questions.explanation: Absent olfactory bulbs, correct. This boy is likely to have Kallmann syndrome, as evidenced by hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and absent sense of smell. Absent olfactory bulbs are present on 75% of MRI scans in these patients. The syndrome results in an isolated gonadotrophin (GNRH) deficiency and, in turn, gonadal deficiencies. This causes loss of libido, loss of secondary sexual hair and amenorrhoea/erectile dysfunction. This patient should be managed with androgen replacement therapy. Fertility can be restored in the majority of patients with either pulsed GNRH or gonadotrophin therapy. Assessment of bone age and bone mineral density is also essential in these patients. A: Normal result. Although with this condition the absence of olfactory bulbs is more common. This is because Kallman syndrome is usually an x-linked mutation in the KAL-1 gene which encodes anosmin-1, causing loss of smell. C: Empty sella. This is more often associated with a defect in the diaphragm and extension into the subarachnoid space (a congenital abnormality), following a pituitary infarction or pituitary tumour treatment. E: Hypertrophied olfactory bulbs. Kallman syndrome is associated with absent, not hypertrophied, olfactory bulbs.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. Over the past year, she has noticed a change in her facial appearance and has been suffering from headaches. Her General Practitioner (GP) has also found it difficult to control her blood pressure and has recently diagnosed her with pre-diabetes. Her blood pressure is 155/88 mmHg; her pulse is 74 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most useful next outpatient investigation?
questions.explanation: The picture here shows prognathism (prominent lower jaw) and widening of the nose, consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. IGF-1 has a long half-life and is elevated in patients with acromegaly. It therefore represents the ideal initial blood test. B: Computed tomography (CT) head. Because of the risk of brain imaging detecting an incidentaloma, a biochemical diagnosis of acromegaly is usually made before proceeding to pituitary imaging. Out of the two options, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred to CT. A: Abdominal ultrasound scan. Ninety-five per cent of cases of acromegaly are related to a pituitary adenoma. An abdominal ultrasound is therefore not a first-line investigation. Even in cases where acromegaly is confirmed and a pituitary scan is negative, an ultrasound scan is unlikely to be sensitive enough to detect a tumour. D: Random growth hormone. Growth hormone release is pulsatile, and growth hormone itself has a very short half-life. This means that a random growth hormone measurement can miss a diagnosis of acromegaly. E: 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Urinary free cortisol is an initial outpatient investigation for Cushing syndrome, characterised by obesity and impaired glucose tolerance, rather than the changes in facial appearance seen here.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with tiredness and loss of libido. This is leading to problems with her relationship. She has had no periods for the past 4 months and has taken three pregnancy tests, all of which have been negative. She takes no medication and currently works as a solicitor. There is a past history of a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 5 years earlier after a return flight to the UK from Australia. She does not have any current plans for pregnancy. On examination, her BP is 122/70 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. Her BMI is 22. Visual fields are normal. Investigations: Haemoglobin 130 g/l, WCC 7.0 x 10^9/L, Platelets 201 x 10^9/L, Sodium 137 mmol/l, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, Creatinine 115 µmol/L, Prolactin 1500 u/l, Pituitary MRI: Micro-adenoma. Which of the following is the optimal way to manage her?
questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists are the intervention of choice for microprolactinoma. A meta-analysis suggested that cabergoline is more efficacious than bromocriptine in normalising prolactin, with a better side effect profile, and it is therefore the treatment of choice for this patient. D: Domperidone. Domperidone is a dopamine antagonist, which is a cause of hyperprolactinaemia. A: Trans-sphenoidal resection. Surgery is not indicated for microprolactinoma unless there is a failure of symptoms to respond to medical intervention or there is significant optic chiasm compression from a macro-adenoma. C: Bromocriptine. Bromocriptine has a slightly less favourable adverse event profile versus cabergoline, but greater evidence exists for safe use in early pregnancy. It is therefore the preferred option in women who are considering starting a family. E: Combined oral contraceptive pill. Combined oral contraceptives are an option for women with a microprolactinoma who don't require the return of fertility, although in this case they are best avoided with the previous history of deep vein thrombosis.

questions.question: A 53-year-old man with type II diabetes attends the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has had diabetes for five years and is currently managed with metformin 1 g twice a day and pioglitazone 30 mg daily. You understand that he suffered a myocardial infarction (MI) while on holiday some five months earlier and has suffered very minor episodes of angina since. He is treated with atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 75 mg, ramipril 10 mg and glyceryl trinate spray, and most recently has had trouble with increasing shortness of breath and peripheral oedema. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 142/80 mmHg. His body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m2. Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin (Hb) 134 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 5.6 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 299 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l, Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/L, Haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%). Which of the following represent the most appropriate management in this case?
options: A. Leave the diabetes therapy unchanged
B. Add a sulphonylurea to the regime
C. Change the pioglitazone to empagliflozin
D. Switch to basal bolus insulin therapy
questions.explanation: This man has a history of ischaemic heart disease and evidence of heart failure. As such, a glitazone is likely to be dangerous with respect to the possibility of worsening his heart failure and increasing the risk of cardiovascular events. For these reasons the pioglitazone should be discontinued. Because his HbA1c is only modestly elevated, a trial of SGLT-2 inhibitor is reasonable, which will control HbA1c and promote modest weight loss, accompanied by a mild diuresis. The class has also now been shown to reduce heart failure, with empagliflozin also having a positive impact on MACE events. A: Leaving therapy unchanged runs the risk of worsening heart failure and fluid retention because of the pioglitazone. B: Adding a sulphonylurea risks increasing the risk of hypoglycaemia for this patient, driving weight gain, and it is not associated with positive cardiovascular outcomes. D: Switching to basal bolus insulin therapy may drive tighter glycaemic control, but it also drives hypoglycaemia and weight gain and may increase the risk of sudden cardiac death because of episodes of severe hypo. E: Without stopping the pioglitazone, it's inappropriate to move straight to adding a GLP-1 agonist.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with ulcerated lesions over both shins. He has a history of type I diabetes mellitus. He has recently lost his job and has poor standards of personal care. He is on multiple daily insulin injections (insulin detemir [rDNA origin] injection as basal insulin and insulin aspart with his meals) and his diabetes control is poor (HbA1c: 79 mmol/mol). His right leg is shown below. Which of the following represents the most appropriate treatment to the non-atrophied areas?
questions.explanation: The image shows shiny pale yellowed lesions with telangiectasia and an erythematous border consistent with necrobiosis lipoidica. Necrobiosis lipoidica is seen in 0.3-1% of patients with diabetes and is more common in females. Around 40-60% of patients with necrobiosis lipoidica have diabetes, and the condition may predate the development of abnormal blood sugar. Treatments with topical steroids, injectable steroids, skin grafting and camouflage creams have been used as therapies. In practice, however, the areas of already atrophied skin respond poorly to steroid therapy. C: Azathioprine, sold under the brand name is an immunosuppressive medication which is used in rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and in kidney transplants to prevent rejection. Common side effects include bone marrow suppression and vomiting. Bone marrow suppression is especially common in people with a genetic deficiency of the enzyme thiopurine S-methyltransferase. Other serious risk factors include an increased risk of lymphoma. Azathioprine is in the purine analogue and anti-metabolite family of medication. It works via 6-thioguanine to disrupt the synthesis of RNA and DNA by cells. B: Oral prednisolone would deteriorate his diabetes control even further. D: This is mainly used in cases of cellulitis which would manifest with an area of erythema accompanied usually by tenderness and increased skin temperature. E: This is used for the treatment of venous ulcers. A venous ulcer tends to occur on the medial side of the leg, typically around the medial malleolus, and is usually shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Venous ulcers are typically 'wet' with a moderate to heavy exudate. The skin surrounding a venous ulcer may be oedematous, and there may be evidence of varicose veins.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with a phaeochromocytoma by the general physicians visits you for a specialist endocrinology appointment. She is on adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine and is awaiting surgery. They are concerned as her calcium is elevated, at 2.75 mmol/l. On examination her blood pressure (BP) is elevated at 148/88 mmHg. You feel a hard mass on the right-hand side of the thyroid. Which test is most important for confirming the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: There is a high index of suspicion that this patient has MEN-2a, and she may well have both parathyroid hyperplasia and medullary thyroid carcinoma. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is the most important diagnosis to confirm, with the pentagastrin test the best way to do this. It measures calcitonin levels at 2 and 5 minutes, however, and a rise in calcitonin is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma. E: PTH may be elevated, but wouldn't confirm or refute an underlying diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma. A: Parathyroid hyperplasia is much commoner than medullary thyroid carcinoma, and it's most important to confirm or refute medullary thyroid carcinoma and hence MEN-2a. C: Ultrasound of the neck is relatively insensitive with respect to identifying small neck masses, and doesn't provide a biochemical diagnosis. D: Random calcitonin is much less sensitive versus pentagastrin-stimulated calcitonin to identify medullary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl of Greek origin comes to the Endocrinology Clinic with failure to maintain normal growth and development. She has Beta-thalassaemia major and receives regular blood transfusions to maintain her haemoglobin (Hb) in the range of 90-100 g/l. You arrange some blood tests: Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin (Hb) 95 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 7.1 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 174 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 5.3 mmol/l, Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/L, Free T4 6.5 nmol/L, 9 am cortisol 52 nmol/L, Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) 2.5 nmol/L, Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) 0.2 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement therapy to begin with?
questions.explanation: This patient has pituitary dysfunction, which has almost certainly been caused by iron overload. Her blood testing is consistent with a diagnosis of pan-hypopituitarism, but it is corticosteroid replacement that is essential first to avoid the possibility of precipitating an adrenal crisis. C: Sex hormone replacement is important, particularly to enable this patient to maintain good bone health, but it can be commenced later. A: Although chronic growth hormone deficiency is associated with tiredness, lethargy and a reduction in muscle mass, it is hydrocortisone that is the more important replacement therapy to start first. D: Thyroxine replacement is essential, but should be begun shortly after hydrocortisone has commenced to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis. E: This is only necessary in patients with adrenal insufficiency who are unable to maintain normal blood pressure control.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man on a visit to his GP has been noticed to have a blood pressure of 145/90 mm Hg. He has a 7-year history of type 2 diabetes, which is currently managed with metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide 160 mg twice daily. His BMI in the clinic was 26. Systemic examination otherwise was normal apart from bilateral peripheral sensory loss and loss of vibration sense up to his knees, consistent with diabetic neuropathy. He has also had laser photocoagulation treatment in both eyes. Other medication of note includes ramipril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin and aspirin, which were started approximately 5 years earlier. Investigations: HbA1c 70.49 mmol/mol (8.6%), Urea 16.7 mmol/L, Phosphate 1.02 mmol/L, Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l, Creatinine (Cr) 225 µmol/L, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.27 mmol/l, Albumin 38 g/l, Chloride (Cl) 115 mmol/L, Bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, Urine protein 0.8 g/24 h, Urine albumin/creatinine ratio 25 mg/mmol. Which next step in his management would be the most appropriate?
options: A. Stop gliclazide and metformin and start a basal bolus insulin regime
B. Reduce the dose of ACE inhibitor by 50%
questions.explanation: This gentleman's renal function precludes the use of metformin. Moreover, the fact that despite being on the maximum dose of gliclazide and a high dose of metformin, his suboptimal HbA1c points towards the need for insulin initiation. A basal bolus regimen would be ideal given his poor renal function. Moreover, it will provide flexibility in terms of dose adjustment and will optimize his glycaemic control. Tight glycaemic control is crucial given that this gentleman has already diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy. Improved control of his hypertension is required, therefore reducing or stopping his ACE inhibitor would be inappropriate. Additionally, the ECG is normal and does not indicate a need for beta-blockade at this point. B: The target blood pressure for diabetics is recommended as <140/80 mmHg, or 125/75 mmHg in type 1 diabetic patients and individuals who have at least micro-albuminuria. ACE inhibitors are renoprotective in patients with a history of diabetic nephropathy, and thus continuing the ACE inhibitor at maximal tolerated dose is recommended. They also have significant effect on reducing the albuminuria. C: It is likely that the creatinine seen here is chronically elevated in the context of diabetic nephropathy and has not been worsened by ACE inhibition. D: This patient needs better management of his hypertension, and the use of a second agent would be necessary. Beta-blockers would not be a first choice unless there is history of atrial fibrillation or coronary artery disease (the ECG is normal here), given the potential worsening effect of some of these on glycaemic control. E: There is no evidence of fluid overload that could justify its use, and it could potentially worsen the renal function.

questions.question: A 73-year-old man comes to the clinic as a referral from his GP, having presented with severe headaches and ischaemic pain in his fingers and toes. The pain increases with heat, and improves if he keeps his hands and feet cold. Most striking is that just taking a few aspirin tablets seemed to improve things for a significant time period. He has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril. On examination his BP is 142/87 mmHg and the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Investigations (sent by the GP): Haemoglobin 123 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 8.1 x 10^9/L, Platelets 821 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 6.2 mmol/L, Creatinine 130 µmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to deal with his hyperkalaemia?
options: B. Start a small dose of furosemide
C. Re-check a fresh sample at the hospital
D. Reassure the biochemistry department that it is related to the high platelet count
questions.explanation: Pseudohyperkalaemia is known to be associated with essential thrombocytosis, the most likely diagnosis here. It is also likely that the sample taken at the GP surgery had spent a considerable amount of time in transit, allowing for in-tube cell lysis to further increase potassium levels. As such, it is sensible to re-check a sample. A: Given that the creatinine is almost in the normal range, it's most likely the elevated potassium is due to pseudohyperkalaemia; as such, the potassium must be re-checked before considering treatment discontinuation. B: This may lead to volume depletion and actually increase the risk of a thrombotic event related to the high platelet count. D: It must be re-checked at the hospital to exclude significant hyperkalaemia. E: This should be started for hyperkalaemia either in the acute setting or where other options for reducing hyperkalaemia in the chronic setting, such as discontinuation of other therapies, have been excluded.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 g BD, liraglutide 1.8 mg daily and glargine 30 mg nocte. He complains of burning pain affecting both feet, much worse at night. Other history of note includes problems with intermittent urinary retention. On examination his BMI is 32, and his BP is 149/82 mmHg. His feet feel warm and his peripheral pulses are easily palpable. Investigations: Haemoglobin 116 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 4.5 x 10^9/L, Platelets 244 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l, Creatinine 145 µmol/l, HbA1c 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%). Which of the following represents the most appropriate first line treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: There is no indication of peripheral vascular disease, and the most likely diagnosis appears to be peripheral neuropathy. NICE guidelines recommend duloxetine, amitriptyline or gabapentin as potential initial therapies. Duloxetine is preferred to amitryptiline because it is associated with a lower risk of urinary retention. C: It is a topical agent used for the treatment of neuropathy in addition to systemic agents, or for patients who are unable to take them. B: This is thought to be less effective than amitryptiline and is associated with increased risk of hyponatraemia. D: Sodium valproate is an alternative therapy for peripheral diabetic neuropathy, but isn't recommended as a first-line option by NICE guidelines. E: This isn't preferred here because of a higher risk of urinary retention versus duloxetine.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of vague left flank pain without any evidence of diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. He is aware of intermittent sweats, particularly at night, that improve with eating. On one occasion, he has fainted between meals. An ultrasound (US) of his abdomen was technically difficult to perform and a computerised tomography (CT) scan was recommended. This revealed a 3 cm mass in the tail of the pancreas. Blood biochemistry was normal. A blood glucose taken after an overnight fast and period on an exercise bike was recorded as 2 mmol/L. A CT guided needle biopsy of the pancreas reveals ill-defined nests of cells separated by vascularised stroma, which stain strongly positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Vasoactive intestinal peptide endocrine tumour (VIPoma)
questions.explanation: Insulinomas are the most common pancreatic endocrine tumour, the incidence being about 1 case per 250 000. Approximately 50% of islet cell tumours are insulinomas. Patients with insulinomas may present with neurological or psychiatric disturbances. An important feature is that symptoms tend to occur at night or early in the morning. The diagnosis is made by demonstrating inappropriately high concentrations of both insulin and C-peptide in the blood, and a blood glucose level of < 2.0-2.2 mmol/l, together with the clinical picture of a hypoglycaemic episode (confusion, altered consciousness, visual disturbances, weakness, sweating, tremulousness and, less commonly, seizures). Provocative testing with an overnight fast followed by exercise on a static bike can be done in a hospital setting. Frequent measurements of the blood glucose concentration should be made during the fast. Only when a low value is recorded should a sample be taken to provide serum for insulin and C-peptide assay. C: Somatostatinomas are associated with glucose intolerance, increased risk of gallstones, diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. A: Patients suffering from a VIPoma present with large-volume secretory diarrhoea, not seen here. B: Gastrinomas are associated with development of the Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and multiple peptic ulcers. E: Glucagonomas are associated with glucose intolerance, increased risk of venous thromboembolic disease and the characteristic rash (necrolytic erythema migrans).

questions.question: A 59-year-old man is referred to the Emergency Department by his General Practitioner (GP). He has recently started ramipril 5 mg for diabetic nephropathy, and the GP is concerned by a deterioration in his creatinine level. According to the GP letter, he has had type II diabetes for the past seven years and was diagnosed with microalbuminuria some three years ago. On examination, in the Emergency Department, he looks well; his blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Investigations: Potassium (K+) 5.0 (4.8 mmol/l on ACEi initiation some 10 days ago), Creatinine 220 µmol/L (185 µmol/l on ACEi initiation some 10 days ago). Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: A. Continue ramipril 5 mg and re-check urea and electrolytes (U&Es) in one week
B. Decrease Ramipril to 2.5 mg daily
C. Increase Ramipril to 10 mg daily
D. Stop ramipril for one week and re-check U&Es
questions.explanation: Although physicians generally consider a rise in creatinine levels of > 20% to be clinically significant, a rise of > 30% is considered significant, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. The rise seen here (185-220 µmol/l) is below 20% and ramipril can therefore be continued. It is, however, prudent not to increase the dose of ramipril at this stage but merely to re-check the U&Es to ensure that no further rise in creatinine has occurred. C: Blood pressure is in the target range, and there has been a rise in creatinine level. For this reason, a further increase in dose should be avoided at this stage. B: The rise in creatinine level seen here on ACEi initiation is below the 20% guidance for possible clinical harm. As such, there is no indication to decrease the ramipril dose at this stage. D: This would have been a reasonable approach, had the creatinine level risen by 30% or more. Given the rise is below the guidance level for concern, there is no indication to discontinue ramipril. E: Withdrawal is only indicated for a significant rise in creatinine level that can be linked to the ramipril prescription. This patient could derive significant potential outcome benefit from an ACEI. Therapy should therefore be continued.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department because she has felt increasingly tired over the past three to four weeks, and now is virtually unable to leave the house due to tiredness, has significant nausea and has been unable to eat for the past 48 hours. She has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, for which she takes 100 mcg of thyroxine daily, and type 1 diabetes, for which she takes a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her pulse is 90 bpm and regular. Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb) 109 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 7.9 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 179 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 127 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 5.6 mmol/l, Creatinine 112 µmol/L, Glucose 8.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 55 mmol/mol (7.2%), Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 1.2 u/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 1 (APS I)
B. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 2 (APS II)
C. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 3 (APS III)
E. Renal tubular acidosis Type IV
questions.explanation: APS II is the most common form of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome and presents most commonly in the third or fourth decade. It consists of Addison's disease plus either an autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus, and may be associated with a number of other autoimmune phenomena such as gonadal failure or coeliac disease. The clinical picture seen here is consistent with a diagnosis of Addison's disease. C: APS III is not associated with adrenal insufficiency. The backbone of APS III is autoimmune thyroiditis, in conjunction with diabetes mellitus, pernicious anaemia or vitiligo. A: The three major components of APS I are: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and autoimmune adrenal insufficiency. D: This patient's symptoms are consistent with autoimmune-mediated glandular failure, rather than secondary failure due to pituitary disease, as exemplified by Hashimoto's thyroiditis. E: Renal tubular acidosis is characterised by deficient aldosterone action. It would fit with the urea and electrolytes picture observed, but it would be inconsistent with the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and Hashimoto's disease seen here.

questions.question: A keen junior doctor studying for his MRCP examination shows the medical registrar an electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded on a 36-year-old woman in the Medical Clinic in the morning. Examination of the patient reveals a normal body habitus with a body mass index (BMI) of 23 kg/m2 but she is hypertensive with a blood pressure of 165/95 mmHg. She takes no medications and apparently complains of lethargy and muscle aches most of the time. The patient had been referred urgently by the general practitioner for investigation for a metabolic abnormality. The ECG is shown below. Based on the ECG, what is the most likely underlying metabolic abnormality?
questions.explanation: This ECG demonstrates the classical picture of a prominent U wave - a small deflection immediately following the T wave, usually seen in V2 and V3. A U wave on the ECG is thought to correspond with after-depolarisation events in the ventricles. A normal U wave is of the same polarity as the T wave, but one-third of the amplitude. The differential diagnosis of prominent upright U waves includes hypokalaemia, left ventricular hypertrophy, some cases of mitral valve prolapse, hyperthyroidism, and quinidine and other type 1A antiarrhythmics. Conn syndrome is characterised by increased aldosterone secretion (primary hyperaldosteronism) from the adrenal gland from a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma. Metabolically, this manifests as suppression of plasma renin activity, hypertension and hypokalaemia. Bartter syndrome is a cause of congenital salt wasting, which presents in childhood with failure to thrive, polyuria and polydipsia. C: The main abnormality associated with hypercalcaemia is shortening of the QT interval. When the calcium level is very high, J waves may also be seen. A: Hyperkalaemia is associated with peaked T waves and later, as the potassium level rises further, with bizarre broadened QRS complexes. D: Hypocalcaemia leads to QT prolongation, although arrhythmias are surprisingly rarely reported in association with low calcium levels. E: Like hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia is associated with QT prolongation. The risk of rhythm disturbance is thought to be higher than for hypocalcaemia.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with bilateral gynaecomastia. He apparently had surgery as a child to correct bilateral undescended testes. On examination, he is tall, with increased arm and leg length. He does have evidence of bilateral gynaecomastia, with small testes bilaterally. Apparently there have been problems with anxiety and bullying at 6th form and he has now left to begin a job. Which of the following would be the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation: The suspicion here, based on history and physical appearance, is a diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome. Both FSH and LH are raised in Klinefelter syndrome, and elevation would be a strong pointer to confirming the underlying diagnosis. Chromosomal analysis would be an obvious further step. Management centres on androgen replacement, cosmetic procedures and access to psychosexual counselling. D: Progesterone levels are not useful in the evaluation of Klinefelter syndrome. A: Although oestrogen levels are elevated in patients with Klinefelter, they are less useful vs raised gonadotrophins in confirming the diagnosis. B: GNRH levels are reduced in Kallmann syndrome; this syndrome is associated with absence of sense of smell, which isn't reported as part of the scenario here. E: Although testosterone is reduced in patients with Klinefelter syndrome, measuring this wouldn't indicate whether the defect was at the level of the pituitary or the testes and hence FSH and LH measurement is more useful.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with a past history of atrial fibrillation (AF) and periods of paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia (PVT) on a 24 hour tape is referred to the Outpatient Clinic with weight loss and tremor. He is clinically hyperthyroid. He takes warfarin and amiodarone. Investigations reveal the following: Thyroxine (T4) 100 pmol/L, Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) < 0.01 uU/L. A colour flow Doppler ultrasound (US) of his thyroid shows increased blood flow. What would be the preferred next management step?
options: B. Start prednisolone 30 mg OD and carbimazole 40 mg OD
questions.explanation: This is an example of type 1 amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism (AIT). The high iodine content of the amiodarone induces release of thyroid hormone (Jod-Basedow effect) and causes hyperthyroidism. In type 2 AIT the amiodarone causes a destructive thyroiditis. Colour flow Doppler ultrasound can be used to differentiate the two: blood flow is increased in type 1 and decreased in type 2. High-dose anti-thyroid drugs are needed to treat type 1 AIT as they have less effect due to the high iodine load. D: Thyroidectomy is rarely recommended as first-line treatment for thyrotoxicosis. Thyroidectomy in a thyrotoxic patient may precipitate thyroid storm. A: Amiodarone should be discontinued if possible, but in this case, given the VT, this decision should be considered carefully in conjunction with a cardiologist. Withdrawal of amiodarone alone will have no immediate effect due to the long half-life of amiodarone. B: Steroids in combination with anti-thyroid drugs help to treat type 2 AIT. However, these have no role in type 1 AIT. E: Radioiodine is not usually effective because of reduced uptake by the thyroid due to high iodine levels.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a three week history of a sore throat associated with lethargy, a reduced appetite and general viral symptoms. She has also felt frequent palpitations recently and increased sweating but these appear to be settling, with the patient now complaining of occasional palpitations. Other symptoms include pain in the lower part of her neck made worse with swallowing and an occasional hoarseness of her voice. She is otherwise fit and well, is not on any medications and is a non-smoker. There is no significant family history. The only positive findings on examination were residual tenderness over her lower anterior neck to palpation and mild tachycardia associated with warm skin to touch. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Thyroid function tests (TFT) show a T4 level slightly above normal and a TSH level of < 0.1 mU/L. The GP diagnoses a viral illness and then commenced carbimazole 20 mg twice a day on the basis of her TFT results. Two months later, the patient again attended her GP but this time complaining of increased lethargy, weight gain and a minor discomfort in the lower part of her neck. What would be the next most appropriate management step?
options: A. Adjust the dose of carbimazole to control the patient's symptoms
B. Stop carbimazole and consider replacement thyroid hormone therapy if symptoms don't recover
C. Refer the patient for an ultrasound scan of the thyroid gland
D. Refer patient for a fine needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid gland
questions.explanation: De Quervain thyroiditis is the most common cause of a painful thyroid gland and causes hyperthyroidism initially, sometimes followed by transient hypothyroidism. The underlying cause is felt to be either a viral infection or the post-viral inflammatory response. The condition is more common in females. The typical course of the disease consists of an acute phase, in which the main complaint is pain, although signs of hyperthyroidism may also be present. This is followed by a transient asymptomatic and euthyroid phase, which evolves into the hypothyroid phase. The hypothyroid state may become permanent in 5-10% of patients, but the vast majority go on to the recovery phase, characterised by normalisation of thyroid structure and function. The treatment is consequently directed towards the control of pain and thyroid symptoms. Initial symptomatic hyperthyroidism can be treated with beta-blockade. Beta-adrenergic blockers are usually the sole form of treatment indicated/required in cases of thyroiditis, although severe, persistent symptoms/signs in may require additional therapy with salicylates and/or glucocorticoids. If hypothyroidism occurs in the late stages, replacement therapy is required and is guided by the TSH levels. D: Fine needle aspiration should always be performed on solitary nodules >10 mm, those <10 mm with suspicious imaging characteristics or on dominant nodules. A: The patient's symptoms are caused by the hypothyroid phase of De Quervain's thyroiditis, rather than the carbimazole. C: Ultrasound scanning should be performed in patients presenting with a single palpable nodule. E: The patient's symptoms are not due to carbimazole. Propylthiouracil and carbimazole are both associated with agranulocytosis and must be stopped if this complication is suspected, and only restarted if a blood count has confirmed that the white cell count is in fact normal.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman who is 22 weeks' pregnant with her second child comes to the clinic complaining of anxiety and palpitations. She is concerned as she is finding it difficult to maintain an adequate weight. On examination, she has a BP of 135/70 mmHg and a resting pulse of 88/min. You palpate a nodule on the left-hand side of her thyroid. Investigations reveal the following: Haemoglobin (Hb) 114 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 5.9 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 172 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/L, Potassium (K*) 4.0 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 95 μmol/l, TSH < 0.05, Free T4 31 pmol/l. Ultrasound reveals a solitary left-sided thyroid nodule. FNA reveals an adenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for her?
questions.explanation: In this scenario, options are limited to manage her thyrotoxicosis. Anti-thyroid drugs would form the mainstay of intervention until after delivery. Both propylthiouracil and carbimazole are options, although the former is not recommended in late pregnancy because of the risk of maternal liver dysfunction. A: This is the option for patients who are unable to tolerate anti-thyroid medication. B: Propanolol offers symptomatic relief only, and will not reduce the risk of fetal loss due to thyrotoxicosis. C: Radioiodine is contraindicated during pregnancy, and is likely to be unsuitable for this patient for a considerable period of time because of the need to avoid exposure to young children. E: Lugol's iodine is used to acutely control thyrotoxicosis when urgent surgery is considered.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with severe dehydration and weight loss. She reports that she has had steatorrhoea for several months and her relatives report that the weight loss has occurred over the same time period. Over the course of her admission, she is found to have a metastatic somatostatinoma. Which of these complications is she most likely to have due to the somatostatinoma?
questions.explanation: Glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus occurs in around 95% of patients with somatostatinoma and is often the first symptom to develop. The classic triad includes diabetes mellitus, diarrhoea and gallstones. Patients commonly also experience weight loss and hypochlorhydria. D: Patients with somatostatinoma are likely to be anaemic, rather than polycythaemic, which may be due to malabsorption owing to the diarrhoea. A: Patients with somatostatinoma often experience hypochlorhydria, not hyperchlorhydria, a state of reduced gastric secretions, since somatostatin inhibits the secretion of gastrin in the stomach which results in reduced chloride levels. B: The most common finding of a patient with a somatostatinoma is glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus. This would cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia. E: Patients with somatostatinoma commonly experience gallstones rather than bladder stones. This occurs because somatostatin inhibits cholecystokinin release in the gallbladder which therefore reduces biliary motility and predisposes to stone formation.

questions.question: A 38-year-old physiotherapist attended for a routine follow-up in the Diabetes Clinic. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus at the age of 11 and unfortunately had a history of both diabetic maculopathy and early diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria. She complained of a 6-week history of raised, tender plaques over the shins (shown below) and, on further questioning, described painful wrists and ankles for the past 6 months. Examination confirmed the presence of the plaques, over which there was clear skin thinning and telangiectasia. Her blood pressure is 147/84 mmHg. A urine dipstick revealed protein +1 and glucose +1. What is the most useful next investigation for her painful joints?
options: B. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody testing
questions.explanation: The patient's plaques are probably unconnected to the wrist and ankle pain but are due to necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. The condition is more common in women and presents in young adults or in early middle life. These erythematous plaques are due to small vessel damage causing partial necrosis of the dermal collagen and connective tissue, with a resulting histiocytic cellular response. The lesions are usually managed with support bandaging and use of topical steroids. The wrist and ankle pain is suggestive of possible arthritis. Both rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes may be associated with the human leukocyte antigen HLA-DR4. Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis, the most probable diagnosis here, and may be positive in advance of any joint destruction. It also stratifies those with rapid disease progression. It is therefore the most useful next step. C: Necrobiosis lipoidica is not associated with generalised complement activation, and so this parameter is likely to be normal. A: Anti-nuclear antibody testing is useful when systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is considered as the underlying diagnosis, although given that joint pains are limited to the wrists and ankles and there is an absence of a photosensitive rash, this is less likely vs a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. D: Although ankle and wrist X-rays are useful in defining rheumatoid arthritis, the absence of changes should not delay treatment. Hence, CCP testing is potentially more useful at this stage of the disease. E: Necrobiosis lipoidica is associated with neither Churg-Strauss vasculitis nor generalised hypersensitivity, and thus IgE measurement has little utility here.

questions.question: A 54-year-old alcoholic is admitted to the Emergency Department complaining of numbness and weakness affecting his hands and twitching affecting his face and jaw. He drinks one bottle of whisky per day and has been suffering from severe diarrhoea for the past 48 hours. On examination, his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. He is clearly malnourished, has multiple spider naevi over his upper chest and back and his abdomen isdisplayed below. While you examine him, he is complaining of numbness and tingling affecting his hands, feet and around his mouth. Serum calcium level is measured at 1.98 mmol/L. You institute calcium replacement; however, 60 minutes later, his calcium has not recovered completely and reads at 2.05 mmol/l. He still has significant symptoms of hypocalcaemia. Which of the following next interventions is likely to be most effective?
questions.explanation: The patient has ascites and multiple spider naevi, which, in the context of alcohol abuse may indicated chronic liver failure. Such patients are often malnourished, resulting in electrolyte loss. This is particularly the case when patients have severe diarrhoea. Hypocalcaemia will often be resistant even to intravenous supplementation when there is concurrent hypomagnesaemia; therefore, magnesium replacement is the correct answer. B: Furosemide is hypercalciuric; it directly increases renal calcium excretion in both the acute treatment and long-term usage. Therefore, this would be an inappropriate drug choice. C: Although thiazide diuretics have metabolic effects contributing to increased calcium uptake as a result of sodium-chloride transport inhibition, these effects will not be enough to adequately increase the calcium levels. Therefore, this is not an appropriate treatment option. D: Recombinant PTH is a theoretical option requiring several days to take effect. Given this patient is symptomatic, it is not an appropriate treatment option. E: Although this patient may require further calcium replacement, because of the resistance associated with hypomagnesaemia, further calcium replacement without magnesium electrolyte correction would not be appropriate.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man with a history of previous injury in a motorcycle accident comes to the clinic with his mother. She looks after him as he has been left with a right arm and leg weakness after a skull fracture and intracranial haemorrhage. He also has epilepsy for which he takes carbamazepine. They complain that he is thirsty all the time and can't stop drinking litres of water and squash each day. His mother herself has significant chronic illness, suffering from chronic left ventricular failure. Investigations: Haemoglobin 134 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 5.9 x 10^9/L, Platelets 203 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 149 mmol/l, Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L, Creatinine 143 µmol/L, Bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, Plasma osmolality 350 mosmol/kg, Urine osmolality 270 after water deprivation, rises to 810 after DDAVP. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: It is highly likely that this man's head injury has led to cranial diabetes insipidus. Whilst it is possible given the clinical history that he may have psychogenic polydipsia, the osmolality results only fit with cranial DI as the diagnosis. Treatment is with intranasal vasopressin; given the possibility of overdose and consequent hyponatraemia, monitoring of U&E is recommended. Carbamazepine may exacerbate hyponatraemia with vasopressin therapy, and therefore close monitoring of U&E and symptom response versus vasopressin dose is even more essential in this case. B: SIADH is associated with relative salt and water overload, accompanied by hyponatraemia rather than the elevated sodium seen here. A: Nephrogenic DI would not show a positive response to DDAVP and is therefore excluded here. D: This is the alternative diagnosis, although the history of head injury and strong response to DDAVP makes cranial diabetes insipidus much more likely. E: Diuretic abuse may be associated with symptoms of dehydration, but elevated bicarbonate would be expected here.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman presents with lethargy on a background of depression and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She takes metformin and gliclazide. Her blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg and she is clinically euvolaemic. Routine biochemical investigations reveal: Sodium (Na+) 120 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/L, Urea 5.6 mmol/L, Creatinine 76 µmol/L, Thyroid function test Normal. Which biochemical test would be most useful in determining her state of water balance?
options: B. Erect/supine renin and aldosterone estimation
questions.explanation: Urine osmolality relative to serum osmolality gives an accurate assessment of the state of the ADH axis. In the absence of other causes (eg CCF), a high urine osmolality relative to serum osmolality in the setting of hyponatraemia is inappropriate. Other tests, such as plasma ADH and detailed urine electrolyte studies, can give similar information, but at much greater expense and difficulty. Sulphonylureas are recognised as a rare cause of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH); the condition is seen most commonly with chlorpropamide and, while this has been replaced by more modern agents such as gliclazide, it is still occasionally seen. C: The fractional excretion of sodium is the percentage of the sodium filtered by the kidney which is excreted in the urine. It is measured in terms of plasma and urine sodium, rather than by the interpretation of urinary sodium concentration alone, as urinary sodium concentrations can vary with water reabsorption. Therefore, the urinary and plasma concentrations of sodium must be compared to get an accurate picture of renal clearance. In clinical use, the fractional excretion of sodium can be calculated as part of the evaluation of acute kidney failure in order to determine if hypovolaemia or decreased effective circulating plasma volume is a contributor to the kidney failure. A: This investigation is for measurement of total protein, it would be useful to diagnose nephrotic conditions. However this investigation would not give any indication of volume status. B: The aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) (ie the ratio of plasma aldosterone to plasma renin activity) is the most sensitive means of differentiating primary from secondary causes of hyperaldosteronism. It is not useful for volume status assessment. D: Plasma ADH would be high in dehydration because it controls the amount of water that is excreted in the urine. ADH levels may be raised and low in certain pathological states such as SIADH or diabetes insipidus therefore it is not the best method to assess fluid status.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department, having been found on the floor by her carer. She is morbidly obese and is prescribed long-term therapy for manic depressive psychosis and hypertension. She arrives with a medication bag containing risperidone, bendroflumethiazide and bisoprolol tablets. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/75 mmHg and a pulse of 95 bpm and regular. Her temperature is 38.1°C There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation of the chest. The abdomen appears soft, and bowel sounds are present. She is drowsy and responds to questions by mumbling incoherently. Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 10.1 x 10^9/l, Platelets (PLT) 189 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 146 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/L, Creatinine 161 µmol/l, Urea 17.2 mmol/L, Glucose 32.1 mmol/L, Bicarbonate 25 mmol/l, PH 7.35. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for fluid replacement?
questions.explanation: The joint British Societies guidelines on the management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic non-ketotic state (HHS) recommend 0.9% saline as the fluid replacement of choice. Assuming insulin replacement is commenced at the same time as saline replacement, there is no reason to expect that use of 0.9% saline will significantly increase serum sodium levels. C: Concentrated saline is only indicated where there is life-threatening hyponatraemia, where it should be given in a High Dependency Unit setting to allow for close monitoring of any increase in the serum sodium level, to prevent it from rising too quickly. A: 0.45% or half normal saline should only be used where osmolality is not declining despite achieving euvolaemia with 0.9% saline replacement. D: Hypotonic fluid replacement with 5% dextrose should only be considered, like 0.45% saline, when osmolality is not correcting despite adequate 0.9% saline replacement. E: Studies suggest that Hartmann's solution (compound sodium lactate) offers no advantage in the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); the guidelines therefore do not recommend its use in HHS.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man attends the Endocrinology Clinic with long-standing type I diabetes mellitus. Unfortunately, he has developed nephropathy, with a recent creatinine (Cr) level measured at 180 µmol/L and microalbuminuria. Last year he received laser treatment to his left eye for severe retinopathy. He is currently treated with a Novomix 30 at a dose of 12 units twice a day. A recent HbA1c was measured at 59.56 (7.6%). You review his home glucose record and find that two hour postprandial glucose is high, at 12 mmol/L, yet he appears to be suffering attacks of hypoglycaemia late in the afternoon before his evening meal, and occasionally before breakfast. His body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m2 Which of the following represents the best advice with respect to his treatment irrespective of patient preference?
options: A. Reduce his portion size in an attempt to take in fewer calories
B. Alter his insulin to a basal bolus regime involving glargine and aspart
C. Increase his BD insulin to 14 units
D. Increase the proportion of short-acting insulin in his mixed insulin dose and increase the dose to 14 units
E. Advise him to snack more in the middle of the afternoon and prior to going to bed
questions.explanation: This man has documented microvascular disease with proven retinopathy and nephropathy. In this population, optimal glycaemic control would be indicated by an HbA1c of 47.54 mmol/mol (<6.5%) if possible. Aspart, as a short-acting insulin, and glargine as an insulin analogue are associated with less hypoglycaemia, would be the most appropriate choice for him. D: This may improve his postprandial blood glucose levels but may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. A: Reducing his portion size may impact on his postprandial blood glucose levels but will increase the risk of late hypoglycaemia. C: Increasing his BD insulin would only exacerbate the problem of late between-dose hypoglycaemia. E: Snacking, but remaining on BD insulin, would only serve to increase his total energy intake and may worsen his glycaemic control.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is admitted for an arthroscopy of the right knee. His admission to the Emergency Department reveals potassium of 5.9 mmol/l, creatinine of 450 µmol/l and urea of 28 mmol/l. Which of the following stems represents the best plan with respect to his surgery?
options: A. He should be commenced on calcium resonium and surgery can proceed
B. He should be given nebulised salbutamol and surgery be postponed by 6 h
C. He is safe to continue with surgery
D. He should be given insulin and dextrose and surgery may proceed
E. Surgery should be delayed until his potassium is below 5.5 mmol/l
questions.explanation: Guidelines for surgery in patients with chronic kidney disease suggest that surgery should be postponed until serum potassium is <5.5 mmol/L In addition, in patients undergoing surgery potassium should be monitored immediately after and then again 4-6 h later. Where surgery is likely to involve significant circulatory compromise and acute or chronic kidney disease may be precipitated, such as in coronary artery bypass surgery, patients should ideally be stabilised on dialysis first. A: Calcium resonium would not work quickly - it takes at least 48 h to signficantly lower the potassium. B: Nebulised salbutamol is only an interim measure to lower potassium as it moves potassium into the cells. However, because it is likely to leak from the cells hours later it is not a definitive treatment. C: Hyperkalaemia can precipitate arrhythmias when patients are given anaesthesia during surgery. Therefore it must be treated pre-surgery. D: Insulin and dextrose is only a 'holding' measure and does not remove potassium from the body, and therefore the patient may become hyperkalaemic later. Dialysis should thus be given first prior to surgery.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. She recently suffered a fall whilst at a nightclub and was knocked out for a few minutes. Since then, over the past few weeks, she has suffered polyuria and polydipsia. She has no past medical history of note, and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, her BP is 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She has a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. Her BMI is 21. Neurological assessment is unremarkable. Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 8.1 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 191 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 146 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/L, Creatinine (Cr) 142 µmol/L, Urea 9.1 mmol/L, Glucose 5.4 mmol/L, Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.21 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis to exclude is diabetes insipidus (DI) due to the head injury, and urine and plasma osmolality is an appropriate non-invasive first step in excluding DI. Inappropriately low urine osmolality in the presence of a raised plasma osmolality is suggestive of the diagnosis, and a water deprivation test would be the obvious next step after this. A: In the absence of focal neurology, a CT head isn't indicated before further biochemistry is obtained. C: The lack of signs of hypo- or hyperthyroidism implies that thyroid function testing is most likely to be normal. D: Urinary sodium is more useful in the assessment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) and of acute tubular necrosis. E: A water deprivation test is the default next investigation after a spot urine and plasma osmolality.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has a history of hypertension which is resistant to dual therapy with 20 mg of lisinopril and 10 mg of amlodipine. Other past medical history of note includes asthma for which she takes a Chinese herbal remedy and a fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 162/95 mmHg and a pulse of 78 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal. The chest is clear, and there are no signs of peripheral oedema. Abdominal examination reveals no palpable masses. Investigations: Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l, White cell count (WCC) 6.4 x 10^9/L, Platelets (PLT) 200 x 10^9/L, Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/L, Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/L, Bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, Creatinine 90 µmol/L, Aldosterone 60 pmol/L (sample taken standing up), Renin 5.4 mU/L (sample taken standing up). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: As well as being used in a range of sweets and as a tobacco additive, liquorice is also used as a cough suppressant as a component of Chinese herbal medicines. In this patient, exposure to liquorice is therefore likely to have come via her traditional asthma medicine. Liquorice poisoning results in low renin and aldosterone, hypertension and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis because glycyrrhizic acid has mineralocorticoid activity. The treatment of choice in this case is removal of the herbal medication; this is likely to result in gradual resolution of her hypertension. B: Conn syndrome is associated with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypertension and hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism, which does not fit with the clinical picture seen here. A: Bartter syndrome is associated with normal blood pressure, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Both renin and aldosterone are elevated in patients suffering from Bartter syndrome. C: Gitelman syndrome is associated with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and normal blood pressure or hypotension. It is also associated with magnesium wasting and borderline low calcium levels. E: Renal artery stenosis is associated with hypokalaemia, hypertension and elevated renin and aldosterone, which does not fit with the clinical picture reported here.

questions.question: A 21-year-old student nurse is admitted to the Emergency Medical Unit having suffered a collapse while on attachment in the Acute Medical Unit. This is the third episode to occur over the past six months. Her past medical history includes mild eczema and infrequent menstruation, which is under investigation. Her grandfather and uncle are noted to have type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, her BP is 110/70 mmHg; her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Her oxygen saturations are 96% on air. Her cardiorespiratory, abdominal and neurological examinations are normal. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 131 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/l | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 137~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.3~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 85~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) | 12~mg/L | 0-10~mg/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 42 IU/L | 5-30 IU/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) | 8~mm/1^h | 0-10~mm/1^h Albumin | 31 g/l | 35-55 g/l Bilirubin | 17~  mu~mol/L | 2-17~  mu mol/l C peptide | 3.0~ng/ml (high) | Glucose | 2.1~mmol/L | Which of the following is the most likely reason for her collapse?
questions.explanation: Sulfonylurea abuse relies on access and intent. Given that this nurse's grandfather has type II diabetes mellitus, she is very likely to have access to sulfonylurea. The elevated C-peptide level in the presence of hypoglycaemia suggests a process which has stimulated endogenous insulin production. This may be a personality disorder or an example of acute psychological stress and an attempt to seek help. Insulin abuse presents with hypoglycaemia and a suppressed C-peptide level. C-peptide is a by-product of insulin production. In insulin overdose, the body stops making endogenous insulin and levels are decreased. This patient has a high C-peptide level and it is, therefore, unlikely that insulin abuse is the cause. Although Addison's disease can cause hypoglycaemia, there is nothing in the clinical history to suggest it as a possible diagnosis, with only mildly abnormal blood pressures and no electrolyte abnormalities. Therefore, it would be unlikely to have caused the collapse. Although this patient has a history of irregular menstruation, which could suggest hypopituitarism, the findings of hypoglycaemia and an elevated C-peptide level do not support this diagnosis. Rather, it is more likely that starvation and the physiological stress from sulfonylurea abuse (that would cause hypoglycaemia and an elevated C-peptide level) are contributing to her oligomenorrhoea. Insulinoma is a possible cause. However, it is significantly rarer as a cause of hypoglycaemia in comparison to sulfonylurea abuse. Given the patient likely has access to sulfonylureas (note the family history of type II diabetes mellitus), as well as the elevated C-peptide level in the presence of hypoglycaemia, this would tend to suggest sulfonylurea abuse rather than insulinoma.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the Admissions Unit. She has a long history of type II diabetes. On examination, her foot is warm and swollen, and she has been suffering vague bony pains in it over the past few months. There is no history of trauma and no obvious skin break. Fundoscopy reveals diabetic retinopathy, and examination of her lower limbs reveals absent sensation to vibration and pinprick to the knees. Her blood pressure (BP) is 155/95 mmHg. A HbA1c level is recorded as 65 mmol/mol. A photo and X-ray of her foot are shown below. What is your next management step?
options: B. Lower limb venous ultrasound scan
questions.explanation: This subacute presentation, with joint swelling and chronic joint pains against a background of long-standing and poorly controlled diabetes, suggests possible Charcot's, in this case of the talo-navicular joint. Non-weight bearing in a cast is the intervention of choice. Bisphosphonates may also be of value in reducing bone turnover. The subacute history is more consistent with Charcot's, especially as there is no obvious potential site of infection. The localised swelling around the ankle joint is more consistent with bony deformity than a venous thrombosis. Clindamycin is optimal oral therapy for osteomyelitis, although it is associated with high risk of development of pseudomembranous colitis. Compression stockings are used in the treatment of chronic venous insufficiency. The picture reveals no evidence of venous ulceration to suggest they are of value here.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with feelings of anxiety. She has lost weight over the past few months and describes palpitations. She has visited her General Practitioner (GP) three x over the past six months and been prescribed a selective serotonin uptake inhibitor (SSRI), although her condition continues to worsen. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 122/70 mmHg. Her pulse is 88 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and she has a fine tremor. The GP conducted some thyroid function tests, which reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 0.05~  mu U/L | 0.17-3.2 μυ/ Free thyroxine (T4) | 20.1~pmol/L | 11-22 pmol/l Free triiodothyronine (T3) | 12.5~pmol/L | 3.5-5 pmol/l What is the best treatment for this woman's underlying condition?
questions.explanation: This woman has triiodothyronine (T3) thyrotoxicosis. Isolated elevation in T3 accompanied by a thyroxine (T4) in the normal range is associated with around 5% of cases of thyrotoxicosis. Thyrotoxicosis is 10 x more common in women than men in the UK. Prevalence is approximately 2% of the female population, with an annual incidence of 3 per 1000 women. Graves' disease is the commonest cause of thyrotoxicosis; other causes include toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma. Assessment of thyrotoxicosis includes thyroid function tests, thyroid autoantibodies and radionucleotide thyroid scanning, where the diagnosis is uncertain. Carbimazole is the mainstay of initial management of thyrotoxicosis, with propylthiouracil an alternative in patients who fail to tolerate carbimazole or for whom it is unsuitable. Therapy for depression may be required, but her mood should be reassessed once thyroid equilibrium is established. Reassurance alone is inappropriate here, since with suppressed TSH, T4 at the upper limit of normal and elevated T3 this patient has confirmed thyrotoxicosis. Although propranolol may be useful for relief of symptoms in the early stages of thyrotoxicosis, use as monotherapy is not appropriate in this situation. Thyroxine is not indicated, given that TSH is suppressed, T4 is at the upper end of the normal range and T3 is elevated.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who is 30 weeks' pregnant comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has found it increasingly difficult to maintain her weight during the past few weeks, and has been suffering from palpitations and anxiety. She has no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a BP of 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 88/min and regular. She has a fine resting tremor and a smooth, non-tender goitre.
