Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 119 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 181  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 84~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Glucose | 4.8~mmol/L | 3.97.1 mmol/l Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | <0.05~mu/L | 0.4-5.0~mu/L Free thyroxine (T4) | 20 pmol/l | 6.5-13.0 pmol/l Anti-thyroid antibody | + | Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: This patient has thyrotoxicosis, potentially due to underlying Graves' disease. The recommended treatment approach is to give enough anti-thyroid drug therapy to maintain thyroid hormone levels in the upper third of the normal range. Carbimazole is the recommended option in late pregnancy because of reports of hepatotoxicity associated with propylthiouracil. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because administration would lead to uptake in the fetal thyroid. Thyroxine does not cross the placenta to any appreciable degree, and therefore block-replace is not recommended in pregnancy. Propylthiouracil may be used in early pregnancy, but in late pregnancy it is not recommended because of risk of hepatotoxicity. Block-replace is not indicated because of thyroxine not crossing the placental barrier.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant is referred by her General Practitioner to the Endocrine Clinic. Over the past week, she has developed symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection and has pain over the thyroid, more marked on the right-hand side than on the left. She has also been feeling rather anxious with palpitations. There is no significant past medical history of note and no family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg; her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular. She has a fine tremor at rest. There is generalised tenderness on palpation of the thyroid, more marked on the right. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 110~g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.7  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets | 191  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/t Sodium (Na+) | 137~mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 82~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | < 0.1 U/L | 0.4-5.0~U/L Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
options: A. High dose carbimazole and thyroxine
questions.explanation: This patient has subacute thyroiditis, for which analgesia with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). such as ibuprofen, is an appropriate initial intervention. Typical symptoms are present, including symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection, pain over the thyroid gland and features consistent with thyrotoxicosis. Symptoms of hyperthyroidism are transient and related to increased thyroxine release rather than to overproduction. Ibuprofen should not be used in the first trimester (risk of miscarriage) or third trimester of pregnancy (risk of closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus in utero and possibly persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn). Maternal use of NSAIDs should be avoided until the beginning of 20 weeks' gestation. If NSAID use is necessary between 20 and 30 weeks' gestation, use should be limited to the lowest effective dose and the shortest duration possible; ultrasound monitoring of amniotic fluid should be considered if treatment extends beyond 48 hours and the NSAID should be discontinued if oligohydramnios is found. Because NSAIDs may cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, the prescribing information for ibuprofen specifically states its use should be avoided starting at 30 weeks' gestation. High-dose carbimazole and thyroxine is incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is transient, not due to overproduction, and block-replace therapy is not recommended in pregnancy. Prednisolone is incorrect. Corticosteroids are avoided in pregnancy, if possible, because of their adverse event profile. Radioiodine is the first-line treatment for Graves' disease. However, given the history of a recent upper respiratory tract infection, combined with a tender thyroid, a diagnosis of subacute thyroiditis is more likely. Furthermore, use of radioiodine is not recommended to treat Graves' disease in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal complications. In such instances, carbimazole is preferred. This patient's pain has precipitated her presentation to hospital. Therefore, it is not considered appropriate to leave her without advice/access to pain-relieving medication.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with decreased libido, vaginal dryness and absence of periods for the past 4 months. Most recently, she has begun to suffer embarrassing milk leakage from her breasts on only minor nipple stimulation. Medication history includes use of the oral contraceptive pill. Prolactin level is 4300 microlU/L and she maintains that she could not possibly be pregnant as she has bought a home test, which is negative. Her BP is normal at 132/72 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular and her BMI is 23. Which of the following is most likely to yield the diagnosis?
options: A. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the pituitary fossa
questions.explanation: Prolactin levels are too elevated to be due to the oral contraceptive pill; with this symptomatic picture it is important to rule out a prolactinoma or other pituitary tumour leading to raised prolactin levels due to pressure effects. MRI scanning is needed to determine tumour size and location. Given her prolactin level, the most likely diagnosis is a micro-adenoma producing prolactin; as such, the management of choice is with a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine or cabergoline in the first instance. Hypothyroidism is associated with elevated prolactin levels, but usually not to this extent, which is more indicative of a prolactinoma. Shop-bought pregnancy tests have an accuracy of above 95%, so pregnancy is unlikely; however, it would be reasonable to perform a re-test to make absolutely sure that it is negative. Elevated prolactin levels are noted in some ovarian and endometrial cancers and with pregnancy, although these are unlikely diagnoses given the absence of abdominal symptoms and negative pregnancy test. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) testing is used in the work-up primarily of precocious and delayed puberty associated with low LH and FSH Levels.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. She has no past medical history of note and only complained to her general practitioner of tiredness and increased thirst over the past few months. Examination is unremarkable. Blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg, and pulse is 70 bpm and regular. The body mass index (BMI) is 23~kg/M2 Primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Which of the following would be considered an indication for surgical referral?
questions.explanation: This question is based on the criteria from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for surgery in asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism. These include creatinine clearance reduced by 30% or more. Young age, rather than older age, is a driver for parathyroid surgery, with age younger than 50 years considered the driver for surgery in the absence of other factors. Serum albumin-adjusted calcium >0.25~mmol/l above the upper limit of normal is considered the cut-off for recommending surgery. Given most hospitals quote a normal range of up to 2.61~mmol/L this is below that threshold. A cut-off of 10~mmol/24 hours is used as the urinary calcium excretion threshold for recommending surgery in asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism. The cut-off for bone mineral density is a T score < - 2.5, indicating a significant risk for fracture linked to loss of bone mineral density.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man is referred to clinic with headaches and a raised fasting glucose of 7.5~mmol/L He has also noticed a change in his facial appearance and enlargement of his hands. Examination reveals prognathism, enlarged digits and bitemporal hemianopia. His BP is elevated at 155/90 mmHg. An oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone levels showed a blood glucose of 11.5~mmol/L at 120 min and also failure to suppress growth hormone levels. An MRI scan of the pituitary fossa revealed an adenoma that was abutting the optic chiasm. Treatment options were explained to the patient and he opted for medical therapy rather surgery (transphenoidal resection of the adenoma). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical therapy for him?
questions.explanation: This gentleman has acromegaly. Acromegaly is usually related to a pituitary adenoma, although it is occasionally caused by ectopic secretion of growth hormone from malignant cells. This results in coarsening of facial features, prognathism and macroglossia. Patients are at increased risk of cardiovascular disease with hypertension and diabetes. Transphenoidal removal of the adenoma would be curative and is the first-line treatment option. Glucagon is used for the treatment of severe hypoglycaemia when the patient is unconscious or unable to receive glucose orally. The excess secretion of growth hormone in acromegaly results in increased insulin resistance and diabetes. Some patients require dietary intervention only, oral hypoglycaemic agents or insulin. In this case, there is insufficient information regarding the glycaemic control of the patient and whether he will require insulin or not. In any case, priority is the treatment of acromegaly since diabetes usually subsequently resolves. Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used for the treatment of prolactinomas as an alternative to cabergoline. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist and is a third-line treatment when surgery, radiotherapy and somatostatin analogues are not effective.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of ischaemic heart disease treated with multiple medications is admitted to the Emergency Admissions Ward with diarrhoea and lethargy. She apparently became unwell with gastroenteritis some 48 hours before admission. Colleagues in the Emergency Department have begun potassium replacement therapy, but the nurses ask you to see her because she still feels 'washed out'. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 105/67 mmHg and a pulse of 85 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft, but there is left-sided tenderness, in keeping with the diarrhoea. Despite 3 litres of fluid replacement (with potassium), the potassium level is still 3.2 mmol/l (2.9 on admission). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Check calcium and treat if low
B. Check magnesium and treat if low
C. Give more potassium via central line
questions.explanation: Hypokalaemia is often resistant to correction with replacement therapy where there is coexisting hypomagnesaemia. Bearing in mind that diarrhoea is associated with substantial magnesium loss, the magnesium level should be measured and corrected if hypomagnesaemia is noted. Giving more potassium via central line will be less effective than first correcting any coexisting hypomagnesaemia. Coexisting hypocalcaemia should have no effect on the body's ability to correct potassium levels. Given diarrhoea is associated with volume loss, amiloride, a potassium-sparing diuretic, is inappropriate in this situation. Starting oral potassium supplements will be less effective than first correcting the magnesium level.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Pregnancy Diabetes Clinic having failed a trial of two weeks' diet and exercise. Her first child was a normal size at birth. She is now 20 weeks pregnant. She has no prior medical history of note. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result Fasting plasma glucose | 6.9~mmol/L Oral glucose tolerance test at 2 hours | 11.4~mmol/L What is the most appropriate next step in this case?
options: B. Diet and exercise advice only
questions.explanation: This woman has gestational diabetes, as evidenced by a raised fasting and 2 h blood glucose. Abnormal glucose tolerance occurs as a de novo event in around 2-3% of pregnant women; unfortunately their long-term risk of subsequent type 2 diabetes is as high as 40-50%. The aim of treatment is to keep blood glucose readings to around 7 mmol/l or below, and to allow mothers to give birth normally (although a number should deliver at 38 weeks' gestation due to excess fetal growth). Women should be offered a further glucose tolerance test at the 6-week check, to rule out the possibility of continued abnormal glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes. Studies have demonstrated that where metformin is instigated as initial therapy, maternal and fetal outcomes are no worse than where patients are prescribed insulin first line, and women gain less weight in pregnancy with greater overall treatment satisfaction scores. Basal bolus insulin therapy is the next intervention when blood glucose levels escape target despite maximal tolerated oral metformin. Although one trial has shown that glibenclamide is effective in controlling blood glucose in pregnancy, it is associated with weight gain and risk of hypoglycaemia, meaning that metformin is preferred. Diet and exercise advice only runs the risk of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia and subsequent adverse fetal outcomes. This is particularly a problem as further weight gain in pregnancy will only exacerbate insulin resistance and worsen glycaemic control. Although oral acarbose does reduce Gl carbohydrate absorption, no large trial of effectiveness in pregnancy has been carried out.

questions.question: A 58-year old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) following collapse. In his possession are empty prednisolone boxes, and he has a steroid user card. He has obvious rheumatoid features on examination and his chest X-ray (CXR) is shown below. He is given intravenous (IV) fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg on lying and 75/40 mmHg on standing. His pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Sodium (Na+) | 131~mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.7~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Urea | 7.8~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 105 umol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Which one of the following would be the most useful addition to the current management?
options: A. Thyroid function test before giving steroids
D. Oral prednisolone 20 mg and fludrocortisone 50 µg
E. Oral prednisolone 40 mg and fludrocortisone 50 µg
questions.explanation: The history of rheumatoid arthritis and steroid user card suggests the patient is on steroids. The fact that he has empty boxes in his possession may mean that he has run out of steroids. As he currently has a pneumonia (the CXR shows multifocal consolidation, worse in the right upper lobe), his need for steroids will be higher than normal. These should be given IV to ensure they are absorbed. Fludrocortisone is often used in the treatment of Addison's disease at a dose of 50-300 µg. There is no indication that this patient has Addison's. Even in new diagnoses of Addison's, mineralocorticoid replacement is not necessary in the acute phase. This is because high-dose hydrocortisone has a mineralocorticoid effect. It is important not to delay the administration of steroids as the patient is systemically unwell and may have missed a number of doses. Oral formulations of steroids are inadequately absorbed and therefore not appropriate in patients who are systemically unwell. Fludrocortisone is often used in the treatment of Addison's disease. There is no indication that this patient has Addison's. Even in new diagnoses of Addison's, mineralocorticoid replacement is not necessary in the acute phase.

questions.question: You review a 32-year-old man with a history of type 1 diabetes who is complaining of tiredness, lethargy and weight loss. He also tells you that he has fainted on three occasions over the past 2 months. He admits to nausea and vomiting. He has been working in Spain for some months. On examination, he is very thin and you notice he is tanned. His blood pressure is 102/65 mmHg, with a postural drop of 12 mmHg on standing. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Thyroxine (T4) | 5.7 pmol/l (10-22) | 10- 22 pmol/l Sodium (Na ) | 132 mmol/l | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.2 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Glucose | 5.8 mmol/l | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Urea | 9.1 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L He has a normochromic, normocytic anaemia. Which one of the following is the best way to diagnose the cause of his symptoms?
options: A. 9 am cortisol and ACTH measurement
questions.explanation: This man has adrenal insufficiency until proven otherwise. This is illustrated by his blood picture of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (levels may have been blunted by vomiting), raised urea and normochromic normocytic anaemia. Nine am cortisol and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) levels are a very sensitive way to detect adrenal insufficiency, with inappropriately low cortisol levels compared to raised ACTH levels indicating a positive diagnosis. Around 70% of cases of adrenal insufficiency occur due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands, adrenal insufficiency occurring with increased frequency in patients with a history of type 1 diabetes or other autoimmune disease. Malignant destruction and infection by tuberculosis are other possible causes. Given this patient has increased skin pigmentation, hypoadrenalism related to adrenal rather than pituitary failure is much more likely here, and hence CT head is not of value. Thyroid dysfunction is likely to be as a result of the severe non-thyroidal illness, and antibody testing is therefore of no value here. Raised thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and reduced T4 levels are often seen at the point of diagnosis of hypoadrenalism. Commencing thyroid hormone replacement may actually worsen the adrenal crisis, and thyroid function testing should be repeated a few weeks after stabilising glucocorticoid replacement. Relative dehydration and increased urinary sodium loss are both likely consequences of hypoadrenalism. Urine assay of sodium and osmolality won't, however, determine the underlying cause. Transferrin saturation is useful in diagnosing haemochromatosis, which does present with increased skin pigmentation, although this is against a background of a type 2 diabetes-like picture with arthritis and erectile dysfunction due to low levels of testosterone.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner, as he is concerned that he has not been experiencing signs of puberty like his peers. He denies any other symptoms and has no past medical history of note. On examination, he is tall but has underdeveloped muscles, and he lacks any facial hair. He has small testicles that measure 4 1~cM2 on orchidometry, and there is little surrounding pubic hair. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Luteinising hormone (LH) | 0.5~mlU/ml | 1.3-8~mlU/ml Testosterone | 2 nmol/l | 10-30 nmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is a cause of delayed puberty due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which is caused by a failure in the development of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurones in the hypothalamus. Along with delayed puberty, reflected in this patient's presentation of small testicles and little pubic hair, patients most typically demonstrate anosmia. Klinefelter syndrome is a reasonable differential diagnosis. It is associated with the 47,XXY karyotype and presents with tall stature, lack of secondary characteristics and infertility. However, Klinefelter syndrome is a cause of primary hypogonadism and in such patients, LH levels would be raised. In contrast, this patient's blood results demonstrate hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Anabolic steroid abuse can cause secondary hypogonadism. However, there is nothing in this history to suggest this is the cause. This patient has underdeveloped muscles; if this were the cause, you would expect overdeveloped muscles. Congenital adrenal hypoplasia is a rare cause of secondary hypogonadism. It presents in childhood with failure to thrive and salt-wasting, which leads to severe disease, resulting in severe volume depletion and electrolyte abnormalities. It is highly unlikely that a patient would reach adolescence without having been previously diagnosed. Haemochromatosis may cause iron deposition in the pituitary gland, which can lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (as demonstrated by this patient's blood results). Typically, haemochromatosis presents after the age of 40 in men and therefore does not tend to cause delayed puberty.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman sees her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of persistent fatigue and difficulty losing weight. She often feels cold and has been constipated. She discussed these symptoms with her mother, who advised that she see her GP because she had experienced similar symptoms when she was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which autoantibody is she most likely to have in her blood?
options: E. Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor stimulating antibody (TSAb)
questions.explanation: These antibodies occur in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are found in patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises iodide ions which is needed for the production of thyroxine and antibodies against this enzyme, therefore, prevent the production of thyroid hormones. This therefore results in autoimmune hypothyroidism. The exact cause is unknown, but Hashimoto's thyroiditis is thought to be more likely to occur if there is a family history of the condition. TSAb antibodies are usually present in Graves' disease and result in stimulation of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. This results in the overproduction of thyroid hormones, and leads to symptoms associated with thyrotoxicosis (tremor, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhoea etc) rather than hypothyroid (proximal myopathy. bradycardia, hypothermia, constipation etc). 21-Hydroxylase antibody is most common in patients with primary hypoadrenalism (Addison's disease). It occurs in 80-90% of patients with this condition and is not associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies are associated with type I diabetes mellitus and stiff person syndrome and are not associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. These antibodies are typically measured when type I diabetes is suspected and is particularly useful if there is diagnostic doubt about which type of diabetes the patient has.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman signs on with a new General Practitioner (GP) and has some routine blood tests. It is after these blood tests that the GP notices a raised corrected calcium level of 2.80~mmol/L and a raised parathyroid hormone (PTH) at 9 pmol/l. There is no history of renal stones, fractures or psychiatric disturbance. Other renal and liver function testing is unremarkable, full blood count is normal and there is no suspicion of underlying malignancy. Bone mineral density is at the lower end of the normal range. Which is likely to be the most appropriate way to manage this woman?
options: D. Calcium and vitamin D therapy
questions.explanation: Definite indications for surgery in hyperparathyroidism, the most likely diagnosis here (American National Institutes of Health consensus) include markedly elevated corrected serum calcium (>3 mmol/l), previous marked hypercalcaemic episode, impaired renal function, renal stones, nephrocalcinosis, substantially elevated urinary calcium and reduced bone mineral density. Patients with hyperparathyroidism kept under observation require annual plasma calcium, renal function and blood pressure checks, repeat bone mineral density check every 2-3 years and renal ultrasound scan. Any significant deterioration in the clinical condition would be an indication for surgery. Surgery should be carried out by a surgeon who does more than 20 parathyroidectomies per year. In parathyroid adenoma the affected gland should be removed; hyperplasia may be managed with partial parathyroidectomy or complete parathyroidectomy, with medical treatment for hypoparathyroidism. In this scenario the patient has mild hypercalcaemia, with no symptoms and no end-organ damage (i.e. nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis), and therefore there is no indication for surgical intervention. Common clinical indications to commence menopausal hormone replacement therapy are: to relieve vasomotor symptoms, to improve urogenital symptoms (long-term therapy is required), to prevent osteoporosis. Oestrogen therapy in postmenopausal women has been shown to cause a small reduction in serum calcium (up to 0.25~mmol/l) without a change in parathyroid hormone. Oestrogen also has beneficial effects on lumbar spine and femoral neck bone mineral density. However, due to risks associated with oestrogen replacement, it should not be used for the sole purpose of treating primary hyperparathyroidism. Calcium replacement is not indicated in primary hyperparathyroidism, since it would deteriorate the hypercalcaemia. Vitamin D can be administered cautiously and at a lower dose in the context of deficiency. Primary hyperparathyroidism can cause mild hypophosphataemia through increased phosphaturia. Phosphate replacement therapy is not indicated.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic with a 4-month history of lethargy and increased urination, particularly at night. She has a past medical history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, for which she takes levothyroxine 125 µg daily. She denies smoking, alcohol and recreational drug use. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, her cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Sodium (Na+) | 144~mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.6 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Urea | 6.8 mmol/l | 1.8-7.1~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 110~  mu mol/L | 50-90~  mu mol/L Glucose | 5.5~mmol/l | 4-7 mmol/l Free thyroxine (T4) | 8.1 pmol/l | 7.9-14.4~pmol/L Plasma osmolality | 320~mOsm/kg | 275-295~mosm/kg Urine osmolality | 220~mosm/kg | 500-800~mosm/kg Results following water deprivation test: Investigation | Result | Normal value Plasma osmolality | 340~mosm/kg | 275-295~mosm/kg Urine osmolality | 290~mosm/kg | 500-800~mosm/kg What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: E. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
questions.explanation: This patient has a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus, given the history of lethargy, polyuria and nocturia, combined with high plasma osmolality and low urine osmolality. Diabetes insipidus can have a central or nephrogenic origin due to deficiency in vasopressin or renal resistance to vasopressin, respectively. There are numerous risk factors for developing diabetes insipidus, including pituitary disease, traumatic head injury, autoimmune disease (eg Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and chronic kidney disease. The initial investigation of choice for diabetes insipidus is a water deprivation test that classically shows an inability to concentrate the urine to preserve plasma osmolality. The persistently low urine osmolality following a water deprivation test confirms a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. This patient is at higher risk of primary adrenal insufficiency, given her autoimmune history. Patients may present with similar symptoms, including fatigue and signs of hypotension. However, due to a lack of mineralocorticoid production, these patients are often hyponatraemic and hypotensive due to salt wasting secondary to lack of Na reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. latrogenic diuretic use is a possible differential diagnosis and would cause a similar picture of low urine osmolality and raised serum osmolality. However, there is often a history of a mental health condition or an eating disorder. A common diuretic that is taken is a loop diuretic such as furosemide. Furosemide can often cause hypokalaemia, making it less likely to be the underlying cause of this patient's presentation. The presentation of diabetes insipidus and primary polydipsia can be similar. However, following the water deprivation test, there should be an expected rise in urine osmolality (>700~mosm/kg) in those with primary polydipsia. The lack of response is more suggestive of diabetes insipidus. Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) presents with low plasma osmolality and raised urine osmolality, as patients have higher serum concentrations of antidiuretic hormone. Therefore, patients with SIADH have increased water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of nephrons and dilutional hyponatraemi3953

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with amenorrhoea. She has not had her first period and feels concerned as her friends all went through puberty several years ago. There is no known medical history or family history of note. On examination, she is 125 cm tall with a weight of 55 kg. Her chest is broad with absent breast development. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Oestradiol | 40 pmol/l | 75-1000 pmol/L Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | 40 mlU/ml | 2-20 mlU/ml Luteinising hormone (LH) | 221  x10^9/L | 1.1-110 mlU/ml Prolactin | 200 IU/ml | 59-619 IU/ml Thyroxine (T4) | 6.5 pmol/L | 7.9-14.4 pmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 10 mU/L | 0.5-5 mU/l Total human chorionic gonadotropin | 1 U/L | < 3 U/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has presented with primary amenorrhoea. She has a primary ovarian insufficiency, given the low oestradiol and raised gonadotropin (LH, FSH) levels. This is combined with a short stature of 125 cm, raised BMI (35~kg/M2) absent breast development and a broad chest, which are all features of Turner syndrome. Autoimmune disorders are associated with Turner syndrome, including hypothyroidism and it is not uncommon to see a raised TSH or low thyroxine level. A pituitary adenoma can cause primary or secondary amenorrhoea. The most common cause of a pituitary adenoma is a prolactinoma. However, the normal prolactin level makes this diagnosis unlikely. Other features of a prolactinoma include lactation, which is not seen here. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal-recessive disorder associated with virilisation at birth, premature adrenarche and precocious puberty. It does not cause primary ovarian failure or absent development of secondary sexual characteristics. Hypothyroidism is an important differential diagnosis to consider, as it is a cause of primary or secondary amenorrhoea. The blood tests show there is a low thyroxine and raised TSH level which indicates hypothyroidism. High BMI is another feature of hypothyroidism. However, short stature and absent breast development are more likely to represent an alternative diagnosis, such as Turner syndrome. It is important to remember that Turner syndrome is associated with autoimmune conditions, including hypothyroidism and this is the most likely reason for the deranged thyroid function tests. Polycystic ovarian syndrome is a common endocrinopathy in young women and is a cause of primary amenorrhoea. It is associated with hyperandrogenism, oligomenorrhoea and metabolic syndrome, with high BMI and insulin resistance. Although it is very important to consider as a differential diagnosis given its prevalence, polycystic ovarian syndrome does not cause short stature or absent breast development.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman was admitted to the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) after a road traffic accident. There were multiple long bone fractures and significant bleeding, and she required a period of mechanical ventilation due to a chest injury. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, which is managed with indapamide, and obesity with a BMI of 31. During her recovery, the orthopaedic surgeons noticed a small goitre. Results obtained 6 days after admission: Investigation | Result | Normal values Free Thyroxine (FT4) | 4.1 pmol/l | 5.8-17.8 pmol/L Free tri-iodothyronine (T3) | 1.5 pmol/l | 5.0-10.0 pmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 0.5 mu/L | 0.4-5.0 mu/l Random cortisol | 1250 nmol/L at 0900 h | 200-700 nmol/L at 0900 h Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her thyroid disorder?
options: E. Repeat thyroid function testing in 3 months
questions.explanation: This patient has a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level, which suggests that she is suffering from 'sick euthyroid' syndrome. This condition, characterised by low tri-iodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) and low or normal TSH, is associated with severe illness and frequently occurs in patients admitted to the ITU. Most physicians advise repeating thyroid function testing in a few months; there is no evidence that patients benefit from thyroid hormone replacement. This patient's level of cortisol is entirely appropriate given her admission to the ITU and road traffic accident. While she is obese, the possibility of co-existent Cushing's disease is unlikely. It might be appropriate to repeat a morning cortisol level a few more weeks into her recovery. Resolution of the underlying illness (in this case the trauma and subsequent surgery) is enough to correct thyroid function. Replacing thyroid hormone, even at low dose, risks driving symptoms of thyrotoxicosis and potentially hindering recovery. Thyroxine 100 mcg/day will drive suppression of TSH and symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Resolution of thyroid dysfunction, accompanied by restoration of T3 and T4 levels, occurs within a few weeks. Thyroid hormone levels are depressed as a result of the acute illness, and thus there is no value in suppressing thyroid hormone production further. Given that T3 and T4 are low, like carbimazole, there is no reason to institute therapy here.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for advice about his blood glucose control. He has suffered a number of significant hypoglycaemic episodes over the past 2 months, which have corresponded with a wish to increase his exercise. He is currently running 15 km per week in 5 km blocks. He takes BD mixed insulin and doesn't alter his dose on the days he exercises. On examination his BP is 125/78 mmHg and his BMI is 27. There are no signs of peripheral neuropathy. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 131 g/L | 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) | 7.6  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 210  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 138 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.4 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine | 90 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/l HbA1c | 50 mmol/ml (6.73%) | < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management with respect to glucose and weight management?
options: A. Reduce his BD mixed insulin dose on the days he exercises
B. Advise him to reduce his exercise
C. Advise him to transfer to a basal bolus regime
D. Advise him to maintain the same insulin dose and take a source of sugar with him when he runs
E. Reassure him that he will adjust to the lower blood sugar and his hypos will subside
questions.explanation: Whilst some patients with type 1 diabetes prefer to take a BD mixed insulin regime because of convenience and number of injections, it is not responsive to changes in routine such as taking intensive aerobic exercise. As such, he should be persuaded to change to a basal bolus regime where he can alter his short-acting insulin dose just prior to when he is planning exercise. This will blunt some of the benefits of exercise in driving a calorie deficit. Reducing his BD insulin is likely to precipitate an increase in his HbA1c because his glucose outside periods of exercise will increase significantly. Exercise is important with respect to maintaining fitness and reducing cardiovascular risk in type 1 diabetes. As such, aiming to reduce his exercise is inappropriate. This runs the risk of reducing awareness of significant hypoglycaemic episodes.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the clinic for review by her GP. She has been worried as she has suffered weight gain of 3 kg over the past 3 months and has not had a period for the past 2 months. There is also some breast tenderness and a feeling of fullness. On examination she looks well and has a normal BP of 125/75 mmHg; other features are entirely normal. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 121 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.6  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/l Platelets | 192  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 140 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.7 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 100 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Prolactin | 1600 mU/L | < 400 mU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prolactin levels rise rapidly in pregnancy, and the symptoms of amenorrhoea, breast fullness/tenderness and weight gain fit very well with this underlying diagnosis. A urine pregnancy test is easily accessible, and should represent the investigation of choice for this patient. Prolactin levels in microprolactinoma are usually slightly higher than those seen here. Although hypothyroidism classically presents with weight gain, it also usually features menorrhagia, whereas this patient reports a two-month period without a period. In macroprolactinoma a much greater rise in prolactin would be expected, with symptoms of optic chiasm compression. PCOS is associated with weight gain, irregular heavy periods and symptoms of hyperandrogenism.

questions.question: A 25-year-old postman presents for review. He is 6 feet 4 inches tall and has signs of delayed puberty and infertility on examination, notably small testes with scanty pubic hair. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | 35 u/L | 1-7 u/l Testosterone | 5 nmol/L | 9-25 nmol/l Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: This is 47XXY, or Klinefelter syndrome. Klinefelter syndrome which is leading cause of primary hypogonadism (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) affects 1 in 1 000 males and involves the loss of Leydig cells and seminiferous tubular dysgenesis. Treatment is with androgen replacement unless testosterone levels are normal. No treatment is possible for associated infertility. Chromosomal disorders such as Klinefelter syndrome, which occur due to loss, gain or rearrangement of one or more chromosomes, have no clear pattern of inheritance and carry a low risk of inheritance in relatives. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism occurs in hypopituitarism, selective gonadotrophin deficiency (eg Kallmann syndrome), systemic illness or severe weight reduction. Fragile-X syndrome is associated with macro-orchidism and learning difficulties in males. We can see from the blood results that FSH is significantly elevated, ruling out hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 and is of course associated with learning difficulties, rather than the specific features of hypoandrogenism seen here. Fragile-X syndrome is associated with learning difficulties and macro-orchidism rather than the small testes seen here. Kallmann syndrome is caused by defective release of GnRH, due to failure of development of the olfactory bulb. LH and FSH are reduced, and patients suffer from anosmia.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man with a history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is managed with a basal-bolus insulin regime comprising glargine and Novorapid™™. He has had type I diabetes since the age of five and has trouble with peripheral neuropathy. On examination his BP is 115/70 mmHg with a postural drop of 10 mmHg, and his BMI is 29. There is glove-and-stocking peripheral neuropathy. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 129 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 184  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 80 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L HbA1c | 56 mmol/mol | < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Urinary ACR | 7.5 mg/mmol | < 3.5 mg/mmol Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step with respect to reducing the risk of renal progression of microvascular complications?
questions.explanation: Evidence suggests that even with normal blood pressure, patients with type 1 diabetes derive benefit with respect to progression of renal disease after micro-albuminuria has become established from angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition. As such, even though his BP is in the normal range it is appropriate to trial this patient on ramipril. Although HbA1c is slightly above target, a dose adjustment for normal eating (DAFNE) course is more appropriate initially versus moving to an insulin pump. Although attaining BP target is important with respect to reducing the risk of microvascular complications, in this case with a systolic BP of 115 mmHg, ACE inhibition is the more appropriate intervention. Metformin may help with weight control in patients with type 1 diabetes and have a small impact in reducing HbA1c, although studies are not powered to detect any impact on outcomes. Given that there is evidence to support use of ACE inhibitors in this situation, reassurance alone is not appropriate.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is overweight and has problems with acne and hirsutism affecting her face and upper chest. She only has a period once every three to four months, and when they occur, they tend to be very heavy. She currently abstains from sexual intercourse and does not wish to become pregnant. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/90 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular. You confirm a male pattern of hirsutism and acne affecting her face and upper chest. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32~kg/M2 Investigations: Investigations | Results | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 131 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 197  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 4.6 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine | 103 mmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Fasting glucose | 6.2 mmol/l | < 7 mmol/l Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | 30 IU/L | 1-25 U/L Luteinising (LH): FSH ratio | 2.1 U/L | 1.1 U/L Testosterone | 4.2 nmol/L | 0.2-2.9 nmol/L Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to control her symptoms?
questions.explanation: This woman has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), for which weight loss is the mainstay of therapy. Greater than 5% loss in weight is associated with improvements in acne, hirsuitism and menstrual regularity, and will also impact on the elevated fasting glucose seen here. In patients who cannot achieve weight loss by lifestyle alone, pharmacological intervention using agents such as high-dose liraglutide may be appropriate. Finasteride is primarily used for reducing hirsuitism and acne in PCOS. In this patient, weight control and managing impaired fasting glucose are important, and only weight loss represents a holistic solution for acne, hirsuitism and impaired fasting glucose. Clomifene is the most appropriate option for ovulation induction. In this case, given her BMI of above 30 and impaired fasting glucose, weight loss is the most appropriate option with respect to long-term outcomes. Given this patient's BMI, she is at an increased risk for venous thrombosis with the oral contraceptive pill, although it may help regulate her menstrual cycle. Metformin is less effective than weight loss in reducing progression to type II diabetes, although it may impact on hirsutism and acne. It could be added in the event that weight loss is insufficient to improve symptoms and fasting glucose.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman was referred to the Genetics Clinic after presenting with intermittent nausea and vomiting and associated abdominal pain. There is concern that she has an inherited disorder, the pattern of which is demonstrated in the genogram below. She has had depression since her teenage years and a peptic ulcer requiring hospital admission last year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the correct answer, as the presenting symptoms are all encompassed by this diagnosis. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is a hereditary endocrine cancer inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. While cancers begin to develop from the teenage years, symptoms tend not to present for several years. The abdominal symptoms with the long history of depression are secondary to parathyroid hyperplasia (95% of patients) and resulting hypercalcaemia. The peptic ulcer is secondary to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, occurring in 75% of MEN1 patients. Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism is an overarching description for genetic disorders which cause hyperparathyroidism without accompanying pathology and is a diagnosis of exclusion. There is no one gene associated with this disorder, and inheritance patterns are uncertain. Additionally, it does not explain the peptic ulcer disease described in the stem. FBHH presents with hypercalcaemia and moderately raised parathyroid hormone (PTH). This presents in an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Typically, most people with FBHH do not present with symptoms; the diagnosis is made based on biochemistry. Furthermore, this diagnosis would not explain the presence of the peptic ulcer, secondary to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. While the symptom pattern could be explained by MEN2 (specifically MEN2A), which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, there are no symptoms of medullary thyroid cancer such as a thyroid nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy. Nearly all patients with MEN2 have medullary thyroid cancer. Furthermore, there is no clear explanation for the peptic ulcer with this diagnosis. HDGC is an umbrella term used to describe a number of genetic anomalies linked to gastric carcinomas. They follow an autosomal dominant method of inheritance. While HDGC has been linked to breast and prostate cancers, there is no link to parathyroid adenomas or depression.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED), having suffered a very severe headache after chasing a man who was stealing his car. Previously fit and well and of normal stature, he was noted to be hypertensive on admission with a blood pressure (BP) of 165/90 mmHg, which later settled to 155/85 mmHg. On further questioning, it was noted that his mother was known to have had 'thyroid cancer', and died at an early age. His GP did routine bloods after he moved house a few months earlier and noted his calcium was elevated at 2.84 mmol/l. What is the most likely unifying diagnosis behind his presentation?
options: D. Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma syndrome
questions.explanation: The history of marked hypertension in this gentleman, coupled with a family history of thyroid carcinoma, should raise the possibility of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN). MEN-2a is characterised by medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid chief cell hyperplasia. It is likely that both this man and his mother carry the same mutation. Around 30% of carriers of an MEN-2a mutation never develop the associated clinical syndrome. The initial diagnostic investigation of choice for phaeochromocytoma is 24 h urinary catecholamine assay. Where the diagnosis is proven, it is sensible to screen for medullary thyroid carcinoma via pentagastrin testing. Conversely, where patients present with medullary thyroid carcinoma, they should be screened for phaeochromocytoma prior to consideration of surgery. Where adequate alpha blockade is not in place prior to surgery, there is a very real chance of hypertensive crisis and possible on-table myocardial infarction. VHL is associated with phaeochromocytoma, although it often presents earlier with balance disturbance due to the presence of CNS haemangioblastomas. MEN-1 is associated with multiple parathyroid adenomas, pancreatic islet cell tumours and pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas being most commonly seen). MEN-2b tends to occur as a sporadic mutation; additional features compared to MEN-2a include a marfanoid habitus and multiple mucosal neuromas. Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma syndrome is associated with the RET mutation, although presentation with phaeochromocytoma would not be expected.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to the endocrine clinic for review. He has been taking amiodarone for the past few months for short episodes of VT diagnosed after a myocardial infarction. During the past 2 months, he has noticed weight loss and heat intolerance, with short runs of an irregular, fast heartbeat. In the clinic he has a BP of 112/82 pulse is 88 and regular. His BMI is 21. Thyroid function testing is abnormal, with a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) suggestive of thyrotoxicosis. Radioiodine uptake scan is normal, as is serum interleukin 6 (IL-6). A most recent ECHO cardiogram ejection fraction is 38%. His amiodarone is discontinued by the cardiologist after the repeat ECHO cardiogram and a 72 h tape, which shows paroxysmal AF but no episodes of VT. Which one of the following options is the best initial therapy for him?
options: B. Carbimazole and potassium perchlorate therapy
questions.explanation: This man probably has amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 1, as exemplified by the presence of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, normal radioiodine uptake and normal interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels. AIT type 1 results primarily from iodine excess and therefore increased hormone synthesis. Type 1 AIT is treated initially with a combination of anti-thyroid drugs and potassium perchlorate therapy. Radioiodine is ineffective at least initially in amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, because of the iodine load already delivered by amiodarone therapy. Prednisolone is a component of therapy for AIT type 2, which is thought to result from a direct toxic effect of amiodarone and is associated with thyroiditis, decreased radioiodine uptake on thyroid scan and raised IL-6 levels. Patients may eventually become hypothyroid because of the destruction of thyroid hormone-producing cells. Surgery should be avoided if possible in a patient with relatively unstable cardiovascular disease; in the event that it is required, acute control of thyroid status is first achieved with perchlorate therapy. It may be considered particularly in cases where amiodarone cannot be withdrawn. Partial thyroidectomy still involves surgical risk, and hence should be reserved for patients who fail to respond to medical therapy where there are no other options.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department for the second time in a month with a syncopal episode. She admits to tiredness, which has increased over the past few months, and says that she has never been keen on physical activity, even at school, because of muscle cramps and easy fatigue. Apparently, one other relative has similar symptoms. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 100/60 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. There is a postural drop of 10 mmHg on standing. Her BMI is 22. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 130 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.6  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 222  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 2.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 90 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO3) | 33 mmol/L | 22-29 mmol/L Glucose | 4.3 mmol/L | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Gitelman syndrome is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner. It presents with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and a metabolic alkalosis. The mutation causing this condition results in a loss of function of the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney. This history provides clues to the genetic nature of the diagnosis by highlighting other relatives with the same symptoms. Bartter syndrome is a condition characterised by hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and hypotension, as seen here. However, typically Bartter syndrome presents in early childhood making the diagnosis less likely here. Classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder in which the production of mineralocorticoids is impaired. This leads to hyperkalaemia as well as significant dehydration from salt-wasting. Further virilisation is a key presenting feature, resulting from increased production of excessive sex steroids. These symptoms typically present in childhood. Conn syndrome is the eponymous name for primary hyperaldosteronism, in which excess aldosterone is released from the adrenal gland. This leads to hypokalaemia. Unlike this clinical scenario, Conn syndrome presents with hypertension. Cushing syndrome results from excess corticosteroids and can lead to hypokalaemia. However, typically patients develop obesity and hypertension (neither of which is present in this case).

questions.question: A 33-year-old female auxiliary nurse presents for review. She has had difficulty with managing her hypertension and is currently taking atenolol 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg, yet her blood pressure is still raised at 165/80 mmHg. She takes beclomethasone 100 mcg BD for asthma, but nil else of note. On examination, she has a body mass index (BMI) of 29, with no obvious abdominal striae. Fasting blood results: Investigation | Result | Normal values Sodium (Na+) | 140 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 2.8 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 90 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/l Bicarbonate HCO3 | 40 mmol/L | 22-29 mmol/l Glucose | 7.1 mmol/l | < 5.9 mmol/L What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: Adrenal adenomas can account for hyperaldosteronism, the likely cause of the profound hypokalaemia and resistant hypertension seen here. Small aldosterone-producing adrenal adenomas are commoner in young women, whereas bilateral adrenal hyperplasia tends to occur later and is commoner in men. The best test for Conn syndrome is to look at renin/aldosterone levels, with antihypertensive medication having been discontinued for around 3 weeks if possible. This is because the pre-existing antihypertensive medications can impact upon the renin:aldosterone ratio. Clearly the diagnosis would be supported if aldosterone levels were raised in the presence of depressed renin levels. Fibromuscular hyperplasia is a cause of hypereninaemic hyperaldosteronism. Although it does cause hypertension, the marked reduction in potassium despite angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition as seen here would not be expected, and a rise in creatinine associated with ACE inhibition would be likely. Diabetic nephropathy fits the criteria for diabetes mellitus, although this is most likely early and is a chance finding here and not the cause of her hypertension. Renal dysfunction in type 2 diabetes is more commonly seen in older individuals and is a product of both sustained hypertension and diabetic nephropathy itself. Cushing syndrome is unlikely given her BMI of 29 and the lack of obvious serious truncal obesity. Essential hypertension is not associated with the marked hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis on blood picture seen here.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man presents complaining of loss of libido and impotence. He finds work and entertaining clients very stressful. Results of blood tests from GP were prolactin 3200 mU/L (< 360), normal thyroid function tests, MCV 100 fl, testosterone low. He admits on further questioning to drinking three glasses of wine per night. There is no reported visual field disturbance. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his impotence?
questions.explanation: This patient's prolactin results are above 3000 mU/l, which is suggestive of a prolactinoma. The diagnostic test of choice would be MRI pituitary; microprolactinomas appear as hypo-intense lesions within the pituitary on T1-weighted scanning. Given the fact that there are no signs of optic chiasm compression, and this patient's thyroid function tests are normal, it would be reasonable to give him a trial of dopamine agonist therapy. Surgery would be kept in reserve for this man if he was resistant or intolerant to drug therapy. Elevation in prolactin due to compression of pituitary stalk is smaller than that seen here. Craniopharyngiomas are less likely to present with hyperprolactinaemia and more likely to present with diabetes insipidus, adrenal failure or pituitary-dependent hypothyroidism. Other focal neurological deficits as a result of local compression are also more likely to be seen. Although there is evidence of alcohol abuse, including the raised MCV, this is unlikely to be the main cause of his problems. Levels of prolactin are usually above 6000 mU/L in macroprolactinoma.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with intermittent double vision on upward gaze. He has diplopia, maximal on looking left and looking down. Examining his eyes, he has mild bilateral proptosis and his eyes look normal, looking straight ahead. His pupils are equal and have normal direct and consensual light reflexes. He is able to look up and down for 10 seconds without tiring. He has no weakness or fatigability in any peripheral muscles. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Free Thyroxine FT4 | 18 pmol/l | 11-22 pmol/l Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | 3.2 μυ/L | 0.17-3.2 μυ/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The differential diagnosis for an eye movement abnormality, which cannot be explained by a single or multiple cranial nerve palsy, is either myasthenia gravis or Graves' disease. Myasthenia is unlikely, as the patient can look up freely for long periods of time. Graves' eye disease can occur with normal thyroid function. The diagnosis can be made by looking for thyroid-stimulating receptor antibodies in the serum. Sixth nerve palsy, or abducens nerve palsy, is a disorder associated with dysfunction of cranial nerve VI (the abducens nerve), which is responsible for causing contraction of the lateral rectus muscle to abduct the eye. The inability of an eye to turn outward results in a convergent strabismus or esotropia, of which the primary symptom is diplopia (commonly known as double vision) in which the two images appear side by side. The condition is commonly unilateral but can also occur bilaterally. The unilateral abducens nerve palsy is the most common of the isolated ocular motor nerve palsies. A complete oculomotor nerve palsy will result in a characteristic down-and-out position in the affected eye. The eye will be displaced outward and downward - outward because the lateral rectus (innervated by the sixth cranial nerve) maintains muscle tone compared to the paralysed medial rectus. The eye will be displaced downward because the superior oblique (innervated by the fourth cranial or trochlear nerve) is non-antagonised by the paralysed superior rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique. The affected individual will also have a ptosis, or drooping of the eyelid, and mydriasis (pupil dilation). Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction in which circulating antibodies cause fluctuant skeletal muscle weakness. Ninety per cent of patients with myasthenia gravis develop ophthalmologic manifestations of the disease, characterised by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Variability in the muscle weakness is a hallmark of myasthenia. The pathophysiology of adult MG is a reduced number of acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the postsynaptic muscle membrane due to circulating anti-AChR antibodies or, less commonly, to antibodies to muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (anti-MuSK), LRP4 and agrin. Myasthenia gravis can mimic almost any painless, pupil-sparing ocular motility disorder, including internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Ptosis may be unilateral or bilateral. The ptosis may be elicited with sustained upward gaze or on repeated eyelid closure. In this case, the patient didn't display any fatigue on physical examination. Fourth cranial nerve palsy, also known as trochlear nerve palsy, is a condition affecting cranial nerve IV, the trochlear nerve, which causes weakness or paralysis to the superior oblique muscle that it innervates. This condition often causes vertical or near-vertical double vision, as the weakened muscle prevents the eyes from moving in the same direction together. Since the fourth cranial nerve is the thinnest and has the longest intracranial course of the cranial nerves, it is particularly vulnerable to traumatic injury.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of difficulties with conception. She is overweight, and has acne and hirsutism. She had an ultrasound recently which noted polycystic ovaries supporting a diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Which hormone excess has caused the hirsutism?
questions.explanation: Androgens are excessively produced by the ovaries in PCOS. This is in part due to an increase in luteinising hormone (LH) levels which are secreted from the pituitary gland. Raised androgens cause symptoms such as hirsutism, conception difficulties and acne. Elevated prolactin might be measured in a patient who is struggling to conceive, or in patients with known PCOS, since prolactin will be raised in around 30% of patients. However, while raised prolactin would impair the chances of conception, it would not account for the hirsutism seen in this patient. Anti-Müllerian hormone is made by preantral follicles and therefore may be raised in PCOS, but it does not cause hirsutism. It does not cause any specific symptoms itself, but a raised level would point towards PCOS. Elevated 17 hydroxy-progesterone may be measured in a patient who presents with hirsutism, as this would point towards a diagnosis of late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia which would cause excessive androgen production, resulting in hirsutism. However, in this case, the patient has known PCOS. SHBG tends to be low in PCOS, rather than circulating in excessive levels. The low level of sex-hormone-binding globulin contributes to the excessive free androgens which circulate and cause hirsutism.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man is admitted to hospital with pneumonia and hyponatraemia with a sodium of 116 mmol/L. He was treated with antibiotics and rapid infusions of 3% hypertonic sodium chloride, but despite initial improvement deteriorated neurologically with fits and subsequent coma the following day. What is the possible cause of his deterioration?
options: A. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
questions.explanation: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, previously known as central pontine myelinolysis, occurs as a result of too-rapid correction of hyponatraemia; ideally correction should not exceed more than 10-12 mmol/l in 24 hours. There is demyelination of the central basal pons or other areas of the brain. Various types of neurological deficits have been described from quadriparesis to coma and death. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the investigation of choice to demonstrate classical demyelination. Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a clinical symptom due to a build-up of cerebrospinal fluid. It is characterised by an abnormal gait, urinary incontinence and potentially reversible dementia. SIADH is defined by hyponatraemia and hypo-osmolality due to inappropriate, continued secretion of ADH despite normal or increased plasma volume, which results in impaired water excretion. In this scenario the sodium was corrected prior to fits. Stroke would not occur as a result of rapid correction of sodium. There is no indication of viral infection in this case. Encephalomyelitis is not associated with sodium correction.

questions.question: A 75-year-old lifelong smoker is seen by his General Practitioner (GP) with a five day history of wheeze and ankle swelling. He is prescribed diuretics along with some other medications but continues to deteriorate. His blood pressure (BP) is 110/60 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg. His pulse is 90 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Sodium (Na+) | 133 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 5.0 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Urea | 28 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 200 μmol/l | 50-120 µmol/l Bicarbonate HCO3 | 16 mmol/l | 24-30 mmol/l Arterial blood gas reveals the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values pH | 7.11 | 7.35-7.45 pCO2 | 7.0 kPa | 4.6-6.0 kPa pO2 | 6.5 kPa | 10.5-13.5 kPa Which one of the following diagnoses best explains the clinical picture and these biochemical results?
options: A. Mixed picture of COPD and cardiac failure with renal hypoperfusion
C. Pre-kidney disease secondary to diuretics
E. Acute kidney disease and fluid overload
questions.explanation: This patient has a respiratory acidosis (pCO2 > 6.5 kPa, pH < 7.35 and hypoxia) and a metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate). It's very likely that he has an element of COPD with chronic CO2 retention and a degree of pulmonary oedema. Treatment with diuretics then leads to renal hypoperfusion, resulting in metabolic acidosis. Severe COPD would produce a respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, which would be reflected by raised bicarbonate level on the ABG. Pre-kidney disease on its own would not cause carbon dioxide retention and hypoxia. Symptoms of acute aspirin (acetyl salicylic acid) toxicity include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, tinnitus, vertigo, altered mentation, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hyperpyrexia and coma. Salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory centre leading to increased rate (tachypnoea) and depth of respiration (hyperventilation). This leads to a fall in pCO2 and respiratory alkalosis. Later, metabolic acidosis occurs due to accumulation of lactic and other organic acids. The most common acid-base presentation is that of mixed respiratory alkalosis-metabolic acidosis. Acute kidney disease and fluid overload would lead to a metabolic acidosis, with perhaps a degree of disordered gas exchange related to pulmonary oedema. It would not directly cause carbon dioxide retention and wheeze.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) because she has fallen twice in the past 2 days. On one occasion, this occurred when she got up out of bed in the morning, and she felt light-headed before falling to the floor. On the other occasion, she had been sitting in a long business meeting, and when it finished, she stood up and again felt light-headed before collapsing. She does not think she lost consciousness on either occasion, and she was not drowsy after the episodes. She did not experience incontinence or bite her tongue. She has otherwise been well recently and does not report any fever. She has a history of poorly-controlled type I diabetes mellitus, for which she takes insulin although she sometimes forgets doses. She has an unremarkable cardiovascular, abdominal, and ear, nose and throat examination. There is no nystagmus. The GP performs an electrocardiogram (ECG), which shows normal sinus rhythm and a QTc interval of 434 milliseconds. What is the likeliest cause of the falls in this patient?
questions.explanation: Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication of diabetes, which can result in postural hypotension and falls. Characteristically, the blood pressure falls rapidly after standing due to a neuronal failure to ensure vasoconstriction. Lying and standing blood pressure measurements would confirm this diagnosis. A fall of   ge 20 mmHg in systolic pressure or of   ge 10 mmHg in diastolic pressure within 3 minutes of standing is abnormal. The fall in blood pressure typically occurs within 2-5 minutes of it being measured. The ECG here shows normal sinus rhythm and a QTc interval of 434 milliseconds (normal). Peripheral neuropathy may occur in many diabetic patients, and this may lead to ulcers which may cause falls, but this would not cause dizziness, as seen here. The normal ECG, along with the lack of any mention of palpitations and the convincing history for postural hypotension, makes an arrythmia less likely. Labyrinthitis can cause dizziness which may cause a person to fall. Typically, dizziness tends to be constant, particularly at first; this is in contrast to this patient, whose dizziness is episodic and situational. The absence of nystagmus also makes this diagnosis less likely. There are no features to suggest that seizures are the cause of this patient's falls. She did not experience any loss of consciousness, tongue biting, incontinence or postictal symptoms, and the context of this patient's history on a background of diabetes makes autonomic neuropathy a more likely cause of the falls.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of galactorrhoea for the past few months. She has a past medical history of chronic kidney disease (requiring peritoneal dialysis), previous hyperthyroidism (successfully treated with carbimazole which was subsequently stopped 2 years ago), and Raynaud's syndrome for which she takes nifedipine. The GP performs a blood test which confirms hyperprolactinaemia (1250 mu/l). What is the most likely cause of hyperprolactinaemia in this patient?
questions.explanation: In CKD, patients may develop hyperprolactinaemia. This is due to the effect of uraemia on the hypothalamus, reducing the release of dopamine which promotes prolactin release. In addition, there is an impaired ability to metabolise prolactin in the kidney: this also contributes to the hyperprolactinaemia, which can cause galactorrhoea. Sexual intercourse, and in particular orgasm, causes a transient rise in prolactin levels, not sexual abstinence. This is thought to be due to negative feedback following orgasm on neurons that regulate sexual motivation and function and therefore contributes to sexual refractoriness. Dopamine receptor agonists, such as bromocriptine, reduce the secretion of prolactin as they increase the inhibition of prolactin secretion. Dopamine receptor antagonists, such as metoclopramide, have the opposite effect and can cause hyperprolactinaemia. Hypothyroidism can cause hyperprolactinaemia, while hyperthyroidism does not. The cause of this is not clear, but hypothyroidism causes thyrotropin hyperplasia in the pituitary gland and sometimes lactotroph hyperplasia as well, which results in hyperprolactinaemia. Verapamil can cause hyperprolactinaemia, but not other calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine. The cause of this is not clear.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man attends the Endocrine Clinic along with his wife with a history of infertility. His General Practitioner (GP) had noted that the patient has gynaecomastia. He had mumps at age eight, and broke his arm aged 14. Otherwise, he has no past history of note. He is on no regular medications. On examination, he is tall, with sparse secondary sexual hair pattern. His testicular volume is less than 5 ml. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value 9 am testosterone | 4 nmol/l | 6-27 nmol/L Luteinising hormone (LH) | Elevated |  Follicle stimulating-hormone (FSH) | Elevated |  What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Low testosterone in the presence of raised LH and FSH suggests gonadal failure. Gynaecomastia and infertility are the two commonest presentations of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY karyotype), which is often but not inevitably associated with reduced secondary sexual characteristics. Oestrogen-producing adrenal tumours are rare and should not result in primary hypogonadism. Adrenocortical adenomas are associated with pituitary tumours in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, but in this case would cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Kallmann syndrome is typified by either anosmia or severe hyposmia. It is also associated with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. Testicular failure following mumps is a rare complication and only occurs following mumps orchitis when contracted after puberty. A pituitary adenoma will cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, resulting in both the LH and FSH being reduced.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic and given a diagnosis of Cushing's disease with a 0.9 cm pituitary adenoma. He has multiple medical problems including severe hypertension currently managed with three agents, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and morbid obesity. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 166/95 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 38. He has bilateral lower limb swelling with severe varicose veins. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 141 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.9  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelet (PLT) | 258  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 3.5 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 132 µmol/l | 50-120 μmol/L Glucose | 15.1 mmol/l | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Proceed directly to trans-sphenoidal resection
questions.explanation: This patient has severe Cushing's with multiple complications including poorly controlled hypertension, diabetes and obesity. As such he is at significant operative risk. Ketoconazole is an effective agent for control of cortisol synthesis prior to surgery. It acts on several of the P450 enzymes, including the first step in cortisol synthesis, cholesterol side-chain cleavage, and conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. A daily dose of 600-800 mg often decreases cortisol production significantly and will help in controlling blood sugar and blood pressure before moving to pituitary surgery. Whilst trans-sphenoidal resection is the preferred option given the presence of a pituitary adenoma, the patient is a high operative risk given his co-morbidities of severe hypertension, poorly controlled diabetes and morbid obesity making this option not the best of those available. Mitotane is used in the treatment of adrenal cancer, rather than in the treatment of pituitary adenoma or Cushing's. Pituitary radiotherapy is considered in patients who have persistently raised adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), but this is usually reserved for patients who have undergone surgery. This patient is too high an operative risk given his multiple medical problems. In addition, he does not have an adrenal adenoma requiring adrenalectomy. The mechanism for ACTH production is via the pituitary adenomas.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by the police. She is convinced that her husband is trying to poison her. Her husband tells you that she is hardly sleeping and seems almost hyperactive at present. She has a first child who is four months old. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 150/85 mmHg, with a pulse of 100 beats per minute (bpm) and atrial fibrillation (AF). Eye examination and thyroid palpation are normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 125 g/l | 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) | 5.7  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 282  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.8 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 90 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/l Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | < 0.05 μU/L | 0.17-3.2 μU/L T4 | 31.2 pmol/L | 11-22 pmol/L Anti-microsomal antibody | + | Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-partum thyroiditis presents with hyperthyroidism in around 1/3 of sufferers some 1-4 months post-delivery. In rare cases thyrotoxicosis may be associated with a psychotic presentation, as seen here. The period of hyperthyroidism is followed by hypothyroidism and then resolution of the condition in the majority of patients; however, 1/3 of women develop permanent hypothyroidism, in which case permanent thyroid replacement is required. Graves' disease is associated with TSH receptor antibodies. However 50-80% with graves disease may have positive anti microsomal antibody. This patient does not have any other features of graves disease and hence it is less likely. The time of presentation is more consistent with post-partum thyroiditis, and patients with Hashimoto's present with hypo-, not hyperthyroidism. Post-partum psychosis can be excluded because of the abnormal thyroid function tests, suggesting that the psychological disturbance is related to thyrotoxicosis. Atrophic thyroiditis is rare, occurs in women aged 40-60 years and is associated with hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman with a history of type II diabetes mellitus comes to the Diabetes Clinic for review. She has been taking metformin for the last three years but is gradually losing control of her blood sugars, with multiple readings of > 10 mmol/l throughout the day. Her current metformin dose is 1 g twice daily (BD). She has a history of hypertension, which is currently managed with ramipril and indapamide. On examination, her BP is 155/85 mmHg and her heart rate is 67 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 32 kg/m² Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 124 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.1  x10^9/l | 4.0=11.0  x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 102 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) | 62 mmol/mol | < 48 mmol/mol Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: This patient is obese and is outside the guidance for good haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) control set by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) at 58 mmol/mol for HbA1c; as such, she requires therapy intensification. Out of the options given, the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor is the most appropriate option because it results in modest calorie spillage into the urine and has positive effects on BP control. Patients, on average, see around 2% weight loss over six months, although in some, much greater weight reduction is seen. Evidence from cardiovascular outcomes among the class (the EMPA-REG study for empagliflozin) suggests a positive impact on cardiovascular outcomes. Sulfonylureas promote weight gain and increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. Glimepiride is therefore suboptimal as a therapy option for this patient.
