Although liraglutide is likely to drive greater weight loss compared to SGLT-2, it is not recommended by NICE guidelines to introduce a glucagon-like peptide 1 at this stage. It is recommended for patients with a BMI of over 35 kg/m². Glitazones promote weight gain and fluid retention, and over the longer term, have a negative impact on bone mineral density. They are therefore best avoided in a relatively young, obese woman. Dipeptidyl peptidase type IV (DPPIV) inhibitors are a possible option after metformin and do not increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. SGLT-2 inhibition, however, is preferred because it promotes greater weight loss and may be associated with positive cardiovascular outcomes, whereas DPPIV inhibitors have a neutral effect on cardiovascular outcomes in reported studies.

questions.question: A 73-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) for his yearly medication review. He has a past medical history of osteoporosis, depression and heart failure. His medications include alendronate, bisoprolol, citalopram, furosemide, ranitidine and spironolactone. His GP performs some routine blood tests, which reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 144 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.3  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 173  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Urea | 6.3 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 73 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Sodium (Na+) | 142 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 2.9 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Which medication is the most likely to be causing the hypokalaemia?
questions.explanation: Furosemide is a diuretic that acts on the kidney and causes electrolyte disturbances, most typically hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and hypochloraemia. It does this by inhibiting the luminal sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter which prevents reabsorption of sodium, chloride, and potassium in the thick ascending loop of Henle. It is, therefore, the most likely culprit medication in this case. Ranitidine is used to treat acid reflux and does not tend to cause electrolyte disturbances. It may be given instead of omeprazole, which may cause hyponatraemia and hypomagnesaemia. Ranitidine may cause nausea or constipation. Alendronate is used to treat osteoporosis. It reduces the action of osteoclasts and may cause hypocalcaemia, but not hypokalaemia, as seen in this patient. Citalopram is used to treat depression and is a potential cause of hyponatraemia as it can cause syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). It does not, however, cause hypokalaemia. Spironolactone is used to treat heart failure and can cause hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) after collapsing at home. She remembers walking to the dining room when she felt faint, had chest tightness and collapsed. When she woke up she called an ambulance. Over the last two years, she has seen her General Practitioner (GP) for chest tightness, palpitations, and dyspnoea, which lasted for minutes at a time. In the last few months, she had developed non-specific pins and needles in her extremities and 'spots before her eyes'. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol socially. Her GP started her on a tricyclic antidepressant two weeks ago for depression. Her mother died of a stroke at age 48. On examination, she is alert, but notably restless, afebrile and has moist palms. Her pulse is 108 beats per minute (bpm) and regular and her blood pressure (BP) is 180/70 mmHg. She has a 2/6 pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex. Chest (including chest X-ray (CXR)) and abdominal examinations are normal, as is a neurological examination. An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm. Urine testing reveals glucose++ and blood+. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 189 g/l | 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) | 6.0  x10^9/l | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 471  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 144 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 3.1 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 75 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Urea | 4.2 mmol/L | 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Glucose | 9.5 mmol/L | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.56 mmol/L | 2.20-2.60 mmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) | 6 mg/L | < 10 mg/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phaeochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-producing tumour within the adrenal gland. (The 'rule of tens', ie 10% familial, 10% are bilateral, 10% are extra-adrenal, 10% are malignant, is no longer tenable, as approximately 30% of phaeochromocytomas are familial; the tumour location and malignancy risk are variable). There is an association with multiple endocrine neoplasia type II in familial cases, and also with the von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome predisposes patients to renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas. As a result, patients may have raised haemoglobin due to a secondary increase in erythropoietin production. This patient does have a raised haemoglobin and therefore needs to be screened for von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Patients present with a variety of symptoms including episodic hypertension, chest tightness, abdominal pain, vomiting, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, pallor and weakness. Symptoms are precipitated by sneezing, stress, surgery and by agents such as cheese, alcohol and tricyclic antidepressants. Glycosuria occurs during attacks in 30% of cases. Tests that help in diagnosis include 24-hour metanephrines measurement, meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) and CT/MRI of the adrenal glands. Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction. Duration of symptom/sign is < 24 h. A normal neurological examination makes this diagnosis unlikely. Cardiac arrhythmias mimic several medical disorders as they can present with symptoms of palpitations (due to arrhythmia per se) or may be due to the haemodynamic consequences (dizziness, syncope, chest pain, light-headedness, weakness, breathlessness, anxiety). In this case, the presence of other features suggestive of phaechromocytomas makes this answer unlikely. Mastocytosis is a condition characterised by excessive mast cell accumulation in one or multiple tissues, and is further divided into two categories: cutaneous mastocytosis (limited to the skin) and systemic mastocytosis, which involves extra-cutaneous organs like the bone marrow and gastrointestinal tract. The most common symptoms are pruritus on exposure to heat or physical irritation and the presence of urticarial pigmentosa, which are yellowish to reddish-brown papules seen on the extremities, chest and abdomen. Coronary vasospasm always presents with predominant chest pain with or without symptoms of nausea, sweating, dizziness, dyspnoea and palpitations. Diagnosis is based on ECG changes of transient ST-segment elevation at the time of an episode and absence of high-grade coronary stenoses on coronary arteriography.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic complaining of frequent falls. On two occasions he has fainted and knocked his head and had to be taken to the Emergency Department, and at other x he was dizzy, but a short period sitting down improved things for him. He has a history of peripheral neuropathy and erectile dysfunction. He takes a basal bolus insulin regime involving insulin glargine and meal time Novorapid™™. He also takes ramipril 5 mg/day for renoprotection and indapamide 2.5 mg. On examination his BP is 145/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 35 mmHg systolic. He has signs consistent with peripheral sensory neuropathy to the mid-shin. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 122 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.4  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 201  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine | 122 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L HbA1c | 50 mmol/ml (6.73%) | < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
questions.explanation: This patient has peripheral neuropathy and almost certainly has significant autonomic neuropathy, which accounts for the large postural drop in his blood pressure. A standing BP of 110 mmHg systolic is clearly acceptable, and therefore the most obvious first step is in stopping his indapamide and monitoring his blood pressure over the subsequent 2-4 weeks. If he still has significant postural hypotension then the next steps would be to add elastic stockings, followed by fludrocortisone. The history of pre-syncope is much more suggestive of changes in blood pressure rather than changes in blood glucose. Excess background insulin is primarily associated with fasting hypoglycaemia, which is not the cause of this patient's collapse given the obvious postural hypotension. Elastic stockings are a potential intervention for patients who have persistent postural hypotension despite discontinuing the thiazide-like diuretic. Fludrocortisone is considered for patients who fail to respond to conservative measures such as elastic stockings. The postural drop in blood pressure points to hypotension rather than hypoglycaemia as the cause of this patient's collapse.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman consults her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of lethargy. She is currently taking fluoxetine for postnatal depression, her child now being five months old. Other past history of note is type I diabetes mellitus, for which she is using a basal bolus insulin regime. Her thyroid hormone tests reveal a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of 7 mU/L (normal range: 0.4-5.0 mU/l) and a free T4 of 8.0 pmol/l (normal range: 10-22 pmol/l). Anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Which of the following most accurately represents her prognosis?
options: A. She is likely to progress rapidly to thyrotoxicosis
B. She is more likely to become euthyroid than to remain hypothyroid
C. She is more likely to remain hypothyroid than to become euthyroid
D. Corticosteroids can improve the chances of becoming euthyroid
E. Permanent thyroxine replacement therapy is likely to be needed
questions.explanation: Postpartum thyroid dysfunction is said to occur in 5-10% of women during the first year after the birth of a child. Hyperthyroidism is said to occur within the first 4 months of pregnancy, the only symptom of which may be tiredness, with hypothyroidism occurring later, at the 3-7-month stage. Often symptoms are mild and non-specific. Spontaneous recovery occurs in the majority of patients within 6-12 months of delivery, although around 40% eventually go on to develop permanent hypothyroidism. Risk of permanent hypothyroidism isn't closely related to the anti-TPO titre at the end of pregnancy because titres progressively fall during the course of pregnancy. In patients with postpartum hypothyroidism, low-dose thyroxine (e.g. 50 µg) may be used to allow for spontaneous recovery to occur with re-checking of thyroid function off therapy after 6 months of treatment. There is no role for corticosteroids in treatment. The hyperthyroid phase presents with non-specific symptoms and may pass undetected. Patients either then become euthyroid or hypothyroid. Around 40% of patients develop permanent hypothyroidism. Long-term thyroxine replacement is only necessary in those patients who develop permanent hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of lethargy. She works in the local pharmacy and has had to ask for increasing amounts of time off work. Apparently there is no past medical history of note, apart from some trouble due to an eating disorder as a teenager. On examination, she looks normal. Her BP is 105/64 mmHg. Her BMI is 20 kg/m². Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 121 g/l | 115-155 g/L White cell count (WCC) | 4.6  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 200  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 134 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 3.1 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 90 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO3^) | 34 mmol/L | 24-30 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient works in a pharmacy, so it is possible she has access to medicine, and we hear she has a history of an eating disorder as a teenager. Thiazide abuse would result in exactly this picture, with normal BP, hypokalaemia and high bicarbonate. Primary hyperaldosteronism is associated with hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, rather than the normal blood pressure seen here. Bartter syndrome may present with a similar biochemical picture, although access to diuretics given she works in a pharmacy is much more likely to be the cause of her symptoms. Although Gitelman syndrome may also present with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, it differs from Bartter in that it is associated with reduced calcium excretion. Liddle syndrome is associated with hypertension, and hence cannot be the diagnosis here. It is caused by a mutation in the epithelial sodium channel.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for a 6-month review after surgery for a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. She presented to the General Practitioner originally with changes in her facial appearance, soft tissue swelling affecting her hands and feet, and impaired glucose tolerance. Her glucose metabolism has returned to normal. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 70 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m² Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 130 g/L | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.2  x10^9/l | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.4 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 90 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Glucose | 5.1 mmol/L | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) | Just above the upper limit of normal |  Which of the following would be most likely to occur as a long-term consequence of acromegaly?
questions.explanation: The underlying diagnosis here is that of acromegaly due to the history of the typical clinical features of growth hormone excess in the setting of a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. Cardiovascular complications are common in acromegaly, including hypertension, arrythmias, biventricular hypertrophy, systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction. This is in direct response to increased levels of growth hormone and IGF-1 causing increased cardiac contractility and increased calcium uptake. The cardiovascular effects have been indicated to reduce life expectancy as much as ten years on average in comparison to the general population. Uncontrolled acromegaly (evidenced by high IGF-1 level) also leads to higher rates of sleep apnoea and insulin resistance. While there is an association between acromegaly and colon cancer (up to 5% of all acromegalic patients) a much higher number of patients have premalignant polyps (up to 30% of all acromegalic patients). Duodenal ulcers are associated with gastrin secreting pancreatic cancers; however, these tumours are rare and duodenal ulceration is not the commonest association with acromegaly. The soft tissue swelling associated with acromegaly gives rise to sleep apnoea. Up to one third of acromegalic patients suffer from obstructive sleep apnoea and treatment of acromegaly variably effects rates of sleep apnoea, but there does tend to be some remission in symptoms following surgery, as per this patient's presentation. Benign uterine tumours are associated with acromegaly rather than uterine cancer.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman who is known to have autoimmune hypothyroidism presents with nausea, vomiting and lethargy. Medication of note includes thyroxine and the oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 110/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 70/min; she has a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing and her pulse increases by 10/min. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 105 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.4  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 201  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 124 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 132 µmol/l | 50-120 μmol/L Calcium (Ca+2) | 2.56 mmol/L | 2.2-2.6 mmol/L There are areas of depigmented skin, as seen in her right hand below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: D. Isolated new onset Addison's disease
questions.explanation: This is the commonest subtype, and includes autoimmune Addison's disease in combination with thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus. There are associations with other autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia, which could explain the anaemia, and primary hypogonadism, vitiligo and myasthenia gravis are also commonly observed. Gastroenteritis is a self-limiting infectious illness causing diarrhoea and vomiting, and is not normally associated with anaemia or hyponatraemia. Type 1 polyglandular syndrome is associated with mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison's disease. The normal calcium here effectively rules out hypoparathyroidism. It also encompasses both autoimmune hypoparathyroidism and hypoadrenalism. This lady possibly does have a new diagnosis of Addison's disease, but in view of her other autoimmune history this option is incorrect. Patients with pernicious anaemia typically present with progressive symptoms of anaemia (breathlessness, chest pain, lethargy) or symptoms of B12 deficiency (motor-sensory polyneuropathy and eventually subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord). It is caused by autoimmune atrophic gastritis, with the presence of anti-parietal cell antibodies.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with a seven year history of type II diabetes has been diagnosed with background diabetic retinopathy at his annual review. He was also recently admitted to hospital with an episode of cardiac failure after an anterior myocardial infarction (MI). He is taking gliclazide 80 mg twice a day as he has failed to tolerate metformin. On examination, his body mass index (BMI) is elevated at 35 kg/m². A recent Hb A1c reading was 7.1%. His blood pressure (BP) 154/85 mmHg. Proteinuria is positive and total cholesterol is 5.4 mmol/l with a high-density lipoprotein (HDL) level of 0.7 mmol/L You are considering switching his blood glucose-lowering medication because of recent weight gain. Which of the following is the most appropriate switch therapy with respect to overall cardiovascular risk in this patient?
questions.explanation: Blood glucose-lowering medications in the GLP-1 and SGLT2 inhibitor class have been shown to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). As such, empagliflozin, which causes glucose excretion and can have positive effects on weight, reduces cardiovascular death and incident cardiac failure, is the most appropriate choice. Although liraglutide has shown a positive effect on MACE, lixisenatide has not shown an impact on MACE events in a secondary prevention type 2 diabetes population. Insulin has no effect in reducing cardiovascular risk, and indeed may increase the risk of heart failure in patients with type 2 diabetes. As such, it is best avoided here. Saxagliptin showed no positive impact on MACE events, although its use was associated with a small increase in cardiac failure episodes during the course of a cardiovascular outcome trial. Sitagliptin shows no positive impact on MACE events, although unlike saxagliptin the use of sitagliptin did not increase the risk of cardiac failure in the context of its cardiovascular outcome trial.

questions.question: A 38-year-old South-Asian man is referred to the Outpatient Clinic. He is currently undergoing treatment for tuberculosis, which is known to involve the renal tracts in this case. The only other past history of note is hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. The infectious disease doctor has referred him to you because of some abnormal tests, which reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) | 6.5 μυ/L | 0.17-3.2 μυ/L Free T4 | 8.4 pmol/l | 11-22 pmol/l Potassium (K+) | 5.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Sodium (Na+) | 131 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/l Computed tomography (CT) scan | Adrenal calcification |  His blood pressure (BP) in the clinic is actually low with a systolic of 100 mmHg. Which of the following actions would be most appropriate in this case?
options: C. Arrange a short synacthen test
questions.explanation: This man is not acutely unwell and you have time to confirm the diagnosis of hypoadrenalism with a short synacthen test. If this is positive then you would consider commencing hydrocortisone replacement. The low BP, coupled with the low sodium and raised potassium, raise the suspicion of hypoadrenalism in this case. Adrenal antibody testing can be extremely helpful in elucidating the cause of suspected adrenal failure. The adrenal calcification suggests the possibility of tuberculosis infection, so that anti-adrenal antibodies are unlikely to be helpful here. His thyroid function tests are abnormal, but you would not commence thyroid hormone replacement at this stage. Commencing thyroxine in a patient with hypoadrenalism may precipitate a rapid deterioration in their condition. It would be most important to confirm the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency, commence steroid hormone replacement and then re-check the thyroid function testing later. Autoimmune thyroid dysfunction is commonly associated with Addison's. Although the suspicion is that this patient is hypo-adrenal, this is likely to be secondary to TB rather than an autoimmune cause. Fludrocortisone replacement is not normally required in the acute stage in the treatment of hypoadrenalism, but can be added once the dose of hydrocortisone is reduced after a few days.

questions.question: A 18-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with diabetic ketoacidosis. He is subsequently diagnosed with type I diabetes mellitus and commences insulin, to which he adapts well. After 3 months of treatment, he begins to feel very dizzy, and, upon checking his capillary blood glucose (CBG), he finds that it is 2.8 mmol/L This happens on three consecutive days. On the fourth day, he decides to stop his insulin treatment, and he subsequently monitors his CBG throughout the day. During the day, his CBG ranges between 5.3-10.2, and he feels well with no dizziness. What is the likeliest cause of the hypoglycaemia seen in this patient?
questions.explanation: Many patients experience a 'honeymoon period' after they are diagnosed with type I diabetes. This typically occurs after around 3 months of treatment and occurs because residual beta islet cells in the pancreas are still able to synthesise a small amount of insulin. The precise mechanism is not understood, but patients tend to require less insulin or even no insulin while it lasts, which can be from months to years. An insulinoma is a rare cause of hypoglycaemia and would not be consistent with the episode of diabetic ketoacidosis and the subsequent diagnosis of type I diabetes. Insulinomas typically present with repeated episodes of unprovoked hypoglycaemia. Adrenal insufficiency does not cause diabetic ketoacidosis, which is what led to the diagnosis of type I diabetes in this patient. Adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycaemia, but he would need steroid treatment to feel better, whereas this patient felt better simply after he stopped the insulin treatment. It is possible that the patient was administering himself too much insulin, but this is less likely to occur suddenly after 3 months of treatment, and this patient adapted well when he was started on insulin. Since this patient was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis and was then successfully treated for type I diabetes for 3 months, it is unlikely that he was misdiagnosed. Given the timing of the symptoms, it is more likely that the hypoglycaemia is due to a 'honeymoon period' and in the future, he will require insulin when this period ends.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman who is 10 weeks' pregnant is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by her General Practitioner (GP). She is suffering from a great deal of tiredness and morning sickness. The GP is concerned about her thyroid function. She has lost 2 kg in weight over the past month. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 115/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 65 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) | 0.2 μυ/L | 0.17-3.2 μυ/L Free T4 | 27 pmol/l | 11-22 pmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: A. Ask GP to repeat thyroid function tests in 2 months
questions.explanation: Suppressed TSH with a small rise in free T4 is a normal finding in 13.5% of women in the first trimester, and 4.5% of women in the second trimester. Hyperemesis gravidarum is the most likely underlying condition. The suppressed TSH with slightly elevated levels of T4 is due to the partial thyroid-stimulating action of beta-HCG. No specific management is indicated. Thyroid function tests are likely to have returned to normal on retesting. Thyroidectomy is indicated for Graves' disease in pregnancy where medical therapy with thionamides is ineffective or contra-indicated. At this stage of pregnancy, without overt symptoms of hyperthyroidism and with TSH and T4 only slightly outside the normal range, thionamides aren't indicated. Like propylthiouracil, carbimazole isn't indicated, because the overserved thyroid blood tests seen here are a normal physiological finding. Radioiodine is contra-indicated in pregnancy, and treatment isn't indicated because the thyroid function tests seen here are not as a result of thyrotoxicosis, but as a result of excess beta-HCG.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology clinic with a 3-week history of anxiety and palpitations. She reports that even when she is resting, she finds that she is tremulous. There is no history of chest pain or shortness of breath and she is eating and drinking well, although she is having difficulty maintaining her weight. She is 18 weeks pregnant. Examination reveals a BP of 125/82 mmHg and a heart rate of 95 bpm and regular. She has a fine resting tremor bilaterally. There is a small, smooth goitre, which is mildly tender on palpation. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | < 0.05 U/L | 0.4-5.0 U/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: It seems this patient has Graves' disease presenting in pregnancy. Although block-replace is the standard intervention outside pregnancy, it cannot be used here as thyroxine does not cross the placenta and there will be a risk of fetal hypothyroidism. Carbimazole is the safest option in the second and third stages of pregnancy, and the dose is titrated to a target TSH level of 0.2-3.0 IU/L. Propranolol is a beta blocker that is generally prescribed with significant caution in pregnancy, as beta blocker use in pregnancy has been shown to be associated with intrauterine growth restriction, fetal bradycardia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are indicated for pain relief in patients suffering from subacute thyroiditis. They are less useful in treatment of Graves' disease and should be avoided in pregnancy. Propylthiouracil has been reported to cause maternal hepatotoxicity after the first trimester. As such, carbimazole is the preferred option for antithyroid therapy. Propylthiouracil is not recommended after the first trimester, and thyroxine does not cross the placenta. Therefore, if block-replace is used where antithyroid drugs are maximised, fetal hypothyroidism is precipitated. This is not an appropriate option because of the use of propylthiouracil and because block-replace is not recommended.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with newly diagnosed type II diabetes. He reports that he leads a healthy lifestyle and is surprised about the diagnosis. His past medical history includes hypertension, which is managed with amlodipine and indapamide. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 88 bpm. His cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable, although he appears to be clammy and sweating. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is soft tissue swelling of his hands and he reports having had to remove his wedding ring due to it feeling tighter than usual. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 149 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.0  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 300  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu moUl Random glucose | 12.1 mmol/l | 3.9-7.1~mmol/l Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm this patient's likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has a clinical picture consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. Usually, IGF-1 measurement varies with age and nutritional status; however, reference ranges exist for comparison. Additionally, IGF-1 has a long half-life and, as such, is a useful measure of growth hormone status. Failure of growth hormone to suppress in response to an oral glucose challenge is the other diagnostic method of choice for assessing patients with possible acromegaly, although this is less convenient following an initial clinic appointment. Although an elevation in fasting plasma glucose level may indicate a diagnosis of diabetes, it will not reveal the underlying cause, which, in this case, is likely to be acromegaly. Prolactin levels may be elevated because of local pressure effects from a pituitary adenoma. However, it will not confirm elevated growth hormone levels. The symptoms seen in this patient fit better with acromegaly, rather than with elevated cortisol levels as a result of hyperadrenalism due to either an adrenal or a pituitary tumour. Growth hormone is released in a pulsatile fashion and has a short half-life. As such, random measurement is not useful in confirming a diagnosis of acromegaly.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of tiredness and malaise, which came on after a short viral illness. She also has pain which appears to be referred to her lower jaw. On examination of the neck the thyroid gland appears to be generally tender and is nodular on palpation. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is measured at <0.05~mU/L (normal range: 0.4-5.0~mU/l) while her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is raised at 45~mm/hour and a technetium scan reveals decreased thyroid uptake. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: De Quervain's thyroiditis is the most common cause of a painful thyroid gland and causes hyperthyroidism initially, sometimes followed by transient hypothyroidism. The underlying cause is felt to be either a viral infection or the postviral inflammatory response. The condition is more common in females. The typical course of the disease consists of an acute phase, in which the main complaint is pain, although signs of hyperthyroidism may also be present. This is followed by a transient asymptomatic and euthyroid phase which evolves into the hypothyroid phase. The hypothyroid state may become permanent in 5-10% of patients, but the vast majority go on to the recovery phase, characterised by normalisation of thyroid structure and function. The treatment is consequently directed towards the control of pain and thyroid symptoms. Initial symptomatic hyperthyroidism can be treated with beta-blockade, but anti-thyroid drugs are of no value since the excess circulating thyroid hormone is due to the release of pre-existing thyroid hormone because of follicular damage rather than from increased synthesis. If hypothyroidism occurs in the late stages, replacement therapy is required and is guided by the TSH levels. Radionucleotide scanning reveals decreased uptake from the thyroid gland. Hashimoto's presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism. On examination there is often a hard goitre which is non-tender. Anti-thyroid peroxidise antibodies are usually raised. Riedel's thyroiditis is characterised by intense fibrosis of the gland. Most patients remain euthyroid. Symptoms of tracheal compression can occur. Radionucleotide scanning is useful in distinguishing between Graves' and other causes of thyrotoxicosis: it will show increased uptake in the whole gland in Graves' disease. Pyogenic thyroiditis is rare and is associated with a pyogenic infection elsewhere. Patients can present with pain and swelling in the neck. and fever. TFTs are often normal.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of polydipsia and polyuria. He is careful with his weight and regularly visits the gym, but still feels that his health is deteriorating and he is actually finding it difficult to maintain his weight and muscle mass. He also complains of diarrhoea and a skin rash which seems to break down and bruise/bleed easily. He has no past medical history, apart from a recent fall from his bike after which he sustained a head injury. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 135/85 mmHg. His pulse is 68 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 25~kg/M2 On dipstick urine testing, there are 2+ of glucose. Which of the following would best explain these findings?
questions.explanation: Glucagonoma is vanishingly rare, with an annual incidence estimated at 1 in 20 million, but it fits the bill here as the only potential cause of secondary diabetes mellitus from the options listed. The fact his weight is normal and he has developed diabetes whilst still maintaining a healthy weight and lifestyle is suggestive of secondary diabetes. Head injury can be a cause of transient diabetes insipidus that usually recovers slowly over the course of a few weeks. Autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with type 1 diabetes, but wouldn't account for the glycosuria seen here. Hyperparathyroidism may be associated with diuresis related to hypercalcaemia, but we are given no evidence here of elevated serum calcium. Insulinomas present with recurrent episodes of collapse due to hypoglycaemia, and gradual weight gain because of compensatory eating.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhoea. She has never had a menstrual period and reports no cyclical abdominal pain. She denies symptoms of hot flashes or night sweats. She has normal breast development (Tanner stage 4) and scant pubic hair (Tanner stage 2). Physical examination reveals a tall stature, a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus, but absent ovaries. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | 85 IU/L | 1.5-12.4 IU/L Luteinising hormone (LH) | 40 IU/L | 1.7-8.6 IU/L Oestradiol | Undetectable | 20-50~pg/ml Karyotype | 45.X |  What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?
options: B. Perform MRI of the brain to evaluate pituitary function
D. Schedule surgical evaluation for ovarian transplantation
E. Initiate cyclic progesterone therapy alone
questions.explanation: The patient has primary ovarian insufficiency likely due to Turner syndrome (45.X karyotype), which causes gonadal dysgenesis and leads to elevated FSH and LH levels. Combined oestrogen-progesterone therapy is recommended to promote secondary sexual characteristics, support bone health and initiate menstrual cycling. Progesterone alone would not be appropriate because the patient requires both oestrogen and progesterone for complete hormone replacement. Oestrogen is necessary for developing secondary sexual characteristics, and progestin is added to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. MRI of the brain is not necessary here because the elevated gonadotrophin (FSH and LH) levels indicate that the amenorrhoea is due to primary ovarian failure, not a pituitary issue. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism would present with low FSH and LH levels. Growth hormone therapy may be considered earlier in childhood for Turner syndrome to improve height, but it is generally less effective after puberty. This patient has already a tall stature, and hormone replacement is the priority at this stage. Ovarian transplantation is not a treatment option for Turner syndrome-related amenorrhoea. Instead, hormone replacement therapy is the standard management to prevent complications of oestrogen deficiency.

questions.question: A 50-year-old retired bank manager attended a 'Well Man' Clinic. He has always enjoyed good health, but has recently developed a dry cough. He takes daily over-the-counter multivitamin tablets. On examination, he is extremely well, with no abnormality detected. Screening investigations reveal: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Creatinine (Cr) | 80~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Urea | 5.0~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Haemoglobin (Hb) | 120 g/l | 135-175~g/l Potassium ( (K+) | 4.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Corrected calcium | 2.82~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/L White cell count (WCC) | 9.0  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L A repeat uncuffed sample with simultaneous plasma parathyroid hormone (PTH) level reveals: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Corrected calcium | 2.86~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/l Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 5.4 pmol/l | 0.9-5.4~pmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Plasma PTH is the best single test for differentiating between hypercalcaemia due to parathyroid overactivity and that due to non-parathyroid causes. Primary hyperparathyroidism can be associated with a plasma PTH level within the normal range. The normal response to hypercalcaemia is suppression of plasma PTH to below the lower reference limit. Levels within the reference limit are inappropriately high and suggestive of parathyroid disease. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is a hereditary disease with autosomal dominant transmission and is characterised by moderate chronic hypercalcaemia and normal or moderately elevated plasma PTH concentrations. The fractional excretion of calcium is lower than in primary hyperparathyroidism, and the urine calcium/creatinine ratio is usually <0.01. The importance of this condition is that hypercalcaemia rarely leads to significant clinical signs and parathyroidectomy is unsuccessful as therapy. Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Hypercalcaemia is a common feature in multiple myeloma where there is frequently calcium elevation, renal insufficiency, anaemia and bone disease. Ten to 15% of patients present with hypercalcaemia in multiple myeloma. The cause is multifactorial, but bone destruction from osteolytic tumour lesions is the main contributing factor. This would not be a cause because PTH and corrected calcium were repeated on an uncuffed sample, with persistent hypercalcemia. Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Hypercalcemia is common in sarcoidosis. This is due to an uncontrolled synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 by macrophages. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 leads to an increased absorption of calcium in the intestine and an increased resorption of calcium in the bone. Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Vitamin D excess is associated with hypercalcaemia because there is an increased absorption of calcium in the intestine and an increased resorption of calcium in the bone.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman complains that she urinates around 6 litres a day and is constantly thirsty. She has a past medical history of diabetes mellitus and bipolar disorder. She takes insulin and lithium and no other medications. She is referred to an Endocrine Clinic. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 134~g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.3  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 183  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Urea | 6.5~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 93~  mu~mol/t | 50-120~  mu~mol/l Sodium (Na+) | 162~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 3.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Random glucose | 13.5~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Water deprivation tests reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Urine osmolarity after fluid deprivation | 243~mOsm/kg | 800-1200~mosm/kg Urine osmolarity after desmopressin administration | 258~mOsm/kg | 1000-1200~mosm/kg What is the likeliest cause of the hypernatraemia seen in this patient?
options: E. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
questions.explanation: NDI would explain all the clinical findings of excessive urination and polydipsia along with the hypernatraemia and the results of the water deprivation test. The pathological problem is the reduced responsiveness of the kidney to antidiuretic hormone (in this case probably caused by lithium). Therefore the urine osmolality does not improve after the dose of desmopressin. CDI would result in hypernatraemia and the same symptoms, but the urine osmolality would improve to greater than 800~mOsm/kg after desmopressin administration. This is due to their being a cranial defect in the production of antidiuretic hormone, so when a synthetic hormone is given, there is a full renal response and improvement in the osmolality. An improvement in urine osmolality would evidence partial diabetes insipidus after administration of desmopressin where the osmolality increases to above 300~mosm/kg but remains less than 800 mOsm/kg. Primary polydipsia is caused by excessive drinking of fluids and may be seen in patients with a history of psychiatric disease such as this patient. However, the water deprivation results are not consistent with this diagnosis since the urine osmolality would be expected to be greater than 800 mOsm/kg, both after water deprivation and after desmopressin administration. This is because there is no defect in the production or sensitivity to antidiuretic hormone in this condition. Therefore when the fluid intake is reduced, there is a normal physiological secretion of antidiuretic hormone, which increases the osmolality. SIADH typically causes hyponatraemia rather than hypernatraemia. In SIADH, there is an excess of antidiuretic hormone, whereas diabetes insipidus is caused by a lack of, or resistance to, antidiuretic hormone.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman is brought into hospital critically ill and with a reduced level of consciousness. Her relatives state she has been increasingly lethargic over the past month and had put on weight. She had been slightly confused, with constipation, and was commenced on antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. She currently takes no regular medication. Her pulse is 55/min, blood pressure 125/98 mmHg, temperature 34 °C, respiratory rate 8/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Examination reveals coarse facial features with dry skin, thin hair and brittle nails. Initial investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values ECG | Sinus bradycardia |  Glucose | 5.9~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Urea | 15.2~mmol/l | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Sodium (Na ) | 127~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.8~mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 223~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L After giving her IV hydrocortisone, which other therapy would you consider?
questions.explanation: Myxoedema coma can be the initial presentation of hypothyroidism, but more usually occurs against a background of long-standing disease where patients are unable to comply with their thyroxine replacement. Patients will have a history of cold intolerance, weight gain, increasing lethargy and constipation. Facial features include general coarsening with periorbital oedema and hair thinning. This is an emergency, and treatment involves intravenous thyroxine and slow rewarming. It is also important to take serum for thyroid function and adrenal function. Coexisting hypoadrenalism is suggested by the hyponatraemia, the hyperkalaemia and a raised urea. Patients may also be hypoglycaemic, although that is not the case here. Treatment with hydrocortisone is recommended until Addison's disease can be excluded. It is important to provide hydrocortisone until Addison's is excluded, as just giving thyroid hormone alone may precipitate an adrenal crisis. The patient is hypothermic and she should be rewarmed slowly in order to improve the chance of neurological recovery. The patient has a normal blood pressure with bradycardia, and therefore there is no indication for aggressive fluid resuscitation. Moreover, she is hyponatraemic, and therefore the correction of sodium levels should be gradual in order to avoid central pontine myelinolysis. Hypertonic saline is indicated in cases of severe hyponatraemia (Na<115~mmol/l) presenting with seizures. In all other cases, hypertonic saline should be administered on ICU or after discussion with an endocrinologist. In our case, the patient is mildly hyponatraemic (Na 127~mmol/L) and this doesn't account for her level of consciousness. Demeclocycline is a semi-synthetic tetracycline antibiotic that can be used off-licence for the treatment of hyponatraemia caused by SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion). It works by reducing the responsiveness of the collecting tubule cells to ADH. In this case, the cause of the hyponatraemia is unknown although it could be due to adrenal insufficiency, and therefore demeclocycline would not be effective.

questions.question: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation has clinical evidence of hyperthyroidism. She is very anxious and complains of palpitations, heat intolerance and difficulty maintaining her weight during the pregnancy. On examination her BP is 120/70 mmHg, with pulse 95/min regular. There is no obvious goitre on neck examination. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 119 g/l | 115-155~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.4  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/t Platelets | 190  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 140~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K*) | 4.5~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 94~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) | <0.05~  mu U/L | 0.17-3.2~  mu U/L Anti-thyroid antibodies | +ve |  How would you propose to manage her?
questions.explanation: There are associated risks for both the fetus and the mother associated with untreated maternal thyrotoxicosis. Unfortunately, thionamides may also cross the placenta and precipitate fetal goitre and hypothyroidism. For this reason patients are usually managed with a dose which keeps their T4 just within the upper limit of the normal range. Carbimazole is associated with rare reports of fetal abnormalities, meaning that propylthioracil is often used in early pregnancy (3 months) with a later switch to carbimazole after the first trimester. Propylthiouracil is now rarely used in late pregnancy because of case reports of maternal hepatotoxicity. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because of accumulation in both the fetal thyroid and the mother's thyroid gland. Although propranolol will treat symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, it won't significantly impact on the risk of miscarriage. Prednisolone doesn't significantly impact on the progression of autoimmune thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy and therefore has no role here.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with headaches, sweating, anxiety and palpitations. She states that members of her family on her father's side have had similar symptoms and have required surgery. She is also complaining of polydipsia and constipation. On examination, her blood pressure is elevated at 165/92. She had two 24 h urinary collections for catecholamines, which were above the upper limit of normal. Her bone profile revealed: Investigation | Result | Normal values Corrected calcium (Ca2+) | 2.71~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7 mmol/L Phosphate (PO43) | 1.1 mmol/l | 1.1-1.45 mmol/l Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 19 pmol/l | 0.95.4 pmol/l Her physician would like to send her for genetic testing. Which condition would he like to test her for?
questions.explanation: Type 2 Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN 2) is a rare familial cancer syndrome caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. MEN 2A patients present with phaeochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia and medullary thyroid carcinoma. This condition [MEN 2B] is characterised by the presence of mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, along with phaechromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma. Clinical hallmarks of [Von Hippel-Landau disease] include the development of retinal and central nervous system haemangioblastomas, which are absent in this case. Moreover, hyperparathyroid hyperplasia is not part of the condition. The main components of MEN 1 are hyperparathyroidism and pituitary and pancreatic tumours. From the pituitary tumours, 25-90% are usually prolactinomas although growth hormone or ACTH secretion has also been described. The pancreatic tumours can be non-functioning, originating from the beta-cells (insulinoma) or originating from non-beta-cells and secreting other peptides such as glucagon, pancreatic polypeptide, somatostatin, chromogranin or gastrin. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is a genetic condition caused in the majority of cases due to loss of function mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) gene, expressed in parathyroid and kidney tissue. The perceived lack of calcium levels by the parathyroid leads to constitutively high levels of parathyroid hormone and therefore hypercalcaemia. Urine calcium/creatinine ratio has to be less than 0.01 in order to consider this condition as a cause for primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic cough with haemoptysis comes to the Emergency Room with severe vomiting and dehydration. His relatives tell you that he has suffered from the cough for over three months and has progressively lost weight. He smokes 40-50 cigarettes per day. On examination, he looks unwell and has a BMI of 18, with a BP of 95/70 mmHg and a pulse of 75/min. There are coarse crackles on auscultation of both lung fields. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 119 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.9  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 198  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 124 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 5.3 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine | 145 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/l What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has an underlying bronchial carcinoma, and whilst adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)-producing tumours are seen which lead to a Cushing-type picture, hypoadrenalism is usually related to the presence of metastases. Severe gastroenteritis with vomiting leads to hypokalaemia; in this case, given that the potassium is at the upper end of the normal range, another cause such as Addison's is more likely. This patient has likely got a lung malignancy, as evidenced by the left hilar mass seen on his CXR and the history. He is hypotensive and hyponatraemic, which is suggestive of adrenal insufficiency. The most common cause in this case would be adrenal metastases, and therefore adrenal metastases is the correct answer. A staging CT will help confirm the diagnosis. Autoimmune adrenal failure is possible but incorrect, as in the context of possible lung cancer, metastases is more likely. Small cell lung cancer has an association with inappropriate secretions of anti-diuretuc hormone (ADH), but it would not explain his symptoms of vomiting and hypotension. It also does not normally present so acutely. There are no infective symptoms to suggest that gastroenteritis is the underlying diagnosis in this case. You would also expect the electrolytes to reveal hypernatraemia associated with dehydration, as well as hypokalaemia from electrolyte loss. We have no abnormal blood tests to suggest an acute kidney injury.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant presents to her General Practitioner with a history of palpitations, sweating, and diarrhoea. She has no past medical history of note and her pregnancy has otherwise been unremarkable. On examination, she has a resting tremor. Her pulse is 100 bpm and regular. Her BP is 118/68 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. Her chest is clear and abdominal examination reveals a gravid uterus correct for her dates. Investigation reveals the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 126 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.2  x10^9/l | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 214  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) | 86 fl | 80-100 fl Sodium (Na+) | 142~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 62 µmol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/l Urea | 4.2~mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin | 6 µmol/l | 2-17 µmol/l Albumin | 38 g/l | 35-55 g/l Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) | 68 U/L | 30-150 U/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 26 U/L | 5-30 U/L Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | 0.01 μυ/ | 0.17-3.2 μυ/ι Free T4 | 36.4 pmol/l | 11-22 pmol/l She plans to breastfeed her baby after delivery. What is the most appropriate therapy?
options: B. Carbimazole till delivery and then switch to PTU
C. Propylthiouracil till delivery and then switch to carbimazole
D. Radioiodine therapy after delivery of the baby
E. Blocking dose of carbimazole with supplemental thyroxine
questions.explanation: The choice here is between carbimazole and propylthiouracil at a dose to control thyroid hormone levels without blocking them completely. What drives the choice between propylthiouracil and carbimazole in this situation is the adverse event profile. Cases of fatal hepatotoxicity have been described with propylthiouracil, and for this reason carbimazole is always recommended in late pregnancy. Neither is recommended in breastfeeding, although if the patient still wishes to breastfeed, switching to propylthiouracil post-partum is potentially the safer option. Lugol's iodine is occasionally prescribed for patients undergoing thyroid surgery, but causes goitre in infants. It is primarily used for short-term control of thyrotoxicosis. Propylthiouracil is not recommended here because of the risk of maternal hepatotoxicity. Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and it is recommended that patients avoid becoming pregnant for six months after therapy. It also presents logistical difficulties in that the woman would not be able to remain in close proximity to her baby for some time after dosing. Carbimazole crosses the placenta but thyroxine does not, so the 'block and replace' approach could render the neonate profoundly hypothyroid.

questions.question: You review a 62-year-old type 2 diabetic who is taking metformin 2 g per day and gliclazide 160 mg per day and ramipril for renoprotection. Recent HbA1c was 68.31~mmol/mol (8.4%) and his blood pressure was 140/75 mmHg. You review his eye photograph that reveals dot-and-blot haemorrhages, cotton wool spots and micro-aneurysms. None are within close proximity to the macula. Which of the following treatments represents the best option for reducing the probability of further deterioration of his diabetic retinopathy over the long term?
options: A. Gradual transition to insulin therapy
B. Addition of valsartan to his blood pressure regime
C. Addition of amlodipine to his blood pressure regime
questions.explanation: This patient's blood pressure is relatively well controlled, yet there is room for significant improvement in his blood glucose. Achievement of the target HbA1c of 53.0~mmol/mol (7.0%) would be associated with significantly reduced progression of retinopathy. Although laser therapy reduces progression of retinopathy, there are no high-risk features currently identified on retinal photography. Addition of ARB to an ACE inhibitor brings little added impact on blood pressure control, with significantly increased risk of hyperkalaemia. As such, it should be avoided. The next step in further intensification of blood pressure control is addition of a calcium antagonist such as amlodipine, although amongst the calcium antagonist class, only diltiazem has been shown to impact significantly on proteinuria. The dose-response curve for gliclazide above 160 mg is fairly flat, and hence there is little value in a further increase in sulphonylurea dose.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with a left Colles' fracture after a relatively minor fall at work. He lives alone and admits that he has difficulty maintaining sexual interest in women. He holds down a normal job although he has recently had time off work with depression. On examination he has sparse secondary sexual hair and small testes. His BP is 138/88 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 126~g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 197  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.7~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 124~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Corrected Ca2+ | 2.2~mmol/L | 2.20-2.60~mmol/L T-score | -3.1 |  Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage him?
questions.explanation: From the history we are given, the suspicion is that this patient has underlying hypogonadism, most probably due to Klinefelter syndrome. Small testes, sparse sexual hair, problems with depression and sexual function are all in keeping with the diagnosis. Testosterone is known to improve bone mineralization and is the treatment of choice here; it is also likely to impact on his sexual function and may consequently improve his depressive symptoms. Unfortunately, due to late diagnosis of Klinefelter, a significant number of patients begin testosterone replacement therapy far too late. This [Raloxifene] is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator used in the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis where bisphosphonates are not tolerated. This [alendronate] would be considered a standard intervention for post-menopausal osteoporosis, but hormone replacement is more important here. This synthetic PTH analogue [Teriparatide] is primarily used in the treatment of severe osteoporosis, with a T-score of below either -3.5 or 4.0 contingent upon age, and is a daily injectable. Replacement with testosterone, usually via an intermittent implant, is more appropriate. Calcium and vitamin D status isn't the primary driver of fracture risk in this patient; hormone replacement is the crucial first intervention.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with vomiting, anorexia, and polyuria. She is a non-smoker. Her GP has been treating her for anaemia with iron supplements, although she tells you this has had little or no effect on feelings of increasing lethargy over the past few months. On examination, her BP is 122/82, pulse is 88 and regular. She looks pale. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Sodium (Na+) | 141~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 3.6~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Bilirubin | 20~  mu mol/L | 1-22~  mu mol/L Urea | 12 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 30 u/l | 7-55 u/l Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) | 280 u/l | 30-150~  mu/L Creatinine (Cr) | 154 µmol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Albumin | 30 g/l | 35-55 g/l Total protein | 85 g/l | 60-83 g/l Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 3.0~mmol/l | 2.2-2.7~mmol/L Phosphate (PO4) | 1.3~mmol/L | 1.1-1.45~mmol/L You start her on IV normal saline. Which one of the following would be the best initial investigation to contribute to the underlying diagnosis?
options: A. Sesta MIBI scan of the neck
questions.explanation: This woman has hypercalcaemia without hypophosphataemia. Therefore, malignancy must be considered. The LFTs show increased globulin fraction (TP-ALB) indicating the possibility of myeloma. Therefore, the most appropriate management in this case is IV saline and a skeletal survey. Treatment of myeloma-induced hypercalcaemia is IV saline rehydration. Furosemide therapy with IV saline can be used as an adjunct to increase calcium excretion. IV pamidronate is also useful in reducing the calcium. In myeloma, hypercalcaemia is primarily due to increased osteolysis and high-dose steroids e.g. prednisolone 40 mg od can rapidly reduce the calcium level. IV pamidronate is also useful in reducing the calcium in resistant cases. The emphasis should be on treating the myeloma with chemotherapy, which will in turn lead to a reduction in the calcium. CT chest is most useful in patients with suspected bronchial carcinoma; the absence of a history of smoking and any reports of a cough counts against this as the underlying diagnosis. This [Sesta MIBI scan] is most useful if a parathyroid adenoma is suspected. Given the phosphate is in the normal range, this is much less likely versus malignancy as the underlying cause of her hypercalcaemia. Her symptoms are entirely consistent with hypercalcaemia, and an abdominal film is unlikely to contribute to determining the underlying diagnosis. Ultrasound is a poor investigation with respect to detecting underlying parathyroid adenomas, and these are not likely to be the cause of hypercalcaemia given that the phosphate is within the normal range.

questions.question: A patient comes to your clinic complaining for 2 months of abdominal pain. He has lost significant weight. He complains of feeling dizzy on standing. He has had a normal upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, colonoscopy and barium follow-through. His blood pressure from lying to standing dropped by 30 mmHg - from 120 mmHg systolic to 90 mmHg. He has abnormal mucosal pigmentation, which is shown below. Which one of the following blood test results might you most expect to see?
questions.explanation: Addison's disease, the most likely diagnosis here, can present with hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, hypoglycaemia, mild acidosis, hypercalcaemia, neutropenia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, anaemia and abnormal liver function tests. It also presents with darkening of the skin in a number of areas, including palmar creases and the buccal mucosa, as seen in this case. In the United Kingdom, non-iatrogenic Addison's disease is most commonly due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands. Adrenal autoantibodies are present in about 75% of cases. The next most common cause is tuberculosis. Other causes include haemorrhage (including during pregnancy), sepsis (including Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome from meningococcaemia), shock, coagulopathy and metastases. Other causes are metastases in over 90% in both glands, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and opportunistic infections associated with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). The most likely diagnosis here is Addison's disease, which can be accompanied by hypercalcaemia. The mechanism is uncertain but is thought to be a combination of increased calcium input into the extracellular space and reduced calcium removal by the kidney. Reduction in calcium removal is probably due to decreased glomerular filtration and increased tubular calcium reabsorption. Both renal factors are secondary to volume depletion. The enhanced calcium mobilization is thought to be of skeletal origin. In Addison's disease, relative lymphocytosis and eosinophilia may be present, which respond to glucocorticoid replacement therapy. In Addison's disease, the most prominent findings are hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis due to the loss of the sodium-retaining and potassium- and hydrogen ion-secreting action of aldosterone.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents for his annual review. Over the past couple of years, he has suffered problems with early satiety, indigestion and regurgitation of food matter but has not lost weight, and now requests investigations. His diabetes is relatively well controlled, with a recent HbA1c of 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%), his Hb is normal at 130 g/l and his ESR is 13~mm/h. You note that he does have a postural drop of 35 mmHg on blood pressure measurement. Which of the following actions is most useful with respect to his Gl symptoms?
options: E. Trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy
questions.explanation: This patient likely has diabetic autonomic neuropathy, manifest in postural hypotension and delayed gastric emptying. Isotope gastric motility studies are the most appropriate way to assess gastric emptying, and treatments involve prokinetic agents such as domperidone, metoclopramide or erythromycin, although response to treatment is generally poor. Treatment of postural hypotension involves mechanical measures such as bedhead elevation and wearing of support stockings. Intake of sodium chloride should be adequate, and fludrocortisone may be added starting at a dose of 50~  mu g/da  gamma. increased up to 400 µg as required. Diuretics, vasodilators and tricyclic antidepressants may exacerbate the condition and, for this reason, review of current medications that may exacerbate postural hypotension is important before commencing further therapy. Upper Gl endoscopy is required as part of the work-up symptoms of indigestion in this patient, but won't reveal the underlying cause. Oesophageal pH monitoring is most useful for evaluating symptoms of oesophageal reflux disease. Although there is a degree of reflux here, it's driven by dysmotility rather than by excess acid production. Although anti-acids may offer some relief, given dysmotility is the primary problem, they are unlikely to bring complete resolution of symptoms. PPIs may reduce stomach acid, but they won't impact on regurgitation of undigested food.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic as she has become increasingly concerned about her weight. She has always been overweight, but has gradually gained 3kg over the last six months. She claims that her diet has remained unchanged and her physical fitness is good. She is taking topical erythromycin for her acne. A pregnancy test is negative, although she does admit to a somewhat erratic menstrual cycle. She has also noticed increased coarse, dark, hair growth on her upper lip. In the clinic, her random blood sugar measurement by finger-prick is 8.0 mmol/L. Which investigation is most likely to point to the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history is consistent with Cushing syndrome or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). If not caused by pregnancy, weight gain is most likely in young people to be caused by increased fat. The causes are: increased caloric consumption disproportionate to energy expenditure; sedentary lifestyle, contributing significantly by TV watching and video gaming; endocrine disorders such as Cushing syndrome; PCOS; hypothyroidism; hypothalamic dysfunction; medications; environmental factors such as poor sleep; gut microbiota; and viruses. Women with PCOS often present with hirsutism and menstrual irregularities. PCOS is also associated with insulin resistance. As per the Rotterdam 2003 criteria for PCOS, two out of the following three should be applicable for a diagnosis of PCOS. • Oligo- and/or anovulation • Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism • Polycystic ovaries (by ultrasound). The ultrasound criterion for defining polycystic ovarian morphology is the presence of 12 or more follicles in each ovary measuring 2-9 mm in diameter and/or increased ovarian volume (>10 ml; calculated using the formula 0.5 x length x width x thickness). One ovary fitting this definition is sufficient to define PCOS. MRI brain would be helpful if pituitary disease, such as Cushing syndrome or hypothalamic disease, was suspected. Here the patient has no specific features to suggest the former. Hypothalamic dysfunction with secondary hypopituitarism is mostly seen in patients with a history of previous surgical treatment for a hypothalamic/pituitary lesion; other causes for hypothalamic dysfunction include inflammatory disease, history of trauma and neoplasia. The typical physical signs of Cushing syndrome, such as facial plethora, round face, abdominal striae, dorsal fat pad and easy bruising (ecchymoses), have not been described in this case. Screening tests would be one of the following: late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements), 24 h urinary free cortisol (UFC) excretion (two measurements) or the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST). Although menstrual irregularities and weight gain are commonly seen in hypothyroidism, the other characteristic features of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and myalgia have not been mentioned in this case. The hair becomes coarse due to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the interstitial matrix, and there is a tendency for hair loss. The distribution of the affected hair is diffuse and does not limit itself to androgen-sensitive distribution like the upper lip. Women with PCOS have insulin resistance and are at increased risk of ischaemic heart disease, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia. An oral glucose tolerance test will help assess the risk for type 2 diabetes and current glucose regulation, but per se it is not useful for diagnosing PCOS.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) with recurrent episodes of penile thrush. He has no other significant symptoms indicating hyperglycaemia. A strong family history of type 2 diabetes is noted and the GP arranges to check fasting plasma glucose. Two samples are checked and the laboratory glucose results are 8.1 and 8.2 mmol/L. Urine is negative for ketones. Haemoglobin A1C, also checked by the GP, is elevated at 74 mmol.mol (8.9%). His BMI is 22 and his BP is 105/72. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
questions.explanation: This man is most likely to have maturity onset of diabetes of youth 3 (MODY3) due to HNF1-alpha mutation (hepatic nuclear factor-1). MODY3 is the cause of 1-2% of type 2 diabetes and makes up around 70% of MODY cases. It presents most commonly in early adulthood and is associated with severe hyperglycaemia in some cases and frequent microvascular complications. One-third of patients require insulin therapy and around one-third may be controlled on oral hypoglycaemic drugs. Sulphonylureas (SUs) would be the initial drug of choice because, at least for the first few years, the capacity to secrete insulin is preserved and the use of SUs restores insulin release, avoiding the need for insulin therapy. The next commonest MODY variant is MODY 2, which results from a glucokinase mutation leading to altered glucose sensing in pancreatic beta cells. In contrast, 90% of MODY2 patients are controlled on diet therapy alone. Sitagliptin potentiates the incretin effect by preventing the breakdown of endogenous GLP-1; it is used as adjunctive therapy in type 2 diabetes. Metformin primarily reduces hepatic glucose output and has minor positive effects on weight control. As such, it is the initial therapy of choice for overweight and obese patients with type 2 diabetes. Basal bolus insulin therapy may well not be required for the majority of patients with MODY for a considerable period of time. Acarbose prevents the breakdown of complex carbohydrates in the gut. Its main use is in patients with type 2 diabetes who have a diet high in starches, such as those who follow a diet high in rice-containing foods.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man with a background of a localised squamous cell lung cancer is admitted to the Emergency Department with worsening confusion. He is thirsty, and, on examination, he has peripheral muscle weakness. His blood results reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 102~g/L | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 12.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 167  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 4.7~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Urea | 6.2~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 145~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Calcium (Ca+2) | 3.2~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/L Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 1.9~pmol/L | 0.9-5.4~pmol/L You are concerned that the patient may have pseudo hyperparathyroidism. After treating the acute hypercalcaemia, what is the most appropriate long term management of the pseudo-hyperparathyroidism?
questions.explanation: Pseudo hyperparathyroidism is often a neoplastic syndrome, whereby the cancer produces parathyroid-related-peptide (PTH-peptide) which has the same effect as PTH. After the acute treatment of hypercalcaemia, the most appropriate management is to treat the underlying disease. In this case, the squamous cell lung cancer might be amenable to surgical excision if it is localised. Calcimimetics, such as cinacalcet, may be given if the hypercalcaemia does not adequately respond to bisphosphonate therapy; this is, therefore, is part of the acute management of hypercalcaemia, rather than pseudo-hyperparathyroidism. Bisphosphonate therapy is part of the acute management of hypercalcaemia. Intravenous (IV) fluids should be given first, and if the patient continues to demonstrate hypercalcaemia after 24 hours, he should be treated with bisphosphonate therapy, eg IV zoledronic acid. Loop diuretics may lower calcium levels but are rarely used in the management of hypercalcaemia and do not have a role in the long-term management. In this condition, the parathyroid gland is acting appropriately. The mechanism for the hypercalcaemia occurs outside of the parathyroid feedback loop, and therefore a parathyroidectomy would not be helpful.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic because of an inability to achieve a pregnancy. She and her husband have been trying for some three years for a child, without success. Her General Practitioner has measured a prolactin level of 2600 mU/l (normal < 360). Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is arranged that demonstrates a microprolactinoma. She elects for treatment with pharmacotherapy. Which one of the following best represents the recommended follow-up for this patient?
options: A. General Practitioner to monitor prolactin levels
B. Monitoring of pituitary hormone axes
questions.explanation: Initially, pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be arranged yearly for patients with microprolactinomas. For patients with macroadenomas or those whose serum prolactin level fails to respond to dopamine agonist treatment (cabergoline or bromocriptine), imaging may be indicated more frequently. The frequency of imaging can reduce once there is suppression of serum prolactin level to the normal range and tumour size remains stable. Patients with visual field disturbance secondary to optic chiasmal compression should have regular visual field examination until maximum improvement is achieved. However, this patient does not have any visual field loss, as she is suffering from a microprolactinoma. Periodic measurement of serum prolactin level is an essential part of monitoring for microprolactinomas. As this patient wishes to achieve pregnancy and has been started on pharmacotherapy, she is best managed in an Endocrine Clinic during initial treatment and through pregnancy. In patients with macroprolactinomas (> 10 mm) which have caused hypopituitarism, patients may be started on hormone replacement. They will therefore require monitoring of the pituitary axes (including testosterone and thyroid function). This patient has a microprolactinoma and this is therefore not required. Initial monitoring of the tumour should be via yearly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and periodic prolactin level measurements. The frequency of MRI monitoring may be reduced once the patient is stable on treatment.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Clinic with a 10-month history of right iliac fossa abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea up to 15 x a day. He had been a heavy drinker in the past, consuming 40 pints of beer a week, but has cut back to 1 pint a day for several years. He has recently noticed that his symptoms became worse when drinking alcohol so has now stopped completely. His wife had noticed that that he has lost weight recently but he was unable to quantify this. He has never smoked but his wife has noticed that he has had some attacks of wheeziness. Examination of his abdomen revealed 3 cm hepatomegaly and an indistinct mass in the right iliac fossa. Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and full blood count were normal, but a small-bowel barium examination revealed a submucosal mass in the ileum. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumours are neuroendocrine tumours that most commonly occur in the Gl tract. They secrete many vasoactive molecules (particularly serotonin), which, in the absence of hepatic involvement, are metabolised in the liver. If these tumours metastasise to the liver, the liver's ability to break down the serotonin produced by these tumours may be overwhelmed; it may then enter the systemic circulation, and symptoms will subsequently develop. It is the phalanx of symptoms produced through serotonin entering the circulation that defines the carcinoid syndrome. Of these symptoms, debilitating diarrhoea - often associated with abdominal pain - is the most common. Flushing (which commonly affects the neck and face) may be associated with wheezing, and telangiectases may result. Alcohol and food intolerances, and exacerbations of symptoms by stress and some drugs, are not uncommon. The classic cardiac findings are of right-sided heart disease, namely tricuspid incompetence or pulmonary stenosis. Examination often reveals hepatomegaly; imaging of the liver reveals metastatic disease. Urinary levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) are normally increased. Treatment with somatostatin analogues (such as octreotide) may improve symptoms, and chemotherapy may also be helpful. Men and women are equally affected by carcinoid tumours, and presentation tends to occur between the ages of 50 and 75 years. Carcinoid tumours are mostly commonly found in the ileum and appendix, but can be located in many other sites, both intestinal and extra-intestinal. Approximately only one-third of tumours metastasise and. consequently, many are asymptomatic. Lymphoma is a recognised complication of coeliac disease, but his lack of Gl symptoms prior to 10 months earlier makes underlying coeliac disease unlikely (although coeliac disease may be subclinical).
