Chronic pancreatitis tends to cause upper abdominal pain and malabsorptive (as opposed to watery) diarrhoea. It is not likely to cause the associated symptoms described in the presentation. Villous adenomas of the rectum are not likely to cause the associated symptoms described in the presentation. IPSID is a proximal small bowel lymphoproliferative condition that tends to present with malabsorption and weight loss. As with coeliac disease, it may progress to lymphoma. It does not describe the full pattern of symptoms described in the scenario.

questions.question: A 46-year-old presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of thirst and lethargy. He had been discharged some two weeks earlier after his third episode of acute pancreatitis in the past year. He admits to alcoholism, drinking three bottles of whisky and at least 30 pints of beer each week. On examination, he looks dehydrated and underweight. His blood pressure is 125/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 92 bpm, his body mass index is 21. Respiratory, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 121~g/L | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 9.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/l Platelets | 232  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 142~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 185~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Glucose | 26.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.5~mmol/l Amylase | 400U/L | < 200 U/L Urine ketones | -ve |  He agrees to begin a detox regime. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage his diabetes?
questions.explanation: Diabetes associated with pancreatitis is due to damage to the endocrine pancreas and associated lack of insulin. This pathophysiology is consistent with the patient's presentation: he is thin, with symptoms of insulinopaenia. As such, exogenous insulin replacement is the only appropriate intervention here. Acarbose reduces absorption of complex carbohydrates from the gut. In this case it won't impact on glucose control and will actually worsen diarrhoea. Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and is therefore expected to have no significant impact on blood glucose levels in this patient. Although gliclazide will have a stimulatory effect on remaining endogenous insulin production, it's unlikely to achieve blood glucose control. Sitagliptin reduces degradation of endogenous incretins; these, however, have little effect on increasing insulin production from a failing pancreas.

questions.question: You are asked to see a 24-year-old woman who is 8 weeks into her first pregnancy. She has suffered vomiting and is finding it difficult to maintain weight. On examination, she is clearly anxious. Her BP is 105/70, with pulse 75 and regular. Her BMI is 22. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 119~g/L | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.7  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 212  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 144~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 3.4~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Glucose | 4.8~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Total Thyroxine (T4) | 185~nmol/L | 58-174~nmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 0.6~mu/L | 0.4-5.0~mu/L Which of the following is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: This patient has increased total T4 with a TSH which is in the normal range. There are no clinical signs of hyperthyroidism. The weight loss and vomiting are most likely to be related to hyperemesis gravidarum. Although normal in this case, TSH itself may be suppressed in 13.5% of patients in the first trimester due to the thyrotrophic effects of beta HCG. There is a twofold increase in thyroid-binding globulin levels in pregnancy due to a combination of reduced hepatic clearance of thyroid-binding globulin and increased synthesis in response to oestrogen. The increased level of thyroid-binding globulin plateaus at 20 weeks and then gradually falls. In this case thyroid binding globulin may be useful in confirming the diagnosis. Although thyrotoxicosis may occur in early pregnancy, the lack of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis here makes that much less likely as the underlying diagnosis, as does the fact that TSH is at the lower end of the normal range rather than being completely suppressed. Propylthiouracil is the treatment of choice for thyrotoxicosis in early pregnancy. Carbimazole is the preferred intervention for thyrotoxicosis in late pregnancy because of the risk of maternal hepatotoxicity associated with propylthiouracil use. Block replace regimens are not used in pregnancy because thyroid hormones do not readily cross the placenta. This patient is not hypothyroid and there is no indication for commencing thyroid hormone.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man who was previously seen in the Endocrinology Clinic for abdominal obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia presents six months later for review after having lost 42 lbs in weight. On examination in the clinic, his blood pressure (BP) is 155/92 mmHg and his body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/M2. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 139 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.9  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 230  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4~mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Low density-lipoprotein (LDL) | 4.4~mmol/l | <3.5~mmol/L Triglycerides | 3.5~mmol/l | 0-1.5~mmol/L High-density lipoprotein (HDL) | 0.7~mmol/L | >1.0~mmol/l Fasting glucose | 6.8~mmol/l(<6.1) | <7~mmol/L Which of the following is true in this case?
options: A. His cardiovascular risk is not increased
B. He does not require anti-hypertensive therapy
C. It would be reasonable to treat him with a statin
D. He should be considered for gastric reduction surgery
E. He is not at increased risk of development of diabetes
questions.explanation: Of particular concern in this patient is the typical lipid pattern seen in insulin-resistant states, with low HDL cholesterol and high triglycerides. Given his increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease, it would therefore be sensible to treat him with a statin. A blood pressure (BP) of 155/92 in a patient with signs of insulin resistance means that intervention with anti-hypertensive therapy is warranted. This patient has signs of insulin resistance, and a low HDL which drives a raised LDL: HDL ratio; as such, cardiovascular risk is increased in this patient. This patient has already lost a significant amount of weight. As such, gastric reduction surgery isn't warranted. A fasting glucose of 6.8 is on the cusp of diabetes, meaning that conversion is likely over the next few years.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department (ED) by her General Practitioner (GP). She gives a history of malaise and weight loss. Most recently she collapsed at home and has suffered from persistent vomiting over the past 24 hours. Other past history of note includes a deep vein thrombosis ( (DVT) in pregnancy and positive screen for anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome. Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 100 and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Sodium (Na+) | 128~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 6.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Urea | 9.1~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 128~  mu mol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Haemoglobin (Hb) | 101~g/L | 115-155~g/L Mean corpusuclar volume (MCV) | 99 fl | 80-100 fl Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) | 41~mm/hour | 1-20~mm/hour Glucose | 3.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.5~mmol/l You arrange for a blood sample to be sent for cortisol and give a bolus of 20% dextrose. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
options: A. Arrange a short synacthen test for the following morning
B. Start prednisolone 30 mg PO OD
C. Start fludrocortisone 100 mcg PO OD
D. Start IV fluid replacement with 5% dextrose
E. Start IV fluid replacement with 0.9% saline and give a bolus of IV dexamethasone
questions.explanation: This woman has anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, which may have led to adrenal infarction, precipitating this presentation with an Addisonian crisis. Autoimmune disease is the commonest cause of Addison's in the developed world, although malignancy and infection (e.g. with tuberculosis) may also be responsible. Initial treatment is with rehydration, and several litres of normal saline may be required during the first 24 h of therapy. A bolus of dexamethasone 4 mg IV should also be given because unlike hydrocortisone, this won't interfere with a synacthen test. Fludrocortisone replacement is not normally required in the acute stage, but can be added once the dose of hydrocortisone is reduced after a few days. This lady is presenting with an Addisonian crisis - you should not wait for a synacthen test prior to commencing therapy. Hydrocortisone is the steroid of choice in the treatment of Addison's. Hypotension should be managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline. Blood glucose should be monitored and hypoglycaemia corrected appropriately, but this usually improves with glucocorticoid therapy.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman is referred to the clinic by the Emergency Department, having been admitted after fainting in the local supermarket. On further questioning it transpires that she has been feeling weak and washed out for quite some time. On examination, her BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse is 75/min. Her BMI is 18. She has calluses on her knuckles but tells you these are due to her job as a landscape gardener. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 109~g/L | 115-155~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.0  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 194  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 140~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K ) | 3.3~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 115~  mu mol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/l Urinary potassium | 0.7~mmoU/L/24 h | 25-100~mmol/24 h Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: D Laxative abuse. This woman is underweight and has symptoms of fatigue which are consistent with hypokalaemia. The fact that she is underweight with a BMI of 18, and has calluses on her knuckles, may point towards induced vomiting and a diagnosis of bulimia, which would fit with possible laxative abuse. Laxative abuse leads to increased Gl potassium loss and renal conservation of potassium, a urinary concentration of potassium of less than 1 mmol/l being highly suggestive of laxative abuse. Urine screening exists for a range of possible laxatives, and the patient should be consented for a urinary laxative screen with appropriate counselling. C Diuretic abuse. The use of thiazide diuretics leads to hypokalaemia through increased potassium excretion in the urine. A Bartter syndrome. This is an autosomal recessive renal tubular disorder characterised by hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia. metabolic alkalosis and hyper-reninaemia with normal blood pressure. Urinary potassium excretion is high due to the inability of the kidneys to retain potassium. B Liddle syndrome. This is a rare hereditary disorder involving increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) which causes the kidneys to excrete potassium but retain too much sodium and water, leading to hypertension. Symptoms are of hypertension, fluid retention hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The urinary potassium excretion is high. E Conn syndrome. Conn syndrome, or primary hyperaldosteronism, occurs due to excess production of the hormone aldosterone by the adrenal glands, resulting in low renin levels Around 66% of cases are due to enlargement of both adrenal glands and 33% are due to an adrenal adenoma that produces aldosterone Most people have hypertension requiring treatment with more than three agents. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypernatraemic, hypokalaemic, metabolic alkalosis. The urinary excretion of potassium is high.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with type II diabetes comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for investigation of chronic diarrhoea. She is taking metformin 2.5 g per day and gliclazide 160 mg. Additional medication includes simvastatin 40 mg and aspirin 75 mg. On examination, she has a body mass index (BMI) of 28~kg/M2 and looks well. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Her blood pressure (BP) is 145/82 mmHg, with no postural drop. There is no evidence of peripheral neuropathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 139 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 229  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.6~mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 130~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Albumin | 40 g/l | 35-55 g/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 35 U/L | 5-30 U/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) | 13~mm/hour | 1-20~mm/hour Small bowel biopsy normal and colonoscopy is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: B Bile salt malabsorption. High-dose metformin is thought to interfere with the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts, leading to reduced reabsorption of bile salts from the ileum. Diarrhoea, in association with metformin therapy, can often be avoided with slow up-titration of the dose. A Autonomic neuropathy. Given the lack of peripheral neuropathy and no postural drop in blood pressure, significant autonomic neuropathy is very unlikely. C Chronic pancreatitis. Clinically significant chronic pancreatitis is associated with malabsorption. The albumin of 40 counts against significant malabsorption. D Coeliac disease. Coeliac disease is associated with anaemia and evidence of malabsorption on biochemistry, neither of which is seen here. The small bowel biopsy effectively rules this out. E NSAID related colitis. Abnormalities on colonic biopsy would be expected in patients with NSAID-related colitis.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man is referred to the clinic with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. He also complains of excessive sweating and worries that his hands have swollen so that his wedding ring no longer fits him. Past medical history includes hypertension, which is managed with amlodipine and indapamide. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and he has a very prominent lower jaw. There is also soft tissue swelling of his hands. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 149 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.0  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 300  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 138~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Random glucose | 12.1~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation towards confirming this man's likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E IGF-1 measurement. There is obvious frontal bossing and prognathism which along with the soft tissue swelling in the hands, hyperhidrosis and hypertension is consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. IGF-1 measurement varies with age and nutritional status, but reference ranges exist for comparison. IGF-1 has a long half-life and, as such, is a useful measure of growth hormone status. Failure of growth hormone to suppress in response to an oral glucose challenge is the other diagnostic method of choice for assessing patients with possible acromegaly, although this is less convenient following an initial clinic appointment. A Fasting plasma glucose. Although an elevation in fasting plasma glucose may indicate a diagnosis of diabetes, it won't reveal the underlying cause. B Random growth hormone measurement. Growth hormone is released in pulsatile fashion and has a short half-life; as such, random measurement is not useful in confirming a diagnosis of acromegaly. C Prolactin measurement. Prolactin may be elevated because of local pressure effects from a pituitary adenoma, but it won't confirm elevated growth hormone. D Random cortisol measurement. The symptoms here fit better with acromegaly rather than with elevated cortisol as a result of hyperadrenalism due to either an adrenal or pituitary tumour.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after her neighbours found her confused at home and called an ambulance. She is unable to give much history. However, her General Practitioner (GP) records state that she has diabetes and hypertension and she has previously suffered from a stroke. Her GP records also note a number of regular medications, including clopidogrel, atorvastatin, linagliptin, Humulin® I, Toujeo® and amlodipine, which were last dispensed two months ago. On examination, she is disorientated and appears dehydrated, but is otherwise well. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value pH | 7.34 | 7.35-7.45 pO2 | 12 kPa | 9.5-14 kPa pCO2 | 7 kPa | 4.6-6.0 kPa Bicarbonate (HCO3) | 21~mmol/L | 22-30~mmol/L Glucose | 27.8~mmol/L | 4-10~mmol/L Urea | 8~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Sodium (N+) | 132~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4~mmol/L | 3.5-5~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 286~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Ketones | 1~mmol/L | <0.6~mmol/L Lactate | 2.1~mmol/L | 0.6-2.4~mmol/L What is the likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation: E Poor adherence to medications. This patient likely has type II diabetes. With many years of insulin resistance commonly experienced in type II diabetes, the pancreatic endocrine function is reduced, meaning that many patients end up on insulin therapy. It is likely that this patient has not been taking her regular insulin regime for many weeks, which has resulted in hyperglycaemia and dehydration. The treatment of choice for this patient would be to start her on a variable-rate insulin infusion (VRII) and intravenous fluids. Once her blood sugar levels have normalised and she is eating and drinking normally, she can be started on an insulin regime based on her requirements from the VRII. C Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state (HHS) is diagnosed with plasma osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg; this can be approximated using the calculation for the plasma osmolarity as: [2(Na2^{+}+K+)+urea+glucose].T This patient's osmolarity is 307.8 mmol/l. Usually, in HHS, the glucose level is > 30 mmol/l and there is no significant ketonaemia or acidosis. Sodium is frequently raised in HHS, as the raised glucose level causes osmotic diuresis and severe dehydration. A Alcohol excess. Alcohol excess may cause poor adherence to medications and mildly raised blood glucose levels in the acute setting. However, blood sugar levels would not be expected to be this high and there is nothing in the scenario to suggest alcohol misuse. B Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). This patient is only mildly acidotic with mildly raised ketone levels. A diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is based on blood glucose level > 11 mmol/l with ketonaemia (blood ketones > 3 mmol/l or urine ketones 2+ or more) and acidosis (pH < 7.3 and/or venous bicarbonate < 15 mmol/l) would not be appropriate. It is more commonly seen in patients with type I diabetes. D Intracranial haemorrhage. Intracranial haemorrhage secondary to a fall and clopidogrel may cause a presentation with confusion. However, it is not known whether the patient has not collected her medications for at least two months, making this less likely.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a two-week history of malaise and anterior neck pain. She explains that she has been suffering from what seems like a severe flu-like illness. On examination, her pulse is 118 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her blood pressure (BP) is 132/74 mmHg. She has a fine tremor and her palms are moist. She has a slightly enlarged, smooth tender thyroid. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Thyroxine (T4) | 40~nmol/L | 11-22 pmol/l Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | <0.01~  mu~U/L | 0.17-3.2~  mu U/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) | 40~mm/hour | 1-20~mm/hour Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: D. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid
questions.explanation: E Subacute thyroiditis. This is a description of subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis, which usually presents with malaise and neck pain. The neck pain can radiate to the ear or occiput. There is often tenderness and nodularity of the thyroid. ESR is often elevated. A Technetium-99m scan shows no technetium uptake by the thyroid. Mild cases can be treated with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), but more severe cases associated with hyperthyroidism should be treated with prednisolone 30~mg/day The prednisolone can be stopped when the T4 normalises. Treatment with carbimazole is not indicated. D Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a C-cell (calcitonin-producing) tumour. It is not associated with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. A Toxic multinodular goitre. A nodular enlarged thyroid gland is expected in toxic multinodular goitre, with a more prolonged period of symptoms of hyperthyroidism. B Graves' disease. Graves' is associated with smooth enlargement of the thyroid, often with only mild tenderness. Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis also occur over a more prolonged period. C Toxic solitary nodule. Toxic adenoma is not associated with generalised tenderness of the thyroid gland, and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis build up over a period of weeks and months.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the Endocrinology Clinic complaining of weakness and lethargy. She has gained 5 kg in weight over the past four months and is finding it increasingly difficult to look after her granddaughter, particularly when she needs to go up and down the stairs. There is a history of mild hypertension which is managed with indapamide, but she is otherwise well. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/92 mmHg; her pulse is 55 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She appears to have thinning hair. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32~kg/M2 and neurological examination reveals evidence of proximal myopathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 112 g/l | 115-155~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.1  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 181  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 127~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.5~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 112~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Creatine kinase (CK) | 352 IU/L | 23-175~IU/L Glucose | 6.1 mmol/L | 3.8-5.4~mmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH). There are several clues in the history to point towards the underlying diagnosis of hypothyroidism, including weight gain, proximal myopathy, hyponatraemia and slight CK elevation. TSH is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis - which is likely to be Hashimoto's thyroiditis as the underlying pathophysiology. B Prolactin. The clinical scenario supports the possibility of hypothyroidism. Prolactin may be useful to support the possibility of a prolactinoma, which is unlikely in this case. A Muscle biopsy. While there is a slight elevation of CK, it is not sufficiently raised to contribute significantly to a diagnosis of myopathy. A muscle biopsy in this case would therefore not be the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis. C Serum and urine osmolality. Although this patient has a low sodium, the serum and urine osmolality are useful in patients in whom you are considering syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), it neither confirms the diagnosis or fits with the clinical scenario in this case. D Synacthen test. Although patients with a low sodium and lethargy should be considered for a short synacthen test, Addison's disease is not consistent with weight gain and therefore is unlikely to be the diagnosis in this case.

questions.question: A 42-year-old Portuguese woman presents to her GP with increasing lethargy. He had seen her twice in the past few months and commenced antidepressants at her last appointment. Most recently, she had been complaining of increasing nausea and vomiting and had lost a considerable amount of weight. On examination, her blood pressure was 105/65 mmHg and her BMI was 21. There was a postural drop of 20 mmHg in her blood pressure on standing, with a corresponding increase in her pulse rate. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Sodium (Na+) | 126 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.8 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 7 mu/L | 0.4-5.0~mu/l Free Thyroxine (FT4) | 7 pmol/l | 10- 22 pmol/l Urea | 10.1 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/l Haemoglobin (Hb) | 101 g/l (normochromic, normocytic), eosinophil count raised | 135-175~g/L Which of the following is the initial treatment of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation: C Hydrocortisone. This patient has the clinical features of adrenal insufficiency, with hyponatraemia, a raised urea, normochromic normocytic anaemia with eosinophilia and a relatively high potassium level despite repeated episodes of vomiting. She should not be treated with thyroxine at this stage: thyroid function testing should be repeated after treatment with corticosteroids. She should be rehydrated, but with N saline. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause of primary adrenal insufficiency. Metastatic carcinoma from lung, breast or kidney primaries is also known to result in adrenal failure. Infiltration due to amyloid, infection due to tuberculosis, vascular haemorrhage or infarction are other documented causes. B Fludrocortisone. This is used for mineralocorticoid insufficiency leading to postural hypotension. In Addison's disease, because corticosteroid replacement therapy usually exerts a mineralocorticoid effect, fludrocortisone is not first-line treatment. A Thyroxine. Mild biochemical hypothyroidism often accompanies adrenal insufficiency, but early treatment of abnormal thyroid numbers, particularly before corticosteroid stabilisation, may further decompensate the adrenal insufficiency. D IV 5% dextrose. Adrenal insufficiency manifesting with adrenal crisis is associated with volume depletion, and therefore normal saline is the appropriate intravenous fluid. E Fluid restriction. Addison's disease is characterised by volume depletion. The hyponatraemia is in the context of the condition, and therefore the most appropriate therapy is fluid replacement with normal saline rather than fluid restriction.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a chest infection. The GP undertakes routine blood tests and notices that her glucose is just into the range for diabetes. He refers her to the Diabetic Clinic, where you see her and take a full history. At the time of the test, she had been unwell for one week with a chest infection. She has no other medical history and is normally fit and well. Her grandmother, mother and sister all have diabetes, which presented when they were young. Her mother's and sister's diabetes is diet-controlled only. Her grandmother has only started to need insulin recently. She has two older brothers who also have diabetes. Her family are all very health conscious and do not smoke, do not drink excessive alcohol and exercise regularly. They all maintain a body mass index (BMI) around 20~kg/M2. Her fasting venous glucose is 12~mmol/L How would you best describe the likely diagnosis in her case?
options: E. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
questions.explanation: E Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). Maturity-onset diabetes is a genetic subgroup of diabetes characterised by autosomal-dominant inheritance, early onset, non-insulin-dependent diabetes and results from a monogenic defect leading to defects of either insulin sensing or insulin release. MODY3 is particularly important to diagnose as many patients initially treated with insulin can in fact be managed with sulphonylurea. C Type-2 diabetes mellitus. The fact that her BMI is 20 makes type 2 diabetes very unlikely as the underlying diagnosis. A Incidental hyperglycaemia. The FPG result of 12 is well into the abnormal range. Coupled with the probable autosomal-dominant inheritance of diabetes, MODY is the more likely diagnosis. B Type-1 diabetes mellitus. The symptoms of hyperglycaemia such as polyuria, polydipsia and lethargy are absent from her presenting complaint. D Metabolic syndrome. Given the BMI of 20 and the autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern. MODY is more likely than metabolic syndrome to be the cause of the hyperglycaemia seen here.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with episodic abdominal pain and a recent episode of acute pancreatitis. He has a history of obesity, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin and amlodipine. He reports consuming alcohol occasionally. Family history is significant for cardiovascular disease in his father, who had a myocardial infarction at the age of 50 years. Physical examination reveals central obesity and hepatomegaly. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Fasting triglycerides (TG) | 15.2~mmol/L | < 1.7 mmol/l Fasting blood gglucose | 8.4 mmol/l | 3.9-5.8 mmol/l Total cholesterol | 5.8 mmol/l | < 5.0 mmol/L High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol | 0.8 mmol/l | > 1.0 mmol/l (men) Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol | 2.2 mmol/l | < 3.0 mmol/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) | 30 U/L | 10-35 U/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) | 35 U/L | 10-40  /L What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's hypertriglyceridaemia?
options: C. Type II diabetes mellitus with metabolic syndrome
questions.explanation: C Type II diabetes mellitus with metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome, often associated with obesity, type II diabetes and insulin resistance, commonly leads to hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL cholesterol levels and other lipid abnormalities. The patient's obesity, diabetes and elevated TG levels are consistent with this diagnosis. B Alcohol-induced hypertriglyceridaemia. Although excessive alcohol intake can cause elevated TG levels, this patient reports only occasional alcohol use, making it an unlikely primary cause of the severe hypertriglyceridaemia observed here. A Familial hypercholesterolaemia. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is typically associated with elevated LDL cholesterol levels and does not commonly present with high TG levels. This condition is unlikely to explain the high TG and low HDL levels in this patient. D Familial combined hyperlipidaemia. Familial combined hyperlipidaemia can present with elevated TG and cholesterol levels, but it typically results in modest TG elevations and is not usually associated with acute pancreatitis at such levels. E Drug-induced hypertriglyceridaemia. Certain drugs, such as beta-blockers and some antipsychotics, can elevate TG levels, but neither metformin nor amlodipine is associated with significant hypertriglyceridaemia, making this an unlikely cause.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man who has both type 1 DM and chronic kidney disease managed with haemodialysis comes to the clinic for review. He was previously noted to have raised PTH and started on CaCO3 and twice weekly vitamin D at the high dose. He has recently begun suffering from depression. He has suffered two previous myocardial infarctions and had a spinal anaesthetic for a total hip replacement in the past year. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 110 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 4.5  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 199  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.2 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine | 634 µmol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 87 pmol/l | 1-6 pmol/l Corrected Ca+2 | 2.2 mmol/l | 2.20-2.60~mmol/L Phosphate (PO4) | 1.45~mmol/L | 0.70-1.40~mmol/L Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step for this patient?
options: B. Increased dose of vitamin D
questions.explanation: D Cinacalcet. This man has hyperparathyroidism, with a PTH that has failed to suppress in response to calcium and vitamin D. As such, the next most appropriate step is cinacalcet. It works as an agonist at the site of the calcium sensor on the parathyroid gland. This leads to a suppression of PTH levels. Cinacalcet may currently be used in patients on renal replacement therapy as an adjunct to vitamin D or phosphate binders. A Parathyroidectomy. Given this patient's history of end stage renal failure, myocardial infarctions and the fact he received a spinal anaesthetic for a hip replacement last year, they are strongly hinting at him being high risk from operative intervention for hyperparathyroidism, and other treatment options should be explored first. B Increased dose of vitamin D. PTH is in not in the treatment range, but calcium is in the normal range. They are on high doses of vitamin D and calcium carbonate and supplementing further with vitamin D is very unlikely to drive down levels of parathyroid hormone. C Sevelamer. Sevelamer is a phosphate binder, and given that phosphate is only just above the normal range, it's not going to significantly impact on the clinical picture seen here. E Aluminium hydroxide. Aluminium hydroxide, an alternative phosphate binder is now used less frequently because of risks of accumulation and the impact on cognitive function.

questions.question: An 63-year-old woman from Saudi Arabia attends the Endocrinology Clinic with her son after referral from her General Practitioner (GP). He has noticed that she has symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and is worried about hyperparathyroidism. On further questioning, you find out she has been taking Rennie anti-indigestion tablets three or four x per day, and has increased these as she has felt progressively more nauseous. Additionally, she is taking a calcium supplement to guard against bone fracture as her mother suffered from fractures late in life. Additional symptoms include fatigue, and, apparently while in Saudi Arabia she was started on sertraline for depression. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 129 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.6  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 145  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) | 18~mm/hour | 1-20~mm/hour Sodium (Na ) | 140~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 5.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 185~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Corrected corrected Ca2+ | 2.85~mmol/L | 2.20-2:60~mmol/L Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | Low | Chest X-ray (CXR) | No focal lesion seen | Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E Milk-alkali syndrome. This patient has a markedly elevated oral calcium intake, as illustrated by her propensity to take both calcium-containing indigestion medications (Rennies is a mixture of calcium and magnesium carbonate) and calcium supplementation to reduce the risk of bone fracture. Additionally, she has various symptoms of hypercalcaemia including the nausea, lethargy and depression reported here. The condition can lead to mild renal impairment, as we've seen with her elevated serum creatinine, but this may well return to normal once calcium intake is reduced. D Hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is a possibility given the patient's age, but the lack of other symptoms, apart from indigestion, and relatively normal blood picture including ESR and haemoglobin, count against this. A Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria. FHH is usually asymptomatic, although some patients may present with renal stones, or very rarely with acute pancreatitis. B Hypoparathyroidism. Hypoparathyroidism is associated with hypocalcaemia rather than the elevated calcium seen here. C Primary hyperparathyroidism. In the absence of the strong history of excess calcium and alkali ingestion here, primary hyperparathyroidism would be considered the main differential, although a normal or slightly elevated PTH, rather than the low value seen here would be expected.

questions.question: An overweight 68-year-old woman with a five year history of type II diabetes mellitus attends for her annual review. She is currently being treated with metformin (2 g total daily dose). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) | 98.91~mmol/mol (11.2%) | <53~mmol/mol(<7.0  %) Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) | 24 | > 60 Creatinine (Cr) | 240~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Total cholesterol | 7.5~mmol/L | <5.2~mmol/L Which of the following represents the most appropriate therapeutic option for this patient?
options: A. Start gliclazide instead of metformin
B. Start gliclazide in addition to metformin
C. Start insulin and continue metformin
E. Start insulin and stop metformin
questions.explanation: E Start insulin and stop metformin. This patient has kidney disease and thus metformin is contraindicated. In addition, her HbA1c is out of control at 98.91~mmol/mol(11.2  %). It is highly unlikely that gliclazide would achieve the necessary level of glycaemic control, and therefore initiation of insulin therapy is the most appropriate therapeutic option. Most patients with type 2 diabetes are initiated on a twice-daily mixed insulin regime, with conversion to a basal bolus regime as an option if sufficient control is not achieved. D Start a statin. The priority is to improve the glycaemic control. Once this is achieved, lipid management with a statin can be considered. A Start gliclazide instead of metformin. Her HbA1c is very high, and therefore the initiation of insulin is more appropriate in order to achieve more rapid glycaemic control. In terms of her renal function, gliclazide could cause hypoglycaemia since its clearance will be delayed. B Start gliclazide in addition to metformin. Metformin has to be discontinued once eGFR is <30. Gliclazide can be used, but there is the risk of hypoglycaemia C Start insulin and continue metformin. Although metformin enhances insulin sensitivity and can be used as adjunctive therapy to insulin, it has to be discontinued in our case since eGFR is <30.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man sees his General Practitioner (GP) due to a persistent and gradually worsening headache over the previous few months. On examination, he is noted to have bitemporal hemianopia, and he is sweaty to touch. His blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg. The patient has no past medical history. An image of the patient is show below: His GP sends a range of blood tests, including Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF-1) as they suspect a diagnosis of acromegaly. Investigation | Result | Normal value IGF-1 | 53 nmol/l | 7.728 nmol/l What is the most likely cause of acromegaly in this case?
options: B. Hypothalamic hypersecretion of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH)
questions.explanation: D Pituitary macroadenoma. Pituitary macroadenomas (diameter more than 10 mm) that secrete growth hormone are the most common cause of acromegaly, accounting for 60-80% of cases. This is often caused by a spontaneous mutation in the somatotroph cells which are responsible for growth hormone secretion. Excessive growth hormone secretion causes the symptoms of acromegaly and the size of the tumour can cause local tumour effects such as headaches, visual field defects (such as bitemporal hemianopia) and cranial nerve palsies. Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acromegaly_facial_features.JPEG A Ectopic growth hormone secretion. Some rare conditions, such as pancreatic islet cell tumours or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, may result in ectopic production of growth hormone, which may lead to the symptoms of acromegaly. On investigation, no mass will be seen on the pituitary gland, and therefore the typical symptoms of mass effect in acromegaly will be absent. It is also possible to have ectopic production of GHRH. This is also rare and most commonly caused by bronchial carcinoid. B Hypothalamic hypersecretion of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH). Hypothalamic tumours, eg gliomas, can secrete excessive quantities of GHRH, which results in pituitary hyperplasia, excessive growth hormone secretion and acromegaly. This is a rare cause of acromegaly. C Pituitary carcinoma. Pituitary adenomas causing acromegaly tend to be benign lesions. It is rare for the lesion to be malignant. E Pituitary microadenoma. Pituitary microadenomas (diameter less than 10 mm) are the second most common cause of acromegaly. They account for between 20-40% of cases and, due to their small size, they tend not to cause symptoms of mass effect, eg bitemporal hemianopia, which is more typical of a macroadenoma.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has been referred by his General Practitioner (GP) for an obvious slowly enlarging mass in the left lobe of the thyroid. He is concerned he might have cancer. Which of the following would increase the likelihood in this patient of underlying thyroid malignancy?
options: B. Strong family history of breast cancer requiring multiple check-up mammograms
C. Abuse of thyroid tablets as a teenager
D. Family history of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
questions.explanation: D Family history of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). FAP is caused by an APC gene mutation on chromosome 5, and is also associated with increased risk of developing thyroid cancer. A Family history of hyperthyroidism. Endemic goitre, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and thyroid adenoma, not hyperthyroidism, are associated with increased risk of thyroid malignancy. B Strong family history of breast cancer requiring multiple check-up mammograms. A familial history of breast cancer is most closely associated with increased risk of ovarian cancer. C Abuse of thyroid tablets as a teenager. Thyrotoxicosis factitia, or abuse of thyroid hormone, is not associated with increased risk of thyroid cancer. E Male sex. Females are three x more likely to develop thyroid cancer than males.

questions.question: A 28-year-old single woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with recent symptoms of sweating, weight loss and palpitations. She tells you that there is a history of thyroid disease in the family and she has recently applied for a job as a nurse because she wants to help people. On examination, she has a BMI of 20, there is no palpable goitre and a tremor is noted. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 125 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.5  x10^9/l | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 138~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium ( (K+) | 4.5~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 90~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Glucose | 5.7~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | <0.05~mu/L | 0.5-4.0~mu/L Free Thyroxine (FT4) | 32.1~pmol/L | 10-22~pmol/L Thyroid scintography | revealed decreased uptake | Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: D Thyroglobulin levels. One possible cause of recent-onset thyrotoxicosis is thyroiditis. Thyroglobulin levels can be used to differentiate thyroiditis and other causes of hyperthyroidism from thyrotoxicosis factitia. Low thyroglobulin levels are associated with a diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis factitia (inappropriate abuse of thyroid hormone), and this is also associated with absence of thyroid enlargement and suppressed TSH in the presence of elevated T4 levels. Decreased isotope uptake is seen on thyroid scanning. Expert psychiatric input is advised in cases such as this one, as presentation of the diagnosis may be met with a hostile reaction and appropriate psychological assessment is required. C Beta HCG. There are no signs of pregnancy, where elevated beta HCG which suppresses TSH is seen. It doesn't normally cause symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. A Thyroid ultrasound scan. Thyroid ultrasound scanning is most useful in identifying small thyroid masses that can't be detected on palpation alone. B Fine needle aspiration biopsy. Fine needle aspiration biopsy is most useful in identifying the histology of cold nodules, identified on ultrasound scan. E Abdominal ultrasound scan. Abdominal ultrasound scanning is useful in identifying intra-abdominal tumours producing thyroid hormone, although these are extremely rare and unlikely to be the cause of symptoms seen here.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department some two weeks after discharge following the birth of her second child. Unfortunately, she suffered a significant period of hypotension due to post-partum haemorrhage and required a 4-unit blood transfusion. She has been feeling increasingly tired with nausea and symptoms of pre-syncope. She looks pale and her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 22~kg/M2. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 110 g/l | 115-155~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8.9  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/ Platelets (PLT) | 171  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 128~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.4~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 110~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Which of the following is the pathology underlying her presentation?
questions.explanation: D Pituitary infarction. Due to increased blood supply during pregnancy, the pituitary gland is susceptible to infarction during a period of hypotension. In this case, a gradual decline of ACTH is likely to have led to reduced cortisol production and driven the adrenal failure. A short synacthen test and pituitary MRI would be useful in confirming the diagnosis, but investigations should not delay corticosteroid replacement. B Bilateral adrenal infarction. Although there was a significant period of time where the patient was hypoperfused, this would be rare to occur in an otherwise well individual. A Autoimmune adrenal failure. The clinical history indicates there was a significant period of hypotension. During this time, the pituitary gland can be prone to infarction which is therefore more likely than autoimmune adrenal failure. C Pituitary haemorrhage. Pituitary haemorrhage, also known as pituitary apoplexy, occurs suddenly and presents in a dramatic fashion as opposed to the subacute presentation above. Typically, patients present with sudden-onset severe headache, visual loss and diplopia. Treatment is surgical. E Renal tubular acidosis type 4. Renal tubular acidosis type 4 would explain the hyperkalaemia. While acquired forms occur in the context of patients with primary adrenal failure, it does not explain the clinical history and therefore is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man, who has had type II diabetes for the past eight years, presents to his General Practitioner for review. He has found it increasingly difficult to maintain his glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) at target on metformin 1 g twice daily (BD) and empagliflozin 25 mg. He has also gained 6 kg in weight over the past year. His past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and benign prostatic hypertrophy. On examination, his blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. The respiratory examination is unremarkable. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and his body mass index is 36~kg/M2. There is bilateral pedal oedema. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 131 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.0  x10^9/L | 4.0-1.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 181  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/| Glucose | 12.1~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L HbA1c | 62~mmol/mol | <48~mmol/mol [for diabetics] Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: A. Add intermediate-acting insulin at night
E. Stop oral treatment and transition to basal bolus insulin
questions.explanation: B Add liraglutide. In this situation, with a body mass index of >35~kg/M2, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines allow for a trial of a glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) analogue. They recommend a reassessment of response to therapy after three months to ensure that adequate HbA1c reduction (> 1%) and weight loss of 3 percent has been achieved. D Refer for bariatric surgery. Although this patient would qualify for bariatric surgery, a trial of GLP-1 agonist therapy is indicated first, given the morbidity associated with a permanent surgical solution. A Add intermediate-acting insulin at night. This patient is significantly obese. As such, although adding intermediate-acting insulin at night may improve his HbA1c, it is likely to result in significant further weight gain and adverse effects, including hypoglycaemia. In particular, in patients with long-term diabetes, hypoglycaemia may risk cardiac arrhythmias, which is an undesirable outcome in a patient with ischaemic heart disease. C Add pioglitazone. Pioglitazone is contraindicated in patients with a history of heart failure due to the risk of fluid retention. Given the presence of oedema on examination and the history of ischaemic heart disease, it is likely that this patient has an element of cardiac failure. E Stop oral treatment and transition to basal bolus insulin. Although basal-bolus insulin can optimise insulin delivery, continuing metformin and the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor seems sensible in this case to limit weight gain on insulin initiation.

questions.question: A 57-year-old non-insulin-dependent diabetic man presented to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of shortness of breath. He was commenced on insulin 4 months ago due to persistent hyperglycaemia despite being on metformin 1 g twice daily (bd) and gliclazide 160 mg bd, and the oral medications were continued. Since being on insulin, he has noticed a weight gain of about 10 kg. He has been a heavy consumer of alcohol and has been treated on multiple occasions for withdrawal symptoms. Other medication includes ramipril, aspirin and atorvastatin. On examination, he had bilateral pitting oedema up to the knees and facial puffiness. Auscultation revealed bilaterally decreased air entry and widespread crackles. Jugular vein pressure (JVP) is elevated. Investigations revealed a normal renal, liver and cardiac profile. Electrocardiogram (ECG) was normal. An echocardiogram revealed a slightly reduced ejection fraction. An admission chest X-ray is shown below. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 102 g/l | 135-175 g/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) | 104 | 80-100 White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 110  x10^9/l | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.5~mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 90 µmol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L HbA1c | 55 mmol/mol | 9.29-53.0~mmol/mol Which of the following would be the most appropriate management step for his symptoms of cardiac failure?
options: D. IV furosemide and oral thiamine supplementation
questions.explanation: D IV furosemide and oral thiamine supplementation. This is a well-established but largely under-recognised clinical scenario of insulin-related worsening of heart failure and fluid overload, which occurs because insulin itself promotes salt and water retention. Thiamine deficiency may also have contributed to his heart failure symptoms. Management of choice is with furosemide to promote salt and water excretion, and thiamine in view of his excessive alcohol consumption. Once his fluid status is stable, if he still has symptoms of heart failure, addition of a cardioselective beta blocker such as bisoprolol may be of value. B Reduce the insulin dosage. Reducing the insulin dose without additional blood glucose lowering therapy runs the risk of deterioration in HbA1c. A Discontinue insulin. HbA1c is virtually at target, and discontinuing insulin risks a significant negative impact on target attainment. C Fluid restriction. Fluid restriction alone won't provide sufficient impact on fluid status to reduce symptoms of heart failure. E Trial of bisoprolol. Beta blockade may improve symptoms of heart failure, but only after fluid overload has been treated with diuretics.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of a lump at the base of his neck. He has noticed that this has become particularly prominent with swallowing and has grown significantly over the past 8 weeks. There is also a problem with diarrhoea over the past few months. Clinical examination reveals a thyroid nodule. On further questioning, it transpires that his mother died during a thyroidectomy some years ago. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 121 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.4  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 140~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 5.2~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 110~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/l Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.85~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/L Ret oncogene | positive | Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Medullary thyroid carcinoma. Ret oncogene positivity raises the possibility of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN-2). Occasionally patients suffer troublesome diarrhoea in response to increased calcitonin levels that cause increased gastrointestinal secretions. We are not given the calcitonin levels here, but it is to be assumed that they are likely to be raised. The thyroid nodule is most likely to be a medullary thyroid carcinoma. Given that his mother died on the operating table, the possibility of MEN-2 with co-existent phaeochromocytoma is further raised. The most appropriate initial screening test would be 24 h urine for catecholamines. MRI with or without meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scanning is useful at a later stage for localising the site of a potential tumour. It is crucial to rule out a phaeochromocytoma, or to manage it appropriately with maximal alpha blockade, before progressing to thyroid surgery. C Follicular thyroid carcinoma. Only a very small proportion of cases of follicular thyroid cancer (<5%) are thought to be related to a familial cancer syndrome. Associated syndromes include (PTEN)-hamartoma tumour syndrome/Cowden syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis/Gardner syndrome, Carney complex type 1, Werner syndrome and Pendred syndrome. B Papillary thyroid carcinoma. Papillary thyroid carcinoma may be associated with RET mutations, but is also associated with mutations in RAS, BRAF and NTRK. The hypercalcaemia here is also more suggestive of MEN-2 because of co-associated hyperparathyroidism. D Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. This is undifferentiated, fast growing and occurs most commonly in an elderly population. E Thyroid adenoma. Thyroid adenomas are not rapidly growing and would not fit with the picture seen here of a potentially cancerous lesion.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. Most recently, he has noticed swelling of his hands and is unable to keep his wedding ring on. His brother also visited from Australia, and thought that his appearance had changed a little. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g BD and gliclazide 160 mg BD. On examination he has soft tissue swelling of his hands and a prominent lower jaw. He is hypertensive, with a BP of 162/90 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 139 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 4.6  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 200  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 140 mmo/l | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.8~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 155~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/l HbA1c | 68.31~mmol/mol (8.4%) | 9.2953.0 mmol/mol (3-7  %) You arrange for him to undergo a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. You look at the low point reached in terms of growth hormone level during the test. Immunoradioassay reveals a growth hormone level of 1.6~mcg/L and you diagnose a growth hormone-producing adenoma. He progresses to surgery, but he then presents 1 year later with a raised IGF-1 level. His diabetes control has worsened a little and again his blood pressure is proving difficult to control. Which of the following would be the most appropriate option for first-line medical therapy for him?
questions.explanation: C Somatostatin analogue. Dopamine agonists are somewhat less effective in the treatment of acromegaly than they are in the treatment of hyperprolactinaemia. For this reason, somatostatin analogues are considered first-line medical therapy. Treatment failures may be considered for pegvisomant, a growth hormone antagonist. Indeed, pegvisomant may be more suitable for patients with particularly marked features of hyperinsulinaemia, as in this gentleman, but currently it is considered a choice only for those who have failed therapy with a somatostatin analogue. B Bromocriptine. It is a dopamine agonist and the alternative to cabergoline as first-line treatment for prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas. A Selegeline. Selegiline, at normal clinical doses, is a selective irreversible MAO-B inhibitor. In larger doses, it loses its specificity and also inhibits MAO-A. It is available in tablet form and is used to reduce symptoms in early-stage Parkinson's disease. A transdermal patch is used to treat depression. D Pegvisomant. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used in the treatment of acromegaly. It is primarily used if the pituitary gland tumour causing the acromegaly cannot be controlled with surgery or radiation, and the use of somatostatin analogues is unsuccessful, but is also effective as a monotherapy. E Pergolide. Pergolide is an ergoline-based dopamine receptor agonist used in some countries for the treatment of Parkinson's disease (PD). PD is associated with reduced dopamine activity in the substantia nigra of the brain. Pergolide acts on many of the same receptors as dopamine to increase receptor activity.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has some blood tests as part of a medical examination for life insurance. She is completely well and takes no regular medication. Apparently another member of her family is noted to have high calcium levels, but has required no intervention. Investigations revealed the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.88 mmol/l | 2.20-2.60 mmol/l Her General Practitioner (GP) therefore conducted some blood tests, which revealed the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | 4.7 pmol/l | 0.9-5.4 pmol/l Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio | < 0.01, indicating relative hypocalciuria | Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) | 30 U/L | 25-82 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH). This lady is well but has elevated calcium. Her parathyroid hormone and serum ACE are normal. Her calcium-to-creatinine ratio is <0.01, indicating reduced excretion of calcium. This is characteristic of FHH, which is a defect in the calcium-sensing receptor (plasma membrane G-protein coupled receptor). No treatment is usually needed. FHH is characterised by hypercalcaemia, relative hypocalciuria, slight hypermagnesaemia and inappropriately normal to high levels of PTH. D Sarcoidosis. Where there is significant sarcoid disease activity, leading to a raised serum calcium, angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are usually elevated. Normal levels seen here count against sarcoidosis as the cause of hypercalcaemia. A Bronchial carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus is associated with production of parathyroid hormone-related PTH (PTHrP), which is a cause of hypercalcaemia, but should actually suppress endogenous PTH production. Other features suggestive of bronchial carcinoma, such as a cough or smoking history, are also absent in this scenario. B Primary hyperparathyroidism. Relative hypocalciuria was previously thought to differentiate between primary hyperparathyroidism and FHH, although population analyses of patients with primary hyperparathyroidism cast doubt on this as a differentiating factor. The inheritance pattern indicating other affected family members does, however, support a diagnosis of FHH. E Paget's disease. Paget's disease is associated with elevated alkaline phosphatase and joint pain, and is usually only associated with hypercalcaemia when patients spend a significant period of time recumbent in bed.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) with a two-day history of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He has returned from a week's holiday in Crete two weeks ago. He says he is worried because he had numerous episodes of unprotected sex. He is feeling weak, has lost his appetite and has lost 6.3 kg (1 stone) in weight. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and often drinks a bottle of red wine for dinner. His mother has type I diabetes mellitus and his father has had a stroke. On examination, his clothes hang loosely and he has a suntan. He is afebrile. His pulse is 60 beats per minute (bpm) while his blood pressure (BP) is 80/40 mmHg. His heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. His abdomen is soft but tender on palpation. Bowel sounds are present. His neurological examination is normal, as is a chest X-ray (CXR). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 110 g/l | 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) | 3.2  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 143  x10^9/l | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 121~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 5.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 65 µmol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.72~mmol/L | 2.20-2.60~mmol/L Urea | 7.2~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Albumin | 34 g/l | 35-55 g/l Glucose | 9.8 mmol/l | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) | 101.3 fl | 80-100 fl Blood film | Macrocytosis | What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C Addison's disease. Over 90% of patients diagnosed complain of weakness, hyperpigmentation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting and hypotension. In addition, the accompanying macrocytic anaemia suggests a diagnosis of pernicious anaemia. Between 70 and 90% of cases of Addison's disease in the UK are caused by autoimmune adrenalitis. The combination of a high ACTH concentration (>80~ng/l) and a poorly responsive Synacthen test is diagnostic of Addison's disease. The raised glucose raises the possibility of co-existent autoimmune diabetes, but the glucose isn't high enough to indicate ketoacidosis. B IV drug abuse. There would be signs of injection drug use, including scars at injection sites (so-called 'track marks') on the skin. When acutely unwell, patients can present with medical conditions affecting one or more system - the cardiovascular system (infective endocarditis, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, etc.); renal system (kidney failure); gastrointestinal system (pancreatitis, cirrhosis, chronic liver disease, infective hepatitis, etc.); central nervous system (dementia, memory impairment, cerebrovascular events, etc.); or respiratory system (lung abscess. pneumonia, chronic obstructive airway disease, TB, etc.). A Gonococcal sepsis. Gonococcal sepsis affects 0.5-3% patients with a sexually transmitted Gram-negative organism called N. gonorrhoeae. It presents as one of the two common syndromes: a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgia without purulent arthritis (also called the 'arthritis-dermatitis syndrome'); or purulent arthritis without associated skin lesions. D Gastroenteritis. Diarrhoea and frequent vomiting are usually present together, but the former symptom conspicuously is absent in this case making this diagnosis less likely. Vomiting can present in isolation in some cases of viral gastroenteritis, but the incubation period is usually shorter (< 72 h). Weight loss in not present in the acute phase. E Diabetic ketoacidosis. There is no weight loss as the presentation is acute, and the patient is significantly dehydrated. Laboratory investigations to confirm the diagnosis include the following: elevated plasma glucose ( (>11~mmol/l). arterial pH  le7.3, serum bicarbonate   le15 mmol/l, positive urine ketones, blood ketones   ge3 mmol/l.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP), complaining of severe problems with central obesity. Her past medical history includes manic depression, hypertension and chronic alcohol abuse. Medication includes sodium valproate, ramipril, indapamide and amlodipine. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 165/90 mmHg and her body mass index (BMI) is 38. She has moon-like facial features, buffalo hump and abdominal striae. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 122 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.6  x10^9/l | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelet (PLT) | 230  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na) | 141~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K) | 4.8~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 123~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Alanine transaminase (ALT) | 105 U/L | 25-55~U/l Fasting glucose | 8.2 mmol/l | <5.6~mmol/L 0900 hours plasma cortisol | 1000~nmol/L | 130-690~nmol/L Midnight plasma cortisol | 400~nmol/L | < 50% of morning level Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C Pseudo Cushing's disease. The answer is Pseudo-Cushing's disease (Option C). It can be challenging to distinguish Cushing's disease from pseudo-Cushing's disease as the clinical presentation is similar. The main clinical clues to pseudo-Cushing's disease in this case are the chronic alcohol abuse and depression. The key biochemical evidence is that there remains diurnal variation in the cortisol level, which would not be seen in Cushing's disease. Often, treating the underlying cause will result in resolution of the symptoms and biochemical disturbances. B Cushing syndrome. Cushing syndrome (Option B) is incorrect. In a patient with Cushing syndrome, the plasma cortisol level would not show diurnal variation, ie the midnight plasma level would not be < 50% of the morning level; this patient's biochemistry clearly shows a drop of > 50%. With her background of chronic alcohol abuse and depression, the best answer would therefore be pseudo-Cushing's disease. A Cushing's disease. Cushing's disease (Option A) is incorrect. In a patient with Cushing's disease, the plasma cortisol level would not show diurnal variation, ie the midnight plasma level would not be < 50% of the morning level; this patient's biochemistry clearly shows a drop of > 50%. With her background of chronic alcohol abuse and depression, the best answer would therefore be pseudo-Cushing's disease. D Impaired glucose tolerance. Impaired glucose tolerance (Option D) is incorrect. A raised glucose level is expected as a result of raised cortisol levels. Diagnosing impaired glucose tolerance requires a fasting blood glucose level of < 7 mmol/l and an oral glucose tolerance test level of 7.8-11.0 mmol/l, which is not the case here. E Simple obesity. Simple obesity (Option E) is incorrect. The patient clearly presents with an abnormal picture and abnormal biochemistry, which simple obesity alone would not satisfactorily explain. There is no doubt that this patient should lose weight.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with type II diabetes comes to the Emergency Department for review. She is not due for follow-up in clinic for two months but has recently started insulin therapy and now has burning pain and weakness affecting her left thigh. Her diabetes has been poorly controlled over the past two years, with an HbA1c of > 69 mmol/mol (> 8.5%) over the follow-up period. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg, and pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Neurological examination reveals evidence of weakness and wasting of the left quadriceps. There is loss of the left knee jerk and slightly diminished sensation over the medial aspect of the thigh. Investigations: Investigations | Results | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 130 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.2  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 295  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine | 118~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L HbA1c | 64mmol/mol (8.0%) | < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) | 32~mm/first hour | 0-10~mm/first hour Creatine kinase (CK) | 64 IU/L | 23-175 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Diabetic amyotrophy. The classical picture of proximal pain and weakness in a femoral nerve distribution is suggestive of diabetic amyotrophy. The underlying pathology is unclear, although the presentation is associated with rapid changes in blood glucose such as those associated with commencing insulin therapy after a period of poor diabetic control. Physiotherapy, coupled with medications, to manage neuropathic pain is the intervention of choice. C Lumbosacral disc prolapse. This is associated with sudden-onset back pain and radiculopathy, usually more marked on one side than the other, rather than the symptoms described here. B Injection site reaction. This is very unlikely, given that patients are not encouraged to inject directly into the thigh on a regular basis and there is no indication of skin changes. D Polymyositis. This is associated with raised CK and generalised proximal muscle pain (in around one-third of patients). E Polymyalgia rheumatica. This is associated with more generalised proximal muscle symptoms affecting both the hips and shoulders, usually worse in the mornings, and a much greater rise in markers of inflammation than that seen here.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with increasing nausea and vomiting over the past 72 h. She has a history of autoimmune hypothyroidism controlled with thyroxine replacement, but has no other significant past medical illnesses. On further questioning, it transpires that she has lost weight and been feeling increasingly lethargic, having passed out twice at work, in the last three months. Examination reveals a BP of 100/80 mmHg, which falls to 85/65 mmHg on standing; her pulse is 80/min and regular. She is slim and tanned with a BMI of 20. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 119 g/l | 135-175~g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 188  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 130~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.9~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 110~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Urea | 10.2~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/l Glucose | 4.1~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 2.1 u/L | 0.4-5.0~u/L Which of the following is the most important step?
options: D. Synacthen test the following day
questions.explanation: A IV hydrocortisone. The presentation here is consistent with Addison's disease. Given the significantly abnormal clinical chemistry, coupled with worsening nausea and vomiting, there is no opportunity to delay initiation of therapy whilst awaiting a Synacthen test. Commencing IV hydrocortisone is therefore the initial intervention of choice. In this case, given the previous history of autoimmune thyroid disease, autoimmune adrenal failure is the most likely cause here. Adrenal insufficiency is excluded in the Synacthen test by an incremental rise in cortisol of > 200 nmol/L and a 30 min value >600~nmol/L One dose of hydrocortisone the previous evening is unlikely to affect interpretation of the test. C Oral fludrocortisone. Oral fludrocortisone is used in patients who fail to maintain postural blood pressure despite adequate corticosteroid replacement. B IV normal saline. Although IV normal saline may temporarily improve blood pressure, it won't impact on the underlying cause, in this case adrenal insufficiency. D Synacthen test the following day. Delaying intervention until after a Synacthen test is inappropriate given the significant hypotension and E Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS). This may reveal adrenal atrophy or calcification, but it won't provide an estimation of adrenal function.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman who has been taking long term amiodarone therapy comes to the clinic complaining of palpitations at rest. On examination her BP is 135/75 mmHg, her pulse is 90/min at rest. Thyroid gland examination is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 119 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 182  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 138 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 130 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | <0.05 U/L | <0.5-4.5 U/L Thyroid autoantibodies | Negative |  Interleukin 6 (IL-6) | Elevated |  You change her amiodarone for another agent. Which of the following is the mainstay of therapy in this situation?
questions.explanation: D Corticosteroids This patient has amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 2, as evidenced by the relatively normal thyroid on clinical examination, lack of marked signs of thyrotoxicosis, elevated IL-6 and negative thyroid autoantibodies. Management of AIT type 2 is very different to the management of AIT type 1, with corticosteroids being the mainstay of therapy. This is because AIT type 2 is the result of a direct effect of amiodarone, which leads to thyroiditis. A Carbimazole Anti-thyroid drugs are the mainstay of therapy for AIT type 1, which is more usually associated with positive thyroid antibodies and there is no rise in IL-6. There is no practical difference in efficacy between propylthiouracil and carbimazole. B Potassium perchlorate Potassium perchlorate is utilised to gain acute control of thyroid function in patients who require urgent intervention, for example because of unstable cardiovascular disease. C Thyroidectomy This is considered for patients who fail to respond to medical intervention alone, usually for AIT type 1. E Propylthiouracil This is an alternative to carbimazole as a mainstay of intervention in AIT type 1.

questions.question: A 21-year-old student nurse presents with frequent episodes of collapse. One of these occurred during a placement in the Emergency Department at the same time as a cardiac arrest. Blood glucose at the time was noted to be 1.4 mmol/l. Other blood tests were unremarkable. On examination straight after an event, her BP was 123/82 mmHg, withpulse is 95/min and regular and she was cold and sweaty. Blood taken at the time confirmed a venous blood glucose of 1.2 mmol/l, C-peptide level was low-normal and insulin levels were markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: C Insulin misuse Hyperinsulinaemia in the presence of a normal or low C-peptide is suggestive of insulin misuse, which is unfortunately a more common occurrence in healthcare professionals who are seeking attention, as is the case here. As here, measurement of insulin, glucose and C-peptide at the time of a collapse is crucial for making the diagnosis. A Insulinoma Insulinoma is a rare occurrence, and is associated with elevated insulin and C-peptide. Overnight fasting, coupled with supervised exercise, is the most commonly used protocol to drive a hypoglycaemic episode. B Sulphonylurea misuse Elevation in both C-peptide and insulin may raise suspicion of sulphonylurea abuse. It is possible to assay levels of commonly used sulphonylureas in urine, and this should be considered. D Alcohol misuse Hypoglycaemia does occur in association with alcohol misuse, but this is commonly following a period of binge drinking and it's unlikely this person could work in a hospital environment whilst having consumed significant amounts of alcohol. E Retroperitoneal sarcoma Hypoglycaemia associated with retroperitoneal sarcoma is extremely rare and is associated with increased levels of IGF-2.

questions.question: A 67-year-old patient who is visiting from West Africa attends the clinic with her daughter. She has had hypertension for a number of years and is managed on a range of agents, including ramipril, indapamide, amlodipine, aspirin and simvastatin. Other past history of note includes a recent left forearm fracture after a fall, an episode of kidney stones and a short period of drug treatment for depression. Her daughter is extremely worried, as she has noticed a change in the appearance of her mother's hands since she last saw her 18 months earlier. Examination in the clinic reveals a blood pressure of 149/85 mmHg and a pulse of 78 bpm (in atrial fibrillation). Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Abdominal and neurological examinations are unremarkable. She appears to have telescoping of the ends of her fingers, although there are no obvious signs of arthritis elsewhere. Investigations: Investigations | Results | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 124 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 8:0  x10^9/t | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 112 μmol/L | 50-120 μmol/L Calcium (Ca2+) | 2.95 mmol/L | 2.2-2.6 mmol/L Phosphate (PO4-) | 0.7 mmol/l (0.8-1.5) | 0.8-1.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C Primary hyperparathyroidism This patient has a relatively normal creatinine level, elevated serum calcium level and reduced serum phosphate level. This clinical picture is most consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism driven either by a single adenoma or four-gland hyperplasia. The X-ray shows the beginning of reabsorption of the terminal phalanges of the fingers on both hands. The intervention of choice is surgery, following localisation of any adenoma with magnetic resonance imaging, technetium scanning or a combination of both. B Pseudohypoparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism classically presents with shortening of the fourth finger of both hands. It leads to calcium levels below the limit of normal. It is caused by G protein-coupled receptor resistance to activation by parathyroid hormone (PTH).
