A Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) FHH is often a benign condition, which presents incidentally with mild to moderate elevation in calcium level on routine blood testing. D Secondary hyperparathyroidism Secondary hyperparathyroidism is driven by hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia and is seen in patients with chronic renal failure. The normal renal function here effectively rules it out. E Tertiary hyperparathyroidism Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops in some patients with secondary disease, when production of PTH becomes autonomous and cannot be limited by correction of calcium and phosphate levels.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy comes to the Endocrine Clinic with his parents. They are concerned about his excessive height. Apparently, he has grown significantly in the past six months and his parents are unable to buy shoes to fit him. He has no significant past medical history apart from severe myopia. On examination, his blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. He is 1.92 m tall and has size 12 feet (his parents are shorter at 1.8 m and 1.62 m). He has large hands, a prominent lower jaw and appears to be perspiring excessively. You note normal secondary sexual characteristics. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 131 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.8  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 201  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/l | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 95 µmol/l | 50-120 μmol/L Glucose | 6.8 mmol/l (fasting) | <7 mmol/L Growth hormone | 15 ng/ml post oral glucose tolerance test | <10 ng/ml Bone age | Consistent with age 19 | Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: D Pituitary gigantism The rapid growth, large hands and feet and normal secondary sexual characteristics alongside failure for growth hormone to be suppressed with an oral glucose tolerance test is highly suggestive of a growth hormone producing pituitary adenoma. A pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is the next investigation of choice. B Familial tall stature His parental height and oral glucose tolerance test result effectively rule out familial tall stature as a diagnosis. A Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disorder that is associated with extensive elastic skin, joint hypermobility and abnormal scar formation. This is not consistent with the clinical scenario - especially the rapid growth. C Marfan syndrome Although patients with Marfan syndrome do have tall stature, it would be unusual for there to be such rapid growth. Aside from the myopia, this patient does not meet any of the other features in the revised Ghent nosology. E Weaver syndrome Weaver syndrome is a bone overgrowth disorder with associated developmental delay. This does not fit the clinical scenario in this case. The patient's rapid growth and the failure for growth hormone to be suppressed is highly suggestive of a growth hormone producing pituitary adenoma.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the Lipid Clinic some 6 weeks after a second episode of acute pancreatitis. He has no past medical history of note apart from hypertriglyceridaemia. He denies significant alcohol consumption. Examination reveals a BP of 135/85 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 23. Investigations; Hb | 139 g/l WCC | 8.1  x10^9/L PLT | 231  x10^9/L Na | 137 mmol/L K+ | 4.3 mmol/l Creatinine | 105 micromol/L ALT | 62 U/L HDL | 0.8 mmol/L LDL | 2.3 mmol/L TGs | 8.1 mmol/L Which of the following is the best way to treat his triglycerides?
questions.explanation: C Fenofibrate The answer is Fenofibrate - Fibrates can lower triglyceride levels by up to 70% in patients with significant hypertriglyceridaemia, and are the initial therapy of choice here. They are also thought to impact positively on plasma viscosity in this situation, hence reducing the risk of vascular events. In patients with mild elevations in TGs, fenofibrate should not be used as it may actually increase the risk of pancreatitis events. A Atorvastatin Atorvastatin, is incorrect, because statins primarily impact on levels of LDL cholesterol. B Cholestyramine Cholestyramine, is incorrect because bile acid binding resins have very modest effects in reducing cholesterol and triglycerides, and are unlikely to significantly impact on this person's markedly elevated triglycerides. D Niacin Niacin is incorrect. Niacin and nicotinic acid derivatives can significantly reduce triglyceride levels. They are poorly tolerated at high dose, however, due to flushing and itching, and may increase the risk of diabetes. In the EU they are only available at low dose as a food supplement. E Omega 3 fatty acids Omega 3 fatty acids is incorrect, this can have very positive effects on triglyceride levels, but in this situation would be the add in of choice to patients not achieving triglyceride target on fibrate alone.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of symptoms of pain and tingling in her hands, which is particularly worse at night. She has an unremarkable past medical history. On examination, Tinel's sign is positive and there is some vague sensory loss over a median nerve distribution; there is also some weakness of the muscles of the thenar eminence. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be the cause of this problem?
questions.explanation: A Hypothyroidism This patient has symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, with pain and tingling at night, thenar eminence wasting and positive Tinel's sign (reproduction of pain and tingling on tapping over median nerve). Associated conditions include hypothyroidism, raised oestrogen levels (oral contraceptive pill or pregnancy), Cushing syndrome and obesity, amongst a number of additional related diseases. Treatment of choice for carpal tunnel syndrome is surgery, although in patients who are surgically unfit, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, locally injected corticosteroids and nocturnal splints may be usefully employed. Even with treatment of hypothyroidism, or birth of the child, symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome may not resolve. E Menopause High oestrogen levels, such as during pregnancy or whilst taking oral contraceptives, are associated with carpal tunnel syndrome. B Anorexia nervosa Obesity is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, due to compression of the median. C Hyperthyroidism Hypothyroidism is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome due to excessive soft tissue/collagenous deposition associated with myxoedem. D Addison's Cushing syndrome (i.e the 'opposite' of Addison's) is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: A 42-year-old type II diabetic woman presents with recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). She has been treated with a number of antibiotics, including trimethoprim and amoxicillin. She still complains of dysuria and some soreness in her groin. Her most recent Hb A1c was 108 mmol/mol (12%). Ultrasound (US) scan abdomen demonstrated no structural abnormalities or evidence of pyelonephritis. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: A Extended spectrum beta-lactamase-producing coli Data from the American Diabetes Association have shown that 9.4% of people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes had a UTI compared to only 5.7% of those without. The most common pathogens isolated from the urine of diabetic patients with UTI were E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae such as Klebsiella spp., Proteus spp., Enterobacter spp. and Enterococci. Multiple courses of antibiotic therapy in these patients, and increased incidence of hospital-acquired and catheter-associated UTI, induce the development of antibiotic-resistant urinary pathogens. Infection with ESBL-producing E. coli is an increasingly recognised cause of infection in diabetes patients and is associated with poor outcomes. ESBLs are enzymes that open the beta-lactam ring, inactivating the antibiotic and consequently conferring resistance to most beta-lactam antibiotics such as pencillins and cephalosporins. Some ESBL isolates have been shown to be resistant to antibiotics commonly used for UTI, such as trimethoprim. Ciprofloxacin is no longer recommended for use in uncomplicated cystitis if there is an appropriate alternative available, due to an increased risk of long lasting or permanent side effects such as tendonitis; however ciprofloxacin may also be ineffective against some strains of ESBL isolates. Carbapenems are generally considered the drug of choice for the treatment of ESBL/E. coli (ESBL-EC) infections. With a half-life of 4 h, ertapenem is commonly used as it is administered only once daily. Fosfomycin is an oral antibiotic agent that has broad activity against multi-drug-resistant pathogen, including ESBL-EC. Another oral antimicrobial agent that can be considered for the treatment of ESBL-EC cystitis is nitrofurantoin. D Neisseria gonorrhoea N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted Gram-negative organism that causes infection in 0.5-3% of patients acquiring it. It presents as one of two common syndromes: a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgias without purulent arthritis (also called the 'arthritis-dermatitis syndrome'); or purulent arthritis without associated skin lesions.. B Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcal aureus (MRSA) MRSA prevalence has risen dramatically in hospital and community settings. Methicillin resistance is mediated by PBP-2a, a penicillin-binding protein encoded by the mecA gene that permits the organism to grow and divide in the presence of methicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics. Risk factors for infection are long-term care residency; recent surgery/hospitalization; long-term indwelling catheters such as in haemodialysis patients; prolonged and repeated use of antibiotics such as cepaholosporins and quinolones; HIV infection and sharing of needles. C Candida albicans Candida urinary tract infections (UTIs) also occur commonly in uncontrolled diabetic patients, but the frequency of occurrence of infection with this organism is lower than that with E. coli. E Chlamydia trachomatis Chlamydia trachomatis is a Gram-negative organism that is sexually transmitted. It causes trachoma, a sight-threatening eye disease endemic to Asia and Africa; urogenital infections; and lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), which is a condition characterised by the development of a painless, stellate genital ulcer followed by the development of inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is the leading cause of infertility in women. Chlamydial urinary tract infection occurs in a small proportion of sexually active women who present with typical symptoms of UTI, but in whom urinalysis reveals pyuria but no bacteriuria.

questions.question: A 19-year-old student presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with delayed puberty. He has so far been unable to form relationships and feels any time he meets a potential female partner everything breaks down at the physical stage. On examination, he has sparse body hair and an underdeveloped penis with small testes. His blood pressure (BP) and body mass index (BMI) are both normal. He is also anosmic. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Testosterone | 5 nmol/l | 9-35 nmol/l Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | 0.69 U/L | 1-25 U/L Luteinizing hormone (LH) | 0.57 U/L | 1-70 U/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 1.2 μυ/ | 0.17-3.2 μυ/ What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: A Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome results from disordered migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-producing neurons into the hypothalamus. This leads to failure of episodic GnRH secretion and subsequent failure of luteinising hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and testosterone production. Seventy-five per cent of sufferers have absent sense of smell (anosmia). It occurs in 1 in 10 000 males, being rarer in females (male: female ratio 4: 1). The syndrome is also associated with an increased risk of cleft lip and palate and sensorineural deafness. The main differential diagnosis is constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP). which is far more common than Kallmann syndrome. A definitive diagnosis of IHH in the absence of a family history or prior genetic testing is difficult to make until the patient reaches at least 18 years of age, unless other suggestive features are present (ie, prior microphallus and/or cryptorchism, anosmia, renal agenesis, skeletal defects, etc). The management of GnRH deficiency includes replacing sex steroids to develop secondary sex characteristics and to build and sustain normal bone and muscle mass. Exogenous gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy are used for ovulation induction in women and for induction of spermatogenesis in men. C Androgen insensitivity syndrome AIS is associated with female external genitalia, rather than the male phenotype seen here. B Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome is associated with small testes and low levels of testosterone, but isn't associated with loss of sense of smell. D Pan-hypopituitarism The normal-range TSH in the absence of symptoms of hypothyroidism counts against a diagnosis of pan-hypopituitarism. E Turner syndrome Turner syndrome is associated with short stature, cardiovascular abnormalities and female external genitalia.

questions.question: A 18-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining that she has not begun began to menstruate and that she has severe acne. On examination, she is found to have hirsutism, a deep voice and severe acne. A photograph of her appearance is shown below: Her GP wonders if she might have non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Which protein is most likely to be defective?
questions.explanation: B 21-Hydroxylase Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is caused by defective 21-hydroxylase in around 95% of cases, due to a gene mutation. This may be classical CAH - where there is a failure to make cortisol and also salt-loss due to a failure of the adrenal glands to synthesis aldosterone; or non-classical CAH - which is milder and causes androgen excess which causes symptoms such as hirsutism, a deep voice and severe acne. Classical CAH tends to be diagnosed when the patient is very young due to failure to thrive, whereas non-classical CAH may be diagnosed later, in late childhood or early adulthood. C Apolipoprotein B This enzyme defect may be seen in some patients with familial hypercholesterolemia. However, as we suspect that she suffers from CAH, it would therefore not be seen in this patient. A 17-alpha hydroxylase This enzyme may be defective in CAH, but this is a rare occurrence. In contrast, 21-hydroxylase deficiency is responsible for around 95% of cases of CAH and is, therefore, more likely to be defective in this scenario. D Thyroid peroxidase Thyroid peroxidase deficiency occurs in patients with congenital hypothyroidism, and not in those with CAH. E Menin Menin is defective in multiple endocrine neoplasia type I as a result of a mutation in the MEN1 gene. This affects the pituitary gland, parathyroid gland and pancreas, but not the adrenal gland, which is affected in CAH.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with headaches and excessive sweating. She also reports joint pain and has noticed progressive enlargement of her hands and feet. She has a past medical history of carpal tunnel syndrome and hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 10 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg once daily. On examination, she has frontal bossing, prognathism with an underbite and an enlarged tongue. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to aid in the diagnosis of this patient?
options: B. MRI of the pituitary gland
C. Random serum growth hormone level
questions.explanation: D Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 This patient has a likely diagnosis of acromegaly, given the history of headaches, sweating, joint pain and enlargement of the hands, feet and facial features. The condition is usually the result of excess growth hormone secretion from the pituitary gland. Growth hormone stimulates the production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), the main tissue mediator of growth hormone. Therefore, the most appropriate initial investigation is to measure the serum levels of this hormone. A raised IGF-1 level is indicative of acromegaly. E Serum prolactin Often, cases of acromegaly are caused by a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. Large adenomas can affect the secretion of other pituitary hormones. Therefore, as part of a general workup of the condition, the levels of pituitary hormones, such as prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone, are measured. However, such measurement is not indicated at this stage. A Oral glucose tolerance test The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is used to confirm the diagnosis of acromegaly in those with a marginally raised IGF-1 level. Since growth hormone levels are normally suppressed by glucose, patients are given a 75-g glucose load and their growth hormone levels are monitored. If the growth hormone level remains elevated, this confirms the diagnosis of acromegaly. Although this investigation is used in the early diagnosis of acromegaly, it is typically used after the measurement of IGF-1 levels. B MRI of the pituitary gland Acromegaly is often caused by a pituitary adenoma. As they enlarge, additional symptoms may present such as headaches or visual field defects. Therefore, imaging of the pituitary gland is often necessary. However, MRI of the pituitary gland is not an initial investigation needed to diagnose acromegaly. Additionally, correlation of the imaging findings with biochemical results (eg IGF-1 levels) is needed. C Random serum growth hormone level Although an elevated random growth hormone level suggests acromegaly, growth hormone levels vary throughout the day, with a short half-life, and are therefore unreliable. For this reason, growth hormone levels are not usually tested in isolation and other measures (eg IGF-1 levels) are used instead.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of thirst and lethargy. She has been feeling unwell for some time, and is now suffering from an erythematous rash that began on her groin but has now spread to involve the buttocks, lower limbs and perineum. The rash is shown below, there is associated glossitis and vaginitis. Fasting blood glucose is raised, at 8.1 mmol/l. On further questioning she admits to weight loss of a few kilograms over the past few months. What would be the most useful investigation to elucidate the reason of presentation in this patient?
questions.explanation: B Glucagon level This lady has diabetes mellitus, with the characteristic rash of necrolytic migratory erythema. The rash results in itchy lesions which blister before eroding and crusting over. Whilst it can affect any body area, it commonly occurs around the genitals, buttocks and lower legs. Her diabetes, therefore may be secondary to a glucagonoma. Glucagonomas are extremely rare, with an annual incidence estimated at 1/20 million. Diagnosis is confirmed on finding raised plasma glucagon levels. Most primary tumours are >3 cm in diameter, 70% are malignant in nature and more than 50% have metastasised at the time of diagnosis. Tumour localisation is usually possible with abdominal ultrasound and/or computerised tomography (CT); where tumours are small, or metastatic spread is being assessed, octreotide scanning may be utilised. The potential for surgical cure is only 5%; octreotide is useful for controlling the rash, although its effects on associated diabetes and weight loss are more variable. Palliative chemotherapy using streptozocin and fluorouracil does produce acceptable reductions of glucagon over a 1-year period. Selective tumour embolisation via the hepatic artery may be of additional value. E Insulin tolerance test Insulin tolerance testing is used in the evaluation of patients with growth hormone deficiency. A Insulin level Insulin levels are most useful in assessment of hypoglycaemia, checked in conjunction with a c-peptide and glucose at the time of an episode. In insulinoma elevated insulin and c-peptide are seen with a low blood glucose. C Somatostatin level Although a somatostatinoma may be associated with the development of impaired glucose tolerance, it is not associated with the characteristic skin rash of glucagonoma seen here. D Oral glucose tolerance test This will merely confirm the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus without elucidating the underlying cause.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman visits the Diabetic Clinic. She was diagnosed with type II diabetes 18 months previously and has been on treatment with metformin modified release 1 g twice a day, pioglitazone 45 mg once a day and gliclazide 80 mg once a day. On examination, her HbA1c level is 75 mmol/mol (9.0%), and blood pressure (BP) is 136/75 mmHg. She has no microalbuminuria. In spite of dietary advice and modification, she remains obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m^2. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to weight and glucose control?
questions.explanation: E Liraglutide 3 mg This patient is obese with poor HbA1c control; as such, rather than an intervention for glucose control and weight loss is appropriate. Liraglutide is licensed for weight loss at the 3 mg dose and was shown in the SCALE diabetes study to drive significant weight loss (6% versus baseline over 52 weeks; see link for JAMA article). D Orlistat Orlistat does achieve modest weight loss, but it is often poorly tolerated due to side effects related to fat malabsorption. Tolerability issues are also seen more frequently in patients where there is concomitant use of metformin. There will also be no short-term impact on glucose control. These factors drive us more towards the use of liraglutide. A Further diet and exercise Given this patient has not lost a significant amount of weight with lifestyle intervention, further measures are required. B Dulaglutide 1.5 mg Dulaglutide 1.5mg is used for glucose control in type II diabetes; although it does impact on weight, effects are more modest versus liraglutide 3mg. C Canagliflozin Canagliflozin is primarily an SGLT-2 inhibitor which reduces glucose reabsorption in the kidney, promoting carbohydrate loss. It is licensed for control of blood glucose in type II diabetes, not for weight loss.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman who is 24 weeks' pregnant is referred to the clinic complaining of increasing tiredness, emotional lability, tiredness particularly in the evenings, and episodes of palpitations. Her GP has put this down to the normal stresses and strains associated with a first pregnancy. On examination she looks tired, her BP is 125/78 mmHg and her pulse is 90/min at rest. You notice that she has sweaty palms. There is a small, smooth goitre on palpation. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 110 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.4x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 182x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.1 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/l Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | <0.05 µU/L | 0.17-3.2 µU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: D Graves' disease Thyrotoxicosis, of which 85% of cases are due to Graves' disease, occurs in 0.1-0.4% of all pregnancies. Whilst her reported symptoms may be reflective of the anxiety experienced by many pregnant women, they seem particularly severe, and the presence of a suppressed TSH points towards the diagnosis. A Hyperemesis gravidarum This may be associated with TSH suppression, but it isn't usually suppressed below the lower limit of quantification, and is not usually associated with frank symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. B Anxiety The goitre, signs of thyrotoxicosis and suppressed TSH effectively rule out anxiety as the cause of symptoms here. C Hashimoto's thyroiditis Hashimoto's thyroiditis is of course associated with hypothyroidism rather than the picture of thyrotoxicosis seen here. E Toxic adenoma A toxic adenoma isn't associated with a goitre, but with a discrete nodule. The suppressed TSH would, however, fit with a toxic adenoma.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP with complaints of fatigue, weight gain and sensitivity to cold over the past few months. She reports no significant changes in her diet or activity level. On examination, she has dry skin and mild periorbital puffiness. Her thyroid gland appears mildly enlarged on palpation, with no nodules. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) | 120 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 6.5x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 250x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na) | 132 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K) | 4.1 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 18 mlU/L | 0.4-4.0 mlU/L Free thyroxine (FT4) | 8 pmol/l | 12-22 pmol/L What is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's symptoms?
options: A. Increased thyroid hormone production due to TSH-secreting adenoma
B. Autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue
C. Decreased synthesis of TSH in the pituitary
E. Increased conversion of T4 to triiodothyronine
questions.explanation: B Autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) is a common cause of primary hypothyroidism where immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland reduces T4 production, leading to a compensatory increase in TSH level. The patient's symptoms and laboratory results are consistent with hypothyroidism due to autoimmune destruction. C Decreased synthesis of TSH in the pituitary If TSH production were low due to pituitary dysfunction (secondary hypothyroidism), both TSH and FT4 levels would be low. Here, the TSH level is elevated, indicating that the thyroid, not the pituitary, is the primary problem. A Increased thyroid hormone production due to TSH-secreting adenoma TSH-secreting adenomas typically cause hyperthyroidism, leading to high levels of TSH and thyroid hormones (triiodothyronine (T3) and T4), causing symptoms including heat intolerance and weight loss. This patient's low FT4 and elevated TSH levels indicate primary hypothyroidism. D Increased thyroxine-binding globulin Increased thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) levels would raise total thyroid hormone levels, but FT4 (the active form) levels would remain normal. TBG changes do not account for the low FT4 and high TSH levels in this patient. E Increased conversion of T4 to triiodothyronine Increased T4 to T3 conversion is not relevant to hypothyroidism, as it would not explain the elevated TSH levels or the symptoms of reduced thyroid hormone levels. In hypothyroidism, both T4 and T3 production are generally low due to thyroid gland dysfunction.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath and a choking sensation, particularly when she goes to bed. She has seen the GP, been given a diagnosis of anxiety and started on sertraline. On examination, she has an obvious multinodular goitre. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 127 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.9x10^9/t | 4.0-11.0x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 194x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) | 4.9 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 100 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 3.5 U/L | <0.5-4.5 U/L Ultrasound (US) Multiple thyroid nodules, very large goitre Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: E Sub-total thyroidectomy The fact this woman has symptoms of thoracic outlet obstruction when she lies flat in bed raises the possibility that she may have significant tracheal compression because of her goitre. There is some debate about whether sub-total or total thyroidectomy is the most appropriate option, with slow re-growth and the possibility of malignant change favouring the latter, but this is countered with increased potential risk of postoperative hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. A Radioiodine Radioiodine is less effective in patients who are euthyroid; it is effective in patients with thyrotoxicosis where increased uptake of iodine is seen. B Carbimazole Anti-thyroid drugs will result in hypothyroidism without resolving the goitre seen here. C Propylthiouracil Like carbimazole, propylthiouracil will result in hypothyroidism without significant resolution of the goitre. D Observation This woman has significant symptoms of thoracic outlet obstruction and is at risk of nocturnal hypoxia.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man who has suffered 5 episodes of pancreatitis related to alcoholism presents to the Emergency Department with thirst, lethargy and loss of weight which has increased in severity over the past 2 months. On examination his BP is 132/90 mmHg, there is a postural drop of 20mmHg on standing. His abdomen is soft and non-tender; his BMI is 21.5. Investigations; Hb | 131 g/l WCC | 7.1x10^9/L PLT | 203x10^9/L Na+ | 138 mmol/L K+ | 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine | 132 micromol/L Urea | 10.2 mmol/L Glucose | 20.1 mmol/L HbA1c | 84 mmol/mol (9.8%) Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his diabetes?
questions.explanation: A Basal bolus insulin The answer is Basal bolus insulin - This patient shows significant features of insulinopaenia, probably related to beta cell loss as a result of repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis. Given he is losing weight and has a very elevated glucose, basal bolus insulin is the only practical intervention. Due to alpha cell loss patients are at significant risk of hypoglycaemia, basal bolus allows much tighter targeting of insulin to requirements versus other regimens such as a BD mixed insulin prescription. E Sitagliptin Sitagliptin, is incorrect because DPPIV inhibitors have very modest effects on glucose, only in patients with significant residual beta cell function, and are associated with increased risk of pancreatitis. B Gliclazide Gliclazide is incorrect because given the random glucose, HbA1c and symptoms, sulphonylureas are likely to be inadequate with respect to controlling blood sugar levels versus insulin. C Liraglutide Liraglutide, is incorrect because of the likely very low levels of residual beta cell function, and risk of pancreatitis associated with GLP-1 agonist use. D Metformin Metformin, is incorrect because the primary role of metformin is to reduce hepatic glucose output, which is not the cause of the diabetes seen here.

questions.question: A young woman comes to the clinic with the diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and decides she would like some treatment. She tells you that her facial hair and acne cause her a great deal of stress. She has a BMI of 23. She is not currently interested in having children and is currently on the oral contraceptive pill (COCP). Which one of the following would be the most appropriate advice?
options: A. There is no treatment available
B. Losing weight will significantly impact on her symptoms
C. Clomifene is the most appropriate intervention
D. Metformin is effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne
E. Co-cyprindiol may be more effective than the COCP
questions.explanation: E Co-cyprindiol may be more effective than the COCP Co-cyprindiol because it contains cyproterone, an anti-androgen, may be more effective than the COCP in controlling acne and hirsuitism and acne in PCOS. C Clomifene is the most appropriate intervention Clomifene is used to induce ovulation in PCOS; hence it is not of value here. A There is no treatment available Co-cyprindrol may offer incremental benefit versus the COCP alone in managing symptoms of hyperandrogenism. B Losing weight will significantly impact on her symptoms This patient's BMI is in the normal range, hence weight loss is likely to have very little impact on her current symptoms. D Metformin is effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne A Cochrane meta-analysis has suggested that metformin is not effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne versus other options such as the COCP or co-cyprindrol.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the clinic with her 5-month-old baby. Over the past few weeks she has been feeling increasingly tired, but the GP has dismissed the problem as the usual tiredness after having a baby. She tells you she feels tired, has put on weight and is constipated all the time, feeling the cold when she goes out. On further questioning, she tells you this wasn't always the case, and that in fact during the first few months she actually felt like she had more energy and could survive on hardly any sleep at all. On examination her BP is 142/70 mmHg, with pulse is 65/min. Her BMI is 28. You notice that her hair and skin are quite dry. Investigations: Hb | 109 g/l WCC | 6.7x10^9/L PLT | 190x10^9/L Na+ | 140 mmol/L K+ | 4.9 mmol/L Creatinine | 100 µmol/L Cholesterol | 6.2 mmol/L TSH | 7.1 U/L Free T4 | 7.1 pmol/l Anti-thyroid antibody | +ve Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: D Post-partum thyroiditis The history here suggests that an early period of possible thyrotoxicosis has now been followed with symptoms of hypothyroidism, with hypothyroidism confirmed on biochemical testing. The timing after the birth of her child suggests this is post-partum thyroiditis. Treatment is with thyroxine replacement, although withdrawal may be possible in some patients who recover normal thyroid function. Recurrence of thyroiditis is common in subsequent pregnancies, however, and in up to 40% permanent hypothyroidism develops. The presence of anti-thyroid antibodies does put her at higher risk of permanent hypothyroidism. C Hashimoto's thyroiditis Hashimoto's disease is the main differential here, although this patient's recent pregnancy makes post-partum thyroiditis more likely. A Graves' disease Graves' disease is characterised by thyrotoxicosis rather than the picture of hypothyroidism seen here. B Subacute thyroiditis Subacute thyroiditis is associated with symptoms of a flu-like illness and pain over the thyroid gland. An initial period of thyrotoxicosis is followed by transient hypothyroidism and then recovery. E Sick euthyroid syndrome Sick euthyroid syndrome is associated with a significant intercurrent illness where abnormal thyroid function tests are noted, for example, in a patient with a prolonged stay on the ITU.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations which have worsened in frequency over the past week, a BP of 130/80 mmHg and she is found to have atrial fibrillation on her ECG. On examination, she has a palpable, smooth thyroid goitre. She is two months postpartum and is currently breast-feeding. Her daughter is very healthy. She has no past medical history. TSH is supressed at less than 0.05 mU/L and is TSH receptor and TPO antibody positive. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis of her goitre?
questions.explanation: A Postpartum thyroiditis This patient has clinical hyperthyroidism and is in the first few months after pregnancy. As such, the most likely diagnosis is postpartum thyroiditis. In women who present with postpartum thyroiditis and have symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, TSH receptor antibodies are found with increased frequency, although TPO antibodies are classically described in association with the condition. A transient period of hypothyroidism follows the episode of thyrotoxicosis, and up to 30% of patients may eventually develop permanent hypothyroidism. D Struma ovarii Struma ovarii is caused by ectopic thyroid tissue, so there is no goitre present. B Pregnancy Pregnancy may be associated with the development of a goitre but thyrotoxicosis is, of course, pathological. C Graves' disease Postpartum thyroiditis may be a harbinger of permanent thyroid dysfunction in some women, but the timing here points us towards postpartum disease rather than diagnosing Graves' at this stage. E Subacute thyroiditis Subacute thyroiditis is associated with symptoms of a flu-like illness, pain over the thyroid gland and thyrotoxicosis. It is not associated with pregnancy.

questions.question: A 18-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is concerned because although she feels she has developed normally as a woman and has a normal sex drive, she has never had a menstrual period. There is no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a BP of 105/72 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. She is 1.8 m tall, and has a BMI of 23. Breast development is normal although pubic and axillary hair appears absent, vulval development also appears to be normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 131 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 181x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 85 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/L Glucose | 5.4 mmol/L | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Testosterone | 21.2 nmol/L | 15-70 nmol/L Karyotyping | 46 XY |  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Androgen insensitivity syndrome The answer is Androgen insensitivity syndrome, (AIS). AIS is associated with normal external female genitalia, (although pubic and axillary hair is absent), primary amenorrhoea, and 46 XY karyotype. Ovaries are absent, undescended testes are common, and some patients present in the first few months with bilateral inguinal hernias, (where testes are identified at hernia repair). As here, testosterone is in the normal male range, although individuals are insensitive to its effects. B Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, is incorrect. This is associated with XX karyotype, later presentation with normal sexual development with symptoms similar to PCOS in the case of non-classical CAH, or virilisation in women with classical CAH. C Kallmann's syndrome Kallmann's syndrome, is incorrect. Kallmann's is associated with absence of sense of smell due to failure of the olfactory bulb to develop properly, and lack of GnRH production, leading to delayed puberty with an XX karyotype. D Primary ovarian failure Primary ovarian failure, is incorrect. This is associated with XX karyotype, and normally with secondary amenorrhoea. E Turner's syndrome Turner's syndrome, is incorrect. Turner's is associated with XO karyotype, hypertension, and short stature, with female external genitalia.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She is otherwise well, apart from lesions on each tibia and some loss of sensation in her feet. The lesions are shown below. Biopsy reveals granuloma formation, with infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: D Topical corticosteroids The appearance in the picture of these ulcerated lesions with their yellow-brown appearance, along with the history of diabetes, points towards the diagnosis of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. These erythematous plaques are due to small vessel damage causing partial necrosis of the dermal collagen and connective tissue, with a resulting histiocytic cellular response. While topical corticosteroids can worsen atrophy, they may be of value in reducing inflammation in early lesions. As such, in this situation, they are the intervention of choice, and systemic steroids are best avoided, if possible, due to their impact on glycaemic control. Small trials support the use of both ciclosporin and hydroxychloroquine as second-line agents. E Hydroxychloroquine It can be used as second-line treatment for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. It can also be used for the management of rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. A Aspirin Antiplatelet agents, such as aspirin, have only limited efficacy in treating necrobiosis lipoidica. A 2016 Cochrane systematic review concluded that further research is necessary before this treatment option can be confirmed to be safe and effective. Most venous ulcers respond to patient education, elevation of foot, elastic compression and evaluation. B Oral prednisolone Topical steroids are indicated for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. Oral steroids can significantly impact on glycaemic control. C Oral ciclosporin Ciclosporin can be used as a second-line agent for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. It can also be used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease and nephrotic syndrome and in organ transplants in order to prevent rejection.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man is admitted to Intensive Care following a motorcycle injury. His computed tomography (CT) head confirms extradural, subdural and subarachnoid haemorrhages. After 6 weeks, he is discharged from hospital. One year later, he is followed up in an Endocrinology Clinic. On review, he is depressed and feels fatigued. On examination, his skin is thin and dry, and he has developed central obesity. He also complains that his sexual libido has markedly reduced. A photograph of the patient is show below: Which hormone deficiency, resulting from traumatic brain injury (TBI), is most likely to cause these symptoms?
questions.explanation: C Growth hormone Chronic growth hormone deficiency can be caused by a TBI and results in symptoms that include fatigue, depression, reduced muscle mass, increased fat mass and reduced libido. This fits the clinical picture presented in this case and explains all of his symptoms on review at the Endocrinology Clinic. B Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) Gonadotropin hormones, including FSH, may be chronically deficient after a TBI which can cause poor libido and fatigue, similar to the symptoms observed in this patient. However, this would not explain the skin symptoms or the central obesity, whereas growth hormone deficiency can explain all of these symptoms. A Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) Levels of ACTH may be deficient in the acute phase after a TBI, but it is rare for this to persist more than a year after injury. The symptoms that this patient has are more in keeping with growth hormone deficiency (fatigue, depression, reduced muscle mass, increased fat mass and reduced libido) rather than ACTH deficiency (abdominal pain, weight loss and nausea). D Prolactin TBI can cause hyperprolactinaemia, particularly acutely. This may cause reduced libido but is due to a hormone excess rather than deficiency. E Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) TSH may be reduced following a TBI, although this is the least common anterior pituitary hormone to be affected. This would cause many of the symptoms that this patient has experienced, such as low mood, fatigue, poor libido, dry skin and weight gain. Still, it is much more common for these patients to experience chronic growth hormone deficiency and not TSH deficiency.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after being found confused by her home help. She has problems with mobility and type II diabetes, and takes a number of medications. According to the carers, she has been increasingly chesty with a cough productive of bloodstained sputum over the past four days. On arrival in the Emergency Department, her blood pressure is 132/88 mmHg, pulse 84 bpm and regular and temperature 38.1°C. There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation. She is drowsy and confused and suffers a short (40 s) tonic-clonic seizure just after you complete your physical examination. Investigations: Investigations | Results | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 121 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 11.9x10^9/L | 4-11x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 199x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 112 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 108 µmol/L | 50-120 µmol/l Glucose | 9.1 mmol/l | 3.5-5.5 mmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP) | 189 mg/l | < 5 mg/l Chest X-ray: Right lower lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention on top of antibiotic therapy?
questions.explanation: C Hypertonic saline This is an emergency situation that cannot wait for fluid restriction or demeclocycline to take effect because of the presence of a significantly reduced conscious level and seizure activity. Bolus 150 mL of 3% NaCl over 20 minutes, 2-3 x as needed, checking Na every 20 minutes. This may be enough acutely to prevent further seizures from occurring. The hypertonic saline must be administered in the High Dependency Unit (HDU) setting, so that close monitoring of serum sodium level can take place to avoid a rapid rise. B Fluid restriction Fluid restriction will correct the sodium level too slowly in this situation where the patient is obtunded and has suffered a seizure. Hypertonic saline under controlled conditions is the most appropriate option to correct his sodium level. A Demeclocycline Demeclocycline results in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and can correct syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) where there is a poor response to fluid restriction. It is not used in this emergency situation. D Isotonic saline SIADH is euvolemic hyponatremia and it is a common misconception that isotonic saline will result in a significant increase in serum sodium level. When urine osmolality is significantly elevated, isotonic saline is a source of free water and can actually worsen hyponatraemia. E Lithium Although lithium results in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, it is not used as a medication in an acute situation for raising serum sodium levels.

questions.question: A 63-year-old HGV driver comes to the clinic for review. He has recently been diagnosed with type II diabetes. Past history of note includes poorly controlled hypertension. He is known to have missed a number of general practitioner (GP) appointments for follow-up. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 132/82 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 34. Investigations; Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 129 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 7.1x10^9/l | 4-11x10^9/L Platelets | 182x10^9/L | 150-400x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.3 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine | 189 micromol/L | 50-120 µmol/L Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) | 32 |  Glucose | 8.1 mmol/L | 3.5-5.5 mmol/L HbA1c | 60 mmol/mol (7.6%) | <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: C Linagliptin The answer is Linagliptin - This patient has obesity, renal impairment and Type 2 diabetes. In this situation an agent that won't lead to further weight gain is most appropriate. Linagliptin is a DPPIV inhibitor subject primarily to hepatic metabolism. This means it can be safely used in patients down to severe renal impairment. It may promote modest weight loss and does not increase the risk of hypoglycaemia; as such it is the default option here. A Basal bolus insulin Basal bolus insulin is incorrect, it is not indicated because it will lead to further weight gain and is associated with increased risk of hypoglycaemia. Starting insulin would mean he could not continue driving the HGV until he could demonstrate stable diabetes control. B Gliclazide Gliclazide is incorrect, increases weight gain and is associated with hypoglycaemia, so as such it should be avoided here. D Metformin Metformin is incorrect, this does not increase weight gain, and does not cause hypoglycaemia; it is however contra-indicated according to the prescribing information and NICE guidelines because GFR is almost at the level where it should be discontinued, (<30). E Pioglitazone Pioglitazone is incorrect, this promotes weight gain and fluid retention, and so because of the weight gain. DPPIV inhibitors are preferred here.

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman visits the Medical Outpatient Clinic for advice. She is hypertensive and has been treated with atenolol for the last two years. While in the clinic, she asks for advice regarding the use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT). She suspects that she is menopausal due to hot flushes, mood swings and lack of periods for the last five months. She has no past medical history of thromboembolism, stroke or breast cancer. However, having read conflicting results about HRT in the press, she is concerned about the risk of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and heart disease. Which of the following statements is correct with respect to HRT (combined oestrogen-progestin therapy)?
options: A. HRT reduces the risk of coronary artery disease
B. HRT has a protective effect on the risk of DVT
C. Risk of strokes is reduced by HRT
D. Risk of DVT is 2-4 x higher in women on HRT
E. HRT has no effect on the risk of DVT
questions.explanation: D Risk of DVT is 2-4 x higher in women on HRT The WHI is the largest available clinical trial on HRT. It was stopped after 5 years - 3 years early because it revealed increased dangers. Older age and obesity added to the risk associated with a regimen of oestrogen plus progestin. Thinner and younger women were at a low absolute risk of DVT, although their risk was still twofold higher among women taking oestrogen plus progestin, compared with women taking placebo. As explained above, the relative risk of DVT is increased 2-4 x in those taking HRT. A HRT reduces the risk of coronary artery disease HERS has shown no reduced risk of coronary artery disease in women taking HRT. B HRT has a protective effect on the risk of DVT Clinical trial evidence from the Heart and Oestrogen/Progestin Replacement Study (HERS) and the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) have shown that oestrogen therapy, with or without progestin, is associated with an increased risk of DVT. C Risk of strokes is reduced by HRT The WHI has shown that the risk of having an ischaemic stroke is increased in those taking HRT due to an increased risk of blood clotting. E HRT has no effect on the risk of DVT As explained above, the relative risk of DVT is increased 2-4 x in those taking HRT.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP) complaining of a painless lump in the lower part of her anterior neck, which was found incidentally as she was fiddling around with her necklace. She is otherwise fit and well and denies any recent chest or throat infections. She is a non-smoker. On examination, the GP confirms the presence of a solitary hard, immobile lump measuring approximately 2 cm in the patient's lower anterior neck, which moves with swallowing and appears to be positioned in the thyroid gland. The patient is apyrexial and the remainder of the physical examination is normal. The patient is referred for a fine needle aspiration biopsy and relevant laboratory studies. The biopsy confirms that the patient has a papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. She undergoes total thyroidectomy and radioiodine treatment. Which of the following is the most useful marker of tumour recurrence?
questions.explanation: C Thyroglobulin: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is the most common thyroid carcinoma and accounts for 80% of such cases. It is a slow-growing and well-differentiated carcinoma but it has a propensity for spread to the cervical lymph nodes. The male to female ratio is 1:3, with females having an overall better prognosis. Risk factors for developing this condition include excessive intake of iodine and external radiation to the neck. Thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation are the mainstays of therapy. Since thyroglobulin is synthesised by well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas, it can serve as a useful tumour marker for assessment of recurrence of the tumour, but only after total thyroid ablation. D Thyroxine: Given that this patient requires thyroid hormone replacement, thyroxine is not useful as a marker of tumour recurrence. A Alkaline phosphatase: Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in the presence of bony metastases from well-differentiated thyroid cancer, although this would be a very late feature. B Beta-HCG: Beta-HCG is useful in the monitoring of malignant germ cell rather than thyroid tumours. E Thyroid-stimulating hormone: Like thyroxine, TSH cannot be used as a marker of tumour recurrence, given that this patient is treated with exogenous thyroid hormone.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman is refered to the Endocrinology Clinic by her General Practitioner (GP) for the management of her type II diabetes mellitus and persistent hypertension. In addition to insulin and metformin for her diabetes, she is also on sertraline and lorazepam for her depression, and carbamazepine for her agonizing post-herpetic neuralgia. On examination, she is obese with a round face and moderate facial acne. She is a heavy drinker. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows failure of suppression of cortisol. A provisional diagnosis of Cushing syndrome is made. However, computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen reveal normal adrenal glands and no evidence of malignancy, and the serum cortisol measurement shows normal daily variation. Further investigations including a midnight cortisol later exclude Cushing syndrome. What was the reason for her failed initial dexamethasone suppression test?
options: A. Interference of metformin with the cortisol radioimmunoassay
B. Variance of baseline cortisol due to fluctuating glycaemic control
C. The induction of the cytochrome p450 system by alcohol and carbamazepine
D. Fluctuating level of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol due to non-compliance with insulin treatment
questions.explanation: C The induction of the cytochrome p450 system by alcohol and carbamazepine: The overnight dexamethasone suppression test is usually used as a screening test for Cushing syndrome. This test has a false-positive rate of up to 2-12% (meaning that a diagnosis of Cushing is suggested incorrectly). Dexamethasone is primarily metabolised by the cytochrome p450 system, specifically by the CYP3A4 isoenzyme. Several drugs such as phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampicin are enzyme inducers, and therefore lead to increased activity of CYP3A4 enzyme, and can thus result in false-positive dexamethasone suppression tests. Considerable increases in cytochrome 450 enzyme activity can be seen in smokers and people who drink alcohol regularly. A Interference of metformin with the cortisol radioimmunoassay: Patients need to be off all oestrogen-containing medication for six weeks prior to any measurements of serum cortisol, but metformin is not known to effect cortisol. B Variance of baseline cortisol due to fluctuating glycaemic control: Whilst patients with diabetes often have slightly higher baseline levels of cortisol, there is no link between raised cortisol levels and poor glycaemic control. D Fluctuating level of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol due to non-compliance with insulin treatment: Non-compliance with insulin treatment is likely to lead to poor glycaemic control, but there is not known to be a link between this and levels of ACTH or cortisol. E Ectopic ACTH production: Ectopic ACTH secretion is most common from a bronchial tumour, and we are given no suggestion in the history of one here. Very high ACTH levels are highly suggestive of an ectopic source of ACTH. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used by some units to help differentiate between pituitary and ectopic sources of ACTH in difficult to diagnose Cushing syndrome, where ACTH fails to suppress when the production is ectopic.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a recent HbA1c of 83.61~mmol/mol (9.8%) asks for urgent clinic review. He complains of a hot, swollen left foot, which has gradually got worse over the past month. On examination, there is increased heat over the tarsal-metatarsal joint and the foot is swollen. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and there is obvious neuropathy. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 121 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 12.1  x10^9/L | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/l Platelets (PLT) | 204  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 140~mmol/l | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 101 µmol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) | 9~mg/L | <10~mg/l Which of the following represents the investigation of choice with respect to the likely diagnosis (where available)?
questions.explanation: B Indium-labelled white cell scan: Although not widely available, an indium-labelled white cell scan is the best way to differentiate between infective causes of this clinical presentation and Charcot's arthropathy. It is more stable with respect to labelling of white cells versus other techniques such as technetium, and is therefore less likely for example, to label areas of increased bone turnover. Charcot's is thought to occur due to increased blood flow as a result of neuropathy. This results in increased osteoclast activity and bone turnover the foot is then susceptible to often very minor trauma and destructive changes take place. Experts recommend immobilisation for at least 3 months in an aircast-type non-weight-bearing plaster. This is to allow bone remodelling/repair to occur. Bisphosphonates are a useful adjunct to the healing process as they reduce osteoclast activity. Whilst insulin therapy is likely to improve glycaemic control and slow further progression of neuropathy, it will not affect recovery of the Charcot's joint. A Technetium isotope scan: Technetium is more likely to label areas of increased bone turnover associated with Charcot's, as well as areas of infection. C Plain radiograph: Plain X-rays may show areas of joint destruction but won't differentiate between infection and Charcot's-driven inflammation. D ESR: Although ESR may be elevated, it is a non-specific marker of inflammation and therefore won't definitively confirm osteomyelitis here. E Joint aspiration: Joint aspiration of a foot is technically difficult and painful. Whilst it may deliver a diagnosis of osteomyelitis, where indium-labelled white cell scanning is available, it's preferred.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man attends the clinic with his partner as they have difficulties with fertility, having tried for a baby for over 24 months with no success. He admits to decreased libido and some problems maintaining his erection. He has also had difficulties with his sense of smell for as long as he can remember. On examination his BP is 120/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 75/min. He has a small penis and sparse secondary sexual hair. Investigations: Hb | 124~g/L WCC | 7.1  x10^9/L PLT | 203  x10^9/L Na+ | 139~mmol/L K+ | 4.4~mmol/l Creatinine | 110~  mu mol/L TSH | 1.2 U/L (0.5-4.5 U/l) Free T4 | 12 pmol/l (10-22) Testosterone | 7.0 nmol/l (9-35) FSH | 0.4 U/ (1-7) LH | 0.2 U/L (1-10) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Kallmann syndrome: This patient has classical symptoms of Kallman syndrome including anosmia, loss of libido, gonadal deficiency, erectile dysfunction and absent secondary sexual characteristics such as pubic hair. The low LH, FSH and testosterone in the presence of a normal TSH fit with the underlying diagnosis of isolated gonatrophin deficiency. GnRH or pulsed gonadotrophin therapy can be used to achieve fertility; in those patients who don't desire fertility, testosterone replacement is an appropriate option. C Mumps orchitis: Orchitis (inflammation of the testicle) is associated with pain, fever, blood in ejaculate, dysuria and penile discharge. None of these symptoms are discussed in the question, nor are there any symptoms associated with mumps infection (swelling of parotid glands, fever, joint pain). Mumps is now quite rare due to current immunisation protocol. B Klinefelter syndrome: Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal disorder characterised by an XXY genotype. Patients tend to present earlier with poor sexual development, small or undescended testes and gynaecomastia. These patients are infertile. The condition is associated with learning disabilities, predisposition to diabetes, breast cancer, long leg height and tall stature. Treatment is with androgen replacement. D Pituitary failure: In this condition you would expect deficiency in all anterior pituitary hormones in addition to GNRH (LH, FSH, TSH, ACTH). E Androgen insensitivity syndrome: In this condition you would expect the FSH level to be normal, smell would be intact and there may be the presence of ambiguous genitalia.

questions.question: A 59-year-old woman presents to the clinic with tiredness. She takes no medication, and her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is in the normal range. She has had a pituitary adenoma in the past that was found to be prolactin-secreting, and she tells you she had some benign tumours removed from her neck. She takes calcium and vitamin D supplements. A picture of her neck is shown below. What is she most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation: C Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1): MEN-1 is associated with the development of parathyroid adenomas (linked to the neck scar and vitamin D and calcium supplementation seen here). The syndrome is also linked to pituitary adenomas, particularly prolactinomas, and endocrine pancreatic tumours. The history seen here is therefore consistent with MEN-1. Around 60% of islet cell tumours do not originate from beta cells, and these are more common in the over-40 population. A Familial medullary thyroid cancer: Medullary thyroid cancer would not explain the presentation with prolactinoma and, as part of a syndrome, is associated with MEN-2. It is not associated with parathyroid adenomas. B Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome: An autosomal dominant inheritance pattern for familial hyperparathyroidism does exist, although it would not explain the presentation with a prolactinoma seen here. D Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2a (MEN-2a): MEN-2 is associated with primary hyperparathyroidism, but it is also associated with phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid cancer, rather than the pituitary tumour reported here. E Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2b (MEN-2b): MEN-2b is associated with a marfanoid habitus, medullary thyroid cancer and phaeochromocytoma.

questions.question: A 21-year-old man who was previously diagnosed with type I diabetes mellitus visits his General Practitioner (GP) for his yearly review. He checks his feet for ulcers occasionally and recently forgot to attend for retinal screening. His urine protein creatinine ratio (PCR) shows evidence of microalbuminuria. He asks his GP whether his diabetes will be life-limiting. What is the most likely cause of death for a patient with type I diabetes?
questions.explanation: A Macrovascular disease: Macrovascular disease is the biggest cause of death in diabetic patients, accounting for around 75% of deaths. This includes coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease and peripheral vascular disease. Atheromas develops more rapidly and progress more quickly in diabetic patients which leads to morbidity. D Neuropathy: Neuropathy develops in many diabetic patients and includes both autonomic neuropathy and peripheral neuropathy which can lead to ulcers and ultimately amputation. Neuropathy can have a significant effect on quality of life. It can lead to ulcers which are prone to becoming infected, which can lead to death, but it is not as likely to cause death as macrovascular disease. B Malignancy: Diabetes is a risk factor for many malignancies, including colon, breast and pancreatic cancer. This does not, however, account for the majority of deaths, unlike macrovascular disease. C Nephropathy: Nephropathy occurs in a significant number of patients with diabetes, and this can lead to a requirement for renal replacement therapy. Ultimately, nephropathy itself is not the biggest cause of death as it causes death in around 5% of diabetic patients. However, the diabetic population with nephropathy are at greater risk of developing cardiovascular disease. E Retinopathy: Diabetic retinopathy may lead to sight loss in patients with diabetes, and this underlines the importance of yearly retinal screening. This has a significant effect on quality of life but does not directly lead to death.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of weight loss and headaches. On examination, he is noted to have a blood pressure (BP) of 175/110~mmHg and 180/102 mmHg on three successive readings at the general practitioner (GP) surgery, despite having been started on an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and calcium channel blocker. He smokes five cigarettes per day. His body mass index (BMI) as measured in the clinic is 23. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Sodium Na | 145~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium ( (K+) | 4.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Urea | 10.6~mmol/l | 2.5-6.5~mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 3.1~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/l Phosphate (PO4) | 0.4~mmol/L | 1.1-1.45~mmol/L What is the likely cause of his presentation?
questions.explanation: D Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2: The patient in this case is young, hypertensive and has hypercalcaemia. The high calcium level can be explained by the presence of parathyroid hypertrophy, and the hypertension is secondary to the presence of a phaeochromocytoma. Both abnormalities may be visualised on ultrasound imaging. Clearly the presence of hyperparathyroidism will be clarified by normal or raised levels on blood testing in the presence of hypercalcaemia. Medullary thyroid cancer doesn't cause hypercalcaemia, it is due to cancer affecting the thyroid C cell line, (which produce calcitonin). There are two forms of MEN II, A and B. Patients with MEN2A and MEN2B experience two main complications, medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) and phaeochromocytoma. MEN2A patients have a predisposition to hypertrophy of the parathyroid glands and subsequent tumour development. MEN2B patients show a variety of additional conditions: a characteristic facial appearance with swollen lips; tumours of the mucous membranes of the eye, mouth, tongue and nasal cavity; enlarged colon; and skeletal abnormalities. MEN2A shows no distinct physical features and must be identified by either measuring hormone levels or finding endocrine tumours. A Extra-adrenal phaeochromocytoma: Although this may explain the hypertension seen here, it wouldn't explain the hypercalcaemia. B Small-cell lung cancer: Small cell lung cancer is associated with the production of ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), leading to features of hypercortisolism. Although hypertension may be a feature, the lack of significant weight gain or dysglycaemia and the modest smoking history count against this. C Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 1: MEN1 is associated with pancreatic endocrine tumours, not with phaeochromocytoma. E Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: This is the syndrome of hypergastrinaemia and recurrent peptic ulceration related to a gastrinoma.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman has been brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by her partner with a one day history of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and vomiting. She has a history of type I diabetes mellitus and pernicious anaemia. Her partner tells you that her General Practitioner (GP) has recently prescribed amoxicillin for a chest infection and that she has lost 12.5 kg (nearly 2 stone) in weight over the last few months. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, she is flushed, disorientated, agitated and jaundiced. Her temperature is 42.1 Celisus . Her pulse is 180 beats per minute (bpm) and irregular. Her blood pressure (BP) is 180/70 mmHg. You detect a third heart sound, her chest is clear and her abdomen generally tender. Her legs are weak proximally and all reflexes brisk. She has some pitting oedema of her lower limbs. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) | 103 g/l | 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) | 17.2  x10^9/l | 4.0-11.0  x10^9/L Platelets (PLT) | 90  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 131~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 2.8 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 165~  mu~mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.82~mmol/L | 2.20-2.60 mmol/l Bilirubin | 64~  mu~mol/L | 2-17 µmol/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) | 140 U/L | 5-30 U/L Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) | 210 U/L | 30-150 U/L Glucose | 19.8~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Neutrophils | 12.6  x10^9/L | 2.5-7.58  x10^9/L Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) | 102.4 fl | 80-100 fl Results of an electrocardiogram (ECG) shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C Thyroid storm: Her past history of diabetes mellitus and pernicious anaemia makes it more likely that she has a further autoimmune disorder. The history of weight loss suggests an underlying thyroid disorder, with the thyroid storm being precipitated by her chest infection. Thyroid storm is a sudden, life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis. Some series suggest a mortality rate of between 30 and 75%. Its manifestations are due to the action of excess thyroid hormone. Fever is the most characteristic feature, with the temperature often rising above 41^ Celisus . There may be evidence of organ damage. The clinical picture is frequently clouded by a secondary infection such as pneumonia or a viral infection. Death may be caused by cardiac arrhythmia (the ECG here shows fast atrial fibrillation), congestive heart failure, hyperthermia or other unidentified factors. The diagnosis of thyroid storm is made entirely on clinical grounds. The results of thyroid function tests will rarely be available soon enough to make the diagnosis. Propylthiouracil followed by a stable iodine preparation (eg Lugol's iodine) is usually given. Propranolol, intravenous fluids, dexamethasone and cooling are also often required. Finally, one must remember to treat the precipitating cause. A Atypical pneumonia: This is caused by 'atypical' pathogens such as M. pneumoniae, Legionella spp, C. pneumonia and C. psittaci. Absence of cough and respiratory signs on physical examination makes this diagnosis unlikely. Incubation period is usually within 10 days, and onset of illness to presentation time is usually within a week. B Diabetic ketoacidosis: Diabetic ketoacidosis usually evolves within 24 h. It is characterised by the triad of metabolic acidosis (7.25 or bicarbonate   le15~mmol/l), hyperglycaemia ( (>13.9~mmol/l) and ketonemia, (  ge3.mmol/l). D Gastroenteritis: Symptom onset is usually acute (  le14~days) and weight loss can occur if the diarrhoea becomes persistent (>14-30 days) or chronic (>30~days) E Adverse drug reaction: Drug reactions to pencillins are either IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated, presenting as immediate (within minutes to hours) or delayed reactions (after days to weeks), respectively. Delayed reactions are more common than immediate reactions. Pruritic or non-pruritic maculo-papular eruptions are a common feature of both types of reaction. Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening immediate reaction that requires emergency treatment. It is characterised by difficulty in breathing, bronchospasm, throat tightness, voice change, recurrent vomiting, light-headedness and hypotension.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man visits an Infertility Clinic on account of inability to sustain an erection. He does have an early morning erection, but when he tries to penetrate his partner, the erection is either too short-lived or too soft to achieve adequate penetration. He has suffered from type 1 diabetes for 30 years. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 155/90 mmHg. He has a normal distribution of pubic and axillary hair, and a normal penis and testes on examination. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 131 g/l | 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 5.9  x10^9/t | 4-11  x10^9/l Platelets | 201  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.9~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine | 110~  mu mol/t | 50-120~  mu mol/l Cholesterol | 5.2~mmol/l | <5.2~mmol/l Triglyceride | 2.1~mmol/l | 0-1.5~mmol/L HbA1c | 57.38~mmol/mol (7.4%) | <53~mmol/mol (<7.0%) Urine | Microalbuminuria |  Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for him?
options: D. Additional blood glucose lowering therapy
questions.explanation: A Sildenafil: Given the duration of this patient's diabetes, the most likely cause of his erectile dysfunction is microvascular disease. As such, moving to oral therapy to improve penile blood flow is an appropriate intervention. In diabetes, high doses of PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil may be needed to achieve a therapeutic effect. B Transdermal testosterone: Given this man is 40 and has morning erections and normal penis, testes and sexual hair, he is unlikely to be significantly testosterone deficient. Of course it is appropriate to assess testosterone levels as part of the work-up for him, but given it's likely these are in the normal range, an impact on sexual function wouldn't be expected. C Psychosexual counselling: Although counselling has an important role in managing sexual dysfunction, he is also appropriate for medical intervention. D Additional blood glucose lowering therapy: Although tight glycaemic control can stay progression of microvascular disease, reversal of existing damage isn't seen. E Referral for penile implant: This is obviously an intervention of last resort in patients who fail to respond to PDE5 inhibitors and prostaglandin-based therapies.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of headaches for the past two months. She has no significant past medical or family history and there is no history of smoking or consumption of alcohol. On examination, her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg and her heart rate is 90 bpm. Auscultation of the abdomen reveals an abdominal bruit left lateral to the umbilicus. Her body mass index is 22~kg/M2. Investigation | Result | Normal value Urea | 3.8~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 120~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Which of the following best describes the changes expected to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation: A Hyperreninaemia, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemia: Hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism is characteristic of renal artery stenosis. The patient is a young woman with newly diagnosed hypertension, along with an abdominal bruit on physical examination. This patient likely has renal artery stenosis, most probably due to fibromuscular dysplasia causing hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism, along with hypokalaemia. D Hyporeninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hyperkalaemia: These findings are typically seen in type 4 renal tubular acidosis. The most common cause is uncontrolled diabetes mellitus which leads to dysfunction of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA). This, in turn, leads to hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism. B Hyperreninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hyperkalaemia: Hyperreninaemic hypoaldosteronism may be seen in patients with septic shock. It could possibly indicate fluid depletion and is associated with an increased incidence of acute kidney injury in such patients. C Hyporeninaemia, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemia: These findings are classical of primary hyperaldosteronism. However, this patient likely has renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia. E Hyporeninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hypokalaemia: Renal artery stenosis results in hyperreninaemia, rather than hyporeninaemia, due to decreased renal perfusion, hence activating the JGA to secrete renin.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has told his general practitioner (GP) that he consumes up to 8 or 9  of fluids per day and is constantly up during the night and day to pass urine. The GP has checked some routine bloods; a fasting blood sugar is 3.4~mmol/L. You arrange a water deprivation test, which reveals the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Maximal serum osmolality after fluid deprivation | 290~mosmol/kg | 278-300~mosmol/kg Urine osmolality after fluid deprivation | 830~mosmol/kg | >750~mosmol/kg Urine osmolality after desmopressin | 841~mosmol/kg | >750~mosmol/kg What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: B Primary polydipsia: Results of the fluid deprivation test are crucial in determining the correct diagnosis here. In this test, patients are deprived of fluids for a period of 8 h or until 5% of body weight is lost. Patients should be weighed hourly. Plasma osmolality is measured 4-hourly, with urine volume and osmolality measurements occurring every 2 h. The patient is then given 2 µg intramuscular (i/m) desmopressin, with urine volume and urine and serum osmolality measured over the next 4 h. Where urine osmolality reaches levels >800~mosmol/kg without desmopressin, then the diagnosis is primary polydipsia. This patient should be offered behavioural advice about slowly reducing his fluid intake. C Nephrogenic DI: Urine osmolality <300~mosmol/kg in the water deprivation test, remaining at <300~mosmol/kg after desmopressin, indicates nephrogenic DI. A Cranial diabetes insipidus (DI): If serum osmolality rises above 305 mOsmol/kg in the water deprivation test, then the patient is said to have DI and the test is stopped. Urine osmolality <300~mOsmol/kg after fluid deprivation, rising to >800~mosmol/kg after desmopressin, indicates cranial DI. D Partial nephrogenic DI: Where urine osmolality at the end of the water deprivation test is intermediate (300-800 mOsmol/kg), and fails to rise above 800 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin, the diagnosis may be partial DI or polydipsia. E Hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism: A picture of hypokalaemia and hypertension, rather than polyuria and polydipsia, would be expected in hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with a long history of Type 1 diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of diplopia. Her diabetes is poorly controlled, despite basal bolus insulin a recent HbA1c has been recorded at 76~mmol/mol (9.1%). She has had previous therapy laser for diabetic retinopathy, has numbness affecting both feet, and a resolved left common peroneal nerve palsy. On examination the right eye is looking down and out, there is a ptosis on the right hand side, and the pupil appears spared. Investigations; Hb | 120 g/l WCC | 7.1  x10^9/l PLT | 201  x10^9/L Na | 137~mmol/L K+ | 5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 132~micromol/L Glucose | 9.3~mmol/L ESR | 9~mm/1^ hour Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her cranial neuropathy?
