questions.explanation: C Diabetes mellitus: The answer is Diabetes mellitus - This patient has previous mononeuritis (common peroneal nerve palsy), and poorly controlled T1DM; as such the most likely cause of the oculomotor nerve palsy seen here is mononeuritis related to diabetes. Symptoms may gradually resolve over a period of 6-8 weeks, and improved diabetes control may positively impact on the degree of improvement seen. B Cerebral infarct: Cerebral infarct, is incorrect, it is very unlikely given that only one cranial nerve is affected. A Anterior communicating artery aneurysm: Anterior communicating artery aneurysms, is incorrect, usually result in visual field defects. (a bitemporal hemianopia) because of optic chiasm compression. D Intracerebral tumour: Intracerebral tumour, is incorrect, it would be associated with gradually worsening symptoms including increasing headaches and other focal neurology, neither of which are seen here. E Vasculitis: Vasculitis is incorrect, it is a possible alternative cause of mononeuritis, although the normal ESR and lack of other features aside from the oculomotor palsy, counts against vasculitis as the alternative pathology.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of persistent loose stools and gradual weight loss over the past 3 months. On examination, she is tachycardic - her heart rate is 110 beats per minute (bpm) and she has a fine tremor. Her eyes have a bulging appearance, shown below: Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Proptosis.jpg The patient also reports sweating despite it being winter. Her GP suspects Graves' Disease. Which autoantibody is she most likely to have in her blood?
options: D. Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor blocking antibody (TBAb)
E. Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor stimulating antibody (TSAb)
questions.explanation: E Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor stimulating antibody (TSAb): TSAb antibodies are usually present in Graves' disease, and result in stimulation of the stimulating thyroid hormone (TSH) receptor, which leads to overproduction of thyroid hormones. The causes the symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, such has tremor, tachycardia, sweating etc. The TSH receptor is also expressed in the orbital fibroblasts and adipocytes, which leads to the eye symptoms associated with Graves disease (building appearance). These do not occur when other non-autoimmune causes of thyrotoxicosis, such as a multinodular goitre, are present. C Islet antigen 2 (IA-2) antibody: These antibodies are associated with type I diabetes mellitus, as they target the beta islet cells of the pancreas. A 21-Hydroxylase antibody: This autoantibody is most commonly found in patients with primary hypoadrenalism (Addison's disease). It occurs in 80-90% of patients with this condition and is not involved in the aetiology of Graves' disease. B Gastrin receptor antibody: Gastrin receptor antibodies are associated with pernicious anaemia and not with Graves' disease. The gastric parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is needed for the absorption of vitamin B12 and therefore, antibodies against these cells result in vitamin B12 deficiency and anaemia. D Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor blocking antibody (TBAb): TBAb antibodies are associated with autoimmune hypothyroidism, eg Hashimoto's thyroiditis. They target the TSH receptor and block their activation, which leads to hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of excruciating abdominal pain in the epigastric region that radiates to his back. He has had four episodes of vomiting in the past two hours and is unable to eat solid foods. The patient does not smoke or consume alcohol. On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 106 bpm. There is severe tenderness on palpation of the epigastric region. The patient appears dehydrated. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Urea | 7.1 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 122 µmol/l | 50-120µmol/l Amylase | 1284 U/L | < 200 U/L Lipase | 1100 U/L | < 140 U/L Triglycerides (TGL) | 11.6 mmol/L | < 1.5 mmol/L Low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) | 4.8 mmol/l | < 3.5 mmol/l After initial stabilisation of the patient with intravenous hydration, which of the following is the best line of management?
options: C. Initiation of atorvastatin and fenofibrate
D. Initiation of fenofibrate and gemfibrozil
E. Initiation of omega-3 fatty acids
questions.explanation: C Initiation of atorvastatin and fenofibrate: This patient has clinical features of pancreatitis, along with biochemical evidence (elevated amylase and lipase levels). The cause of pancreatitis is likely due to severe hypertriglyceridaemia (triglycerides (TGL)>11.5 mmol/l). In addition, the low-density lipoprotein level is slightly elevated. In these patients, it has been found that initiation of a combination of statin and fibrate, along with dietary modification, decreases the future risk of pancreatitis and premature atherosclerosis. A Initiation of atorvastatin: Initiation of statin alone in a patient with pancreatitis secondary to hypertriglyceridaemia is unlikely to achieve an adequate reduction of triglycerides to sufficiency reduce the risk of future repeat episodes. B Initiation of evolocumab: Evolocumab, a proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type 9 inhibitor, is being investigated as part of a clinical trial but is not recommended as standard of care in a patient with pancreatitis secondary to severe hypertriglyceridaemia (TGL=11.5~mmol/L). D Initiation of fenofibrate and gemfibrozil: Initiation of two fibrates does not confer an added benefit and may increase the incidence of hepatitis. E Initiation of omega-3 fatty acids: While omega-3 fatty acids may be useful, in addition to statins and fibrates, they are not recommended as monotherapy as the minor reduction in triglyceride levels is unlikely to result in a sufficient reduction of the risk of repeat episodes.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man who has had type I diabetes mellitus for 27 years comes to the clinic for review. He has bilateral lower limb sensory loss consistent with peripheral neuropathy and background diabetic retinopathy, but is otherwise well. Current insulin regime is 8 U TDS of short-acting insulin (Actrapid®) with 20 U/ day of intermediate insulin (Insulatard®). Apart from recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia (4 x/week), he feels he is doing well. His BP is 135/70 mmHg, with pulse 80/min and regular. His BMI is 23. HbA1c is 66 mmol/mol (8.2%) and a recent creatinine was measured at 135 micromol/L. Morning glucoses are in the range of 6-22 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in his regimen?
options: A. Reduce his Actrapid® by 6 units/day
B. Reduce his Insalotard® by 6 units/day
C. Change his Insalotard® to insulin glargine at 20~units/day
D. Increase his Actrapid® by 6 units/day
E. Change his regime to 12 units of Mixtard® twice/day
questions.explanation: C Change his Insalotard® to insulin glargine at 20 units/day: This patient is missing his HbA1c target and suffering nocturnal hypos, as evidenced by his symptoms and some of the morning glucose values (22 mmol/l being potentially reflective of a counter-regulatory response to hypoglycaemia). Because he is missing the HbA1c target, it would not really be appropriate to reduce his insulin dose. Switching to glargine is likely to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia whilst improving target achievement, because it is a 'peak-less' insulin. E Change his regime to 12 units of Mixtard® twice/day: BD mixed insulin is not tailored as appropriately to meal x as a basal bolus regimen, and as such it isn't recommended for patients with type 1 diabetes. A Reduce his Actrapid® by 6 units/day: The profile of glucose testing suggests possible episodes of hypoglycaemia at night; as such, reducing the dose of Actrapid® won't impact significantly on this patient's glucose control. B Reduce his Insalotard® by 6 units/day: Given that the HbA1c is above target, this is suboptimal versus switching to an insulin analogue. D Increase his Actrapid® by 6 units/day: This won't significantly impact on nocturnal hypoglycaemia, but may drive increased food intake and suboptimal weight control.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of extreme fatigue and increasing generalised abdominal pain. He reports a 3-day history of vomiting, diarrhoea and dizziness. He was recently diagnosed with HIV and was started on antiretroviral therapy 3 weeks previously. On examination his pulse rate was 120~beats/min and blood pressure was 100/50 mmHg. His cardiovascular. neurological and abdominal examinations were normal. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal Values Sodium (Na+) | 128~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.6~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/l Glucose | 3.0~mmol/L | 3.9-7.1~mmol/L Urea | 8.5~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/L Virology at the time of HIV diagnosis: Cytomegalovirus IgG | + HbsAb | + HbsAg | - Previously his electrolytes had been within the normal range. What is the most useful bedside test to aid in diagnosis?
options: A. Blood pressure in each arm
questions.explanation: D Postural blood pressures: This patient is suffering from an Addisonian crisis, as evidenced by the low sodium and raised potassium, low blood pressure and dizziness, abdominal pain and vomiting. This is probably due to an immune reconstitution syndrome after starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV. In this patient's case, he is CMV IgG positive and therefore the cause may be CMV adrenalitis. If this was felt to be the case, ganciclovir should be used in treatment. Postural blood pressures will demonstrate a significant drop. He should be treated with IV hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. C Exercise oxygen saturations: These are sometimes used as a bedside test to gather evidence of PCP pneumonia in HIV-positive patients. This patient has presented in an Addisonian crisis: this explains his low sodium and raised potassium, abdominal pain and vomiting, dizziness and low blood pressure. The most appropriate bedside test would be postural blood pressures, expecting to see a significant drop. Patients can develop Addisonian crises as a result of an immune reconstitution syndrome after antiretroviral therapy is started; in this case, the patient is CMV IgG positive and therefore this may be as a result of CMV adrenalitis. A Blood pressure in each arm: This patient has developed an Addisonian crisis, as evidenced by the low sodium, raised potassium, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, and low blood pressure. This can occur as part of an immune reconstitution syndrome once antiretroviral therapy is started in HIV; it may have been caused by CMV adrenalitis, as this patient has previously been exposed to CMV (hence he is IgG positive in serology). The most appropriate bedside test would be postural blood pressures: you would expect to see a significant postural drop in an Addisonian crisis. B ECG: This patient is in the midst of an Addisonian crisis: this explains the low sodium and raised potassium, low blood pressure and abdominal pain, vomiting and dizziness. An ECG will not help in the diagnosis of Addison's: instead the patient should have postural blood pressures taken, expecting to see a significant drop. Addisonian crises can occur as a result of an immune constitution syndrome after antiretroviral therapy for HIV is started: in this case, the patient is CMV IgG positive and therefore this may be CMV adrenalitis. E Urinalysis: This patient has developed an Addisonian crisis: he has a low blood pressure, tachycardia, hypoglycaemia, dizziness, abdominal pain and vomiting, and bloods show a low sodium and a high potassium. This is probably due to an immune reconstitution syndrome as a result of starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV; in this patient's case, he is also CMV IgG positive and therefore it is possible that this has been caused by CMV adrenalitis.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man attends the Hypertension Clinic describing a three month history of episodes of headaches and dizziness. In addition, he often experiences vague central abdominal discomfort. He feels that he has lost some weight recently, though this may be related to a low-fat diet he has been trying. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 152/90 mmHg. In addition, there appears to be thyroid swelling which has not previously been noted. His bone profile reveals a corrected calcium of 2.74 mmol/l. He also had an oral glucose tolerance test with his General Practitioner (GP), who was concerned about the weight loss, which was normal, hence excluding the diagnosis of diabetes. Which one of the following is most likely to be the cause of his hypertension?
questions.explanation: D Phaeochromocytoma: The episodic symptoms of headache and dizziness, the hypertension, the hypercalacaemia and the thyroid mass fit better with a phaeochromocytoma in the context of MEN 2A. MEN 2 presents with medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaechromocytoma. The third component could be parathyroid hyperplasia (MEN 2A) or mucutaneous neuromas and marfanoid habitus (MEN 2B). E Graves' disease: Graves' disease can cause a diffusely enlarged, non-tender goitre and also mild hypercalcaemia in the acute phase (thyrotoxicosis). However, dizziness, abdominal pain and hypertension are not features of the condition. A Cushing's syndrome: Cushing syndrome is a cause of secondary hypertension but would not cause weight loss. The typical feature is weight gain with central distribution. B Addison's disease: Addison's could be considered in the context of dizziness and abdominal pain, but hypertension would be unusual in this condition. It mainly resents with postural hypotension, nausea, abdominal pain and hyperpigmentation. C Abuse of growth hormone: Abuse of growth hormone is another cause for secondary hypertension. It may also lead to weight gain, insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance, which is not the case in this scenario.

questions.question: You review a 52-year-old man who describes having undergone pituitary surgery (and 'some treatment' after the operation), a while ago. He now complains of feelings of lethargy, reduced energy and vitality. On examination, he has increased central abdominal adiposity and has reduced grip strength. He is already taking thyroid and cortisol replacement, and blood testing suggests these are adequate. Full blood count (FBC). urea and electrolytes (U&E) and liver function tests (LFTs) are unremarkable. Which of the following would be the best investigation to perform next?
options: A. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa
questions.explanation: E Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1): In light of this man's previous pituitary surgery, it is possible that he has growth hormone (GH) deficiency. Clinical features of growth hormone deficiency include impaired well-being, reduced energy and vitality, reduced muscle mass and exercise tolerance, decreased sweating, increased cardiovascular risk and increased fracture risk (osteoporosis). A serum IGF-1 concentration lower than the lower limit of normal in a patient who has pituitary disease confirms the diagnosis of GH deficiency. Even a normal value does not exclude GH deficiency; further investigations would be indicated here. A Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa: We know that pituitary anatomy is likely to be abnormal in relation to previous surgery, and further imaging won't inform as to abnormalities of gland function. B Insulin tolerance test: Insulin tolerance testing to induce hypoglycaemia is a potential option for investigation, although this is unpleasant for the patient. Other options, such as the arginine-growth hormone-releasing hormone test, are preferred where these are available now. C Glucose tolerance test: Oral glucose tolerance testing is utilised in the evaluation of acromegaly, not growth hormone deficiency. D Serum prolactin: An elevated serum prolactin would neither confirm or refute growth hormone deficiency, and this is not therefore a preferred next investigation.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a history of watery diarrhoea over the past three months and intermittent facial flushing. He does not have any past medical history, has not been abroad in the last six months, and does not take any medications. He appears very dehydrated and is referred to the Acute Medical Unit (AMU) in the local hospital. On admission to hospital, he has blood tests which reveal the following: Investigation | Result | Normal value Arterial pH | 7.32 | 7.35-7.45 Arterial pCO2 | 4.3 kPa | 4.7-6.0 kPa Arterial pO2 | 14.2 kPa | > 10.5 kPa Arterial HCO3 | 18.1~mmol/L | 22.0-26.0~mmol/L Sodium (Na+) | 137~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium ( (K+) | 3.1~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Urea | 6.5 mmol/l | 2.5-6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 93~  mu~mol/l | 50-120~  mu mol/L Calcium ( (Ca+2) | 2.74~mmol/L | 2.2-2.7~mmol/L Magnesium (Mg) | 0.45~mmol/L | 0.6-1.1~mmol/L In addition, a stool culture returns negative for bacterial and fungal infections. A computed tomography (CT) scan finds a lesion on his pancreas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E VIPoma: VIPoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumour which hypersecretes vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) causing watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and acidosis. The tumours are found on the pancreas, and more than half are malignant. Other features of VIPoma include facial flushing, and therefore, this diagnosis explains all the clinical findings for this patient. A Bacterial infection: A bacterial infection is unlikely given the absence of fever and the negative stool culture. A bacterial infection could cause dehydration and explain the biochemical results, but it would not explain the facial flushing or the pancreatic mass. B Insulinoma: An insulinoma would explain the finding of a pancreatic mass, but it would typically cause episodes of hypoglycaemia or the diarrhoea and flushing that this patient is experiencing. C Laxative abuse: Laxative abuse could cause the diarrhoea and the biochemical abnormalities but would not explain the pancreatic mass or the flushing. There is also no indication from the patient's history to suggest an abuse problem. D Pancreatitis: Pancreatitis could explain the biochemical derangement seen here, but this is usually due to vomiting rather than diarrhoea. Pancreatitis causes inflammation of the pancreas but does not tend to cause a pancreatic mass or flushing.

questions.question: A 51-year-old man presents to the Ophthalmology Clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly deteriorating vision. He has not had previous eye concerns and does not regularly wear glasses. His eyes are not painful but his vision is constantly blurred. He has not seen his General Practitioner for the past 12 years but reports that he has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes amlodipine 10 mg once daily, and he has no known allergies. His BMI is 35~kg/M2. His eyes are examined and shown below: What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: C Pan-retinal photocoagulation: This patient's fundoscopy shows multiple flame haemorrhages and neovascularisation with associated pre-retinal haemorrhages. This is in keeping with a diagnosis of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, a retinal consequence of chronic and under-controlled diabetes mellitus. Although there is not a known diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, the raised BMI puts this patient at higher risk for having the condition. The most important treatment of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, particularly in advanced disease, is with pan-retinal photocoagulation. This is because proliferative disease puts the patient at risk of vitreous haemorrhage. A Antivascular endothelial growth factor: Antivascular endothelial growth factor plays an important role in the management of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. However, in severe diseases with multiple pre-retinal haemorrhages and neovascularisation, the treatment of choice is with pan-retinal laser photocoagulation. B Escalate antihypertensive treatment: Hypertensive retinopathy is a reasonable differential diagnosis to consider, given the history of hypertension and onset of blurred vision. However, the ocular findings in hypertensive retinopathy include arteriolar narrowing and, in severe cases, cotton-wool spots and retinal haemorrhages. However, proliferative disease is not a feature of hypertensive retinopathy and suggests an alternative diagnosis. D Topical corticosteroids: Topical corticosteroids are used in the management of inflammatory ocular conditions (eg anterior uveitis associated with inflammatory bowel disease). However, it is not used in the management of proliferative diabetic retinopathy and should be avoided in this case. E Topical timolol: Topical timolol is a beta-blocker used in the management of acute angle-closure glaucoma. It works by reducing aqueous humour production and, therefore, intraocular pressure. Fundoscopy findings of acute angle-closure glaucoma include an increased cup-to-disc ratio. However, proliferative retinopathy is not a feature and suggests alternative pathology.

questions.question: A woman is 32 weeks' pregnant. She is taking propylthiouracil 150 mg daily for thyrotoxicosis. On her check-up, she complains of heat intolerance and palpitations, and repeat thyroid function tests confirm that thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is < 0.1, and T3 and T4 are also elevated. Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step?
options: D. Stop propylthiouracil and start carbimazole
questions.explanation: D Stop propylthiouracil and start carbimazole: In pregnancy, PTU is only recommended in guidelines for the first trimester of pregnancy. After this time, a switch to carbimazole is recommended because of the risk of maternal liver toxicity associated with PTU use. This patients should be switched to carbimazole and the PTU not up-titrated. E Arrange for partial thyroidectomy: Thyroidectomy should be considered in cases of allergies/contraindications to both anti-thyroid drugs in patients who are not compliant with drug therapy, and in women in whom euthyroidism cannot be achieved even on large doses of anti-thyroid drugs. If surgery is indicated, the second trimester is the optimal time. Thyroidectomy is often followed by a gradual, but not immediate, disappearance of TSH receptor antibodies, and withdrawal of anti-thyroid drugs in the mother after thyroidectomy may lead to isolated foetal hyperthyroidism. A Increase propylthiouracil dose: Both carbimazole, at a suggested daily dose of 10-20 mg, and propylthiouracil (PTU), at a dose of 150 mg bd, are acceptable for use in pregnancy, although PTU tends to be the more popular choice. PTU may be more protein-bound and so less is transmitted to the foetus, but compliance with carbimazole is generally better. In addition, there is evidence that PTU may be associated with maternal hepatotoxicity in late pregnancy. precipitating a change to carbimazole as the most appropriate in that case. B Radioiodine treatment: Radioiodine treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy, since radioiodine crosses the placenta and can cause congenital hypothyroidism. Following radioactive iodine treatment, men should avoid fathering a child for four months, and women should avoid conceiving for six months. C Induce delivery: In cases of thyrotoxicosis not responsive to anti-thyroid drugs, or in cases of non-compliance, thyroidectomy is then recommended (ATA Guidelines 2017).

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman is reviewed after attending for a well woman clinic. She finds it difficult to control her weight, often feels tired, and currently has very heavy periods. Apart from this she doesn't have any particular concerns. On examination her BMI is 32 and her BP is 155/92 mmHg. Otherwise clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 132 g/l | 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) | 4.5  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 201  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 140~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K*) | 4.5~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 132~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Total cholesterol | 6.1~mmol/L | <5.2~mmol/l Fasting serum triglyceride | 3.2 mmol/l | 0-1.5~mmol/L Which of the following tests is most likely to contribute to determining the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E TFTs: The difficulty with weight control, menorrhagia and hypertriglyceridaemia are all features consistent with hypothyroidism. TSH is likely to be elevated above the normal range, with low T3 and T4. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism, and the condition is managed with thyroid hormone replacement. Once thyroxine is commenced, periods improve and hypertriglyceridaemia usually begins to resolve without intervention with statin therapy. B HbA1c measurement: Significantly elevated blood glucose is unlikely to be seen, and even if HbA1c is abnormal it won't illustrate the reason for her weight gain and menorrhagia. A HDL measurement: HDL may be low but it's not contributing to the underlying diagnosis. C LFTS: There may be a small elevation in transaminases, but this won't confirm the underlying cause of her symptoms. D Prolactin: Prolactin is elevated in hypothyroidism, but thyroid function tests should exclude hypothyroidism as the underlying cause before other investigations are undertaken.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic after she complains of urinating 'constantly' during the day and night. She estimates that she urinates 5 litres of urine a day. Two years previously, she was involved in a road traffic accident (RTA), where she suffered a traumatic brain injury (TBI) and was admitted to intensive care (ITU). A water deprivation test confirms that she has cranial diabetes insipidus (DI), and she is started on desmopressin treatment which causes a rapid improvement in her symptoms. What of the following best describes the pharmacological action of the desmopressin?
questions.explanation: D Vasopressin analogue: Diabetes insipidus (DI) is caused by a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and may occur idiopathically or due to a precipitating cause, such as a TBI. DI may occur as a result of a deficiency in production of ADH from the pituitary gland (cranial DI) or due to impaired renal responsiveness to ADH (nephrogenic DI). The treatment of cranial DI is with desmopressin, which is an ADH analogue. It primarily acts on V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts, which rapidly increases the reabsorption of water into the bloodstream, providing symptomatic relief. A Dopamine receptor agonist: An example of a dopamine receptor agonist is bromocriptine, which may be used in the treatment of a pituitary prolactinoma since it suppresses the release of prolactin and gradually causes shrinkage in the size of the tumour. This has no value in the treatment of DI. B Somatostatin analogue: Somatostatin analogues, such as lanreotide, stimulate the somatostatin receptor and may be used to treat acromegaly which results from a pituitary growth hormone-secreting tumour. Somatostatin inhibits the secretion of growth hormone and has no value in the treatment of DI. C Tetracycline antibiotic: Demeclocycline is a tetracycline antibiotic and is used in the treatment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). It acts on the collecting tubules in the kidneys and reduces their responsiveness to antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In DI the problem is reduced ADH secretion rather than the increased ADH. E Vasopressin antagonist: Vasopressin receptor antagonists, such as vaptans, are used in the treatment of SIADH, where there is an excess of ADH, rather than the deficiency of ADH, seen in DI.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents to the clinic because of problems with the physical side of her relationship. She is concerned that her breasts leak milk after only minimal stimulation from her boyfriend, and that intercourse is difficult as she has significant problems with vaginal dryness. She also reports that she has not had a period for the past 4 months. The only other history of note is that she was given metoclopramide by a locum doctor for a recent episode of gastroenteritis. On examination her BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. You can produce milk on minimal breast stimulation. She has some peripheral field visual loss. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 127 g/l | 115-155~g/L White cell count (WCC) | 7.6  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 203  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na ) | 138~mmol/L | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 4.4~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol Creatinine | 100~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Prolactin | 1005~mU/L | <400~mU/L Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) | 7.2 μυ/ | 0.17-3.2~  mu U/L Free T4 | 16.2 pmol/l | 11-22~pmol/L Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) | 0.5 U/L | 1-25 U/L Luteinizing hormone (LH) | 0.5 U/L | 1-70 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Non-functioning pituitary adenoma: The prolactin isn't raised enough to be consistent with a macroprolactinoma, and the peripheral visual field loss raises the possibility of a large tumour. The low FSH and LH are consistent with this; the raised TSH may be due to the fact that non-functioning adenomas may occasionally secrete small amounts of TSH. This woman should undergo a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to further characterise the tumour. However, it is likely that surgery will be the mainstay of therapy as the tumour is highly unlikely to respond significantly to somatostatin or dopamine agonists. The elevated prolactin here is likely related to pressure on the pituitary stalk. Pressure on the pituitary stalk causes an elevation in prolactin levels which stimulates milk production. B Metoclopramide-related hyperprolactinaemia: Drug-related hyperprolactinaemia is usually associated with a lesser rise in prolactin, to <1000. C Microprolactinoma: Microprolactinomas are not associated with visual field loss, and a greater rise in prolactin would be expected in microprolactinoma. D Macroprolactinoma: Macroprolactinomas are associated with the visual disturbance seen here, although a rise in prolactin to at least 5000 mU/l would be expected. E Pregnancy: Although pregnancy is associated with a rise in prolactin, it isn't associated with the visual field defect seen here.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with weight loss and polyuria. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 125/82 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. His body mass index (BMI) is 23~kg/M2. You also note that he has vitiligo. Investigations conducted by the GP revealed the following: Investigation | Result | Normal Value Sodium (Na) | 125 mmol/l | 135-145~mmol/l Potassium  (K+) | 6.0 mmol/l | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Urea | 8.0~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) | 120 µmol/l | 50-120 µmol/l Glucose | 12.5 mmol/l | 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Corrected calcium (Ca+2) | 2.35 mmol/l | 2.20-2.60~mmol/L Free Thyroxine fT4 | 8.0 pmol/l | 11-22 pmol/l Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 7.2 mU/l | 0.17-3.2~mU/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: D Polyglandular syndrome type 2: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is the association of primary adrenal insufficiency with primary hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes. sometimes, primary gonadal failure is present as well. Both type 1 and type 2 polyglandular syndrome are associated with vitiligo and pernicious anaemia. A Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency: LAL deficiency, also known as Wolman syndrome, is characterised by primary adrenal failure, hepatosplenomegaly and steatorrhoea. B DIDMOAD syndrome: DIDMOAD syndrome is characterised by Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy and Deafness and is a mitochondrial rather than an autoimmune disorder. C Polyglandular syndrome type 1: Type 1 polyglandular syndrome is characterised by two or more of the following: hypoparathyroidism (90%), primary adrenal insufficiency (60%), chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, primary gonadal failure and primary hypothyroidism. E Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1: MEN1 is associated with pancreatic tumours, including insulinomas and glucagonomas, rather than the development of adrenal insufficiency and diabetes seen here.

questions.question: A 72-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is managed with metformin 1 g BD and pioglitazone 30 mg. On examination, he has a large necrotic, malodorous ulcer over the right medial malleolus. You notice that he has bilateral peripheral oedema and varicose veins. Peripheral pulses are easily palpable and capillary return is normal. Dopplers done by the chiropody team in the clinic are also within acceptable limits. His pioglitazone is discontinued and a transition to insulin therapy is planned. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Haemoglobin | 109~g/L | 135-175~g/L White cell count (WCC) | 5.4  x10^9/L | 4-11  x10^9/L Platelets | 200  x10^9/L | 150-400  x10^9/L Sodium (Na+) | 139~mmol/l | 135-145~mmol/L Potassium (K+) | 5.0~mmol/L | 3.5-5.0~mmol/L Creatinine | 182~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) | 27~mg/L | 0-10~mg/L Wound swab | scanty faecal flora |  Which of the following treatments is likely to be the most effective?
questions.explanation: B Multi-layer compression bandaging: The fact that peripheral arteries are palpable and the normal Dopplers exclude the ischaemic origin of the ulcer. The location strongly suggests that this man's ulcer is venous. As such, the optimal management is compression bandaging. His white count is normal and the CRP is only just above normal, and thus infection is not likely to be the primary cause of his ulcer. Dressings may be employed that encourage de-sloughing, rather than progressing to definitive surgical debridement. A Surgical debridement under GA: Surgical debridement is usually performed on diabetic foot ulcers that are infected and neuropathic, ischaemic or mixed in origin. C Oral metronidazole: Depending upon sensitivities, an antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity, such as co-amoxiclav, may also be required. Metronidazole is reserved for ulcers where anaerobic infection is strongly suspected. D Varicose vein stripping: This procedure is done under general or local anaesthetic to aid in the treatment of varicose veins and other manifestations of chronic venous disease. It is mainly performed when the symptoms are quite severe (pain/discomfort). E Mobilisation: Rather than mobilisation, elevation of the leg above the level of the heart and rest, to reduce peripheral oedema, is the recommended course of action.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. She is usually managed with basal bolus insulin but has omitted a number of doses due to a row with her boyfriend. On examination her respiratory rate is 35/min she is drowsy, confused and smells of pear drops. Which of the following results would fit best with her arterial blood gases?
questions.explanation: D pH 7.1: pCO2 3.0 mmol/l; pO2 11.1~mmol/L: The characteristic picture of metabolic acidosis with hyperventilation and the smell of pear drops is typical of diabetic ketoacidosis. Hyperglycaemia with a relatively normal pH is of course seen in patients with hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma, typically found in the elderly population with type 2 diabetes who retain enough residual insulin production to avoid becoming ketotic. A pH 7.4: pCO2 3.0~mmol/l; pO2 12.1~mmol/L: Drowsiness with respiratory compensation accompanied by a pear drop smell would always imply a metabolic acidosis due to diabetic ketoacidosis until proven otherwise. B pH 7.5; pCO2 3.0~mmol/l; pO2 7.4~mmol/L: This implies an alkalosis, and with a low CO2 this would be respiratory in origin. C pH 7.25; pCO2 6.7 7~mmol/l; pO2 7.4~mmol/L: The pCO2 here is elevated, which implies a respiratory rather than a metabolic acidosis. E pH 7.4: pCO2 6.7~mmol/L; pO2 6.7~mmol/L: A normal pH is inconsistent with this presentation, and the elevated pCO2 implies a respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner for a check-up for his type II diabetes mellitus which is controlled by metformin. He was diagnosed with diabetes 11 years ago after an inferior myocardial infarction (MI). On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 160/95 mmHg and his body mass index is 26~kg/M2 He has normal fundi and examination of his feet shows normal sensation and peripheral pulses. As well as his metformin he takes ramipril 2.5, amlodipine 5 mg once a day and simvastatin 40 mg at night. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal value Cholesterol | 4.6~mmol/l | <5.2~mmoll Urea | 7.4~mmol/L | 2.5-6.5~mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) | 109~  mu mol/L | 50-120~  mu mol/L Haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) | 57.38~mmol/mol (7.4%) | <53~mmol/mol(<7.0  %) Albumin: creatinine ratio | 3.8~mg/mmol | <3.5~mg/mmol Which of the following is likely to have the greatest impact on this patient's future risk of complications?
options: A. Adding a fibrate to statin therapy
C. Escalating the dose of ramipril to 5 mg once daily
E. Switching from ramipril to losartan
questions.explanation: C Escalating the dose of ramipril to 5 mg once daily: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest a target blood pressure (BP) of 140/80 mmHg in type II diabetes. First-line antihypertensive drug treatment should be with an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. This patient also has microalbuminuria; a sign of diabetic nephropathy. Normally, ACE inhibitors significantly reduce the risk of all-cause mortality in patients with diabetic kidney disease and the dose should be escalated to the highest dose tolerated by the patient. D Starting a sulfonylurea: The NICE guidelines suggest a target HbA1c of <53~mmol/mol(<7  %) in patients with type II diabetes mellitus. However, the ACCORD trial showed no benefit of aiming for an HbA1c of <47.54~mmol/mol (6.5%) in late-stage disease in patients who also have a positive cardiovascular history. A Adding a fibrate to statin therapy: The action to control cardiovascular risk in type II diabetes (ACCORD) trial investigated the addition of fenofibrate to statin therapy but found no impact on future macrovascular events. B Adding insulin: If initial drug treatment with metformin has not continued to control HbA1c to below the person's agreed threshold for intensification, consider dual therapy with metformin combined with one combining a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone or a sulfonylurea. Insulin is only normally considered if dual therapy has not achieved adequate glycaemic control. E Switching from ramipril to losartan: For adults with chronic kidney disease and type II diabetes, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) or an ACE inhibitor (titrated to the highest licensed dose that the person can tolerate) should be offered if the ACE is 3 mg/mmol or more. Given that this patient appears to be tolerating treatment with an ACE inhibitor, there is no indication to switch to an ARB, although the dose should be intensified to the highest dose that can be tolerated.

questions.question: You review a 36-year-old woman who presents to the Emergency Department with anxiety and palpitations. She has an 8-month-old child. Over the past 4 months, she has lost 5 kg in weight but puts this down to all the work looking after her baby. You notice she has obvious chemosis and her facial appearance isshown below. Which of the following best fits the underlying diagnosis of her systemic condition?
questions.explanation: A Graves' disease: There is obvious proptosis and lid retraction which, along with chemosis, is consistent with Graves' ophthalmopathy and thyrotoxicosis. Graves' ophthalmopathy occurs due to local accumulation of glycosaminoglycans; 75% of Graves' patients develop the disease within 1 year of ophthalmopathy occurring. The condition can be worsened by smoking and by hypothyroidism post-radioiodine treatment. If visual impairment, with blurring or visual field loss, or pain occurs, then this is a sign of optic neuropathy, and the patient should be referred to an ophthalmologist for treatment. Standard therapy involves a portfolio of treatment modalities that may include systemic corticosteroids, radiotherapy or orbital decompression, or a combination of treatments. In patients with thyroid eye disease undergoing radioiodine treatment, post-radioiodine hypothyroidism should be avoided because of the risk of worsening Graves' eye disease. For this reason, patients are stabilised on a block-replace regimen before moving to radioiodine therapy. Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Proptosis_and_lid_retraction_from_Graves%27_Disease.jpg. D Toxic thyroid adenoma: Toxic thyroid adenoma is associated with thyrotoxicosis, but not with the eye signs seen here which are related to Graves'. B Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Hashimoto's disease is associated with goitre, but not with thyroid eye disease, and leads to hypothyroidism not thyrotoxicosis. C Riedel's thyroiditis: This leads to fibrotic disease of the thyroid gland and to hypothyroidism rather than thyrotoxicosis. E Postpartum thyroiditis: While postpartum thyroiditis may be associated with a transient period of thyrotoxicosis and TSH-r antibodies, eye signs consistent with Graves' are not a feature of the condition.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman attends the GP 3 months after the birth of her second child. She complains of an increasing inability to cope over the past few months and frequent tearfulness. On examination, her BP is 132/72 mmHg, her pulse is 66/min and regular, her BMI is 28 and she tells you she has gained weight over the past 2-3 weeks. Investigations: Investigation | Result | Normal values Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | 8.5 mu/l | 0.45.0 mu/l Free Thyroxine (FT4) | 6.5 pmol/l | 10-22 pmol/l Anti TPO antibodies | + |  Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: C Post-partum thyroiditis: Postpartum thyroiditis is said to develop some 3-7 months after pregnancy and is often associated with mild symptoms such as tiredness or depression. It is said to occur to varying degrees in 5-7% of women, and in 30-52% of cases anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Permanent hypothyroidism is said to develop in around 40% of patients, with increased frequency in patients with positive anti-TPO antibodies. Standard treatment for postpartum hypothyroidism is low-dose thyroxine (around 50 µg), with a withdrawal period after 6 months to measure recovery of thyroid function. A Grave's disease: Graves' disease is associated with thyrotoxicosis rather than the picture of hypothyroidism seen here. B Hashimoto's thyroiditis: This is the major differential, but the timing of her symptoms means that postpartum thyroiditis is potentially more likely, and there is potential to recover from the hypothyroidism seen here. D Sub-acute thyroiditis: Subacute thyroiditis is associated with flu-like symptoms and pain over the thyroid gland rather than the picture seen here. E Riedel's thyroiditis: This is associated with dense fibrosis of the thyroid gland and notable changes in the anterior neck, not seen in this patient, and not associated with the post-pregnancy period.

questions.question: A 21-year-old man presents for review with concerns about his sexual function. He has recently begun a relationship with a woman and is unable to become sexually aroused. Past history of note includes repair of cleft lip and palate. On examination, he is normal height and is thin. He has failure of development of secondary sexual characteristics. Other history of note includes a lack of sense of smell, which he puts down to an accident as a toddler. He wishes to settle down with this woman and may start a family soon. Investigations: Investigation | Result Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | Normal Luteinizing hromone (LH) | Low Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | Low Testosterone | Low Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: C Pulsed GnRH therapy: This patient is thought to have Kallmann syndrome and a failure of GnRH, and hence LH, FSH secretion. The history of cleft palate defect and lack of sense of smell both fit best with this as the most likely diagnosis. It is due to disordered migration of GnRH-producing neurones to the hypothalamus. It has an incidence of 1 in 10,000 males, with a male to female ratio of 4:1. Anosmia is present in 75% and there is an increased association with cleft lip and palate. Pulsed GnRH treatment is needed to restore LH and FSH release. It needs to be continued for as long as fertility is required. Once his family is complete, switching to testosterone therapy may be more convenient for him. B Continuous GnRH therapy: As natural GnRH release is pulsatile, continuous therapy fails to lead to LH and FSH release. A Testosterone supplementation: Although this restores secondary sexual characteristics, it doesn't restore fertility and is therefore not appropriate here. D FSH therapy: FSH can be used to induce fertility, but it is thought to be potentially less effective than pulsed GnRH therapy. Long-acting preparations of FSH do exist, though, which may be more convenient with respect to administration. E LH therapy: LH can be used in conjunction with FSH to induce fertility in women with Kallmann syndrome.
